fr1_title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence and Big Data 2023-2027
fr1_justif: The Strategy treats AI literacy as part of Strategic Objective 2 and explicitly calls for educating all actors (public private civil society and end users) about digital tools and AI (pp.17–18). It operationalises this through Program 2 in the Action Plan (p.23) and two key measures which includes integrating AI learning into the education system (basic knowledge programming and ongoing training). It also states on p. 31 the need to update some existing curricula (from basic education to continuing education) so as to add subjects relating to AI and big data management.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Affairs and Digitalisation (lead coordinating body) supported by the Steering Committee Technical Committee and Program Support Units as set out under the Implementation Mechanism (Chapter 41 pp4243)
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy requires curriculum reforms across the full education pipeline stating that curricula should be updated from basic education to ongoing training to include AI and big data subjects and that every student should receive basic knowledge of how AI works (Action 2.1 p.31). This covers primary/secondary (“basic education”) and tertiary/continuing education (“degree courses” and “ongoing training”). It also states among the goals that Basic specialized programming training and continuing education courses are offered in various institutions (p. 17).
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy supports AI programmes or courses within the formal system by requiring an update of curricula from basic education to ongoing training and include AI and big data subjects ensuring every student gains basic AI knowledge (p.31). It also links this to Program 2 (strengthening human capabilities) (pp.21–23). However it does not explicitly establish new dedicated AI institutions nor does it identify specific universities/schools or legally create AI faculties; the focus is curriculum integration and training roll-out not institutional creation.
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: It supports resources for AI education by proposing to equip training facilities (universities institutes training and research centres) to work on AI and big data including setting up work rooms and FabLabs and promoting partnerships (Action 3.1 p.33) so there are resources allocated for AI education. However it does not explicitly provide teacher training (e.g. training-of-trainers pedagogy support teacher certification) for AI education.

fr1_title: Law No. 2017-20 establishing the Digital Code in the Republic of Benin
fr1_justif: The Digital Code’s personal data protections create redress routes relevant where AI is used via automated decision-making (including profiling). Controllers must inform people about automated decision-making and the right to lodge a complaint with the Authority (Arts. 415-416 pp. 130-131). Affected persons can lodge a complaint with the Authority receive updates and then pursue judicial recourse (Arts. 448-450 p. 144). It also provides effective remedy before the competent administrative court if the Authority fails to act within 90 days plus compensation and liability for material/moral damage (Art. 451 p. 144).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Under the Digital Code (Law No. 2017-20) the personal data protection regime explicitly carves out defence national security and public safety processing from its general scope.Book V provides that processing relating to public safety defence the investigation and prosecution of criminal offences and the essential interests of the State is subject to special derogations laid down by other laws rather than the ordinary data protection rules (Book V Scope of application p.114–115).Accordingly defence and security activities are explicitly excluded or treated under special regimes not fully subject to the standard transparency and explainability obligations.
fr1_body_name: Personal Data Protection Authority (APDP)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The Digital Code does not establish mechanisms for AI harm specifically but it would apply where an AI system processes personal data and causes harm (e.g. automated decision-making). It grants a right to an effective judicial remedy where data-protection rights are violated (Art. 450) the right to complain to the Authority and allows recourse to the competent administrative court if the Authority fails to act within 90 days; it also provides compensation and liability against controllers/processors (Art. 451) and states that legal actions to obtain redress are brought before the competent courts.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: The Code creates state-based non-judicial channels that could handle AI-related grievances where AI is used in digital services or personal data processing but it does not establish an AI-specific ombuds or tribunal. It (i) defines a “Complaint” as a written request submitted to the Regulatory Authority; (ii) requires operators to maintain an effective complaints-handling mechanism; and (iii) allows individuals to file a complaint with the Authority (data protection authority) where rights requests are not handled within the deadline.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

fr1_title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence and Big Data 2023-2027
fr1_justif: The Strategy 2023-2027 addresses linguistic diversity under Action 1.2 – Implementation of AI solutions. In the Education sector (p.55) it promotes natural language processing and speech recognition to translate local languages into French and facilitate inclusive digital learning. While not a comprehensive cultural inclusion framework these measures constitute a strategic recognition of linguistic diversity within AI projects emphasizing local language accessibility and the involvement of national actors in solution development
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Affairs and Digitalisation (lead coordinating body) supported by the Steering Committee Technical Committee and Program Support Units as set out under the Implementation Mechanism (Chapter 41 pp4243)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy includes initiatives under Action 1.2 – Implementation of AI solutions particularly in the Education sector where natural language processing (translation of local languages to French) and speech recognition are planned. These elements address aspects of linguistic diversity. However the strategy does not articulate overarching objectives policy measures or recommendations to ensure AI systems broadly reflect cultural diversity or inclusivity beyond specific projects
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence and Big Data 2023-2027
fr1_justif: The Strategy addresses the indicator at a high level by emphasizing the importance of designing and implementing AI systems with due regard to overarching principles explicitly referencing the planet prosperity and sustainability (p. 35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Affairs and Digitalisation (lead coordinating body) supported by the Steering Committee Technical Committee and Program Support Units as set out under the Implementation Mechanism (Chapter 41 pp4243)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element2_justif: The strategy calls for impact analyses and monitoring of AI solutions throughout their lifecycle considering values like “the planet” and “sustainability” (Action 4.1 p. 35) and aims to foster accountability and promote the obligation to report among AI actors (Section 4.3 p. 44). However it does not explicitly assign developers the obligation to measure or report energy usage or the environmental impact of their models in measurable terms.
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: Law No. 2017-20 establishing the Digital Code in the Republic of Benin
fr1_justif: The Digital Code is a comprehensive and binding document that governs all digital-related activities in the Republic of Benin. Although it does not specifically address artificial intelligence it provides a general framework for digital technologies and prohibits any form of discrimination or unfair treatment. Its provisions on fairness transparency (Art. 17) and personal data protection impose non-discrimination obligations in automated processing (Art. 19 - 20). Articles 149 and 150 also enshrine these principles in Benin's digital action within the Digital Code. (See page 53 - Section II)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: According to Article 4 state infrastructure dedicated to public safety or national defense as well as the use of frequencies allocated directly to these administrations do not fall within its scope. These facilities are governed by a specific decree of the Council of Ministers. Furthermore terrestrial broadcasting companies (radio and television) are also excluded with regard to their production and broadcasting activities. Thus the Code establishes a clear framework while recognizing that certain sensitive and strategic functions of the State require separate regulation to guarantee national security and sovereignty.
fr1_body_name: Personal Data Protection Authority (APDP) Regulatory Authority for Electronic Communications and Postal Services (ARCEP-Benin) Beninese Agency for Universal Electronic Communications and Postal Services (ABSU-CEP)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

fr1_title: Law No. 2017-20 establishing the Digital Code in the Republic of Benin
fr1_justif: The Digital Code addresses Human Oversight by curbing reliance on solely automated decisions and requiring safeguards that enable human determination. In Book V Art. 401 states that no judicial decision assessing a person’s behaviour may be based on automated processing including profiling so a human decision-maker must remain decisive (p.125). It further defines automated processing as exploitation “without direct human intervention” (p.15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: According to Article 4 state infrastructure dedicated to public safety or national defense as well as the use of frequencies allocated directly to these administrations do not fall within its scope. These facilities are governed by a specific decree of the Council of Ministers. Furthermore terrestrial broadcasting companies (radio and television) are also excluded with regard to their production and broadcasting activities. Thus the Code establishes a clear framework while recognizing that certain sensitive and strategic functions of the State require separate regulation to guarantee national security and sovereignty.
fr1_body_name: Personal Data Protection Authority (APDP) Regulatory Authority for Electronic Communications and Postal Services (ARCEP-Benin) Beninese Agency for Universal Electronic Communications and Postal Services (ABSU-CEP)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Code has no AI-specific “human control” rules but it requires safeguards for automated processing (incl. profiling) that produces legal or similarly significant effects. No judicial decision assessing a person’s behaviour may be based on automated processing including profiling so a human decision-maker must remain decisive (Art. 401 p.125). It prohibits basing judicial decisions on automated processing and bars decisions with legal/significant effects being taken solely by automated processing; where exceptions apply safeguards include allowing the person concerned to “effectively assert their point of view” (Art. 401 p.125). It also prohibits controllers must carry out a data-protection impact assessment to assess necessity/proportionality and define risk-mitigation measures and review it when risks change (Art. 428 p.135).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The Code does not expressly identify “sensitive sectors” like medicine but it prevents full automation for high-impact decisions. It prohibits judicial decisions involving an assessment of a person’s behaviour from being based on automated processing (incl. profiling) and bars decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects from being taken solely by automated processing. Where an exception applies safeguards are required including enabling the person concerned to “effectively assert their point of view” (Art. 401 p.125).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence and Big Data 2023-2027
fr1_justif: The strategy tackles public-sector AI skills via Strategic Objective 2 (“Strengthen human capabilities in AI and big data management”) which flags insufficient trained resources and calls for training and awareness for stakeholders including public actors (pp.17–19). It creates Programme 2 (“Strengthening the human capacities of stakeholders in AI professions and jobs”) (pp.21–23) and sets actions: integrate programming/continuing education (Action 2.1 p.31) deploy AI capacity-building for public and private stakeholders and users (Action 2.2 pp.31 & 25) and big-data capacity-building (Action 2.3 p.32).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Affairs and Digitalisation (lead coordinating body) supported by the Steering Committee Technical Committee and Program Support Units as set out under the Implementation Mechanism (Chapter 41 pp4243)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy includes a government-wide capacity-building thrust: Strategic Objective 2 is to “strengthen human capabilities in AI and big data management” noting the need to train and raise awareness among stakeholders including public actors (Strategic Objectives pp.17–18). It then sets Action 2.2 to implement a capacity-building programme for public and private stakeholders and users on AI (Actions p.25; details p.31). However it does not expressly set a tailored upskilling plan for the judiciary or a full “risks” curriculum.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The Strategy supports ongoing skills development by planning “basic specialised programming training and continuing education courses” as an expected effect under Strategic Objective 2 (Strengthen human capabilities in AI and big data management) (p.17). It then operationalises this via multi-year capacity-building actions: Action 2.1 integrates basic programming + continuing education into the education system (p.31) and Action 2.2 runs a capacity-building programme for public and private actors and users on AI (pp.25 & 31) spanning several years (p.31).

fr1_title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence and Big Data 2023-2027
fr1_justif: The Strategy treats reskilling/upskilling as a core objective: Strategic Objective 2 is to “strengthen human capabilities” in AI and big data management (Section 1.4; pp.16–18). It creates Program 2: Strengthening human capabilities of actors in AI professions and positions (Section 2.1–2.2; pp.21–23) with actions to integrate AI training into the education system (basic programming and ongoing courses) and roll out capacity-development programmes for AI for public/private actors and end users (Action 2.1–2.2; pp.31; plan of action p.23).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Affairs and Digitalisation (lead coordinating body) supported by the Steering Committee Technical Committee and Program Support Units as set out under the Implementation Mechanism (Chapter 41 pp4243)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy sets objectives and measures to strengthen human capabilities through AI education training and capacity-development programmes (Program 2; pp.21–23) and includes an Action Plan with skills-related actions (pp.23 31). However it does not clearly specify government-funded or subsidized programmes targeted at workers displaced or affected by AI nor dedicated funding instruments for worker reskilling. The measures are framed broadly (education and training across actors) rather than explicit worker-focused subsidy schemes.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Law No. 2017-20 establishing the Digital Code in the Republic of Benin
fr1_justif: While the law primarily regulates general data processing Article 415(13) explicitly imposes an obligation to inform the data subject about the existence of automated decision-making including profiling as referenced in Article 401. In such cases the controller must provide meaningful information about the logic involved as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of the processing for the data subject.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Under the Digital Code (Law No. 2017-20) the personal data protection regime explicitly carves out defence national security and public safety processing from its general scope.Book V provides that processing relating to public safety defence the investigation and prosecution of criminal offences and the essential interests of the State is subject to special derogations laid down by other laws rather than the ordinary data protection rules (Book V Scope of application p.114–115).Accordingly defence and security activities are explicitly excluded or treated under special regimes not fully subject to the standard transparency and explainability obligations.
fr1_body_name: Personal Data Protection Authority (APDP) This is the most applicable body for the Transparency and Explainability indicator Under the Digital Code (Book V) the APDP is mandated to supervise and enforce compliance with personal data protection obligations including transparency duties information to data subjects and safeguards relating to automated processing and profiling These functions directly underpin explainability and transparency in AI-enabled data processing- Electronic Communications and Postal Regulatory Authority (ARCEP Benin)- Beninese Universal Service Agency for Electronic Communications and Postal Services (ABSU-CEP)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The document clearly promotes transparency regarding automated decision-making as Article 415(13) requires informing individuals about the existence of such processing and providing meaningful information about the logic involved as well as its significance and consequences. However it does not explicitly require disclosure of broader elements such as the system’s overall purpose or data sources and therefore does not fully address all aspects of clarity referenced in the question.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The Code does not impose an AI-specific duty to explain “decision-making logic” in hiring or loan contexts. However it (i) restricts high-stakes solely automated decisions by providing that no decision producing legal effects or significantly affecting a person may be taken solely on automated processing intended to evaluate aspects of personality (Art. 401); and (ii) imposes transparency obligations on data controllers to provide information about processing in a concise transparent intelligible and accessible way (Art. 418 linked to Arts. 415 - 416)
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

fr1_title: Child Online Protection (COP) Guidelines for Policy-Makers (Localized for Bhutan 2023)
fr1_justif: The Guidelines address children’s rights by recognizing AI-driven risks to their development privacy and wellbeing. Algorithmically curated content and inappropriate material are discussed (Quick References pp. 9–11) highlighting threats to autonomy and participation. Children’s right to privacy and data protection is emphasized across age groups (pp. 9–11). Crucially the General Guidelines for Industry (Quick References p. 14) explicitly mandate identifying and mitigating adverse impacts on children’s rights requiring safety- and privacy-by-design approaches including privacy-preserving AI.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: The guidelines address algorithmically driven manipulation and exploitation. It identifies a key threat as 'Algorithmically Filtered Content for Manipulation' noting that 'Exposure to content that is algorithmically manipulated with the intent to influence can significantly shape a child’s development' (3.-COP-Guidelines-for-Policy-Makers.pdf p. 11). It also warns against 'embedded marketing' (p. 10) and 'Unwanted Advertising' raising concerns about the 'commodification of children’s data' (p. 12). The guidelines instruct parents to 'Address Advertising and Misinformation' and discuss 'inappropriate or misleading ads' with children (1.-Quick-Reference_COP-Guidelines-for-Stakeholders.pdf p. 6).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: The document assigns obligations to industry actors including developers and deployers of AI to identify prevent and mitigate adverse impacts of digital technologies on children’s rights (1.-Quick-Reference_COP-Guidelines-for-Stakeholders.pdf General Guidelines for Industry p. 14). It recommends adopting safety- and privacy-by-design principles implementing age-appropriate design and leveraging privacy-preserving AI to protect children online (p. 14 clauses 1 3 and 5). But the guidelines remain high-level and do not define enforceable obligations technical standards or accountability mechanisms specific to AI system development and deployment.

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: National Data Governance Framework (NDGF) (2025)(Bhutan)
fr1_justif: PILLAR THREE (Data Security & Protection page 14): Mandates minimum data security requirements including encryption of data 'in use' by AI systems access control mechanisms multi-factor authentication security protocols aligned with international standards and data breach detection/notification within 72 hours—directly applicable to AI system operations. Section 2.3.2(k) explicitly requires: 'Ensure AI systems align with legal and user safety standards in their data usage'—binding safety requirement for AI. PILLAR FIVE (Critical Information Infrastructure Protection page 16): Establishes cybersecurity framework protecting government data infrastructure
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Data Governance Committee
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: Section 2.3.2 mandates encryption access control multi-factor authentication and threat detection to ensure data security in software development lifecycle and network infrastructure but not mentions explicit security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

fr1_title: (Draft Law) General Law on Artifiical Intelligence (PL 558/2024-2025) (Chamber of Deputies) (Bolivia)
fr1_justif: Art. 8.1 mandates responsible AI development for social well-being while Art. 10(c) requires developers to establish internal oversight and error-correction mechanisms. Arts. 14–15 enforce risk assessment and mitigation especially for high-risk systems. Crucially Arts. 22–24 establish the Supervisory and Enforcement Authority responsible for monitoring inspection and compliance. These provisions address human oversight through institutional supervision and accountability mechanisms. However the framework does not explicitly mandate human-in-the-loop systems or a specific right to human review of automated decisions.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The draft bill does not expressly require 'meaningful human control' or mandate that AI remain an assistive tool rather than replacing human judgment. However Arts. 14–15 require risk assessment and mitigation for high-risk systems introducing preventive oversight. Art. 10(c) mandates internal oversight and error-correction mechanisms while Arts. 22–24 establish a Supervisory Authority for monitoring and regulatory control. While these provisions support institutional accountability the bill lacks explicit mandates for human-in-the-loop systems or guaranteed human review in critical decision-making contexts
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: Bill for the Promotion Management and Use of Artificial Intelligence (Chamber of Deputies) (Bolivia)
fr1_justif: The document directly addresses Impact Assessments through mandatory obligations to prevent mitigate and address risks associated with AI systems. Articles 10 11 12 13 and 14 establish risk classification and mitigation measures. Article 15 establishes mandatory impact assessments for AI systems used by both public and private entities
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The document has a proactive risk management by requiring prevention and mitigation of potential impacts of AI as one of the purposes of the bill (Title III). In Art. 10 it mentions that safeguard fairness act in respect internal mechanism of oversight must be took into account while developing AI systems. Art. 11 12 13 establish risk measurement parameters and Art. 14 introduces risk mitigation measures. However it is based more on sanctions than prevention and does not include educational or informational aspects or participatory actions by different sectors to prevent violations or reduce risks.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems
fr1_title: (Draft Law) General Law on Artifiical Intelligence (PL 558/2024-2025) (Chamber of Deputies) (Bolivia)
fr1_justif: Article 26 establishes a public registry for AI systems requiring providers to disclose their objectives algorithmic logic and personal data utilized. Critically it mandates that developers and users as responsible parties keep this information updated whenever changes occur in technical characteristics or data processing. Furthermore Article 27 empowers the Artificial Intelligence Supervision and Oversight Authority (ASFIA) to monitor these systems. ASFIA is authorized to demand information from both public and private sectors to ensure a robust mechanism for risk mitigation and ongoing compliance.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
fr1_element1_justif: The bill explicitly states in Article 26 that developers providers and responsible users of AI systems must register in a public registry in which they declare the explanatory foundations and objectives operational characteristics and type of personal data they use. A specific AI authority (ASFIA) must supervise intervene and determine the risk and mitigation procedures for these systems.
fr1_element2_text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
fr1_element2_justif: Yes it is mentioned in different parts. Articles 5 to 9 mention aspects of privacy proper use security and responsibility with regard to data use. Articles 10 to 15 include impact assessment and mitigation measures. Articles 16 to 19 include provisions related to data protection. Finally Article 26 through the public register of AI systems requires the type of personal data used to be specified. However it is important to note that the training process is not specified but only a general reference is made to the development and use of these technologies.
fr1_element3_text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
fr1_element4_text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

fr1_title: (Draft Law) General Law on Artifiical Intelligence (PL 558/2024-2025) (Chamber of Deputies) (Bolivia)
fr1_justif: Art. 5.1 mandates an ethical framework for AI based on dignity transparency and safety. Art. 15.2 promotes inter-institutional cooperation for ethical and operational testing. Art. 18 establishes the right to access and rectify personal data within AI systems. Art. 21 promotes digital literacy and AI human rights awareness to ensure informed decision-making. Finally Art. 26 creates a Mandatory Public Registry for high-risk AI. Developers must disclose system objectives algorithmic characteristics and data classifications with a strict obligation to keep this information updated whenever technical or data processing changes occur (Art. 26.3).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: Art. 26 creates a Mandatory Public Registry for high-risk AI. Developers must disclose system objectives algorithmic characteristics and data classifications with a strict obligation to keep this information updated (Art. 26.3). However it is not clear whether this obligation applies to non-high-risk AI systems
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: Art. 26 creates a Mandatory Public Registry for high-risk AI requiring developers to disclose objectives algorithmic characteristics and data classifications (Art. 26.3). Art. 12 defines High-Risk AI Systems specifically including those used for: (5) evaluating subjects for public assistance; (6) determining creditworthiness; (7) assessing probabilities of committing legal infractions; and (8) classifying subjects as potential crime victims; among others.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: Art. 17 mandates explicit informed consent for personal data collection by AI systems. Under Art. 18 data owners have the right to access processing information and request rectification for inaccuracies. To ensure accountability Art. 20 guarantees access to judicial resources in cases of fundamental rights violations or damages caused by AI. Finally Art. 21 promotes digital literacy and AI human rights awareness across all developmental stages emphasizing ethics and data science to empower informed citizen decision-making

fr1_title: Data Protection Act 2024 (Act No. 18 of 2024) (Botswana)
fr1_justif: The Botswana Data Protection Act 2024 addresses redress in AI-related contexts though it does not explicitly mention AI. Its provisions apply to automated and algorithmic processing. Section 49 regulates automated decision-making granting data subjects the right to human intervention and to contest automated decisions. Section 38(7)(b) requires controllers to inform data subjects of their right to complain and seek judicial remedy. Section 80 enables complaints for contraventions and Section 72 requires redress mechanisms in binding corporate rules.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Information and Data Protection Commission
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The Botswana Data Protection Act 2024 provides structured access to redress and remedies through the Information and Data Protection Appeals Tribunal covering aspects such as its continuation (s.85) composition (s.86) jurisdiction (s.87) tenure and removal of members (ss.88 - 90) appeals process (ss.95 97) and related procedural matters (ss.91 - 96). While these provisions enable individuals to challenge decisions and seek remedies the Act does not explicitly address AI or harms caused by AI systems meaning that any redress for AI-related harms would need to be pursued indirectly under general data protection frameworks.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

fr1_title: Data Protection Act 2024 (Act No. 18 of 2024) (Botswana)
fr1_justif: The Botswana Data Protection Act (2024) addresses fairness and non-discrimination in the context of AI through provisions governing automated decision-making and personal data processing.Section 19 establishes a core principle that personal data must be processed “lawfully fairly and transparently” which applies to AI systems that process personal data. Section 49 provides a key safeguard by granting data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing or profiling that produce legal or similarly significant effects and requires measures such as human intervention and the right to contest decisions. Section 37 complements this by imposing transparency obligations requiring information
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

fr1_title: Data Protection Act 2024 (Act No. 18 of 2024) (Botswana)
fr1_justif: The Botswana Data Protection Bill/Act 2024 explicitly tackles human oversight and determination in the context of automated decision-making (often relevant for AI systems) in Section 49. It gives data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing including profiling. Where such processing is permitted (e.g. with explicit consent or for contracts) the controller must implement suitable safeguards which include the right to obtain human intervention to express one’s point of view and to contest the decision.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Information and Data Protection Commission
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: the Botswana Data Protection Act 18 of 2024 does not include a standalone explicit policy provision promoting “meaningful human control over AI systems”. What the Act does rather is impose rights and safeguards related to automated decision-making (i.e. requiring that individuals not be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing and entitling them to human intervention and contestability) mainly in Section 49. These ensure procedural checks when automated decisions affect individuals but they are framed as data subject rights not broad regulatory objectives about purpose or philosophy of AI governance.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: General Law for the Protection of Personal Data (LGPD)
fr1_justif: The LGPD addresses access to redress and remedy in the context of AI particularly regarding automated decision-making. Article 20 grants individuals the right to request a review of decisions based solely on automated processing ensuring a pathway to contest such outcomes. Article 18 provides complementary rights (e.g. access correction deletion objection) enabling individuals to challenge unlawful data use. Additionally Article 18(§1) allows complaints to the national authority (ANPD) and Article 22 ensures the possibility of judicial remedies. Together these provisions establish mechanisms for redress including administrative and judicial avenues.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Article 4(III) of the LGPD explicitly excludes data processing carried out for public security national defense state security and criminal investigations from its scope. It further clarifies that such activities must be governed by separate specific legislation (§1) confirming that defense and security are outside the framework’s direct applicability.

fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

According to Article 17 Article 17 providers of information technology products or services aimed at children and adolescents or likely to have access to them must regularly review artificial intelligence tools with the participation of experts and competent agencies in order to disable the system and ensure security. Art.22 Art. 22. prohibits the use of profiling techniques including emotional analysis augmented and virtual reality for this purpose.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

fr1_element2_justif: Training a qualified technical team and creating job opportunities to retain talent is fundamental to fostering AI ecosystems that promote collaboration between companies; universities and government to drive innovation (p.12). Actions under the training qualification and dissemination axis (p. 74) establish: an AI training program with introductory scholarships at competitive rates for the training; attraction and retention of talent to increase the supply of highly qualified AI professionals and reduce the gap between academia and industry. Under the AI for business innovation axis (p. 87): salary supplement scholarships for AI talent retention.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Brazilian Strategy of Artificial Intelligence
fr1_justif: The legislation regulation and ethical use axis (p. 17-23) suggests AI risk analyses through the preparation of environmental safety and human rights impact reports; the creation of whitelists and blacklists for certain rules and algorithmic analyses; the adoption of transparent and auditable methodologies for the development of AI systems data sources procedures and project documentation; and the development of voluntary and consensual standards to manage the risks associated with AI applications. Furthermore the adoption of regulatory sandboxes for research development (p. 37) and public safety (p. 50). Productive sector axis (p.40) establishes specific objectives accuracy indicators of technology developed.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Science Technology and Innovation
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The legislation regulation and ethical use axis (p. 17-23) establishes AI risk analysis through impact reports but does not define risk thresholds performance or quality parameters. Only the productive sector axis (p.40) recommends the investment programs establishing specific objectives and accuracy indicators of the technology developed. Sandboxes are also suggested for the public safety axis (p. 50) and research and development (p. 37) and it is recommended that they be monitored by a competent authority to assess opportunities and risks; however parameters and limits are not established.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: In the research development innovation and entrepreneurship area (pp. 36-38) regulatory sandboxes are cited as important mechanisms for organizations developing innovative products and services using personal data. However no strategic action has been defined in this regard. The answer is partial as the mechanisms outlined in the framework do not apply throughout the AI system life-cycle
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

fr1_title: Brazilian Strategy of Artificial Intelligence
fr1_justif: The strategic axis legislation regulation and ethical use (p.17-23) includes: encouraging the production of ethical AI by funding research projects aimed at applying ethical solutions particularly in the areas of responsibility/accountability and transparency known as the FAT matrix; encouraging transparency and responsible disclosure regarding the use of AI systems (p.23); Encourage transparency and responsible disclosure regarding the use of AI systems and promote compliance by such systems with human rights (p.23). There are no specific actions for explainability a general recommendation for specific funding for research or pilot programs to create explainable and transparent AI (p.16).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Science Technology and Innovation
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: In the AI governance axis (page 25) the strategy defines that the idea of transparency can be translated into the adoption of transparent and auditable methodologies for the development of AI systems; data sources and project procedures and documentation. While this approach aims to promote data sources; decision-making logic and public trust; no strategic action in this regard has been established.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The thematic axis of strategic actions: legislation regulation and ethical use. It states that explainability is a right protected by the General Data Protection Law so informing individuals about the existence of AI-based decision-making processes is a prerequisite for exercising the right to review automated decisions (p.21). Furthermore it defines the action of creating and implementing best practices or codes of conduct relating to the collection implementation and use of data encouraging organizations to improve their traceability while safeguarding legal rights (p.23).

fr1_title: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Bulgaria until 2030
fr1_justif: The Concept treats AI literacy as a central pillar emphasizing education reform lifelong learning and awareness-raising across society. It frames AI literacy not only as technical skills but also as ethical legal and social understanding of AI. Knowledge and Skills Base: The document highlights the need to create knowledge and skills for the development and use of AI to achieve competitiveness and trust (s. 2.3 4 Vision and Goals; 4.2) Education System Reform: calls for reforms across all levels of education—from schools to universities—to integrate AI-related content and digital skills (s.5.3); Lifelong Learning (s.5.3 - Vocational training and continuing education).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Interdepartmental Working Group
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: Section 5.3. specifies a list of specific measures that will contribute to the development of the knowledge base and skill set needed to work in the AI field as well as to work in an environment using AI apps in the Secondary&Higher education and Vocational training and continuing education. Digital skills training in the Primary education is also briefly mentioned - see page 20 line 7). The Concept mentions  the measures laid down in the document 'AI in Education and Science' (2020) by Ministry of Education and Science. Creation of a critical mass of specialists with higher education the most developed EU countries are planning solid investments in university structures and doctoral programs in AI and Introduction of AI in schools (p.15
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: STEM centers and disciplines: see section 5.3 first paragraph; Establishing AI-oriented profiles in the curricula of appropriate bachelor's specialties in the professional fields 'Informatics and Computer Science' 'Communication and Computer Engineering' and Creating and maintaining special talentprogrammes (second and third bullet in 'Higher education' section 5.3); promotion of interdisciplinary (hybrid) academic training programmes (fourth bullet in 'Higher education' section 5.3);
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: Updating the university educational programmes for training teachers and staff for educational management by developing the competencies of teachers to work with information digital technologies and AI regarding the changing nature of teaching as well as the use of AI-supported systems for school system management (bullet 6 in 'Higher education' section 5.3). Others: Implementing AI in university management (bullet 8 in 'Higher education' section 5.3). Ministry of Education and Science develops policies and tools to promote innovative teaching practices and methods (paragraph 1 of section 5.3). Also see Section 2.3 'Education and lifelong learning' and section 4.2. and section 6 Creating AI applications for educational purposes

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

fr1_title: EU GDPR
fr1_justif: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).
fr1_body_name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: It is mandatory to establish an independent supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint including a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) including age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

fr1_title: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Bulgaria until 2030
fr1_justif: For this indicator emphasis is on equal access fairness and inclusivity in AI systems. Introduction: refers to EU’s vision of “trustworthy AI” with requirements such as diversity non-discrimination and fairness ensuring universal design and equal access. Section 2.2. AI as a Driver of Digital Transformation (pp. 10-11) – Notes the role of AI in machine translation and language localization (e.g. e-commerce platforms digital assistants) directly addressing Bulgaria’s multilingual context and cultural diversity. Section 5.5 Raising awareness and building trust in society – Stresses the need for public trust and inclusivity. Section 6 paragraph Software industry and Creating AI applications for educational purposes.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Interdepartmental Working Group
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
fr1_body_name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related to gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
fr1_body_name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities including equality bodies can voluntarily investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targeting gender-specific.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
