fr1_title: National Digital Economy Master Plan 2024 - 2034 (Gambia)
fr1_justif: The document includes AI as part of the digital economy's foundational framing (5). Under Pillar 6 of the plan on Digital Literacy and Skills it notes that 'The government can provide training programs for public sector workers to improve their digital skills and increase efficiency in their work...this can include training in... artificial intelligence tools.' (50). Relevant additional projects in digital skills development include: The Smart City Planning Training project targeting urban planners and local authorities (56) and Digital Skills for Law Enforcement (58). Other additional projects and flagship projects under Pillar 6 while not specifically mentioning the public sector seem to be open to both the public and private sector.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy (MoCDE) and the Gambia ICT Agency (GICTA)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The plan is very broad and just provides that 'The government can provide training programs for public sector workers to improve their digital skills and increase efficiency in their work...this can include training in... artificial intelligence tools' (50) and then introduces some general flagship and additional projects for digital skills. Projects seem to be more geared to applications of AI (and other rdigital technologies) rather than its risks and ethical considerations).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The plan proposes dedicated digital leadership roles within government but these are framed around digital transformation broadly — not AI specifically. It proposes assigning aChief Digital Officers (CDO) to every ministry to 'oversee IT investments processes and policies' with agreed minimum qualifications and adequate payroll to attract and sustain competencies (24). It proposes mandatory Chief Information Security Officers (CISO) and Data Protection Officers (DPO) in all ministries (60) with a networking platform and competency development model. And it proposes an AI Ethics Council (74) in partnership with global experts to 'guide the ethical development and deployment of artificial intelligence technologies' and formulate policies.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The plan states that 'digital literacy and skills are constantly evolving and it is essential to develop a culture of lifelong learning to ensure that individuals and organizations are equipped to keep pace with these changes' (51). The 'Virtual Government Training Programs' (28) are framed as providing 'continuous learning' and enhancing the efficiency of government officials. The cross-cutting themes section identifies the need for the public sector to 'be prepared to leverage new and emerging technologies' and calls for 'clear policy legal and regulatory frameworks to empower public servants to adopt and implement automation and other technologies' (78).

fr1_title: National Digital Economy Master Plan 2024 - 2034 (Gambia)
fr1_justif: The document includes AI as part of the digital economy's foundational framing (5). Pillar 6 is dedicated to Digital literacy and skills and various programs mention AI and/or emerging technologies specifically while others will also be applicable. Emerging Technologies Training (56): 'introduce participants to cutting-edge technologies such as AI....to develop expertise in these technologies preparing individuals for future job opportunities in emerging fields. Data Science Bootcamps: training participants in 'data analysis machine learning and predictive modeling' (58). Digital Skills Training Centers: serve as hubs for delivering comprehensive digital skills training to individuals of all ages including on emerging technologies (52).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy (MoCDE) and the Gambia ICT Agency (GICTA)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The plan contains extensive provisions for skills development programs that encompass both upskilling (enhancing existing competencies) and reskilling (training for new roles) for the digital economy which includes AI (51-58) to be developed by the government. It seems as if the key programs are to be funded by the government while the government will work with partners locally and globally to mobilize the needed resources for additional projects but due to not being explicitly stated whether they are government funded or subsidized partially is more appropriate.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: The 'Digital Skills Scholarships' initiative will would 'provide financial support to deserving individuals especially from underserved communities to pursue digital skills training and certifications' and aims to 'ensure that talented individuals are not hindered by financial barriers and can contribute to the digital economy effectively and sustainably' (53). However aside from that scholarship there are no explicit incentives outlined for workers to participate in these programs.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: National Data Policy 2025: The Gambia (Draft)
fr1_justif: The Gambia National Data Management Framework forms part of the Policy and Layer 5 (Innovation & Emerging Technologies) specifically provides for 'Ethical AI and algorithmic transparency: Development of principles tools and oversight mechanisms to ensure fairness explainability and inclusivity in automated decision-making systems' and 'Artificial intelligence governance: Establishment of regulatory and policy frameworks for responsible AI development and deployment including algorithmic accountability and risk management.' (p. 28). Additionally one of the overarching data policy guiding principles is to 'Promote a trustworthy and secure data ecosystem that is ethical by design transparent and accountable to data subjects.' (p.16).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The policy includes 'Ethical AI and algorithmic transparency' as a management domain (p 28) and mentions establishing regulatory and policy frameworks including for algorithmic accountability (p 29). Includes transparency in guiding principles: 'ethical by design transparent and accountable to data subjects '(p. 16). However the Policy lacks specific provisions: No requirement to disclose why an AI system is being used;  No mandate to reveal what data sources feed AI systems;  No concrete requirements for explaining how AI arrives at decisions; No requirements for public registers or documentation of AI systems notice requirements when AI is being used or user rights to receive explanations.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

fr1_title: Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection
fr1_justif: The document addresses access to redress and remedy in the AI context mainly through rules on automated decision-making and profiling. Article 19 provides procedural safeguards by allowing individuals to contest decisions based solely on automated processing express their views and request human involvement. While Article 19 does not establish a full right to remedy or compensation Articles 52 61 and 62 complement it by addressing remedies and liability outlining mechanisms for redress accountability and enforcement in cases of violations arising from automated data processing.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Article 2 clause 2 states: This Law shall not apply to the processing of data for the purposes of national security (including economic security) defence intelligence and counter-intelligence activities;
fr1_body_name: Personal Data Protection Service (PDPS)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection establishes judicial and administrative appeal mechanisms that may apply to AI-related harms but only indirectly. Article 22 (“Right to appeal”) allows data subjects to challenge decisions of the Personal Data Protection Service before a court including in cases involving Article 19 on automated decision-making. However this appeal is directed against an administrative decision not against an AI system AI deployer or harm caused by AI as such. Articles 52 61 and 62 further provide general remedies and liability for unlawful data processing which may encompass AI-driven automated processing but the law does not establish AI-specific judicial mechanisms or objectives for redress.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: The Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection establishes state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms through the Personal Data Protection Service (PDPS) (Article 49). Data subjects may submit complaints concerning unlawful personal data processing including automated decision-making under Article 19. Article 52 further empowers the PDPS to examine violations issue binding instructions require corrective measures and apply administrative sanctions. While these mechanisms may be used in cases involving AI-driven automated processing they are limited to data protection infringements and do not constitute a dedicated redress framework for AI systems AI deployers or harm caused by AI as such.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection does not explicitly include requirements or incentives for companies or developers to create their own grievance or complaint-handling mechanisms related to harms caused by AI systems.However it contains indirect obligations that functionally require organizations to ensure individuals can exercise their rights — which includes responding to complaints. see article 17 clause C

fr1_title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
fr1_justif: The document lists detailed steps to mitigate the bias factors (see article 9 clause 4)
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: National Bank of Georgia
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The document defines bias as an inclination or prejudice in the data and/or algorithm that systematically gives an unfair advantage to an individual or a group and listes detailed steps to promote fair outcomes (see article 9 clause 4)
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The document does not explicitly recommend specific measures to prevent the amplification of existing social biases. However it addresses stereotypical biases and provides detailed steps to mitigate them thereby encompassing this topic as well (see article 9 clause 4)
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: Article 9 clause 4 provides detailed steps to mitigate bias throughout AI lifecycle.

fr1_title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
fr1_justif: While the document doesn't use terms like 'human-in-the-loop' it mandates human control across the model lifecycle: Article 6 allows replacing model parameters based on expert judgment if validation is unsatisfactory. It requires monitoring 'overrides' made by experts to identify model limitations; (Articles 5-8 11) A qualified person independent of development must approve a model's launch. For regulatory models NBG's human assessment determines approval; The second line of defense must consist of staff with the expertise to critically analyze mathematical logic and assumptions. Transparency: Transparency requirements ensure humans can interpret 'black box' outcomes and explain the logic to customers.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: National Bank of Georgia
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The document very generally states that ongoing monitoring of models should include the analysis of overrides made by expert judgment with appropriate documentation. It also mentions human judgment through requirements for expert validation ongoing human monitoring bias checks and explainability. And does not go into details (see articles 6 7 9 9.5).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The document does not explicitly address preventing full automation in sensitive sectors. However it limits full automation within the financial sector by requiring human expert validation ongoing human monitoring and bias checks for all AI/ML models (Art. 6 7 9).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The document does not explicitly use the phrase 'responsible individuals for AI oversight' but it establishes a rigorous accountability framework through Articles 3 4 6 7 and 9. It mandates that entities define specific roles and responsibilities across three independent lines of defense to oversee and manage model risks. Article 6 allow for 'expert judgment' to intervene and override model results when they are unsatisfactory. Furthermore Article 9 stipulates that the entity remains the 'responsible person' for the model even when outsourced. For regulatory models Article 11 specifically requires submitting a 'list of people who are responsible for the model' to the National Bank.

fr1_title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
fr1_justif: In accordance with the Regulation on Data-driven Statistical AI and Machine Learning Model Risk Management issued by the National Bank of Georgia financial institutions must follow specific standards for model integrity: Impact Assessment: Under Article 5 Clause 10 development tests must evaluate how specific assumptions influence results and identify conditions where a model's effectiveness may decrease. Risk Management: Per Article 1 Clause 4 users must maintain a risk management system proportionate to the model's complexity and its potential impact on the institution's material risks. This framework ensures that AI and statistical tools are both transparent and aligned with a bank's/firm's overall risk profile.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: National Bank of Georgia
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: While the law includes provisions for proactive risk management it falls short of explicitly promoting a broad organizational culture regarding societal or environmental impacts. Instead it focuses on technical and material risk. Article 5 Clause 10 mandates that development testing - an essential step before deployment - must evaluate the impact of assumptions on results and identify when effectiveness decreases. While this establishes a rigorous legal requirement for impact assessment within a risk management framework the scope remains primarily focused on the model user’s material risks (Article 1 Clause 4) rather than broader ethical or environmental promotion.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The document explicitly states the need to include impact assessment as an essential component of model development testing prior to deployment (article 6 clause 2) as well as to ensure its monitoring by users after deployment (article 6 clause 5b). Article 4 assigns responsibilities to the first line (developers/users) for development testing and risk management. Article 6 states that the second line of defense is responsible for internal validation and staff performing this validation must have knowledge skills and expertise proportional to the model’s complexity to ensure rigorous assessment of model risks.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
fr1_justif: the document addresses safety and security mainly through its model-risk management framework. It mandates that all AI ML and statistical models used by supervised entities must undergo rigorous internal validation testing and monitoring to prevent losses from incorrect model design data use or implementation. The regulation requires data quality controls (completeness accuracy timeliness audit trace) and establishes a “three lines of defense” structure—development independent validation and internal audit—to ensure transparency accountability and reliability. These provisions collectively safeguard the integrity stability and secure operation of models within financial institutions. (Article 5. Model building and testing)
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: National Bank of Georgia
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes explicit provisions related to establishing performance thresholds and quality benchmarks for AI systems. In particular it requires model testing and monitoring to include process verification and benchmarking (Article 6 Clause 5(b)). In addition internal policies and procedures must define the target accuracy of models and the permissible level of error alongside validation testing and procedures for reviewing and responding to unacceptable errors (Article 3 Paragraph 2). Together these provisions ensure that AI systems are evaluated against predefined performance standards to operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The document includes safeguards and fallback procedures to address AI system failure or unexpected behavior. Article 8 Clause 3 establishes an emergency safeguard by requiring the restriction or suspension of a model when there are significant changes in model risk or breaches of risk appetite. Additionally Article 6 Paragraph 5(b)(ii) provides a human-in-the-loop fallback allowing expert judgment to replace validation results or parameters when validation is unsatisfactory and alternative data or models are unavailable. Together these provisions function as mitigation and emergency protocols to limit potential harm.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The document establishes comprehensive requirements for pre-deployment testing validation and documentation to ensure technical robustness across the AI system lifecycle. Article 5 mandates documented model objectives methodology assumptions data quality standards and extensive testing (including accuracy checks sensitivity analysis scenario testing and transparency assessments) prior to deployment. Article 6 further requires independent internal validation covering model inputs calculations and outputs supported by documented conceptual soundness reviews robustness testing and risk-based validation intensity. Together these provisions ensure technical robustness before deployment and throughout ongoing model use.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

fr1_title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
fr1_justif: Article 5 clause 10 (page 4) states that the model should be transparent and allow for explanation and interpretation. To ensure transparency the model’s logic technical content and potential biases must be examined during the validation process. The requirement for transparency becomes even more significant when the model’s decisions directly affect consumers and the decision-making
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: National Bank of Georgia
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The decree states that the model should be transparent and should allow for explanation and interpretation. In order to ensure transparency the logic and technical content of the model and existence of the bias should be checked during the model validation process. Also the user of the model should contribute to the education and awareness of consumers about the decision made by using machine learning and artificial intelligence. Moreover there is the need to describe data sources as well as the model development process and assumptions. See articles 5 9 and 11.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: There is no differentiation between high-stakes and low-stakes systems. The decree generally states that the model user should increase the transparency of the decision made by employing the model. In order to ensure transparency the model developer should if necessary be able to explain to the customer the logic of the model decision. See article 9
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: Article 9 states: In order to ensure transparency the model user should if necessary be able to explain to the customer the logic of the model decision.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the German Federal Government (2020 Update)
fr1_justif: AI literacy is framed as a societal competence: under “AI skills for all” the update aims that “every citizen” is well informed about AI’s opportunities and challenges to “demystify” AI and strengthen digital skills for everyday dealings with AI (Society “AI skills for all” p.25). It operationalises this via the free online course “Elements of AI” for the full breadth of the population including those without prior knowledge (p.25). It also commits to adapting education and training curricula across school vocational and higher education plus continuing training at companies (p.11)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The German Federal Government
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy states: 'Education and training curricula are being adapted' mentioning school vocational and higher education (p. 11). For the Tertiary level it funds the 'implementation of AI in the curriculum content' (p. 26) and development of AI-related degree programs via the 'AI in Higher Education' initiative. The Strategy does not distinguish between primary and secondary school but it mentioned the STEM Action Plan (p. 12) to promote AI literacy and the integration of AI-specific modules which is for primary and secondary school (https://stip.oecd.org/stip/interactive-dashboards/policy-initiatives/2025%2Fdata%2FpolicyInitiatives%2F99998575). The Strategy also includes vocational training via the INVITE platform (p. 26).
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy includes clear measures to establish AI programs within formal education. Centrally it funds the establishment of 100 new AI professorships for AI teaching (p. 10). Through the 'AI in Higher Education' program it finances the development of AI-related degree programs and the 'implementation of AI in curriculum content' (p. 12 27). The Strategy strengthens AI provision mainly in higher education: it is “of vital importance” to secure specialists “through university courses” (p.10). It will foster innovation in higher education “such as the AI-supported development of university courses” (p.11). It will also support international students through dedicated DAAD AI programs (p. 10).
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The National AI Strategy madates the integration of AI into the curricula for future academic staff (p. 11 26). It expands the 'AI trainer programme' and funds 'train-the-trainer' initiatives to create a network of qualified educators (p. 17). For resources it develops an 'AI-supported online portal' for vocational training and uses the STEM Action Plan to provide AI-related learning clusters for schools (p. 11).

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

fr1_title: EU GDPR
fr1_justif: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).
fr1_body_name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: It is mandatory to establish an independent supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint including a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) including age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the German Federal Government (2020 Update)
fr1_justif: The National Strategy explicitly links preventing discrimination and bias to the inclusion of 'social diversity' within development teams going beyond just gender (p. 24: Security robustness and sustainability of AI). In the cultural sector the Strategy funds AI projects for the 'preservation development accessibility networking and communication of cultural programmes' (p.30). It also emphasises developing AI skills to verify media content specifically to ensure diversity of opinion (p.30). The strategy also aims to establish 'AI made in Europe' as a trademark rooted in 'common European rules and values (p. 2: Summary p.13).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The German Federal Government
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy does not explicitly mention preventing cultural stereotypes or erasure of linguistic diversity. However it does include a general prevention objective: under “Safety robustness and sustainability of AI” it states that AI use must ensure effective protection against discrimination manipulation and misuse and argues that reflecting societal diversity in developer teams helps prevent bias and discrimination “from the very outset” (p. 24).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: Law on increasing energy efficiency in Germany (Energy Efficiency Act - EnEfG)
fr1_justif: The EnEfG law implements the EU Energy Efficiency Directive (EED) at a national level and regulates the environmental footprint of data centres where AI workloads run. It mandates that data centers with a load of =300 kW meet strict performance metrics such as a Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of =1.2 (Section 11) for new facilities and an Energy Reuse Factor (ERF) of 20% by 2028 (Section 11(2)). By requiring 100% renewable energy use by 2027 and annual reporting to the Energy Efficiency Register (Section 11(5)) the EnEfG ensures that AI growth aligns with national climate goals. For reporting data center operators must submit annual energy and water usage data to the Energy Efficiency Register (RZReg) (Section 13).
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Defense and security are explicitly excluded from the scope of the EnEfG through Section 21. This section stipulates that the mandatory energy reduction targets for public bodies and the requirement to implement management systems do not apply to the field of National Defense. These exemptions ensure that the Act's stringent technical standards such as waste heat reuse or renewable energy quotas  do not jeopardise the operational readiness or security-critical infrastructure of the Bundeswehr. While the defense sector is encouraged to contribute to sustainability through separate strategies it remains legally exempt from the EnEfG.
fr1_body_name: The Federal Office for Economic Affairs and Export Control (BAFA)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: Section 11 establishes binding Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and waste heat reuse (ERF) targets for data centers effectively preventing 'excessive energy consumption' at the hardware level. It also mandates 100% renewable energy by 2027 for these facilities. However it lacks specific provisions for e-waste management which is handled under the ElektroG and does not regulate 'resource-intensive' software practices or algorithmic efficiency directly. The Act focuses on the efficiency of the 'where' AI is trained rather than the 'how' of its development.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element2_justif: Section 13 requires data center operators to report detailed energy metrics to a national register. Section 15 obliges these operators to inform their customers including AI developers of the specific energy consumption related to their service use. This provides developers with the necessary data to assess their environmental impact. However the EnEfG does not directly legally obligate software developers to report on their AI models; that specific requirement is handled by the EU AI Act which mandates energy reporting for General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models.
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
fr1_element3_justif: The Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) explicitly promotes these efforts through binding technical mandates in Section 11. It establishes a strict PUE target of = 1.2 for new data centers effectively mandating advanced cooling technologies. It also dictates a transition to 100% renewable energy by 2027 (Section 11.5) and enforces waste heat reuse (ERF) of up to 20% by 2028. Regarding water Section 13 and Annex 3 require operators to report total water consumption and efficiency indicators to a national register. While water efficiency targets are currently focused on transparency rather than binding limits the Act creates a comprehensive legal baseline for reducing the environmental footprint of the infrastructure powering AI.

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related to gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities including equality bodies can voluntarily investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targeting gender-specific.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.

fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) including the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems
fr1_title: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Federal Administration (Germany)
fr1_justif: The Guidelines address public disclosure by prioritizing transparency to ensure administrative action remains traceable. Guideline B6 (p. 22) mandates that federal authorities disclose their AI use as transparently as possible to foster public trust. This involves implementing internal and external labeling and documentation obligations. Guideline A5 (p. 16) specifically requires marking AI-generated content when shared with the public. Furthermore the framework promotes 'Explainable AI' (p. 7) requiring that the logic and data basis of AI results be reproducible and understandable for affected citizens.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: In the footnote of Section 3 (p. 10) it states that deviations from the guidelines are permissible in justified cases such as for military or national security purposes.
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
fr1_element1_justif: The Guidelines encourage a public inventory. Under Guideline B6  the Federal Administration operates the “AI Oppportunity Marketplace' (MaKI) described as an AI-transparency register offering an overview of AI use and authorities are encouraged to register deployed systems (pp. 22-23). This is a recommended practice rather than a binding obligation to list all systems with specified fields.
fr1_element2_text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
fr1_element2_justif: The Guidelines recommend transparency and documentation for AI use in federal bodies but stop short of mandating public disclosure of training data or publishing impact-assessment results. Under “Transparency regarding government AI use”(p.22) they urge authorities to consider labelling and documentation duties and refer to AI Act transparency obligations (Arts 48 50). They also state IT leads must be able to provide information on authorised AI systems (p.17). However no rule requires disclosure of datasets rationales or DPIA/FRIA outputs (Guideline B6 notes on MaKI and Guideline B1). Guideline B7 regulates data disclosure by minimising data sharing including preventing reuse of inputs for model training via account settings (p.23).
fr1_element3_text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
fr1_element3_justif: The Guidelines promote transparency about administrative AI use (Guideline B6) including use of the MaKI transparency register but stop short of prescribing exhaustive public fields. They simultaneously require authorities to decide AI use “in light of information security data protection and secrecy” and note disclosure limits where national security considerations apply (Guideline B1). They also prescribe data-minimisation and pseudonymous registration practices that constrain what may be disclosed publicly (Guideline B7).
fr1_element4_text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
fr1_element4_justif: The Guidelines urge authorities to provide explanations that users and affected persons can understand including recognising when they interact with AI and where feasible tracing the basis on which results were produced (p. 7). Guideline B6 (p.22) also stress making AI as transparent as possible to build public trust but does not mandate plain-language public-facing explanations for each system.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the German Federal Government (2020 Update)
fr1_justif: The document addresses Public Procurement of AI by expanding the KOINNO center to provide public buyers with specialised training and guidelines (p. 22). It prioritises 'AI made in Germany/Europe' by revising guidelines to facilitate access for start-ups through innovation partnerships (p. 16 22). The strategy mandates that procurement processes define standard requirements for the traceability and verifiability of AI systems to ensure transparency (p. 14 24). Furthermore it utilises 'learning and experimentation spaces' for administrations to test AI applications ensuring they meet ethical and technical standards before being awarded contracts (p. 21).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The German Federal Government
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy mandates the expansion of the Centre of Excellence for Innovative Procurement (KOINNO) center (p. 22). The Strategy also articulates requirements that should guide the selection and use of AI systems including traceability non-discrimination and verifiability (pp. 21 23). In addition it promotes “learning and experimentation spaces” to test systems’ ethical and technical robustness before wider deployment (p. 21). Finally its “AI made in Europe” framing emphasises responsible public-interest development (p. 2).
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element3_justif: The Strategy does not create a binding legal mandate requiring vendors to disclose training data or model details. However it recommends preventing “black box” AI through policy and standards: it calls for AI to be transparent predictable and verifiable when adapting the regulatory framework (p. 21 p.23). It frames rules norms and standards as part of a quality infrastructure to underpin trust in products and services (pp.19-20). This support transparency objectives but stop short of a vendor disclosure mandate.
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
fr1_element4_justif: The National AI Strategy prioritises digital sovereignty by fostering an 'AI Made in Germany/Europe' ecosystem (p. 2 13 24). It explicitly uses public procurement as a steering tool expanding the Centre of Excellence for Public Procuremen (KOINNO) and giving more consideration to start-ups and SMEs in public contracts (p. 22). The Strategy promotes innovation partnerships to co-develop AI with domestic providers reducing dependency on foreign technology and preventing vendor lock-in (p. 16 22). Furthermore it links procurement to sovereign infrastructures like GAIA-X to ensure data and model control (p. 12 18 28).

fr1_title: AI Strategy for the Justice System (KI Strategie in der Justiz)
fr1_justif: The AI Strategy for the Justice System highlights public-sector skills. Under Action area 5.7 “Strengthen AI competence of justice personnel” it states that sufficient AI competence among justice staff is a key prerequisite for introducing procuring and using AI systems (p. 34). It then sets measures: G1 “Roles and competence profiles” (defining competence needs and potential specialist roles) G2 “Knowledge-transfer formats and training/support materials” and G3 “Training” (cross-Länder training concepts and continuing training and awareness offers) (pp. 34–35).
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: Federal-State Commission for Information Technology in the Judiciary (BLK) AI working group of the Federal-State Commission for Information Technology in the Judiciary (BLK-AG AI)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy contains measures to upskill and reskill justice personnel including the judiciary and justice administration by defining roles and competence profiles complementary to the judicial personnel (p. 35 G1) developing exchange and knowledge sharing of materials beneficial for all members of the judiciary (p. 35 G2) and (after examination) will offer further training and awareness-raising programs as needed regarding AI competence (p. 35 G3). However it is sector-specific to the justice system and does not establish a government-wide upskilling strategy (p. 4).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The Strategy foresees continuing training and professional development: it plans the cross-federal-state (Länder) development of training concepts and further training and awareness-raising programs as needed regarding AI competence (p. 35 G3). It also frames the Strategy as continuously updated in response to 'technological and economic developments” (p. 4).

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the German Federal Government (2020 Update)
fr1_justif: The National AI Strategy establishes comprehensive government-funded reskilling programs. It prioritises “skills development and continuing training at companies” and links this to the Federal Government’s National Skills Strategy (p. 11). It also states that information and skills-development schemes are being expanded including the “AI trainer programme” at the Mittelstand 4.0 Centres of Excellence and related train-the-trainer support (p. 17). The annex further lists creating an AI-supported online portal for continuing vocational training and launching INVITE projects for digital continuing education (p. 26).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The German Federal Government
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The National AI Strategy establishes comprehensive government-funded reskilling programs. It prioritises “skills development and continuing training at companies” and links this to the Federal Government’s National Skills Strategy (p. 11). It also states that information and skills-development schemes are being expanded including the “AI trainer programme” at the Mittelstand 4.0 Centres of Excellence and related train-the-trainer support (p. 17). The annex further lists creating an AI-supported online portal for continuing vocational training and launching INVITE projects for digital continuing education (p. 26).
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
