fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) including the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems
fr1_title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
fr1_justif: Art. 14 (p.9) requires public administrations to ensure citizens’ “knowledge of the functioning” of AI systems and the “traceability” of their use. It also mandates technical organisational and training measures to guarantee responsible use. These provisions establish transparency duties regarding how government AI operates ensuring that individuals are informed when administrative processes rely on AI tools.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly excludes the framework of this law from developments in intelligence defense and national security fields so the framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.
fr1_body_name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
fr1_element2_text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
fr1_element3_text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
fr1_element3_justif: The law sets broad principles: Art. 4 (p.3) requires clear simple information to users while ensuring protection of personal data and privacy. Art. 14 mandates transparency but also respects autonomy and legal responsibilities. However it does not define detailed criteria distinguishing publicly disclosable information from security-sensitive content.
fr1_element4_text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
fr1_element4_justif: Art. 14 (p.9) requires public administrations to ensure citizens’ “knowledge of the functioning” of AI systems and the “traceability” of their use. Art. 4 (p.3) requires communications to be in “clear and simple language” ensuring understandable explanations of how AI affects individuals. Art. 7 similarly gives users a right to be informed of AI use in health.

fr1_title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
fr1_justif: The law addresses AI procurement in Art. 5(d) (p. 4) requiring public e-procurement platforms to prioritise AI solutions that ensure national data-center localisation disaster-recovery and business-continuity capabilities and high standards of security and transparency in training and development. It also mandates compliance with competition non-discrimination and proportionality principles in awarding AI contracts.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly excludes the framework of this law from developments in intelligence defense and national security fields so the framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.
fr1_body_name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element1_justif: Art. 5(d) instructs public e-procurement platforms to prioritise AI solutions ensuring data localisation security disaster-recovery and transparency in training and development (p.4). These criteria introduce AI-specific ethical/technical considerations beyond traditional IT procurement but the law does not create full procurement guidelines or procedures.
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element3_justif: Art. 5(d) requires AI models to ensure “high standards of transparency in training and development methods” (p.4). This establishes a transparency expectation but does not require vendors to disclose training data model architecture or avoid black-box systems.
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
fr1_element4_justif: Art. 5(d) directs procurement platforms to prioritise AI solutions where strategic data are processed in national data centres with disaster-recovery and continuity also located in Italy (p.4). This creates a sovereign procurement preference supporting national infrastructure and local AI providers.

fr1_title: Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024–2026
fr1_justif: The Strategy sets multiple actions to develop AI skills in the public sector. PA.1 (p.22) promotes awareness methodological guidance and understanding of AI risks. PA.3 (p.23) requires training staff in advanced AI-related technologies. PA.6 (pp.24–25) creates AI-focused upskilling programmes and postgraduate training within the National School of Administration and other PA training schools. The overview (p.21) highlights the need to build AI-specific competencies across the public administration.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: PA.1 (p. 22) establishes a government-wide approach to build AI awareness competencies and understanding of risks across the public administration. PA.6 (pp. 24–25) introduces national upskilling programmes and postgraduate AI training through the National School of Administration and PA training schools confirming a coordinated government-wide reskilling effort.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The implementation section creates coordination and governance structures and assigns responsibilities across PA bodies (p.21) and PA.1 (p. 22) promotes internal competence centers for AI guidance. However the Strategy does not establish specific “AI champion” roles such as Chief AI Officers or permanent expert teams in each department.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: PA.6 (pp.24–25) establishes continuous upskilling programmes and advanced training for civil servants to maintain AI-related competencies over time. PA.1 (p.22) also emphasizes ongoing awareness and capacity-building activities to keep pace with evolving AI risks tools and methodologies.
fr2_title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
fr2_justif: The only indirect reference is in Article 15 which requires judicial authorities to understand AI systems used in justice but it does not mandate or outline training programs. There are no sections establishing AI-related training for public administration personnel
fr2_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr2_defence_and_security_justif: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly excludes the framework of this law from developments in intelligence defense and national security fields so the framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.
fr2_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr2_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr2_element2_justif: The law designates AgID and ACN as national authorities with supervisory and guidance roles on AI (Art. 20) and establishes the AI Observatory on Labour (Art. 12). These bodies act as institutional hubs supporting responsible AI governance. However the law does not create AI champions inside ministries or assign roles specifically responsible for fostering AI innovation within individual agencies.
fr2_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

fr1_title: Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024–2026
fr1_justif: The Strategy explicitly prioritises AI-related reskilling and upskilling. It states “no worker can be left behind” and “roll out a robust programme of incentives for reskilling and upskilling initiatives” (pp. 29). Action F.5 provides “training and professional development courses on AI to retrain and update workers’ skills” (pp. 33-34). Supply-chain academies offer structured reskilling  (p. 33). PA.6 mandates postgraduate AI training for public administration employees  (p. 24).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Department for Digital Transformation - Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) - FAIR Foundation
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy explicitly commits to government-supported reskilling and upskilling. It states Italy will “roll out a robust programme of incentives for reskilling and upskilling” to retrain workers (p.30). Action F.5 mandates “training and professional development courses on AI to retrain and update workers’ skills” (p.33). Supply-chain academies funded via FSC support worker reskilling (p.34). FSC funds are the Development and Cohesion Fund an Italian national financial instrument that finances interventions to reduce economic social and territorial imbalances between different areas of the country. Originally known as FAS (Fund for Underutilised Areas) it works in conjunction with European Structural Funds to promote sustainable growth.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: High-risk AI systems must be designed to enable deployers to understand system outputs and use them including the purpose performance levels known limitations and input data specifications (Art.13). Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and techniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). General-purpose AI providers and generate synthetic AI system content need to be published as technical documentation (Art.50 53). It is mandatory to register in the EU public database before deploying the high-risk AI (Art.49).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); including explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure taken and main element (art.86).

fr1_title: Data Protection Act 2020 (Jamaica)
fr1_justif: Section 12 (“Rights in relation to automated decision-taking”) of Jamaica’s Data Protection Act (p. 22 approved in 2020 according https://oic.gov.jm/page/data-protection-act) establishes that individuals have the right not to be subject to decisions that significantly affect them when these are based solely on automated processing and it also entitles data subjects to request that such decisions be reconsidered or remade with human involvement
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Part V Exemption to Data Protection Standards or to Disclosure to Data Subject Requirements (p. 48) covers this. Section 33 (p. 48) deals with National Security. Section 33 (1) talks to exemptions for the purpose of national security.
fr1_body_name: Information Commissioner
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: It includes limited safeguards related to automated decision-making and human accountability in section 12 (p 22). There it mentions explicitly human supervision of decisions related to “the individual’s performance at work creditworthiness reliability or conduct” so it covers critical areas. However it does not refer to “meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: Data Protection Act 2020 (Jamaica)
fr1_justif: Section 6(2)(d) of the Data Protection Act 2020 (pg. 14) requires data controllers to inform data subjects of the logic involved in automated decision-making processes directly addressing explainability requirements. Section 12 (pg. 22) further reinforces transparency by entitling individuals to request reconsideration of automated decisions that significantly affect them ensuring data controllers must be accountable for the reasoning behind such decisions. Together these provisions establish a transparency and explainability framework applicable to automated processing in Jamaica.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Part V Exemption to Data Protection Standards  or to Disclosure to Data Subject Requirements (pg. 48) covers this. Section 33 (pg.48) deals with National Security. Section 33 (1) talks to exemptions for the purpose of national security.
fr1_body_name: Information Commissioner
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: Section 6(2)(d) of the DPA 2020 (pg. 14) requires data controllers to inform individuals of the purpose and logic of automated decision-making upon request. Section 12 (pg. 22) further entitles individuals to request reconsideration of automated decisions significantly affecting them. However coverage is partial because transparency obligations are reactive rather than proactive require payment of a fee and don't explicitly address data sources or mandate public disclosure of how AI systems operate. The DPA doesn't require systematic publication of information about AI system design or functioning.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: Section 12 of the DPA 2020 (pg. 22) entitles individuals to know when decisions significantly affecting them are based solely on automated processing and to request reconsideration with human involvement. Section 6(2)(d) (pg. 14) further requires data controllers to inform individuals of the logic involved in automated decision-making upon request. However coverage is partial because the DPA doesn't explicitly require organisations to provide detailed explanations of the specific factors or weightings that led to a particular outcome falling short of a full right to explanation as understood in AI governance standards.

fr1_title: Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI at the primary and secondary education level (Japan)
fr1_justif: The Guidelines from the Ministry of Education Culture Sports Science and Technology (MEXT) stress that children should learn to use tools like generative AI [p.3]. They also define teachers’ roles: to use generative AI effectively in schools teachers must attain core AI literacy understanding how it works and its characteristics to build a foundation for appropriate classroom use [p.7]. In addition students should gain a scientific understanding of generative AI its operation societal effects and related laws systems and etiquette and learn to apply it to identify and solve problems [p.9].
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The Guidelines outline the importance for children to master technologies such as generative AI as tools [p. 3] and the role of teachers stating that to effectively utilize generative AI in schools teachers are required to acquire a certain level of AI literacy such as understanding the mechanisms and characteristics of generative AI as this will also help to create the foundation for appropriate use in educational activities [p.7]. However there are no specific notes regarding curriculum reforms and it does not apply to the tertiary level.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The Guidelines define the role of teachers: to effectively utilize generative AI in schools teachers are required to acquire a certain level of AI literacy understanding the mechanisms and characteristics of generative AI which helps build the foundation for appropriate use in educational activities [p.7]. They also state that the principles should be used as reference materials for teacher-training courses and for addressing issues when using generative AI as teaching content [p.19]. Boards of education are also expected to publicize and share precedents teaching materials and know-how and to leverage external resources such as teacher-training universities and service providers [p.21].

fr1_title: AI White Paper 2024 New Strategies in Stage II Toward the world's most AI-friendly country (Japan)
fr1_justif: The White Paper treats AI-facilitated misinformation as a critical safety and governance concern. It highlights how generative AI can produce fake images videos and audio that enable fraud and undermine trust [p.16] and how such AI generated misinformation (especially during disasters and accidents) can become life-threatening [p.19]. It also warns of AI’s role in election interference and democratic disruption [p.19]. To counter this it urges legal measures for faster deletion of illegal content platform transparency literacy campaigns and public-private development of detection technologies [pp.20–21] linking misinformation control to preventing harm and maintaining public safety.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: AI Safety Institute (AISI)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The White Paper includes measures to prevent AI from generating or spreading misinformation but does not mention hate speech harassment or violence explicitly. It notes safeguards against producing illegal or dangerous content such as weapons or terrorism-related material though “the model still struggles with malicious uses such as prompt injection” [p.19]. It further calls for government and platform action to speed up deletion of illegal AI-generated content and enhance transparency [p.20]. While these provisions address misinformation risks they do not extend to preventing hate speech or AI-enabled harassment.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: The White Paper urges “institutional arrangements” to speed deletion of illegal AI-generated content and to make platform operational status transparent [p.20]. It distinguishes appropriate governance for developers versus providers/users [p.17] and recommends minimum legal obligations on safety and transparency for high-risk AI cases [p.18]. It also promotes labeling/source attribution of AI-generated content to boost transparency of information [p.19].
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI at the primary and secondary education level (Japan)
fr1_justif: The guidelines adopt a human-centered rule: AI use must not violate fundamental human rights; humans make final decisions and bear responsibility [§2 Basic Concept – Human-centered principle p.7]. Student use must follow age restrictions and as needed parents’ understanding/consent [Key points for utilization p.19; Checklist p.25]. Students are instructed not to input personal information [p.19] and teachers check outputs for bias [p.19]. Transparency is required: cite AI use and inform parents of its purpose/nature [p.20]. Educators consider students’ developmental stage [Checklist p.25].
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The guidelines protect children’s data and privacy by teaching students not to enter personal information into AI tools [p.19] and ensuring educational information security [pp.21 22]. According to the Guidelines the use of Generative AI must also respect age limits and potentially require teacher supervision and/or parents’ prior understanding [p.19].
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: While the guidelines place some obligations on deployers (schools/boards) to ensure safe and age-appropriate use [p.19] and gives recommendations for handling personal data of the students [p.21] they do not assign any design duties to developers.

fr1_title: Governance Guidelines for Implementation of AI Principles Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
fr1_justif: The Guidelines recommend to AI system developers to take cultural differences into account and increase the diversity of the team when developing AI systems to ensure that the diversities found in Japan are also well recognized in the discussion [p.26; 69-71].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The guidelines recommend that AI system developers take cultural differences into account and increase the diversity of their team when developing AI systems to ensure that the diversities found in Japan are also well recognized in the discussion [p.26; 69-71]. This also includes specific recommendations for AI developers such as using specific data sets that avoid unfair discrimination and utilizing a highly diverse team when screening for diversity and sensitivity in AI outputs [pp. 70-72].
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: The guidelines recommend that AI system developers take cultural differences into account and increase the diversity of their team when developing AI systems to ensure that the AI outputs will entrench/impair any unfair discrimination based on certain social attributes [pp.71-72]. To be more specific AI developers are requested to use data sets that avoid unfair discrimination and utilizing a diverse team screen outputs of the AI for diversity and sensitivity [pp. 70-72].
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
fr1_element3_justif: The guidelines do recommend that AI system developers increase the diversity of their team when developing AI systems [p.71]. Specifically AI developers are requested to use data sets that avoid unfair discrimination and utilizing a diverse team screen outputs of the AI for diversity and sensitivity [pp. 70-72]. Furthermore the Guidelines stipulate that AI systems intended for provision to other countries and regions should be designed with due consideration for local regulations customs and cultural factors ensuring appropriate functionality and adaptability across contexts.

fr1_title: The Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
fr1_justif: The Guidelines emphasizes that the development and expansion of more advanced AI is a significant impact on the environment due to the large amounts of electricity required [p.27]. Evaluation point 11 of the Procurement Check Sheet (Appendix 3) [p.62 of the PDF] explicitly states providing or using a generative AI system that considers environmental impact; for example by using models trained on hardware featuring energy-efficient semiconductors. It lists Documentation that clarifies superior environmental performance in terms of power consumption etc. as examples for supporting this goal.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The guideline does not apply to government information systems handling confidential information related to national security the maintenance of public safety and order as well as information that may potentially become confidential [p. 6].
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: The guidelines only specifically address measures and best practices for reducing power-consumption by using energy-efficient technology (see Evaluation Viewpoint 11) but nothing related to e-waste.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element2_justif: Under 'Developing and providing environmentally conscious generative AI systems' the guidelines recommend supporting measures like documentation that clarifies superior environmental performance in terms of power consumption etc. see Evaluation point 11 of the Procurement Check Sheet (Appendix 3) [p.62 of the PDF].
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: AI Guidelines for Business Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
fr1_justif: The Guidelines promote fairness by promoting the elimination of harmful bias/discrimination tied to protected traits and respecting human rights and cultural diversity [pp. 16 23].They require bias controls across the lifecycle of AI systems (data models/algorithms prompts and external services) to prevent unfair outcomes [p.23]. They also call for timely human intervention to mitigate automation bias and correct unfair results [p.17].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: They require bias controls across the lifecycle of AI systems (data models/algorithms prompts and external services) to prevent unfair outcomes [p.23]. They also call for timely human intervention to mitigate automation bias and correct unfair results [p.17].
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The Guidelines state that during the development provision or use of an AI system or service it is important that each AI business actor makes efforts to eliminate unfair and harmful bias and discrimination against any specific individuals or groups based on race gender national origin age political opinion religion and so forth [p.16]. Based on the fact that biases which that results in unreasonable disadvantage to specific individuals or groups which cannot be rationally explained cannot be completely eliminated from the process of training data the Guidelines suggest to make sure AI models are trained with properly represented data sets and check AI systems assume no bias [p.28].
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: They require bias controls across the lifecycle of AI systems (data models/algorithms prompts and external services) to prevent unfair outcomes [p.23]. They also call for timely human intervention to mitigate automation bias and correct unfair results [p.17]. These obligations are explicitly extended to AI Developers Providers and AI Business users [p.23].

fr1_title: New Female Digital Talent Development Plan (Japan)
fr1_justif: The plan links gender equality to AI by noting how AI is reshaping daily life and work making AI skills essential for workers [pp. 2 4] and emphasizing women’s acquisition of AI/cloud skills to raise productivity and deliver services [p.4]. It also notes AI tools’ rapid spread and the need for women to keep skills updated [pp. 2 4]; and pairing this with measures that promote women’s economic independence and career advancement via digital upskilling pathways and targets for women’s leadership (30% executives by 2030) [p.3].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Economy Trade and Industry (METI) Gender Equality Bureau Cabinet Office (translated as Headquarters for Promoting Gender Equality)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
fr1_element3_justif: The plan explicitly promotes increasing women’s participation in the AI and digital workforce. It expands education-training benefits to include courses on “digital skills including AI” [p.6] encourages companies to update women’s AI/cloud skills [p.2] and links these initiatives to the national goal of 30% women in leadership positions by around 2030 [p.3].

fr1_title: AI Guidelines for Business Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
fr1_justif: The guidelines emphasize the necessity of having timely human intervention rather than letting AI make decisions alone and also advocate for implementing measures to protect human judgement from AI influence [pp.1517].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: While the guidelines emphasize the necessity of having controllability and timely human intervention rather than letting AI make decisions alone advocate for implementing measures to protect human judgement from AI influence [pp.1517] and state the importance of AI being a tool to the human [p.11] they do not specifically refer to any critical areas but more so do so in a general manner.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: While the guidelines emphasize the need for timely human interventions rather than letting AI make the decisions alone [p.17] they do not highlight any specific sensitive sectors.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The guidelines state that when developing providing or using an AI system or service it is important that each AI business actor executes its accountability to stakeholders within reasonable extent [p.19] and recommend to appoint someone as the person responsible for executing its accountability in each AI business actor [p.20]. However they do not assign any specific obligations for oversight and intervention.

fr1_title: AI White Paper 2024 New Strategies in Stage II Toward the world's most AI-friendly country (Japan)
fr1_justif: The White Paper states that “the basis of Japan’s strategy is to continuously assess and reduce risks” [p.18]. It calls for ongoing updates in response to technological and business changes and close cooperation between government and industry to promote risk reduction [p.18]. To address serious risks the government should consider reviewing existing laws and regulations [p.19] and promote preventive measures [p.20]. It also emphasizes Sharing advanced use-cases of AI and quantitative and qualitative impacts in public and private sectors [p.9] and developing internationally consistent safety evaluation and red-teaming methods including checking tools and test implementation methods [pp.20–21].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: AI Safety Institute (AISI)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The White Paper promotes a proactive approach to AI risk management by requiring businesses to “voluntarily and continuously assess and reduce risks” and to “update measures in response to changes in technology and business” [p.18]. It also calls for cooperation between government and industry and emphasizes internationally consistent evaluation methods and testing for AI safety [pp.20-21]. Moreover in areas where AI malfunctions or systemic risks could have significant consequences - such as the negative impact of AI on elections - the government is asked to review existing laws and encourage preventive measures [p.19-20]. However it does not explicitly require pre-deployment evaluation of societal ethical or environmental impacts.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The White Paper instructs businesses to “voluntarily and continuously assess and reduce risks” associated with AI and to regularly update these measures as technology and business environments evolve [p.18] and emphasizes collaboration between government and industry to ensure effective risk mitigation and highlights the need for consistent evaluation methods and testing including red-teaming to enhance AI safety [pp.20-21]. While these provisions certainly promote ongoing assessment and mitigation they stop short of assigning any kind of specific obligations to developers or users to conduct comprehensive impact assessments covering risks to individuals or society it is again more of an abstract assessment than formal obligation.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems
fr1_title: The Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
fr1_justif: These Guidelines are intended for gov. staff involved in procurement and use of GenAI [p. 6] and are organized around evaluation viewpoints (EV) that function as a practical checklist. Within this framework the they suggest optional requirements such as enabling reasonable disclosure or information-sharing by planners or providers to ensure that relevant prompts or system parameters are not concealed (EV8 having technical measures or documentation in place that allow end users to distinguish AI-generated outputs from human-generated information (EV13) and emphasize the need for management and oversight mechanisms that allow the system’s overview origins and operations to be verified through logs and technical specifications (EV21).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The guideline does not apply to government information systems handling confidential information related to national security the maintenance of public safety and order as well as information that may potentially become confidential [p. 6].
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
fr1_element1_justif: While the Guidelines note the importance of having managements in place to ensure that the overview origins and operations of the system model and data can be verified from logs and technical specifications etc. (Evaluation Viewpoint 21) they do not suggest the establishment of a public registry/inventory meaning that those logs are just for internal assessment and verifiability.
fr1_element2_text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
fr1_element2_justif: The Guidelines suggest as an optional requirement to be able to provide disclosure or share information to the planner to a reasonable extent in order to make sure that parts of the prompts or parameters entered into generative AI systems are not concealed. (Evaluation Viewpoint 8) and having technology or documentation in place to that provides mechanisms for end users to distinguish outputs by generative AI systems from information output by humans (Evaluation Viewpoint 13).
fr1_element3_text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
fr1_element3_justif: The Guidelines suggest to be able to provide disclosure or share information to the planner to a reasonable extent in order to make sure that parts of the prompts or parameters entered into generative AI systems are not concealed (Evaluation Viewpoint 8). The 'reasonable extent' note most likely contains privacy and safety considerations but there is no clear outlining of such.
fr1_element4_text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
fr1_element4_justif: The guidelines recommend having technology or documentation in place that provides mechanisms for end users to distinguish outputs by generative AI systems from information output by humans (Evaluation Viewpoint 13). This is due to concerns about the manipulation of information and public opinion through the dissemination of misinformation and deepfakes generated by AI [p.26]. However there are no specific provisions regarding a clear and accessible explanation on any specifics regarding how AI system works nor the terminology used in doing so.

fr1_title: The Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
fr1_justif: The Guidelines emphasize the need for all individuals involved in the procurement of generative AI within each ministry or agency  understanding both the benefits and risks of generative AI and measures for mitigating the risks associated with generative AI [p.10]. It also notes the importance of Identifying and disseminating best practices for the procurement [p.17] checks on procurements [p. 19] and comply with laws regulations and guidelines related to government information systems when procuring generative AI [p.29]. They also recommend utilizing a 'Procurement Check Sheet' to organize the requirements for procuring generative AI systems [pp.36 39].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The guideline does not apply to government information systems handling confidential information related to national security the maintenance of public safety and order as well as information that may potentially become confidential [p. 6].
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element1_justif: The document establishes AI-specific procurement through detailed AI-tailored requirements set out in the 'Procurement Check Sheet' and 'Contract Check Sheet'  [pp.36–39]. They require procurement specifications to address points unique to Gen AI including AI governance of suppliers appropriate input/output and data handling prevention of false or harmful outputs protection of personal data transparency and explainability security and safeguards for public-use cases (e.g. disclosure). Procurement requirements are structured as mandatory “Basic Requirements” and optional requirements and are complemented by contract-level provisions on quality assurance embedding responsible AI considerations directly into procurement practice.
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

fr1_title: The Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
fr1_justif: The Guideline addresses Public Sector Skills Development by requiring systematic training and literacy-building for government staff. It mandates education on responding to information-security incidents and risk cases specific to generative AI systems (Evaluation Viewpoint 4) and requires role-tailored training to ensure appropriate literacy technical knowledge risk awareness and ethics for personnel involved in development and operation of generative AI (Evaluation Viewpoint 5). Guiding Principle 8 further highlights education reskilling and stakeholder support as central components of ensuring AI literacy within the public sector [p.31].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The guideline does not apply to government information systems handling confidential information related to national security the maintenance of public safety and order as well as information that may potentially become confidential [p.6].
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The Guideline mandates several training-related measures but does not form a unified government-wide upskilling strategy nor does it include the judiciary. The Chief AI Officer must conduct trainings to enhance AI literacy among government staff [p.19] and provide sessions on input data and hallucinations [p.34]. It requires education on information-security incidents and generative-AI-specific risk cases (Evaluation Viewpoint 4) and role-specific literacy technical knowledge risk awareness and ethics (Evaluation Viewpoint 5). Guiding Principle 8 highlights AI literacy education reskilling and stakeholder support [p.31].
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The Guideline assigns a dedicated role within each ministry or agency the Chief AI Officer (CAIO) to act as the central authority for AI governance. The CAIO is mandated to promote generative AI utilization monitor systems ensure risk management handle risk cases and conduct trainings to enhance AI literacy among government staff [p.19]. The CAIO also formulates and revises internal rules disseminates the guideline and delivers training sessions on issues such as input data and hallucinations [pp. 33 34]. These responsibilities position the CAIO as an AI champion providing expert guidance and supporting responsible AI innovation across government.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes multiple provisions that support ongoing professional development and continued training. It requires the Chief AI Officer to conduct trainings to enhance AI literacy among government staff and provide updated guidance on issues such as input data and hallucinations [p.19 p.34]. It mandates education and training on responding to information-security incidents and risk cases specific to generative AI (Evaluation Viewpoint 4) and role-tailored training ensuring literacy technical knowledge risk awareness and ethics (Evaluation Viewpoint 5). Guiding Principle 8 further emphasizes education literacy and reskilling [p.31] reinforcing the need for continuous skill development.

fr1_title: AI Guidelines for Business Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
fr1_justif: The Guidelines note that AI use can be viewed as a solution to some social challenges such as decreasing labor caused by a declining birthrate and aging population [p. 2]. Consequently the Guidelines prognose that work tasks will vastly change due to AI and advocates to take the necessary steps to ensure that the persons engaged in AI in each AI business actor acquire AI literacy [pp. 21 23] to discuss actively about education and reskilling to promote new ways of working [p. 21 23] and provide educational opportunities so that various people can acquire a deeper understanding of benefits of AI [p. 21].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: While the guidelines advocate to take the necessary steps to ensure that the persons engaged in AI in each AI business actor acquire AI literacy [pp. 21 23] to discuss actively about education and reskilling to promote new ways of working [p. 21 23] and provide educational opportunities so that various people can acquire a deeper understanding of benefits of AI [p. 21] they do not include any specific establishments of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs but instead keep it vague and open-ended how these 'necessary steps' should look.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
fr1_element3_justif: Among the Common Guiding Principles for AI Business actors involved in advanced AI systems [p. 24] the Guidelines outlines the importance to provide support for the improvement of literacy [p. 25] and to support digital literacy initiatives [p. 32]. Each AI business actor is expected to provide the persons engaged in AI in the AI business actor with the necessary education to gain the knowledge literacy and ethical views to correctly understand and use AI in a socially correct manner [p. 21]. However all of these are just recommendations not actual requirements and they are not intended to mitigate job displacement caused by automation but  rather remedy decreasing labor caused by a declining birthrate and aging population [p. 2].

fr1_title: AI White Paper 2024 New Strategies in Stage II Toward the world's most AI-friendly country (Japan)
fr1_justif: The white paper highlights AI safety and security as central to Japan’s balanced governance approach. It promotes voluntary risk assessment and reduction complemented by minimal regulatory measures for high-risk systems [p.18]. To strengthen safety infrastructure it proposes enhancing the role of the AI Safety Institute (AISI) in evaluation red-teaming and international collaboration [pp.20-21]. Further emphasis is placed on research into AI vulnerabilities and the creation of a secure data environment that fosters responsible innovation [p.21].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: AI Safety Institute (AISI)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The document recommends ensuring AI safety and reliability through evaluation methods with international consistency and the activities of the AI Safety Institute (AISI) including “checking tools and red-teaming test implementation methods” [p.21]. However it does not specify concrete performance thresholds or quantitative quality benchmarks for AI systems. The focus is seemingly more on establishing frameworks and procedures for ongoing assessment rather than defining fixed operational standards.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: While the document notes the importance of addressing systemic risks in critical sectors such as finance medicine and transport where AI malfunctions could have severe impacts [p.16] and recommends that the government review existing laws and regulations in such areas [p.19] t does not explicitly mention safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols as concrete mechanisms to mitigate harm from AI failure aside from the safeguard of clearly indicating whether content has been AI-generated or not [p.19] but this is more a measure against misinformation than failure or unexpected AI behaviour.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The document refers to the need for AI safety evaluation methods and recommends that the AI Safety Institute (AISI) conduct “investigations standards etc. necessary for AI safety assessment including checking tools and red-teaming test implementation methods” [p.21].  However there is no explicit requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation throughout the entire AI system lifecycle. The focus remains on general safety assurance and ongoing evaluation.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: The document explicitly identifies risks of malicious attacks such as data poisoning and cyberattacks as major AI-related threats [p.16] and recommends actions to counter them. It calls for R&D on exploitation of AI vulnerabilities and on technologies to defend against attacks embedding vulnerabilities in AI [p.21]. It also urges cooperation between public and private sectors to strengthen cybersecurity expertise and international collaboration through the AI Safety Institute (AISI) [p.21] thereby introducing clear security-oriented obligations and measures.

fr1_title: AI Guidelines for Business Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
fr1_justif: The guidelines outline the importance that each AI business actor provides stakeholders with information to the reasonable extent necessary In order to ensure verifiability relating to decisions made by AI [pp.18 23]. They also recommend to establish a situation that allows the origin of data and decisions made during the development provision or use of the AI system or service to be traced forward and backward to the extent that is reasonable and technically possible [p.19] and improving explainability and interpretability for relevant stakeholders [pp.19 23].
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The Guidelines state that when developing providing or using an AI system or service based on the social context when the AI system or service is used it is important that each AI business actor provides all stakeholders with information to the reasonable extent necessary and technically possible while ensuring the verifiability of the AI system or service [p.18]. To that end they recommend that in order to ensure verifiability relating to decisions made by AI record or store logs of AI training processes inference processes rationales of decisions made by AI and the like (for example input/output generated when developing and using the AI system or service) to the extent possible based on the data amount or contents [pp.18 23].
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: While the Guidelines provide some specific measures and objectives to entities developing and using AI (AI Developer AI Provider and AI Business User [p.23]) such as ensuring verifiability and improving traceability via  Documentation of system architectures and the like or  Providing relevant stakeholders with information [pp. 18 19 23] these recommendations are meant as general guidance for Businesses involved in AI but are not specifically highlighted for any high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

fr1_title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
fr1_justif: The Strategy addresses AI Literacy in pages 15 to 17 (First Objective: Building Capacities and Developing Jordanian Skills). Mainly in subsections on Raising Awareness Education and Digital Literacy. and the Integration of AI topics into school university and vocational curricula (p. 17).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) National Council for Entrepreneurship and a Steering Committee
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The First Strategic Objective – Building Capacities and Developing Jordanian Skills (pages 15–17) explicitly calls for integrating AI concepts and digital literacy into school university and vocational curricula promoting early exposure to AI education and alignment with future labour-market needs.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy mentions on page 15 'Initiative to develop specialization in artificial intelligence at universities' and the 'Elaboration of professional and technical training programs in the field of artificial intelligence'. It also encourages AI-related programs in universities and technical institutes and partnerships with academia (page 17) .
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

fr1_title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
fr1_justif: The Code of Ethics explicitly integrates access to redress and remedy under Section 5 (Responsibility and Accountability p. 19). It requires all parties developing or operating AI systems to provide affected individuals with simple accessible and prompt complaint mechanisms (point 2) and to address and correct any negative effects or harms caused by AI systems including serious material or moral damage (point 4). These provisions align with non-judicial redress and remedial accountability principles.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: Page 19 (Section 5 points 2 & 4) calls on entities developing or operating AI systems to provide accessible uncomplicated complaint channels for affected individuals and to address and correct harms caused by AI.

fr1_title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
fr1_justif: In the Inclusiveness and Justice section on page 14 the Code emphasizes on 'ensuring the fairness of artificial intelligence techniques and not to be biased discriminated or targeted against any group or component of society''.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The Inclusiveness and Justice section on page 14 explicitly states that it is 'Ensuring respect protection and promotion of diversity inclusiveness and impartiality in all stages of development [...] where bias is the favoritism that results from AI systems due to the use of incomplete erroneous or biased data sets or that results from individuals who design and/or train artificial intelligence systems by creating algorithms that reflect intended cognitive biases or factual biases resulting from social intolerance or institutional discrimination. Bias can enter through: building the system collecting data or preparing a set of data governed by certain features or analyzing or treating it in a discriminatory manner.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: Section Inclusiveness and Justice on page 14 explicitly states 'Working on ensuring the fairness of artificial intelligence techniques and not to be biased discriminated or targeted against any group or component of society'. While the section about Risks on page 29 states against 'Marginalization of some groups and bias towards certain groups at the expense of others or the marketing of some negative extremist and violent ideas'.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: Not entirely but partially since the Code states on page 31 that it is 'Encouraging developers and researchers in the field of artificial intelligence to determine the benefits and risks of dealing with developed systems through the available means as a prototype work that shows how this Code of ethics was used for guidance and the principles contained therein are applied'. It indirectly (or rather broadly) implies it.

fr1_title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
fr1_justif: The National AI Code of Ethics addresses Gender Equality only in a limited and indirect manner. On page 9 the document states that AI systems should ensure inclusiveness and impartiality by avoiding bias linked to specific data categories explicitly including gender alongside race and religion. However the framework does not contain gender-specific objectives measures or implementation mechanisms. As such Gender Equality is acknowledged at the level of bias prevention rather than addressed as a standalone or substantive policy area.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: In the Code of Ethics the Legal Reference explicitly lists fairness and impartiality in AI decision-making 'by focusing on data related to color race religion or gender' alongside transparency and privacy protection. (page 9) Under Inclusiveness and Justice the Code requires AI to be inclusive fair transparent and impartial across all stages of development and use. (page 14) Hence the Code ethically expects prevention of gender bias/discrimination thought it frames these as principles rather than audited sanctionable duties.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
fr1_justif: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) addresses it in the Humanity and Society section on page 13 emphasizing that AI must respect human dignity role and status in society by “not forcing humans to submit to artificial intelligence decisions without granting AI the right of human intervention.” This principle underscores that humans retain ultimate control and decision-making authority over AI systems ensuring accountability and preventing full automation of judgment.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) explicitly promotes meaningful human control. On page 13 it calls for preserving “human dignity role and status… without forcing humans to submit to AI decisions.” On page 28 it cautions against “believing that AI is superior to humans… and relying on it to make decisions absolutely without interpreting outputs in proportion to the circumstances and general context.” However the document does not define critical areas establish mandatory human-in-the-loop requirements or provide procedural safeguards or enforcement mechanisms. Human control is articulated normatively rather than operationalized through concrete measures.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: AI Regulatory Framework for the banking sector (2025) (Jordan)
fr1_justif: The AI Regulatory Framework for the Jordanian Banking Sector (CBJ 2024) mandates banks to conduct AI-specific impact assessments prior to system deployment (Sec. 2.4 & 6.1–6.2). Institutions must evaluate ethical operational and cybersecurity risks document decision-making logic and maintain a centralised AI-incident log. These assessments feed into the CBJ’s supervisory reviews through FinCERT and compliance audits ensuring that AI applications undergo structured risk evaluation human oversight and accountability throughout their lifecycle to prevent harm and ensure transparency.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The framework promotes risk management and risk assessment (p.6 21) and limiting potential risks (p.5).
