'An organization is required to conduct periodic impact assessments of artificial intelligence techniques in proportion to the level of risk arranged for each application to assess privacy risks the likelihood of bias or any deviation from the objectives of intended use' (p.13).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The framework mandates institutions to conduct periodic impact assessments of AI (p. 13): 'in proportion to the level of risk arranged for each application to assess privacy risks the likelihood of bias or any deviation from the objectives of intended use. High-risk artificial intelligence applications should be subject to the reviews of AAC-Kra and Mu-kr to ensure that they are carried out in a responsible and consistent manner'.  Furthermore AI systems should comply with all regulations guidelines frameworks and circulars applying to the sector as well as the data protection law (p.14). However risks for individuals and the society to be mitigated are not listed.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

fr1_title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
fr1_justif: The framework addresses the indicator by explicitly recognising the risk that AI adoption may “lead to the loss of traditional jobs” and proposing mitigation measures such as workforce retraining and rehabilitation (p. 31). It further establishes the principle that AI systems should act as “a complement to the existing workforce not a replacement for it” (p. 7) thereby directly framing AI deployment in relation to labour protection. By acknowledging displacement risks and outlining concrete measures to address them the strategy goes beyond a purely economic focus and aligns with the indicator’s inclusion of protection against job loss due to automation.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) and National Council for Entrepreneurship
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Jordan Artificial Intelligence Policy 2020
fr1_justif: The framework addresses the indicator by explicitly identifying public procurement as a key mechanism for AI adoption stating that “government’s procurement mechanisms are the main drivers to adopt smart solutions in the public sector” and calling for a review of procurement legislation to facilitate this (p. 6). It further outlines concrete priorities for shaping this process including the promotion of open-source solutions and the empowerment of Jordanian entrepreneurs and start-ups as suppliers of AI systems (p. 6).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Ministerial Committee for AI (the Committee)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

fr1_title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
fr1_justif: The Jordan AI Strategy (2023–2027) prioritizes capacity building under its First Objective (pp. 15–18) outlining initiatives to train civil servants through awareness programs technical and professional AI training and the establishment of professional standards. It also highlights education and digital literacy development across levels. Additionally the Third Axis: Data and Skills (p. 29) emphasizes training public sector cadres to enhance performance and innovation.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) National Council for Entrepreneurship and a Steering Committee
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy sets a government-wide framework for upskilling public servants through awareness workshops technical training and education reform (pp. 15–18 29) but does not include the judiciary. It builds foundational understanding of AI’s applications and risks for civil service only not judges or courts.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

fr1_title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
fr1_justif: In the Strategy page 18 (Capacity Building and Upgrading Skills and Competencies) and page 30 (Risk Management). The first explicitly highlights a focus on specialized training programs for graduates and workers to build AI-relevant technical skills (p. 18). While the Risk management requires “modernization and rehabilitation projects to pave the way for employees to change their work area” (p. 30).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) and the National Council for Entrepreneurship
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The  Risk Management (pages 30–31) emphasize preparing the workforce for AI-driven market changes through reskilling and rehabilitation programs and modernization projects to help employees shift work areas. However the Strategy does not specify government funding or subsidies for these programs.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
fr1_justif: The Jordan Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan (2023–2027) addresses AI safety and security mainly under Objective Four: Ensuring a legislative and regulatory environment that supports the safe deployment of AI (page 21) and Risk Management (page 30 & 31). It mandates continuous review of laws to manage risks protect privacy and strengthen public trust. It promotes adherence to the National AI Code of Ethics includes cybersecurity measures and requires safeguards to prevent misuse and ensure reliable explainable and safe AI applications.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) National Council for Entrepreneurship and a Steering Committee
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: Cybersecurity is recognized as a priority sector (pages 22 & 23) and referenced in Risk Management (pages 30–31) which calls for preventing data breaches ensuring privacy and updating cybercrime and cybersecurity laws. However these are broad policy aims not direct obligations for AI developers or operators.

fr1_title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
fr1_justif: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) explicitly addresses Transparency and Explainability across several sections. Page 9 lists Transparency among the key legal references guiding the Code. A full section on Transparency appears on page 18 detailing requirements for clarity explainability and disclosure in AI systems. On page 24 the principles for virtual environments emphasize responsibility transparency and integrity. On page 27 under Ethics of Scientific Research it mandates structural transparency in data flow and results.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) partially addresses this provision. Page 18 (Transparency section) promotes clarity on AI system purpose data sources and explainability requiring disclosure of how systems function and the rationale behind their outcomes to foster trust. However while it emphasizes transparency and user understanding it does not detail mechanisms for continuous disclosure or the full decision-making logic of AI systems.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) (p. 13) states that humans must not be forced to submit to AI decisions without the right to intervene aligning with the spirit of human oversight and contestability. Combined with the Transparency principle (p. 18) it implies a right to question AI outcomes. Yet it does not explicitly grant or operationalize an individual right to receive detailed explanations or the reasoning behind decisions.

fr1_title: Conceptual Framework for the Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in the System of Secondary Technical and Vocational and Post-Secondary Education for 2025–2029
fr1_justif: The Concept treats AI literacy as a foundational competence for both learners and teachers. For learners AI literacy is embedded in formal curricula through Digital Literacy and Informatics covering AI concepts ethics data protection and algorithmic thinking (Chapter 1.2) and conceptualised as a basic skill comparable to reading and writing under Priority 1: Educational Content (Chapter 3.1) including extracurricular programmes and partnerships. Teacher AI literacy is addressed through the development of AI competencies aligned with UNESCO frameworks (Chapter 1.4) and a structured professional development model (Chapter 3.3). Learners’ AI literacy proficiency is formally monitored within the evaluation framework (Chapter 4.3).
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: JSC Taldau designated as the body responsible for coordinating monitoring and evaluation of the Concept (Chapter 42) Ybyray Altynsarin National Academy of Education responsible for methodological support development of the Open Methodological Complex AI ethics guidance and implementation of Priority 5 (Chapters 32 and 35) JSC National Centre for Professional Development rleu (NCPC rleu) responsible for teacher professional development and AI competency training (Chapters 14 and 33)
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The framework includes explicit curriculum reforms across multiple education levels. It mandates the integration of AI-related content into formal curricula through Digital Literacy (introduced from grade 1) and Informatics (Chapter 1.2). For secondary education it details staged age-appropriate AI learning and expansion of subject content (Chapter 1.2; Chapter 3.1 – Priority 1: Educational Content). For tertiary-level pathways it addresses technical and vocational and post-secondary education granting institutions autonomy to embed AI within general basic and professional modules aligned with labour-market needs (Chapter 1.2). These reforms are operationalised through an implementation mechanism and monitored (Chapters 3 and 4).
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The framework mandates inclusion and expansion of AI content in formal curricula (e.g. Digital Literacy and Informatics) and the planned introduction of AI modules ensuring structured AI learning pathways (Chapter 1.2; Chapter 3.1). It further establishes institutional mechanisms and programmes to support AI education including the creation of AI Labs within the national education infrastructure to pilot AI tools and develop teaching resources (Chapter 3.4 – Research and Innovation). In addition it outlines formal teacher training and certification programmes (Chapter 3.3).
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The framework addresses teachers’ AI competencies and training needs (Chapter 1.4 – Digital Competencies of Teachers) and establishes a structured professional development pathway aligned with international standards (Chapter 3.3 – Priority 3: Professional Development of Teachers) including staged training (Acquire–Deepen–Create) certification and continuous learning. It also provides methodological resources through the development of an Open Methodological Complex offering lesson scenarios practical assignments ethical guidance and AI-safe materials (Chapter 3.2 – Priority 2: Methodological Support for Teachers).

fr1_title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
fr1_justif: The Draft Law explicitly addresses the risks of AI-facilitated misinformation and manipulation through synthetic content. Article 1(4) defines “synthetic results of AI systems” as images videos audio text or combinations that imitate people or events that did not occur. Article 17(3) prohibits the creation and use of AI systems that:- Use manipulative methods to distort individual behavior to cause or threaten harm.  - Classify individuals based on behavior or traits for discriminatory purposes. - Generate or distribute content prohibited by Kazakh law. These clauses directly regulate the creation and spread of deceptive AI-generated content and behaviors linked to misinformation and social manipulation.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) only indirectly addresses prevention. Article 17(3) prohibits AI systems that:- Exploit emotional vulnerability to cause harm;- Conduct profiling that could result in discrimination;- Create or distribute synthetic outputs (e.g. text video audio) if their content is prohibited under Kazakhstan law. Article 21(2)–(3) requires synthetic AI results to be marked and accompanied by warnings with responsibility placed on owners/holders.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) contains limited but relevant provisions. Article 17(3)(1) prohibits AI systems that use manipulative methods to distort behaviour or force individuals to make decisions that may cause harm or create a threat of harm which is directly relevant to tech-facilitated violence. Article 18(2) requires owners or holders to take immediate measures including suspension or termination when such risks are identified. Article 7(2) provides procedural safeguards through transparency and objection rights and Articles 8(2) and 24 establish accountability and compensation for harm under existing law.
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
fr1_justif: The Draft Law addresses redress and remedy indirectly. Article 24 provides that harm caused by AI systems shall be compensated in accordance with the Civil Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan establishing a general pathway for redress.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” affirms users’ rights to object to automated processing and request explanations (Articles 7 and 16) and states that AI system owners are legally responsible for harms caused by their systems. Article 24 provides that harm caused by AI systems shall be compensated in accordance with the Civil Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan enabling individuals or groups to seek judicial redress.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

fr1_title: Conceptual Framework for the Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in the System of Secondary Technical and Vocational and Post-Secondary Education for 2025–2029
fr1_justif: The framework embeds children’s rights as a core condition for the use of AI in education. The Mission statement requires AI to be used in the best interests of the learner prioritising the rights of the child and the role of the teacher (Introduction). Chapter 2.1 (Ethical and Legal Principles) establishes the principle of protecting the rights of the child and pedagogical responsibility requiring human oversight in significant decisions safeguarding dignity and safety and guaranteeing the right to appeal. The same chapter mandates privacy and personal data protection and prohibits discrimination ensuring inclusiveness for learners with special educational needs. Chapter 2.2 reinforces children’s autonomy via academic integrity.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: JSC Taldau designated as the body responsible for coordinating monitoring and evaluation of the Concept (Chapter 42) Ybyray Altynsarin National Academy of Education responsible for methodological support development of the Open Methodological Complex AI ethics guidance and implementation of Priority 5 (Chapters 32 and 35) JSC National Centre for Professional Development rleu (NCPC rleu) responsible for teacher professional development and AI competency training (Chapters 14 and 33)
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: While the measures are not child-exclusive in technical detail they are clearly applied to children as the primary rights-holders in educational AI systems. Chapter 2.1 (Ethical and Legal Principles) establishes the principle of legality and personal data protection requiring lawful processing data minimisation limited retention and appropriate security measures for educational data. It also links AI use to enhanced safeguards and human oversight in education contexts. These protections are reinforced by transparency and accountability requirements including clear rules for AI use and oversight (Chapter 2.1) and by monitoring compliance with ethical norms within the Monitoring and Evaluation framework (Chapter 4.2-4.3).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: The document includes general safeguards aimed at preventing harm to children from AI but it does not explicitly address all risks such as targeted advertising or commercial exploitation. Chapter 2.1 (Ethical and Legal Principles) establishes the principle of protecting the rights of the child and pedagogical responsibility requiring human oversight safeguarding learners’ dignity and safety and prohibiting discriminatory or harmful AI use. Chapter 2.2 (Pedagogical Principles) further limits inappropriate use by requiring age-appropriate application academic integrity and ensuring AI does not replace independent thinking. Transparency and mandatory labelling of AI-generated content also reduce risks of manipulation (Chapter 2.1).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: The framework  assigns certain obligations to deployers but it does not comprehensively regulate AI developers in a child-specific design sense. Chapter 2.1 (Ethical and Legal Principles) requires AI systems used in education to comply with fairness non-discrimination transparency data protection and human oversight explicitly linked to protecting the rights of the child. Chapter 2.2 (Pedagogical Principles) mandates age-appropriate use of AI and prohibits replacing learners’ independent thinking placing responsibility on those deploying AI in schools. Also Chapter 2.3 (Technological and Administrative Principles) introduces a risk-based approach and requires that only AI systems listed in a trusted registry may be used in schools.

fr1_title: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence for 2024-2029 (Resolution of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 592 of 24 July 2024)
fr1_justif: The Concept actively promotes cultural and linguistic diversity by prioritizing AI tools that strengthen the Kazakh language. In Section 5 Chapter 2 Direction 4 (Scientific Research and AI Technologies) it mandates the development of the Kazakh Large Language Model (KazLLM) and expansion of Kazakh-language tokens and semantic units. It also supports the multilingual AI translator Tilmas covering Kazakh Russian English Turkish Tatar and Uzbek and the creation of Kazakh text-to-speech technologies ensuring AI systems function across languages and cultural contexts.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: the Ministry of Digital Development Innovation and Aerospace Industry (MDDIAI) Sectoral Council on AI Development and the Committee for AI and Innovation Development within the Ministry of Digital Development Innovation and Aerospace Industry
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The Concept contains explicit measures promoting AI systems that support cultural and linguistic diversity. In Section 5 Chapter 2 Direction 4 (Scientific Research and AI Technologies) it mandates the creation of the Kazakh Large Language Model (KazLLM) to expand AI capabilities in the national language including increasing Kazakh-language tokens and semantic units. It also supports the multilingual AI translator Tilmas (Kazakh Russian English Turkish Tatar Uzbek) and development of Kazakh text-to-speech technologies ensuring AI tools are responsive to diverse languages and cultural contexts.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
fr1_justif: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (September 2025) includes limited but explicit references to environmental impact. Article 8.3 states that the creation and operation of AI systems must account for energy efficiency and aim to reduce negative environmental impact. Article 18.1–2 outlines AI risk management obligations (that could include environmental risks based on Article 8.3) requiring system owners to regularly assess and update risk mitigation measures across the AI lifecycle. While these provisions are general they reflect an emerging legal acknowledgment that AI development must consider sustainability and ecological safety.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (September 2025) addresses environmental concerns but does so only in general terms: Article 8.3 requires that during the development and operation of AI systems actors must ensure energy efficiency and minimize environmental harm. However the law does not explicitly mention the prevention of excessive energy consumption e-waste or regulation of resource-intensive AI models.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
fr1_justif: The draft AI law embeds fairness and non-discrimination as core legal principles. Article 6 (Fairness and Equality) requires that AI systems respect human dignity and rights and prohibits discrimination based on race nationality language religion beliefs or other status. Article 17(3) bans the creation or use of AI systems that classify individuals based on biometric data (e.g. to infer race religion political views) for discriminatory purposes.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (2025) promotes fairness by prohibiting discrimination based on language nationality race religion and other traits (Article 6). Article 4 establishes fairness and equality as a core principle of AI regulation. It also bans AI systems that classify individuals by biometric data for discriminatory purposes as well as systems exploiting vulnerabilities related to age disability or social status (Article 17(3)). Article 10(2) and Article 20 require the use and audit of high-quality lawful and representative datasets indirectly addressing bias risks in AI outputs.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: Article 17(3) expressly prohibits AI systems that classify individuals using biometric data to infer race political views religious affiliation or similar characteristics for discriminatory purposes as well as systems exploiting vulnerabilities linked to age disability or social status. Article 6 (Fairness and Equality) mandates that AI systems be created and operated in a manner that excludes discrimination. Article 10(2) requires the use of high-quality and representative datasets while Article 20 mandates audits assessing data quality and lawfulness helping reduce bias embedded in training data.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

fr1_title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
fr1_justif: Article 6 requires AI systems to respect citizens' rights ensure fairness and equality and prohibit discrimination based on sex and other characteristics. Article 4 lists “fairness and equality” as a core principle of state AI regulation. These provisions establish explicit protections against gender-based bias in AI design and deployment.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: Article 6 of the Draft Law requires that AI systems be developed and used with respect for fairness equality and the rights of citizens explicitly prohibiting discrimination based on sex and other attributes. This directly supports the prevention of gender bias in AI tools and systems.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: The Draft Law assigns general obligations to all entities developing and using AI systems to ensure fairness and equality and to prevent discrimination including on the basis of sex (Article 6). However it does not contain gender-specific responsibilities or enforcement mechanisms uniquely targeting gender equality outcomes.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
fr1_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) strongly emphasizes human oversight. Article 9 states that AI must preserve human autonomy and free will placing human life and rights as the highest value. Article 17 introduces restrictions on fully autonomous AI systems especially those that may manipulate or exploit users without human awareness. Article 21 requires labeling of AI-generated content and prohibits automated decision-making that significantly affects individual rights without compliance with data protection rules. Collectively these provisions ensure that human actors remain in control and informed of AI decisions
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) promotes meaningful human control by prioritizing human autonomy rights and free will in Article 9. Article 17 introduces a classification of AI system autonomy and restricts fully autonomous systems that act without user awareness or outside legal frameworks. These provisions ensure that AI serves human interests and does not override human judgment.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: Article 17 of the Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) classifies AI systems based on their level of autonomy and prohibits the use of fully autonomous systems that make decisions without human awareness or legal basis. While this indirectly covers sensitive sectors the law does not explicitly mention specific domains like law enforcement or medicine.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) does not mandate naming specific individuals but it does assign accountability to system owners and operators. Article 17 outlines restrictions on AI autonomy requiring developers and owners to ensure systems do not operate unlawfully. Article 22 (machine-readable forms) also emphasizes formalized control mechanisms. While not detailing individual responsibility the law partially addresses oversight and accountability by assigning duties to legal entities managing AI systems.

fr1_title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
fr1_justif: The Draft Law addresses impact assessments through a risk-based approach. Article 17 defines categories of AI systems by degree of risk (low medium high) and autonomy. Article 18 establishes a formal risk management process requiring owners/operators to identify analyze and mitigate both intended and unintended risks throughout the AI system’s lifecycle. This includes annual risk updates and mandatory suspension if prohibited risks are detected. Article 15(2)(3) requires documentation of the system depending on its level of impact on safety rights and public order. Article 20 mandates audits including evaluating data quality and illegal functionalities. These provisions functionally amount to a mandatory impact assessment.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) includes provisions that encourage proactive risk management but does not fully address societal ethical and environmental impacts in all aspects. Article 17 categorizes AI systems by risk levels (low medium high) and Article 18 mandates a risk assessment for all systems particularly high-risk AI. This implies evaluation of safety reliability and societal risks before deployment. However the law does not explicitly require evaluations of ethical or environmental impacts as part of the risk assessment.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) requires AI system owners and operators to assess risks but it does not explicitly mandate comprehensive Impact Assessments. Article 17 classifies AI systems by their risk level (low medium high) and requires the identification and management of risks associated with their use but it focuses primarily on technical and safety risks.  Article 18 mandates the risk assessment for both intended and unintended uses of AI systems requiring owners to take action to mitigate any foreseeable risks. However the law does not explicitly mention conducting comprehensive impact assessments.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) provides some transparency and accountability measures but does not explicitly grant the public the right to access the findings of impact assessments. Article 7 ensures that users are informed about automated decision-making including the ability to seek explanations of AI system outcomes which promotes transparency and accountability. Article 21 requires that AI-generated content (e.g. synthetic outputs) be labeled and Article 18 ensures that high-risk systems are documented for compliance with transparency and safety standards.

fr1_title: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence for 2024-2029 (Resolution of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 592 of 24 July 2024)
fr1_justif: The Concept addresses AI-related reskilling and upskilling in Section 5 Chapter 2 (Approaches) Direction 3: Human Capital. It mandates implementing reskilling and upskilling programs mentorship for AI instructors and allocating 15% of Tech Orda vouchers for AI training (Direction 3 item 1). It also provides for integration of AI modules into higher and vocational education and creation of regional competence centers to train 25000 specialists (Direction 3 items 1-4). Workforce forecasting is revised to align training with AI-driven labour needs (Direction 3 item 3).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: the Ministry of Digital Development Innovation and Aerospace Industry (MDDIAI) Sectoral Council on AI Development and the Committee for AI and Innovation Development within the Ministry of Digital Development Innovation and Aerospace Industry
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The AI Concept 2024–2029 includes explicit measures for government-supported reskilling and upskilling in response to AI-driven labour market demands. In Section 5 Chapter 2 (Approaches) Direction 3: Human Capital it mandates: Reskilling and upskilling programs funded through national initiatives; Allocation of 15% of Tech Orda vouchers specifically for AI training (Direction 3 item 1); Creation of regional competence centers to train specialists (Direction 3 items 1-4); Integration of AI modules into education to develop workforce skills.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: The AI Concept 2024–2029 includes financial support elements but they apply to specific groups rather than all workers. In Section 5 Chapter 2 (Approaches) Direction 3: Human Capital the Concept directs that 15% of Tech Orda vouchers be allocated to AI training in private schools - this is a government subsidy supporting reskilling. 'The Tech Orda program provides government-funded grants of up to 600000 KZT for citizens aged 18–45 to study at private IT schools.' (Direction 3: Human Capital).  It also mandates the creation of competence centers and public AI courses but the document does not specify direct financial incentives for individual workers beyond these voucher-based supports.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
fr1_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” includes detailed provisions to ensure the safety and security of AI systems.  Article 10 requires AI operators to implement protective measures against unauthorized access system misuse and data breaches. Article 17(3) prohibits the use of AI systems that can lead to mass violation of human rights such as covert surveillance emotion detection or social profiling without consent.  Article 18 requires AI system owners to conduct risk assessments document their systems and ensure the reliability of high-risk AI applications. The law mandates immediate suspension of AI systems if they pose foreseeable harm and outlines criteria for classifying systems as critical infrastructure.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) requires developers and owners of AI systems to ensure accuracy reliability and safety especially for high-risk systems (Article 18). It mandates documentation of system functionality and risk levels and obliges operators to prevent malfunctions and unauthorized access (Article 10). However the law does not define specific quantitative performance thresholds or technical benchmarks such as accuracy percentages or error tolerances which would qualify as explicit quality standards.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) includes explicit safeguards and emergency measures to mitigate harm from AI system failure or unexpected behavior. Article 11(1)–(3) requires AI systems to be created and operated safely exclude misuse and obliges owners and holders to conduct risk management to eliminate potential threats. Article 18(1) establishes continuous risk management throughout the AI system lifecycle including identification of foreseeable risks and predictable misuse. Crucially Article 18(2) requires immediate measures including suspension or full termination of an AI system where risks related to prohibited harmful functionalities under Article 17(3) are identified.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) includes documentation and assessment obligations that directly support technical robustness across the AI lifecycle. Article 15(2)(3) requires owners and holders to maintain documentation on AI systems proportionate to their impact on safety rights and public order. Article 18(1) establishes continuous risk management throughout the lifecycle including identification and assessment of foreseeable risks and predictable misuse. Article 20 requires audits of AI systems including assessment of data quality and the absence of prohibited functionalities. Together these provisions address lifecycle robustness.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) includes explicit security obligations for AI system operators. Article 10 requires developers and users to implement measures preventing unauthorized access data breaches and illegal storage or processing of personal data. Article 18 mandates the management of foreseeable risks including technical and operational threats that may lead to harm.

fr1_title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
fr1_justif: The Draft Law embeds “transparency and explainability”  among the foundational principles of state regulation in the AI domain (Article 4). Article 7 mandates that users receive full information on the operational characteristics and limitations of AI systems and grants individuals subject to automated decisions the right to be informed to object and to seek protection. Article 21 requires that  -Users be informed when goods or services are produced using AI systems. Synthetic results (e.g. AI-generated content) must be labeled in machine-readable form. Article 22 adds that legal information must be encoded to support automated recognition.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: Article 4 establishes transparency and explainability as a fundamental principle of AI regulation. Article 7 requires that users be informed about the operational characteristics and limitations of AI systems. Article 16(4-5) entitles users to receive explanations regarding AI-generated outcomes affecting their rights and to request information about the data on which decisions were based. Article 21 mandates disclosure when goods or services are produced using AI systems and requires clear labeling of synthetic AI-generated content and Article 22 ensures that machine-readable formats support transparency of legally significant data.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) assigns obligations to AI providers to inform users about the functioning and consequences of AI systems (Article 7). However it does not explicitly require context-specific explanations nor does it define what constitutes a “meaningful explanation.”
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: Article 7 of the Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) grants individuals the right to be informed about the consequences of AI-based decisions affecting them and to seek protection of their rights. However it does not fully articulate a right to receive a detailed explanation of the decision-making process or the key factors that influenced the outcome.

fr1_justif: Sections 57–66 of Kenya’s Data Protection Act establish enforcement and redress mechanisms. fr1_title: Concept: Digital Transformation of the Kyrgyz Republic for 2024-2028
fr1_justif: The Concept promotes AI literacy primarily through education and capacity-building initiatives. Chapter 2 §5 “Artificial Intelligence” (p.7) outlines measures to introduce AI training programs in higher education institutions covering AI machine learning neural networks and big data. In particular training of the following specialties: Data Scientist Data Engineer AI Architect DataArchitect AI Project Manager. The document also establishes a National Council for AI Development tasked with popularising AI and involving schoolchildren and students in the process of AI learning and teaching AI technologies (p.7). The Action Plan (Task No.12) operationalises these commitments through concrete measures related to AI education.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Council for AI Development
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The Concept includes curriculum-related measures but coverage is uneven across education levels. It provides explicit provisions for higher education calling for the introduction of training programmes in universities in areas such as artificial intelligence machine learning neural networks and big data (§5 “Artificial Intelligence”). At earlier levels the document refers more generally to the development of digital skills through a digital education platform and training initiatives for the population including students (pp. 12–13) but does not explicitly mention AI-specific curriculum reforms at primary or secondary levels.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The document explicitly provides for the establishment of AI-related programs within formal higher education institutions. It calls for the introduction of training programs in universities in fields such as AI machine and deep learning neural networks and big data and specifies new AI-related specialties including Data Scientist Data Engineer AI Architect and AI Project Manager (§5 Artificial Intelligence p.18). While it focuses mainly on tertiary education references to education at the school level relate primarily to digital education systems and general digital literacy rather than to AI-specific learning content (pp.13–14).
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: It provides for a unified register of teachers and educators which includes information on their professional development and digital competence (p.13–14) and aims to improve teachers’ digital skills through digital education platforms. However while it highlights digital and data literacy training it does not yet specify structured AI-specific teacher training programs or dedicated teaching resources for AI education (§5 Artificial Intelligence).

fr1_title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
fr1_justif: The Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (2024) ensures Access to Redress and Remedy in AI through several provisions. Article 84 grants individuals the right to object to automated decision-making and to appeal such processing to a regulator or court. Articles 67 119 162 and 170 establish complaint and dispute mechanisms for digital services while Article 90 designates the State Agency for Personal Data Protection as the complaint-handling authority. Articles 194–196 outline developer and operator liability for AI-related harm.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (2024) includes provisions reinforcing judicial mechanisms for remedy in cases involving AI systems. Article 84 grants individuals the right to appeal automated decision-making including AI-based processing before a regulator or court. Articles 67 119 162 and 170 further establish judicial and administrative review procedures for digital rights violations. These collectively ensure access to judicial remedy for harms caused by AI or automated systems.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: The Digital Code  includes provisions for state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms. Articles 90 119 162 170 and 190 establish the role of sectoral regulators (e.g. in personal data telecom and the national digital ecosystem) to handle complaints and disputes including those involving AI systems. These regulators act as non-judicial bodies empowered to investigate issue binding decisions and ensure redress for digital and AI-related grievances.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: Articles 119 and 196 require digital service providers and users of high-risk AI systems to ensure mechanisms for handling complaints halting harmful AI use and informing affected individuals. These obligations function as grievance and redress mechanisms at the company or developer level ensuring accountability and protection for individuals harmed by AI systems.

fr1_title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
fr1_justif: The Digital Code addresses children’s rights in the digital environment including AI systems through Article 81 “Peculiarities of processing children’s personal data.” (p.56). It establishes safeguards for lawful processing of children’s data requiring that it be in the child’s interest and subject to protection of fundamental rights and freedoms. Processing is only permitted under specific legal grounds or with consent of a legal representative while children aged 14+ may give consent themselves. It also mandates child-accessible language for consent requests and obliges controllers to prevent unlawful processing.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The Digital Code (Art. 81) includes explicit provisions on the protection of children’s personal data and privacy. It restricts processing of children’s data to specific lawful grounds (e.g. vital interests healthcare justice public health security research) and requires parental or guardian consent when no other legal basis exists. It also mandates clear accessible language for children’s consent and obliges data controllers to prevent unlawful processing directly safeguarding children in digital/AI-related environments.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: The Digital Code (Art. 81) provides safeguards for the processing of children’s personal data requiring that it be in the child’s interest with special protections and parental/guardian consent where necessary. These measures indirectly prevent potential misuse of AI systems to exploit or manipulate children’s data. However the Code does not explicitly address risks such as targeted advertising algorithmic manipulation or exposure to inappropriate content. Thus it covers protection of data but not the full scope of AI-related harms.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: Art. 81 assigns obligations to all data controllers (“owners of records”) to ensure children’s personal data is processed only under strict conditions with safeguards to protect rights and freedoms and with parental consent where required. It also requires information and consent requests to be presented in clear accessible language for children. However the Code does not explicitly impose obligations on AI system developers or deployers to ensure systems are safe age-appropriate or beneficial for children.

fr1_title: Program Development of the state language and improvement of language policy in the Kyrgyz Republic for 2021–2025
fr1_justif: The Programme addresses cultural and linguistic diversity in connection with AI by promoting the digitalization of the Kyrgyz language through AI-based tools. On p.4 it links language dissemination to the “Digital Kyrgyzstan 2019–2023” strategy calling for automated systems and AI-powered applications. Chapter 5. Digitalization of the State Language (p.29 sections 8.3–8.4) further details the development of AI translation products to and from Kyrgyz and the creation of infrastructure for their dissemination supporting the preservation and wider use of the state language in digital spaces.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: The National Commission on the State Language under the President of the Kyrgyz Republic
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The Programme promotes the use of AI for the development and expansion of the Kyrgyz language in the digital space but does not extend its scope to a wide range of cultures and languages. On p.4 it states that automated systems and software operating on AI principles will be developed to expand the Kyrgyz language on the Internet. In Chapter 5 Digitalization of the State Language (pp. 8–9) tasks include developing an AI-based translation tool for Kyrgyz to and from other languages and creating technical infrastructure to support Kyrgyz-language AI products. These provisions address linguistic diversity with a strong emphasis on Kyrgyz but they do not explicitly cover cultural pluralism or responsiveness to multiple cultural contexts.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
fr1_justif: The Digital Code addresses Environmental Impact in the context of AI by identifying the environment as a protected good potentially affected by AI systems in Article 1(41). Then Article 192 explicitly includes the environment among protected goods requiring AI developers and users to minimize risks of environmental harm and ensure accountability. Article 193 mandates risk assessment for all AI systems including impacts on the environment. Article 171 also ties digital systems regulation to preventing harm to the environment.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
fr1_justif: The Digital Code establish foundational fairness and non-discrimination principles that apply across all digital technologies including AI systems. Article 3 establishes fairness and proportionality principles and prioritizes individual interests. Article 41 guarantees non-discrimination principle in digital identification ensuring equal rights regardless of identification status. Article 113 prohibits discrimination in digital services based on gender race language disability ethnicity religion or other status. Article 176 promotes equal competition among telecom operators.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The Digital Code includes provisions that indirectly promote fairness in AI outcomes. Article 124(4)(4) mandates methods for checking data samples for bias while Article 191–193 require AI systems to ensure accuracy explainability and minimize risks to protected goods (life rights equality). It also guarantees equal and non-discriminatory access to digital services (Article 5). However it lacks explicit fairness metrics or auditing mechanisms for AI.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The Code contains multiple provisions (Articles 71–72 83–84 113(6)) that explicitly prohibit discriminatory data processing based on different grounds and provide redress mechanisms thereby helping prevent AI systems from amplifying societal bias.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

fr1_title: National Strategy of the Kyrgyz Republic to achieve Gender Equality by 2030
fr1_justif: The National Gender Equality Strategy 2030 of Kyrgyzstan explicitly links gender equality with AI (section 5.7. pp. 40-41) which mandates training-of-trainers on new academic standards and subjects including artificial intelligence cybersecurity and neural networks alongside the development of training modules and video lessons. This aims to strengthen women’s participation in STEM and reduce gender gaps in emerging technologies.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Labor Social Security and Migration of the Kyrgyz Republic
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
fr1_element3_justif: It promotes women’s participation in STEM and AI-related fields. Section 5.7 (pp. 40–41) mandates training modules and video lessons on AI cybersecurity and related subjects for students at KSTU and OshTU targeting increased access for girls and women. Earlier sections also highlight the need to reduce gender gaps in education and technology sectors (pp. 15 section 1.4. - p. 28) and to boost women’s representation in the technology field workforce.

fr1_title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
fr1_justif: The Digital Code addresses Human Oversight and Determination through explicit provisions: Article 57(2) grants the right to human oversight of automated decisions; Article 122(1) mandates that health-related decisions be made only by humans. And Chapter 23: Artificial Intelligence Systems: Article 191(4) introduces the principle of effective human control requiring human oversight in AI use; Article 192(3) assigns responsibility to AI owners for preventing harm; Article 196(1)(3) obliges users of high-risk AI to ensure effective control of system operation.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: Article 191(4) establishes the principle of effective human control requiring that AI use remains under human oversight. Article 122(1) mandates that critical areas such as health-related decisions be made only by humans ensuring human judgment in critical areas. Articles 192–196 further require risk management accountability and continuous human supervision of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifecycle.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (2025) includes explicit provisions preventing full automation in sensitive sectors. Article 122(1) states that decisions concerning an individual’s health including diagnosis can only be made by humans (principle of human decision-making). This establishes a clear prohibition of full automation in the medical field and sets a precedent for similar human oversight in other high-risk areas.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The Digital Code assigns explicit obligations for human accountability in AI use. Article 192(3) requires AI owners and users to take all necessary measures to minimize risks and bear responsibility for any harm caused. Article 196(1)(3) mandates users of high-risk AI systems to ensure effective human control and designate individuals responsible for such oversight. These provisions ensure identifiable human responsibility and intervention authority over AI decisions.

fr1_title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
fr1_justif: The Digital Code addresses AI-related Impact Assessments through two mechanisms. Article 82 establishes requirements for impact assessments on personal data protection prior to automated decision-making or large-scale data processing including risk management and stakeholder consultation. Article 193 introduces a hazard assessment for AI systems mandating evaluation of potential risks to protected interests at design deployment and modification stages aligned with global practices.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The Digital Code promotes proactive risk management by requiring AI system owners to conduct a hazard assessment before deployment as outlined in Article 193. This assessment evaluates potential risks that AI systems may pose to protected societal interests and must be performed at design implementation and modification stages following global best practices.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: Article 193 of the Digital Code assigns clear obligations to AI system owners to conduct hazard assessments at key stages - during design before deployment and after significant changes. These assessments must identify and mitigate risks AI systems may pose to protected interests aligning with the principle of proactive risk management and societal protection. In the Code 'hazard' refers to the risk of harm that an AI system may cause to protected interests which include life and health rights and freedoms the environment defense capability national security and public order (Art. 193(1) Art. 192(1)). Assessments must identify and mitigate such risks and be published openly.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: Article 193(4) of the Digital Code (2025) mandates that the results and methodology of AI system hazard assessments be published on the owner’s website in a clear and understandable form and as open data. This provision ensures public access to assessment findings enabling transparency and accountability regarding the societal impacts of AI systems.
