fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: It introduces a User Rights Framework allowing individuals to request explanations of AI-driven decisions and dispute them if necessary and proposes product liability standards clarifying responsibility when AI systems cause harm (Sec.5.1 5.2 p. 23–26). Additionally public input mechanisms and feedback systems allow stakeholders to raise concerns about AI deployment (pp. 23 5.6.5. Feedback Mechanisms).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: It establishes an AI governance structure including a national regulator responsible for overseeing AI development and implementation (Sec. 5.6.1 5.6.5. pp. 25–26). It also introduces a User Rights Framework allowing individuals to request explanations and dispute AI-driven decisions and provides feedback and public input mechanisms through which users and stakeholders can raise concerns about AI deployment (Sec. 5.6.1 5.6.5. pp. 17 23–26). However it does not clearly establish a dedicated non-judicial complaint body or formal grievance resolution procedure for AI-related harms.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

fr1_title: Child Online Protection Guidelines (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: The framework addresses children rights in the digital environment which explicitly includes AI automated systems and algorithms (p.3). The guidelines describe children online rights (p. 4) child online obligations (p.5)obligations of mobile and internet service providers (p. 6) obligations of content service providers (p. 7) what children need to know to be safe online (p. 7) and duties and tips for parents (p.8-9).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: P.4: Right to Privacy and data protection. 'Children have a right to private and family life in the digital environment. Children’s personal data must be protected and processed lawfully for specific purposes and with clear consent of the children and/or their parents or guardians'. AI is not mentioned but it is covered in the definition of the digital environment (p.3).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: The guidelines recommend to 'use scanning and filtering technology to ensure child user safety and users are not exposed to inappropriate content' (p.6). Also the content service provider should restrict 'access of children to harmful or inappropriate content through adopting measures such as age-verification age classification of content etc (p.7). However targeted advertising is not mentioned.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: As the framework implements the ITU Guidelines on Child Online Protection 2020 it provides for obligations of content service providers. Those include parental consent for using children information integrating child rights considerations into all appropriate corporate policies processes on how cases of child online abuses are reported and handled create a safer and age-appropriate online environment by restricting access of children to harmful or inappropriate content through adopting measures such as age-verification age classification of content (p. 7). However the design of AI systems is not mentioned.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: The plan supports cultural/linguistic diversity mainly through inclusion and accessibility measures: it proposes “Localized Training” to “develop content in local languages” (Implementation Plan—Training 7.2 p.36–37) and targets “underrepresented communities” in “Public Awareness Campaigns” (2.3 p.38). It also sets core ethics values (fairness non-discrimination inclusivity) that help counter exclusion in AI governance (Guidelines p.54; Guiding Principles p.13–14).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: Partially: it supports linguistic accessibility through “develop content in local languages” (Training 7.2 p.36–37) and emphasizes inclusivity/non-discrimination (Guiding Principles p.13–14; Ethics Guidelines p.54). However it does not set explicit technical requirements that AI systems be culturally/linguistically representative (e.g. dataset coverage or localization standards for deployed models).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: Partially: it commits to addressing bias and discrimination (Guiding Principles 5.4.2.1–2.4 p.13–14) and includes “Bias Mitigation Programs… to prevent discrimination and promote equity” (Policy statements p.17; Implementation measures p.59–60). But it does not specifically mention cultural stereotyping cultural erasure or linguistic dominance as distinct risks.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: The plan ties AI growth to sustainability via infrastructure measures. Under Objective 4 (“Building and providing AI infrastructure”) it requires local data centres to “meet international energy efficiency standards to minimize environmental impact” and references AI in sustainability as an emerging focus area. These are cross-cutting prescriptions rather than sector-specific rules.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: Mentions minimizing environmental impact via data-centre energy-efficiency standards but no specific limits on model training energy/e-waste.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
fr1_element3_justif: Calls for meeting “international energy efficiency standards” for data centres; renewables and specific cooling technologies are not detailed.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: The draft embeds fairness non-discrimination and inclusion as core principles (Guiding Principles p.14). It operationalizes these via Ethical Oversight Committees to monitor deployments (Objective 6 p.16) Regular audits and reporting on safety/ethics (p.17) and Bias-mitigation programs to identify and reduce discriminatory outcomes (p.17). It also creates Public Input Mechanisms so affected groups can raise concerns about unfair impacts (p.17). Together these provisions target fairness throughout design deployment and oversight.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Core values include fairness and non-discrimination; bias-mitigation programs and fairness-inclusive audits operationalize this (pp. 13 17 23).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The draft sets out Bias Mitigation Programs defining bias-handling standards mandating bias audits for fairness/equity and providing tools and training (pp. 17 60). It also requires regular audits with criteria that include fairness and provides regulatory oversight/enforcement (pp. 58–59). Ethical Oversight Committees monitor deployments with focus on fairness accountability transparency (p. 56) and risk-assessment standards for high-risk systems explicitly include bias detection (p. 57).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The draft assigns lifecycle duties to developers/deployers to surface and reduce bias. It (i) sets core principles incl. fairness and non-discrimination that bind organizational practice (p.54) (ii) requires risk-assessment standards with bias detection before deployment (p.57) (iii) mandates regular audits with criteria covering fairness plus periodicity and transparent reporting (pp.58–59) and (iv) establishes bias-mitigation programs with bias audits tools and training (p.60).

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: The document addresses human oversight through safety and risk-management provisions. Under AI Safety Protocols (Sec.2.1-2.2 pp. 56–57) it mandates risk assessment and mitigation protocols for high-risk AI systems including scenario testing stress testing and fail-safe mechanisms before deployment. It also requires human-in-the-loop safeguards explainability features and real-time monitoring allowing human intervention when systems fail or produce harmful outcomes (Sec. 3.1-3.2 p. 57). Additionally the Compendium of International Best Practices (p. 69) emphasizes transparency and explainability in AI decision-making to ensure accountability.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The document promotes human oversight in high-risk AI systems through safety and risk-management provisions. Under Section 3. AI Safety Protocols it requires safeguards such as human-in-the-loop mechanisms explainability features and real-time monitoring enabling human intervention when systems fail or produce harmful outcomes (pp. 56–57). It also promotes transparency and explainability as part of responsible AI governance (p. 69).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The document recognizes sensitive sectors and requires safeguards for high-risk AI systems. Under Section 3. AI Safety Protocols it mandates risk assessment and mitigation measures for AI used in sectors such as healthcare finance and public safety including human-in-the-loop mechanisms explainability features and real-time monitoring to enable human intervention (pp. 56–57). However it does not explicitly state that full automation is prohibited or prevented in those sectors. It only encourages oversight and intervention.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: Impact/risk assessment is operationalised through mandatory risk assessment + documentation before deployment and ongoing audits. In 6.2 “AI Safety Protocols” (p.57) the plan sets risk assessment standards (bias data security reliability) and requires scenario/stress testing + fail-safes for high-risk AI. It also mandates human-in-the-loop explainability and real-time monitoring (p.57). 6.2 “Regular Audits and Reporting” (pp.58–59) adds periodic audits transparent reporting and regulator oversight.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The plan requires pre-deployment risk assessment + documentation and sets technical/ethical risk standards. In 6.2 “AI Safety Protocols” (p.57) it mandates standardized risk protocols (bias data security reliability) plus scenario/stress testing for high-risk AI. However it does not clearly require a comprehensive assessment of societal ethical and environmental impacts as a single integrated “impact assessment” before every deployment.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: Obligations are created through required risk documentation and compliance mechanisms. 6.2 “AI Safety Protocols” (p.57) calls for legal requirements for risk assessments and documentation before deployment and introduces penalties/suspension for non-compliance. Ongoing duties are reinforced in 6.2 “Regular Audits and Reporting” (pp.58–59) requiring periodic audits reporting templates independent auditors and regulatory oversight—supporting identification and mitigation of risks to individuals and society.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: Transparency provisions exist but an explicit public right of access is not clearly codified. In 6.2 “Regular Audits and Reporting” (p.58) the plan requires transparent reporting and states that key results should be accessible to stakeholders and regulators. In 6.2 “Ethical Oversight Committees” (p.56) it also proposes publishing reports/findings to maintain public trust. However it does not clearly establish a legal right for the public to obtain full assessment findings on demand.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: The plan underscores “Building AI capacity … across the public sector and society” as a key focus with training programs education support and awareness campaigns (p.7). fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: The document promotes AI-related reskilling and upskilling initiatives to help the workforce adapt to AI-driven economic changes. It proposes technical training and vocational programs that teach workers how to use AI tools develop data analysis and machine learning skills and transition into new AI-related roles (pp. 33–34 “Technical Training Programs”). The policy also includes skill gap assessments and role-specific training modules to address industry needs. Additionally it sets targets for participants in reskilling and upskilling programs (see table point 7 p. 64) and recommends strategies to mitigate automation impacts through workforce training and social protections (p. 70 Sec. 8).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes provisions for government-supported reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to AI-driven labor market changes. It proposes technical training and vocational programs aimed at teaching workers how to use AI tools and transition into new roles created by AI (pp. 33–34 “Technical Training Programs”). These initiatives involve public institutions such as MICSTI the Ministry of Education and Training the AI regulator and the AI policy maker (p. 33). The policy also establishes targets for participants in reskilling and upskilling programs to support workforce adaptation (p. 64) and highlights strategies to mitigate the socio-economic impacts of AI through workforce training (p. 70).
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes recommendations aimed at mitigating workforce disruption caused by AI by promoting training and development programs for workers affected by automation. It proposes technical training and vocational upskilling programs to help workers adapt to AI-driven changes in the labor market and acquire skills such as AI operation data analysis and working with AI-powered systems (pp. 33–34 “Technical Training Programs”). These programs include upskilling for existing roles and reskilling for new AI-related jobs such as AI system monitoring (p. 34). The policy also calls for strategies to address the socio-economic impacts of AI through workforce reskilling and upskilling initiatives (p. 70 Sec. 8).

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: Under Guiding Principles – Safety and Reliability it states that AI systems should be safe reliable and operate as intended and that risks and unintended consequences should be prevented (p. 13 Sec. 5.4 1.1–1.2). It proposes security and misuse prevention measures including preventing AI use in terrorism cyberattacks phishing and harmful surveillance and establishing mechanisms to identify and mitigate AI-related threats (p. 14 Sec. 6.1–6.2). The policy also mandates safety protocols human-in-the-loop safeguards monitoring audits and regulatory oversight to ensure safe deployment and compliance (pp. 57–59).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The document promotes the reliability and safe functioning of AI systems but does not establish explicit quantitative performance thresholds or benchmarks. The Guiding Principles state that AI systems should be safe reliable and operate as intended and should avoid unintended harm (p. 13 Sec. 5.4 1.1–1.2). It also encourages research and standards to reduce risks from advanced AI (p. 13 Sec. 5.4 1.3). Additionally the policy recommends audits monitoring and evaluation of AI system performance and safety (pp. 57–59). However specific measurable accuracy or performance benchmarks are not defined so the criterion is only partially addressed.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The document includes safeguards and mitigation measures to address potential AI system failures or harmful outcomes. It recommends human-in-the-loop mechanisms real-time monitoring and system design that minimizes harm and enables quick intervention in case of failures (pp. 57–58 “Mandate Mitigation Measures” Sec. 3.1–3.2). It also requires risk assessments before deployment and regulatory compliance mechanisms to prevent unsafe systems from being deployed (p. 57 Sec. 4.1). In addition regular audits monitoring and regulatory oversight are proposed to detect risks and ensure corrective actions (pp. 58–59 “Regular Audits and Reporting”). These provisions function as safeguards and response mechanisms for AI risks.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes measures requiring evaluation and documentation before AI systems are deployed. It proposes legal requirements for risk assessments and documentation prior to deployment to ensure compliance and safety (p. 57 Sec. 4.1 “Enforce Regulatory Compliance”). The policy also recommends monitoring auditing and reporting on AI system performance safety and compliance throughout operation (pp. 58–59 “Regular Audits and Reporting”). These provisions support pre-deployment validation and ongoing oversight across the AI lifecycle contributing to technical robustness and accountability.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: The document addresses security risks related to AI misuse but does not establish detailed technical security obligations specifically for protecting AI systems from cyberattacks or adversarial manipulation. It calls for preventing the harmful or illegal use of AI including cyberattacks phishing and other security threats (p. 14 Sec. 6.1–6.2 “Security and Prevention of Misuse”). The policy also promotes monitoring safeguards and regulatory oversight mechanisms to mitigate risks associated with AI technologies (pp. 57–59). However it does not define specific cybersecurity requirements or adversarial robustness measures for AI systems so the criterion is only partially addressed.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (Second Draft) (Lesotho)
fr1_justif: The draft embeds transparency/explainability as core principles (e.g. clear purpose traceability) in the Guiding Principles (pp. 11–12). It requires organizations to document system purpose data sources and decision logic keep audit trails undergo regular/independent audits and publish monitoring reports (Audit/Monitoring & Reporting Standards pp. 18–20). It also creates Feedback & Public Input Mechanisms so people can query/contest AI decisions and receive meaningful explanations (pp. 33–36). High-risk uses face enhanced disclosure and oversight (pp. 19–20).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The draft promotes clarity by requiring transparency/explainability in the Guiding Principles - systems must state their purpose document data sources/provenance and make decision logic traceable (pp. 11–12). The Audit/Monitoring & Reporting Standards mandate documentation audit trails regular/independent audits and public reporting reinforcing clarity of how systems operate (pp. 18–20). Feedback & Public Input Mechanisms let affected people query decisions and obtain meaningful explanations (pp. 33–36).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The draft establishes an individual right to an explanation for consequential AI decisions. The Transparency & Explainability principle requires disclosures of system purpose data sources and decision logic “in understandable terms” (p.27). Audit/Monitoring & Reporting Standards require record-keeping and explainability for high-risk AI to support user inquiries (pp.31–33). Feedback & Public Input Mechanisms and the Regulator’s dispute-resolution channel provide routes to request and receive explanations (pp.34–35; 25–26).

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence National Policy (Libya)
fr1_justif: The National AI Policy mentions the need to adjust curricula to adapt to the pace of new technology development 'adapt education in Libya to ensure that young students acquire modern science technology engineering and mathematics skills by developing a long-term action plan to modernise and develop primary and secondary education' and 'building the capacities of teachers in the context of AI' (p.12).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Council/Authority (exact name to be determined) in accordance with decision issued by the Council of Ministers
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The policy explicitly states that the Ministry of Education should modernize education and adjust school curricula to reflect the AI and digital era. It also emphasizes developing a long-term action plan to modernise and develop primary and secondary education (p.12). Furthermore it states that 'the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research should develop an action plan to amend university curricula and higher education programmes to ensure greater focus on emerging technologies including artificial intelligence' (p.12). All levels of education are thus included in curricula adjustment and modernization.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The framework states that 'work must be done to build effective teacher capabilities for the student in addition to attracting the necessary competencies and training and guiding them on how to deliver artificial intelligence programs when needed' (p.12). However it does not specify the scope duration certification or mandatory nature of teacher training nor does it detail teaching materials or institutionalized professional development programs. For indicator purposes this qualifies as affirmative but early-stage support for teacher training rather than a fully developed teacher AI education framework.

fr1_title: National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (Libya)
fr1_justif: The charter assigns accountability to developers and deployers for ensuring transparency oversight and responsiveness to user harm. It states that 'Responsibility for the ethical implications of the use of artificial intelligence technologies lies with all those involved in the development and dissemination of these technologies and the legislative bodies must establish laws and mechanisms that guarantee the right of individuals and society to sue to hold accountable and to challenge the decisions of artificial intelligence.Compensation laws must be clear when damage is caused by AI decisions including liability for bias violation of privacy or negative impacts on employment' (p.7).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: While remedy is not directly addressed it is stated that 'the legislative bodies must establish laws and mechanisms that guarantee the right of individuals and society to sue to hold accountable and to challenge the decisions of artificial intelligence.Compensation laws must be clear when damage is caused by AI decisions including liability for bias violation of privacy or negativeimpacts on employment' (p.7).
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

fr1_title: National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (Libya)
fr1_justif: Equity and Fairness Section in the National Charter on page 7 (Arabic Version) of the document highlights the connection between AI and Child protection non-discrimination and accountability. 'Applications must limit discrimination based on race gender age disability wealth or political opinion.' (p. 6 in the translated document). In addition: 'The use of artificial intelligence systems by children minors with special needs or limited technical capabilities must It also states that the use of artificial intelligence systems by children minors persons with special needs or those with limited technical abilities must be carefully considered with the necessary measures put in place to protect them and ensure that they are not harmed.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: The Charter contains a broad obligation to protect children minors and vulnerable users from harm when interacting with AI systems (p. 7 Arabic p. 6 English). It also includes universal clauses on privacy fairness and lawful data use but does not contain specific provisions or mechanisms addressing the prevention of AI-enabled exploitation manipulation targeted advertising or exposure to harmful content targeting children in particular.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children

fr1_title: National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (Libya)
fr1_justif: Principle 11 of the national charter specifically focuses on environmental sustainability. The principle aims to 'Ensure that artificial intelligence technologies do not unnecessarily drain energy resources while increasing their effectiveness and efficiency to reduce their carbon impact on the environment thus contributing to meeting the challenges of climate change' (p.9) Principle 8 on page 14  translated document) also highlights more broadly its objective to ensure that AI systems achieve tangible and sustainable benefits for individuals society and the environment throughout their entire lifecycle.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) directly acknowledges the environmental costs of AI and calls for their prevention. In Principle 11: Environment and Sustainability (p. 9 of translated document) it urges developers and users to ensure AI technologies 'do not unnecessarily drain energy resources” and to improve efficiency to reduce their carbon footprint. This reflects a clear objective to curb resource-intensive AI development and deployment.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (Libya)
fr1_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) explicitly identifies fairness and non-discrimination as one of its twelve ethical benchmarks set out in the section titled “Ethical Principles of Artificial Intelligence” on page 6 of the document. The detailed articulation of this benchmark then follows on page 7 under the subsection Fairness and Equity which states that AI systems must be inclusive avoid sustaining or deepening social injustice and must “limit discrimination or bias based on race color sex language age disability political or non-political opinion wealth or any other status'.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) identifies Fairness and Equity as a core objective calling for AI systems that are inclusive; accessible and free from discrimination or bias. It urges developers to promote equality; ensure fair outcomes and prevent harm to groups based on traits such as gender; age; disability or opinion (p. 7). The Charter also recommends using diverse datasets and fair algorithmic design to minimize bias in decision-making.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) explicitly calls for preventing AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying societal biases and discrimination. In Section 3: Fairness and Equity (p. 7) it instructs that AI applications must limit bias based on race color gender language age disability political opinion or any other status. It also warns against sustaining or worsening social injustice through algorithmic decisions. However the Charter provides no procedural or enforcement measures.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) assigns broad ethical obligations to AI developers and deployers to identify and reduce bias in AI systems. In Section 3: Fairness and Equity (p. 7) it calls for ensuring algorithmic fairness using diverse datasets and avoiding discrimination based on race gender age disability or other characteristics. It also stresses the need to prevent social injustice and promote inclusivity in AI development. However the Charter does not specify concrete procedures or technical standards for measuring or mitigating bias across the AI lifecycle.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence National Policy (Libya)
fr1_justif: In the section on principles underpinning the national AI policy (p.6) one of the key principles highlighted is Equality and Justice: Full respect for the rule of law and alignment with human values in ensuring fairness equality and justice in how artificial intelligence systems treat all individuals regardless of race gender class or culture. Unjustified bias and preferential treatment must be avoided. In section 5 of the policy on the design and use of AI systems one of the objectives cited is ensuring that there is no discrimination or bias in favor of a particular group within the algorithms of artificial intelligence systems (p.13)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Council/Authority (exact name to be determined) in accordance with decision issued by the Council of Ministers
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: In section 5 of the policy p. 13 on the development and use of Ai systems the AI body is responsible for ensuring that there is no discrimination or bias in favor of any particular group within the algorithms of artificial intelligence systems. Furthermore under the equality and justice principle: it is required 'equality and justice in the treatment of all individuals by artificial intelligence systems regardless of race gender class or culture and bias and unjustified preferences must be avoided' (p. 6).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (Libya)
fr1_justif: The principle aims to determine the extent of human intervention required within decision-making processes or operations in AI applications Regulations should be applied that allow for human intervention or automatic shutdown of the system in case of malfunction especially when such failure affects human safety. The Charter encourages the creation of controlled testing environments to enhance responsible oversight in the field of research and innovation. 'Those responsible for the different stages of the life cycle of an AI system must be identified and accountable for the results of these systems while enabling human oversight' (p.7)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) explicitly emphasizes meaningful human control over AI systems through Principle 9: Human Oversight (p. 8). It requires that the level of human intervention in AI decision-making be determined by the system’s risk level and ethical implications ensuring continuous monitoring and accountability by identified human operators. It is stated that 'Artificial intelligence systems must be prevented from developing in a self-sustained way that overrides human capabilities' (p.8).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) includes provisions that indirectly prevent full automation in sensitive sectors by emphasizing the importance of human oversight and ethical judgment. In Principle 9: Human Oversight (p. 9) it requires that the level of human involvement in AI decision-making be determined according to the system’s risk and ethical implications ensuring human accountability in high-impact contexts especially when it affects human safety (p.8). While the Charter does not specify sectors such as law enforcement or medicine it clearly conveys that human intervention must remain essential where AI decisions carry significant ethical or societal consequences.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) explicitly requires entities using AI to designate responsible individuals to ensure oversight and accountability. In Principle 6: Accountability and Integrity (p. 9) it mandates that roles and responsibilities be clearly defined among developers service providers and users ensuring that all parties are answerable for AI system outcomes. Although non-binding this provision establishes an ethical obligation for organizations to assign named human overseers who can monitor intervene and assume responsibility for AI decisions throughout the system’s lifecycle.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence National Policy (Libya)
fr1_justif: On page 12 the policy calls for “training and qualifying local expertise” and “providing mid-term training programs” to build institutional capacity within administrative bodies explicitly linking AI adoption to skills development in government institutions. Further on page 12 the policy recommends “periodic awareness programs for employees of the public sector ” and “partnerships between public and private institutions to disseminate AI knowledge and skills” confirming a structured objective to equip public servants with foundational AI competencies rather than imposing binding training requirements.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Council/Authority (exact name to be determined) in accordance with decision issued by the Council of Ministers
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The National Artificial Intelligence Policy of Libya includes recommendations for government-wide up-skilling of public servants but it does not extend these provisions to the judiciary. On page 12 the policy frames capacity building as a national priority and calls for “training and qualifying local expertise” and “mid-term training programs” to strengthen institutional readiness within administrative bodies while page 14 recommends “periodic awareness programs for public sector employees” and partnerships to disseminate AI knowledge
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The National Artificial Intelligence Policy of Libya includes recommendations supporting ongoing capacity development but does not impose a formal requirement for continuous professional development. On page 12 it refers to “mid-term training programs” and ongoing efforts to “train and qualify local expertise” indicating recognition of the evolving nature of AI skills. Additionally page 14 recommends “periodic awareness programs for public sector employees” which suggests continuity but the policy stops short of mandating structured lifelong AI professional development frameworks

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence National Policy (Libya)
fr1_justif: On page 12 the policy also commits to “preventing brain drain ensuring appropriate employment opportunities and providing mid-term training for local experts while attracting foreign expertise”. Finally page 14 expands these aims by requiring “periodic awareness programs for public sector employees and partnerships between public and private institutions to spread AI knowledge and skills” and instructs “the Ministry of Education to adapt schooling so young students acquire modern science technology engineering and mathematics skills.”
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Council/Authority (exact name to be determined) in accordance with decision issued by the Council of Ministers
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: On page 12 the policy instructs the government to “train local expertise and attract foreign experts to benefit from their experience in this field ensuring mid-term training (five years)” clearly implying a state-backed training and reskilling program. Similarly page 14 calls for “periodic awareness programs for public sector employees and partnerships between public and private institutions to spread AI knowledge and skills among public employees.”. However grants or subsidies are not mentioned nor is the objective to help workers to adapt from their current work to new job market demands.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
fr1_element3_justif: The policy states that : 'The relevant authorities in the public and private sectors must take measures and implement programs to develop and rehabilitate the workforce’s skills in artificial intelligenceorganize specialized training courses for their employees in applications that use artificial intelligence and encourage innovation' (p.13). However job displacement caused by automation is not mentioned as a threat to mitigate.

fr1_title: National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (Libya)
fr1_justif: The principle aims to 'prevent potential risks and ensure safety during the development and use of artificial intelligence technologies.”  (page 8) The principle also stipulates that the collection use management and any handling of data used in AI technologies must comply with the applicable laws and regulations in Libya. It is necessary to ensure the quality of the data that feeds AI technologies in terms of accuracy and soundness and such data should be subject to technical auditing and review when needed. Data governance and the protection of personal data must be guaranteed and any individual or entity that violates data privacy shall be held accountable.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: On page 4: 'appropriate mechanisms and systems responsible for conducting designing deploying and monitoring quality tests must be developed before and after their implementation'. p.7: 'The security and integrity of AI systems must be monitored and tested continuously to ensure that they achieve their intended purposeand any problems detected should be addressed through ongoing risk management as needed'. However documentation of these tests and the exact aspects to be tested are not mentioned.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

fr1_title: National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (Libya)
fr1_justif: The principle defines transparency as ensuring that AI decision-making processes are clear and understandable to users and stakeholders. It requires responsible and timely disclosure clear justifications for AI system results and providing information that helps individuals understand outcomes including key factors used in decisions.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) explicitly promotes clarity and openness in how AI systems function to strengthen public trust. In Principle 1 transparency and interpretability (p. 5) it requires that AI decision-making processes be clear and understandable 'this includes providing information that helps individuals understand outcomes such as the key factors that have been relied upon in making decisions' with responsible and timely disclosure of information about a system’s purpose data use and logic. It establishes an ethical expectation that AI developers and operators communicate how their systems work to ensure accountability and informed user understanding.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The Charter states that : Institutions and users must be transparent about algorithms that make decisions that affect the individuals whose personal data is used. However it does not mandate that entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The Libyan National Charter for the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2025) recognizes an ethical right for individuals to receive explanations for AI decisions that affect them. In Principle 1 (p. 6) and reinforced in the Accountability and Integrity section (p. 10) it grants people the ability to challenge AI outcomes and requires that they be provided with clear understandable information about the factors and logic behind those results. While this establishes an important right to explanation and contestation it does establish explicitly the right to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome.

fr1_title: Lithuanian Action Plan for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies 2023-2026
fr1_justif: Measures relating to financial instruments focusing on funding participation in AI summer camps/courses/internships for university professors researchers and AI specialists working in companies (p. 22). Specifically identify high-quality summer camps/courses/internships/conferences for professional development in Lithuania or abroad and invite university professors researchers and business specialists to submit funding applications. Participation is funded up to 100% for universities and researchers (p. 22).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Innovation Agency connect to the Minister of Economy and Innovation
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The measures aim to identify and fund high-quality summer camps/courses/internships/conferences for university lecturers researchers and AI specialists working in companies (p.22). However no action is related to institutionalized education.
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The DSA addresses misuse through platform duties (not “AI tools” generally): VLOPs/VLOSEs must assess and mitigate systemic risks linked to their services and “algorithmic systems” (Arts. 34–35) including risks relating to illegal content (e.g. illegal hate speech/cyber violence). It does not impose a general ban on AI tools creating misinformation
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

fr1_title: EU GDPR
fr1_justif: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).
fr1_body_name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: It is mandatory to establish an independent supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint including a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) including age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

fr1_justif: Guidelines for the development of the Lithuanian language in the digital media and for the advancement of language technologies in 2021-2027 aimed at ensuring the full use of the Lithuanian language in the digital media consolidating and maintaining the status of the Lithuanian language in the information society promoting the development of technologies adapted to the Lithuanian language and improving the quality of services based thereon (art.2 1). However the focus is on Lithuanianization rather than diversity or representativeness.

Hybrid and AI technological solutions adapted to the Lithuanian language must be improved. However is not clear if it is mandatory for all sectors supping still guiding only the public sector.

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
fr1_body_name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related to gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
fr1_body_name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities including equality bodies can voluntarily investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targeting gender-specific.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
