fr2_title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
fr2_justif: The law addresses AI-facilitated misinformation and violence through explicit prohibitions and duties. It bans AI systems that generate simulated audiovisual or textual content for fraud disinformation or digital violence unless they include authentication and visible labeling mechanisms (Art. 38.V). General duties prohibit AI from inducing harmful violent or manipulative outcomes (Art. 35.V). For children specifically AI systems that promote violence hatred discrimination or disseminate false distorted or decontextualized information are prohibited including synthetic sexually exploitative material (Art. 63 Ch. XIV)
fr2_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr2_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr2_element1_justif: it prevents AI tools from creating/disseminating misinformation and enabling digital violence by banning AI systems that generate simulated audiovisual/textual content for fraud disinformation or digital violence unless they include authentication and visible labeling (Art. 38(V) Ch. X p. 33). It also covers hate/violence mainly in the child-protection chapter prohibiting AI that disseminates false/distorted/decontextualized information and content promoting violence/hatred/discrimination (Art. 63 Ch. XIV pp. 46–47). However it does not fully detail broader “harassment”/hate-speech controls for all contexts.
fr2_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr2_element2_justif: It assigns transparency/traceability/audit and incident-reporting duties to developers/operators/users (e.g. periodic technical audits traceability/explainability reporting incidents and biases) (Ch. IX; Arts. 35–37; pp. 32–33). It also requires safeguards for simulated content linked to fraud/misinformation/digital violence via authentication + visible labeling (Art. 38(V) p. 33). However it does not set detailed “platform content moderation policies” as such.
fr2_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr2_element3_justif: It grants protection and redress rights via: (a) liability of any public/private operator and joint liability when multiple entities are involved (Ch. XIII Arts. 52–53 p. 41); (b) a right to full reparation and access to courts/defenders/autonomous bodies and administrative complaint mechanisms (Art. 57 pp. 43–44); and (c) complaint/review/remedy mechanisms including complaints against platforms or entities operating the system with required accessible channels plus appeals and precautionary measures (Ch. XXVIII Arts. 136–138 pp. 78–79).
fr2_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr2_element4_justif: It does not mention “gender-based harassment” explicitly but it targets related harms. It bans AI systems that generate simulated content for “fraud disinformation or digital violence” without authentication/visible labeling (Ch. X Art. 38(V) p. 33). It also prohibits AI that generates/disseminates child sexual exploitation material including hyperrealism “deep lies” (Ch. XIV Art. 63(V) pp. 46–47). And it embeds non-discrimination on gender as a guiding principle (“Equity”) (Defs. p. 8).

fr1_title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
fr1_justif: The Federal Bill for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of AI (April 2025) establishes a comprehensive redress framework. Art. 5.XVII defines Algorithmic Harm Redress as a legal administrative or technical mechanism for affected persons to obtain restitution compensation or corrective measures against unfair or discriminatory automated decisions. Art. 56 grants affected persons the right to full reparation and access to courts public defenders autonomous bodies and administrative mechanisms. Arts. 131–138 (Ch. XXVII–XXVIII) establish complaint review and appeal procedures including precautionary measures against AI systems causing harm.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: Right to Access Courts for Full Reparation: Persons affected by the development implementation or use of artificial intelligence systems shall have the right to access courts public defenders' offices autonomous bodies and administrative complaint mechanisms to demand full reparation for damages. The imposition of sanctions must guarantee the right to a hearing adequate defense and access to administrative or judicial review mechanisms. The National Council for Artificial Intelligence and the National Algorithmic Audit Platform may issue opinions alerts and technical reports that serve as evidence or technical references in the corresponding administrative civil or criminal proceedings. Arts. 56575960132133135 & 138.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: Art. 7 designates existing state-based bodies as competent authorities for the law's application and surveillance including the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) for monitoring fundamental rights compliance and the Federal Consumer Protection Agency (PROFECO) for user protection. Art. 22.VI assigns the PNAA the function of receiving and addressing citizen complaints about unjustified opaque or discriminatory automated decisions. Art. 56–57 confirm that affected persons may access non-judicial administrative and autonomous-body mechanisms for redress without being required to resort to courts.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: Art. 37.VI requires developers of high-risk AI systems to establish update security and incident-reporting protocols with care channels for affected persons. Art. 37.VIII guarantees people the right to access question and appeal automated decisions that affect them. Arts. 131(iv) 133 135 establish complaint and review procedures including accessible channels through which persons may file complaints against entities operating AI systems and seek precautionary measures and remedies.

fr1_title: General Law on the Rights of Girls Boys and Adolescents (Mexico)
fr1_justif: Children and adolescents enjoy the right to universal access to Information and Communication Technologies as well as to broadcasting and telecommunications services including broadband and the Internet as established in the Political Constitution and the Federal Telecommunications and Broadcasting Law (Art. 101 BIS). The State must guarantee safe access and use of the Internet by promoting policies for the prevention protection response and punishment of cyberbullying and all forms of ICT-facilitated violence (Art. 101 BIS 3 added DOF 24-12-2024). These provisions apply to AI systems as technologies encompassed within the ICT framework (Arts. 11-12 101 BIS - 101 BIS 3).

Retailers and lessors are specifically required to 'demand proof of age' for games classified as exclusively for adults. he State is obligated to 'guarantee access to and safe use of the Internet' and promote policies for the 'prevention protection care and punishment of cyberbullying and all forms of violence that cause harm to their privacy

fr1_title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
fr1_justif: The draft law establishes non-discrimination and algorithmic justice as a guiding principle requiring AI systems to avoid direct or indirect discrimination based on ethnic origin gender sexual orientation age social status disability or any other personal condition (Art. 6.VIII). Equity is defined as an AI-specific obligation to eradicate perpetuation of inequalities (Art. 5.VII). Persons affected by discriminatory automated decisions may demand suspension of the system correction of results and compensation (Art. 44.II). The PNAA is mandated to audit datasets for structural biases and differential impact risks (Art. 22.I).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Art. 6.VIII establishes non-discrimination and algorithmic justice as a guiding principle requiring AI systems to avoid disproportionate impacts on any group. Art. 22.I mandates the PNAA to audit training datasets identifying structural biases representativeness deficiencies and differential impact risks. Art. 22.II requires evaluation of AI models using technical metrics of fairness and parity. Art. 37.VII obliges high-risk system developers to certify that training data is representative ethical verifiable and free of structural biases. Art. 43 authorizes the RENSIA authority to conduct random audits and impose corrective measures for non-compliance.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: Art. 44.II prohibits AI systems from discriminating based on ethnic origin gender age religion sexual orientation disability socioeconomic status ideology language or any other protected category. Persons affected by discriminatory automated decisions may demand suspension of the system correction of results and compensation. Art. 6.VIII requires all AI systems to be designed and implemented to avoid direct or indirect discrimination on any of these grounds. Art. 46.III obliges developers to avoid training data that reproduces unjustified or structural biases directly targeting discrimination at the source of AI development.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: Art. 46.III obliges developers to avoid training data that reproduces unjustified or structural biases. Art. 46.II requires technical and legal impact assessments before commercialization. Art. 49 mandates Algorithmic Impact Assessments for high-risk systems explicitly requiring analysis of differentiated risks by gender age disability and ethnicity. Art. 22.I assigns the PNAA the function of auditing datasets throughout the AI lifecycle to identify structural biases and differential impact risks. Art. 37.VII requires certification that training data is representative and free of structural biases prior to deployment.

fr1_title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
fr1_justif: The draft addresses gender equality mainly as non-discrimination inclusive governance and anti-bias controls. It defines “Equity” to prohibit discrimination by gender and sexual preferences (Art. 5.VII pp. 7–8) and sets “Non-Discrimination & Algorithmic Justice” as a governing principle (Art. 6.VIII pp. 12–13). It requires gender parity in the National AI Council (Arts. 15–16 p. 22). It mandates audits of training data for representativeness and “differential impact” (Art. 22.I p. 26) and gives people the right to challenge discriminatory automated decisions (Art. 44.II p. 36). It also calls for participation of women and LGBTIQ+ in AI decision-making (Art. 103 p. 66).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: It sets anti-discrimination principles and some controls but not full mandatory bias-audit regimes for all high-risk uses. It prohibits discrimination by gender and sexual preferences under “Equity” (Art. 5.VII pp. 7–8) and adopts “Non-Discrimination & Algorithmic Justice” as a principle (Art. 6.VIII pp. 12–13). It requires audits/monitoring to identify “differential impacts” and data representativeness (Art. 22.I p. 26) and gives a right to contest discriminatory automated decisions (Art. 44.II p. 36). But it does not mandate sector-specific bias audits (e.g. hiring/credit/health) with standard metrics or explicit gender-bias testing protocols.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: It assigns broad duties to prevent discrimination but does not spell out detailed gender-specific developer/user obligations. It applies to all public/private entities handling AI (Art. 3 p. 6) and sets binding principles of Equity (no discrimination by gender/sexual preferences) (Art. 5.VII pp. 7–8) and Non-Discrimination & Algorithmic Justice (Art. 6.VIII pp. 12–13). It requires audits/controls to detect differential impacts and ensure data representativeness (Art. 22.I p. 26) and creates governance duties via the National AI Council (Arts. 15–16 pp. 21–22). But it lacks explicit requirements like “use gender-diverse datasets” standardized gender-bias audits or user-side transparency duties tailored to gender equality.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
fr1_element3_justif: The bill supports increasing representation mainly via policy objectives not concrete programs. It calls for strengthening the AI ecosystem by promoting participation of women and LGBTIQ+ in training/R&D and decision-making (Art. 103 p. 66). It also mandates gender parity in the National AI Council (Arts. 15–16 pp. 21–22) which can influence priorities and resource allocation. But it does not establish specific initiatives such as scholarships mentorship/funding schemes hiring targets or mandatory workforce gender reporting for AI companies/institutions.

fr1_title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
fr1_justif: The draft law addresses human oversight through several provisions. Article 6(d) grants users the right to request review and appeal of automated decisions affecting their rights. Article 26 requires entities using AI for automated decisions to guarantee that those decisions are explainable and subject to human review. Article 27 establishes that individuals may request review before the OR-IA and appeal before an independent body in case of rejection. Article 38(III) additionally mandates qualified human supervision for AI systems interacting with children. These provisions collectively address accountability obligations human review of automated decisions and individual appeal rights.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: It includes extensive provisions measures and principles to promote meaningful human control and ensure AI remains a tool to assist not replace human judgment particularly in critical areas. The document establishes human control through the following points: Guiding Principle (Meaningful Human Oversight); Individual Rights and Review; Reinforced Control in Critical/Strategic Sectors; Obligation for High-Risk Systems
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: Article 6(d) grants users the right to request review and appeal of automated decisions affecting their rights (p. 25). Article 27 further establishes that individuals affected by automated decisions may petition the OR-IA and in case of rejection appeal before an independent body (p. 34). However these rights are reactive mechanisms — available upon request — rather than proactive obligations requiring mandatory human oversight before or during automated decisions. The framework therefore partially addresses individual rights to human review.

fr1_title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
fr1_justif: The draft bill defines Algorithmic Impact Assessment (AIA) as the estimation of harm an AI system may cause to the population (Art. 5.VIII). High-risk AI systems — those with significant impact on human rights life health or public safety — are subject to strict design requirements and conformity assessments (Art. 5.XIII). The Risk Traffic Light System classifies all AI systems by their potential impact on fundamental rights health the environment and democratic institutions (Art. 5.XXIII). The Precaution Principle requires that innovation be guided by prior ethical social and environmental impact assessments (Art. 6.XV).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: Article 6(XV) establishes the Principle of Precaution and Proportionality in Innovation mandating that technological innovation be guided by the precautionary principle avoiding implementation without prior ethical social and environmental impact assessments. Article 25 requires that all high-risk AI systems undergo evaluation by the PNAA before registration in the National Registry (RENSIA) establishing pre-deployment assessment as a mandatory requirement. Together these provisions establish a culture of proactive risk management applicable to all actors before deployment.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: art. 25 establishes that AI systems classified as high-risk must undergo a PNAA evaluation before registration in the RENSIA constituting a mandatory pre-deployment impact assessment for high-risk actors. The PNAA is assigned technical functions to audit training datasets identify structural biases and differential impact risks and evaluate AI models against metrics of equity explainability and traceability (Arts. 21-22). However these obligations apply specifically to high-risk systems; comprehensive AIA obligations for all developers across risk levels could not be confirmed from the available text
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

fr1_title: Decree adding various provisions to the Federal Labor Law regarding digital platforms (Mexico)
fr1_justif: Article 291-J regulates assignment algorithms: 'through algorithms or similar mechanisms' must be transparent clear and known to all workers. It requires platforms to develop an 'algorithmic work management policy' explaining: consequences of complying or failing to comply with instructions (waiting times travel etc.); impact of customer ratings; incentives & penalties affecting the intensity frequency & pace of work; existence & rules of categories that positively or negatively affect task assignment; & other criteria affecting access to future tasks bonuses & sanctions with the aim of reducing information asymmetry. Article 291-P requires human oversight for decisions interrupting a worker's connection & linking.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: Chapter IX Bis protects platform workers from AI-driven discrimination through multiple provisions. Article 291-J mandates that task assignment algorithms be transparent clear and known to all workers and requires platforms to publish an algorithmic management policy disclosing criteria affecting task access penalties and incentives. Article 291-P requires that decisions interrupting a worker's connection or access be subject to human review. Articles 291-I and 291-R extend full labour rights and non-discrimination protections to workers governed by algorithmic management including those previously lacking formal employment contracts.
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: Article 291-J requires platforms to develop and publish an algorithmic work management policy that explains: criteria governing task assignment; consequences of compliance or non-compliance with instructions; the impact of customer ratings; incentive and penalty structures affecting work intensity and frequency; and rules of any categorisation system affecting future task access or sanctions. Article 291-K further requires disclosure of how algorithmic systems interact with workers' rights and conditions directly addressing transparency in AI-driven labour management.
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work
fr1_element3_justif: Article 291-I explicitly extends all collective labour rights recognised under the Federal Labor Law — including the rights to unionise strike and collectively bargain — to platform workers operating under algorithmic management systems. Given that task allocation performance monitoring and access to work in this sector are governed by algorithms the reinforcement of collective rights directly addresses workers' capacity to organise in response to AI-driven changes in working conditions. This fills a prior legal gap where gig workers were excluded from collective protections.

fr1_title: Initiative with Draft Decree to Reform the Articles 153-CY and 153-K of the Federal Labour Law
fr1_justif: This Senate bill filed November 5 2024 proposes two operative reforms to the Federal Labor Law. Article 153-C introduces a new mandatory obligation for employers to provide AI competency training to workers. Article 153-K requires the National Committee on Concertation and Productivity — convened by STPS and the Secretaría de Economía — to incorporate AI skills into its national training and productivity recommendations. Together these provisions establish a binding legal basis for employer-led AI reskilling directly addressing workforce adaptation to AI-driven transitions.

fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI

fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
fr1_element3_justif: The proposed addition of fraction II to Article 153-C establishes a direct mandatory obligation for employers (patrones) to provide AI competency training to their workers specifically to ensure they can understand and apply AI tools adopted in the workplace. This constitutes a binding requirement for companies to invest in workforce development as a response to AI-driven automation directly addressing the risk of worker displacement resulting from technological transition.

fr1_element4_justif: The law partially addresses cybersecurity obligations. Art. 37.VI requires high-risk systems to establish update and security protocols. Art. 38.VII prohibits AI systems that facilitate cybercrimes unauthorized data hacking or attacks against critical infrastructure. Art. 5.XIV(g) classifies such systems as prohibited AI. However no dedicated chapter establishes specific obligations to protect AI systems against adversarial interference manipulation of training data or model-level cyberattacks.

fr1_title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
fr1_justif: The draft law establishes explainability and algorithmic transparency as a foundational guiding principle requiring AI systems to operate under mechanisms that allow their decisions processes and criteria to be understood for accountability and oversight (Art. 6.VI). An entire chapter (Ch. XVI Arts. 83–90) is dedicated to explainability transparency and algorithmic traceability mandating differentiated explainability for different user profiles technical documentation and prohibiting black-box systems. Developers and operators of high-risk systems must ensure meaningful explanations adapted to citizens authorities and technical auditors (Art. 85).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The principle of transparency and explainability is a foundational pillar of the proposed law with an entire chapter dedicated to it. The law mandates clarity on how AI systems operate through a comprehensive set of principles rights and obligations for developers and users: Guiding Principles and Definitions; Rights of Users and Affected Persons (Public Trust); Specific Obligations for Clarity (Decision-Making Logic and Data Sources). The 'principles section' (Chapter III) Article 36 and Chapter X all contain specific provisions that promote clarity on how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic which serves to foster public trust.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: This requirement is a core tenet of the proposed law addressed through the guiding principles of Explainability and Transparency.Key Provisions and Obligations: Right to an Explanation (Chapter XI); Obligation for High-Risk and Strategic Systems (Chapter IX & XII); The Principle of Explainability (Chapter III & XVI); The entire Chapter XVI is dedicated to 'EXPLAINABILITY TRANSPARENCY AND TRACEABILITY ALGORITHMIC'
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: Art. 44.IV grants every person the right to know in reasonably understandable language the reasons and criteria behind automated decisions significantly affecting them with high-risk systems required to provide explainability mechanisms tailored to specific profiles. Art. 84 recognizes the right to request and receive a reasoned explanation of the data used criteria applied and system logic leading to the decision. Art. 85.II specifies that affected individuals must receive a detailed description of the process followed data used how it was weighted and what options exist to challenge or reverse the decision (Ch. XVI).

Page 11 Clause 9.18 and Page 32 Clause 14 call for skill-based training and awareness programs to ensure equal access and participation of children senior citizens minorities persons with disabilities and other marginalized communities. Page 13 Clause 9.30 and Page 38 Clause 24 aim to reduce learning inequality through AI tools such as NLP and personalized learning. Additionally Page 18 Clause 10.1.1 mandates guidance on fairness and human rights in AI while Page 15 Clause 9.60 and Page 53 Clause 49 address mitigating biases and harms
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Women Children and Senior Citizens provincial and local levels National AI Centre
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The document promotes equitable participation and addresses some bias-related risks but does not provide detailed technical measures to ensure AI systems produce unbiased outcomes. Page 11 Clause 9.18 and Page 32 Clause 14 promote equal access and participation of marginalized groups in AI development and use. Page 13 Clause 9.30 and Page 38 Clause 24 aim to reduce learning inequalities through AI-based educational tools. Additionally Page 15 Clause 9.60 and Page 53 Clause 49 call for measures to mitigate harms from misinformation deepfakes and personal biases. However the policy does not specify concrete mechanisms such as bias auditing or algorithmic fairness assessments.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The document acknowledges risks related to bias and promotes inclusive participation but does not provide detailed safeguards to systematically prevent discriminatory AI outcomes. Page 15 Clause 9.60 and Page 53 Clause 49 call for preventive and control measures to mitigate harms caused by misinformation deepfakes and personal biases in AI systems. Additionally Page 11 Clause 9.18 and Page 32 Clause 14 promote equal access and participation of marginalized groups in AI development and use. While these provisions support inclusivity and awareness of bias the policy does not specify concrete mechanisms (e.g. bias audits or impact assessments) to prevent discrimination based on protected characteristics.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

fr1_element1_justif: The policy includes provisions for capacity-building across all three tiers of government (Strategy 8.4 p. 8–9) and mandates skill-based training for policymakers and public sector employees (Clause 9.19; Implementation Plan Action 15 p. 12/33). fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy (2025) (Nepal)
fr1_justif: The document addresses reskilling and upskilling in response to the workforce impacts of AI. Clause 9.23 (p.11) proposes reskilling programs at the central provincial and local levels to minimize job losses that may result from AI adoption. Clause 9.24 (p.11) also calls for upskilling programs for the workforce in the Information Technology sector. These initiatives are reiterated in the Policy Implementation Plan (p.35 S.N. 19–20) which outlines actions to implement reskilling and upskilling programs to support workforce adaptation to AI-driven technological change.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Communication and Information Technology Ministry of Education Science and Technology Provincial and Local Government National AI Center
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: The framework promotes AI-related education and skills development by prioritizing study and research in AI and developing skilled professionals through universities and educational institutions (p.8 sec. 7.2; p.9 sec. 8.5). It also mentions coordination with national and international organizations related to AI (p.7). However the document does not explicitly establish partnerships between government educational institutions and private companies to jointly develop curricula focused on AI-related skills.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy (2025) (Nepal)
fr1_justif: The document addresses AI safety and security by emphasizing the development of a responsible and reliable AI ecosystem. It highlights the need for proper data management digital infrastructure and governance to ensure the safe and responsible use of AI technologies (pp. 4–5). The policy also sets objectives to build a sustainable and reliable AI ecosystem and strengthen AI governance (Section 6 p. 7). Additionally it proposes benchmarking standardization and certification of AI systems to ensure quality safety and reliability (Section 9.5 p. 10) and the creation of a regulatory sandbox to support the safe development and testing of AI systems (Section 9.10 p. 10).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Information Communication and Technology and National AI Center
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes measures related to establishing quality benchmarks for AI systems. It proposes undertaking benchmarking standardization and certification of AI systems developed and used in Nepal to ensure their quality safety and reliability (Section 9.5 p. 10). These measures imply the creation of performance and quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems function reliably under defined conditions. Additionally the policy supports the safe testing and development of AI systems through a regulatory sandbox (Section 9.10 p. 10) which further contributes to assessing system performance and reliability before deployment.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes some measures related to testing and validation of AI systems. It proposes benchmarking standardization and certification of AI systems developed and used in Nepal to ensure their quality safety and reliability (Section 9.5 p. 10). It also recommends the creation of a regulatory sandbox for the safe development and testing of AI systems (Section 9.10 p. 10). However the policy does not explicitly require systematic pre-deployment testing validation procedures or lifecycle documentation requirements for AI systems.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy (2025) (Nepal)
fr1_justif: The document addresses transparency by stating the need for “transparent AI systems” (Section 2.2 p.6) and assigning the AI Regulation Council responsibility to guide AI development with a focus on fairness transparency and accountability (Section 10.1.1(a) p.18). It also requires data management prioritizing ethics privacy and transparency (Section 10.3.1(c) p.20).

fr1_body_name: The AI Regulation Council National AI Centre and AI Excellence Centres
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The document promotes transparency and responsible AI use but does not comprehensively address all elements of operational clarity. It highlights the development of ethical responsible and transparent AI systems (Section 2.2 p.6) and assigns the AI Regulation Council a role in providing guidance on transparency and accountability in AI development and use (Section 10.1.1(a) p.18). It also requires AI data management to prioritize ethics privacy and transparency (Section 10.3.1(c) p.20). However it does not specifically require disclosure of AI system purpose data sources or decision-making logic to the public.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

To assist in classroom translation SLO provides 'curricula tools sample teaching materials conferences and reports' (p. 60). The document doesn't mention AI literacy but encompasses it within the broader digital skills explanation throughout the document.

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

fr1_title: EU GDPR
fr1_justif: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).
fr1_body_name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: It is mandatory to establish an independent supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint including a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) including age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

fr1_title: The Government-wide vision on generative AI of the Netherlands
fr1_justif: It emphasizes supporting open and public language models trained on underrepresented languages such as Frisian Papiamento and sign language to ensure accessibility and equal representation (p.13 Section 3b – Challenges and risks). It also explores participation in the Alliance for Language Technologies (ALT-EDIC) to strengthen European cooperation on linguistic technologies (p.37 Section 5c – Shaping and applying laws and regulations). It highlights opportunities for Generative AI to enhance accessibility and inclusion noting its ability to translate large volumes of text accurately (p.10–11 Sec. 3a) and adjust language levels to make government information more accessible (p.10).
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: Algorithms Coordination Directorate (DCA) and Government AI Validation Team (Rijks Al-validatieteam)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: For Linguistic Diversity: The document provides concrete actions such as encouraging the development of AI models for specific minority languages like Frisian and Papiamento and launching a national Dutch-language model (GPT-NL) to create local alternatives.(Pages 13-14). For Cultural Representation: It directly addresses the need for cultural representativeness by first identifying the risk of bias from developers with 'one-sided perspectives' and then recommending a solution: inclusive development methods like 'democratic AI' which involves a 'representative selection of people' in the creation process. (Page 25)
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: It highlights that “training data may contain biases or one-sided perspectives that are then reproduced by the model” (Section 2.1 p. 11) acknowledging the risk of cultural stereotyping and emphasising responsible data practices to avoid such outcomes. To actively prevent the erasure of linguistic diversity the framework includes direct actions to support less-dominant languages.(Page 13). It also talks about developing Dutch GPT or more eurocentric GPTs to decrease reliance on dominant cultures.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
fr1_element3_justif: The framework assigns some obligations related to datasets particularly for government procurement and through the broader legal framework of the AI Act. However the adaptability of all systems to various cultural and linguistic contexts is framed more as a high-level objective and recommendation rather than a direct obligation. The document acknowledges the need for representative and unbiased training data(p.26) noting that “an important risk of generative AI is the representativeness of the training data: these may contain biases or one-sided perspectives that are then reproduced by the model” (p. 11).

fr1_title: The Government-wide vision on generative AI of the Netherlands
fr1_justif: Sustainability is one of the four guiding principles ensuring that AI development supports both prosperity and climate goals. The document stresses that the development and deployment of generative AI must not negatively affect the climate or ecosystems. It also recognises substantial energy demand and climate change as key environmental risks arising from generative AI’s lifecycle (Sec. 3b p. 12).
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: Algorithms Coordination Directorate (DCA) and Government AI Validation Team (Rijks Al-validatieteam)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: The vision establishes sustainability as a key principle.(p.27). The document states that the development and deployment of generative AI 'should not have an unwanted impact on our climate and ecosystems'. It explicitly states the government 'will not use technology if it causes great harm to people and the planet'(p.28). The document recommends that sustainability 'should be promoted by focusing on energy-efficient training processes and delivery with priority given to the use of renewable energy sources.(p.28). The document doesn't cover anything specific regarding e-waste.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
fr1_body_name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities including equality bodies can voluntarily investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targeting gender-specific.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
