fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: The NAIS addresses AI literacy mainly under Pillar 3: Accelerating AI Adoption and Sector Transformation (pp. 38-43) and its Guiding Principles (p. 29). It calls for increasing AI literacy among stakeholders (Sec. 3.3.1 p. 41) and empowering citizens with the knowledge and skills to engage with AI (p. 29). It mandates a comprehensive AI skills development programme including teacher training (p. 41). Across the strategy it stresses building national AI capacity urging skill development (p. 35) warning of AI literacy shortages (p. 36) and setting a goal to expand AI professionals within five years (p. 34).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The NAIS only partially addresses curriculum reform across education levels. It proposes a comprehensive AI skills development programme and teacher training to embed AI concepts into learning including curriculum reform and reskilling initiatives (Strategic Pillar 3 Sec. 3.3.1 p. 41). It also seeks to improve the public education system (p. 35) and emphasizes tertiary education through AI Centres of Excellence and the EduAI Hub (Sec. 1.1.3 p. 15). However while tertiary reforms are explicit there are no specific provisions for distinct primary or secondary curriculum reforms.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: Under Pillar 2 (Strategy 2.3.2 p.37) the NAIS calls for the creation of AI Centres of Excellence (CoEs) at local universities to develop industry-specific AI solutions train next-generation AI talent and nurture skilled professionals. It also mandates developing AI-driven training and education systems to expand diverse AI talent (Pillar 3 Strategy 3.3.1 p.41). The strategy references existing initiatives like National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (NCAIR)  and the EduAI Hub at the University of Lagos confirming tertiary-level implementation within Nigeria’s AI ecosystem.
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The NAIS explicitly includes teacher training and resource provision for AI education. It mandates a comprehensive AI skills development programme with a specific focus on teacher training (Strategic Pillar 3 Sec. 3.3.1 p. 41) to embed AI concepts into learning. This aligns with the broader goal of building a digitally competent workforce (Introduction p. 14) and improving the public education system. While resource provision is implied rather than detailed teacher tra

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: Page 50 of the strategy identifies misinformation as one of the societal risks associated with AI systems and further provided that strategies should be developed to mitigate each risks including misinformation in page 53. But does not specifically address AI- facilitated misinformation and violence
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy focuses on mitigating known AI vulnerabilities that facilitate misuse by acknowledging the risk of 'misleading models' and systems being easy to 'mislead and manipulate with variations in input' (Section 1.6.1 Page 48). The overarching AI Risk Management Framework (Objective 5.1 Page 46) is the mechanism intended to prevent or mitigate the amplification of these risks but it lacks direct provisions for hate speech harassment or violence (p.50- 52).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: The strategy addresses the underlying issues that facilitate gender-based harm but lacks a specific explicit provision against the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence. Objective 4.2 (P. 45) mandates establishing a legal framework that protects human rights and fundamental freedoms. Furthermore Objective 4.1 (P. 44) mandates an AI Ethics Assessment Framework designed to address ethical implications including bias and discrimination which are the recognized root causes of such harm. These measures provide a high-level preventive foundation against gendered misuse but the strategy lacks a dedicated measure specifically targeting the harassment and violence manifestation of the harm.

fr1_title: Nigeria Data Protection Act
fr1_justif: Where the existence of automated decision-making including profiling the significance and envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject and the right to object to and challenge such processing (section 27). Any data subject whose rights have been violated through automated processing may present a complaint with the National Commission (section 46) seek compliance and enforcement orders (sections 47 48) institute civil proceedings for damages (section 51) and invoke the right to human review of automated decisions (section 37). Data controllers and processors found in violation are subject to administrative fines (section 49).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: This Law does not apply to the processing of personal data carried out by one or more persons exclusively for processing by a competent authority to the extent necessary for national security(section 3).
fr1_body_name: Nigeria Data Protection Commission
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: A private right of civil action enabling any data subject harmed by unlawful data processing to institute proceedings before a Nigerian court and seek compensation (section 51). The National Commission can support a judicial review (section 50). The judicial pathway is available but remains confined to data protection violations; there is no dedicated AI judicial mechanism.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: The National Commission is primarily a state-based non-judicial mechanism for AI-related grievances (section 46) empowering any data subject or their representative to lodge a complaint with the Commission regarding violations of the Act including those arising from automated processing. The Commission is obligated to investigate complaints and may issue compliance orders (section 47) and enforcement orders (section 48) requiring controllers to cease unlawful processing rectify violations and implement remedial measures.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: Data controllers to inform data subjects of their right to lodge a complaint with the national commission (section 27). It covers the automated processing of data; there is no provision in terms of the developer of AI either a specific phase in the cycle of data or the AI lifecycle.

fr1_title: Nigeria Data Protection Act
fr1_justif: The law refers to the Rights of the Child Act (section 65) where a child is defined as any person under the age of 18 – they do not have the legal capacity to independently consent to the processing of their personal data (section 31). Consent for processing must be obtained from parents or legal guardians. Controllers must adopt consent verification mechanisms checking if it was given by an authorized adult (section 31). Therefore no data subject including children will be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing including profiling (section 37) with applicable and explicit exceptions. A data privacy impact assessment is also required (section 28).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: This Law does not apply to the processing of personal datacarried out by one or more persons exclusively for the purpose of processing by a competent authority to the extent necessary for national security (section 3).
fr1_body_name: Nigeria Data Protection Commission
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The Act applies to all personal data processing carried out by automated means (section 2). Children below the age of 18 have no legal capacity to consent to the processing of their personal data and parental or guardian consent is mandatory; data controllers must implement verification mechanisms to confirm such consent has been obtained (section 31). Where automated decision-making including profiling is employed data subjects must be informed of its existence significance and envisaged consequences in a clear format appropriate to the class of data subjects targeted (section 27).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: Data controllers targeting children through automated systems must incorporate consent verification mechanisms from adults or guardians into those systems as a condition for lawful operation (Section 31). However the law does not provide explicit provisions regarding design standards or obligations for solutions that use automated data processing before going to market or that operate on continuous processing.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: The Strategy promotes a Nigeria-centric approach ensuring local communities provide cultural context and define safety thresholds (p.14). It commits to diversity in AI R&D under the 'Inclusivity and Shared Prosperity' principle (p.28). Art. 4.1.1 establishes a High-Level AI Ethics Expert Group (AIEEG) with diverse stakeholders to guide implementation. Furthermore Art. 4.1.2 mandates the development of National AI Ethical Principles aligned with Nigerian values specifically highlighting decoloniality humanity inclusion and solidarity.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy promotes AI that reflects Nigeria’s social and cultural diversity explicitly noting that “replicating Nigeria’s social context and cultural diversity with AI tools… will drive AI accessibility across education agriculture healthcare and other sectors” (Pillar 3 p.38) and reinforcing this in Section 3.1 Drive Locally-led AI Innovation (p.38) which reiterates that locally-led solutions should mirror Nigeria’s social context. Its Vision/Guiding Principles (p.28) commit to inclusivity and representation in AI research and deployment. However while cultural diversity is well covered in principle the document does not explicitly require support for a wide range of languages nor does it set concrete enforceable measures.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: The strategy contains explicit measures to prevent cultural bias its Guiding Principles call to “actively promote diversity and representation in AI research development and deployment” (p.28) and Pillar 4: Responsible & Ethical AI Development requires ethical principles addressing fairness non-discrimination and decoloniality to counter dominance of foreign or majority cultures (p.44). The strategy also flags the risk of biased non-representative systems (pp.37 - 38). However while cultural protection is explicit the document does not separately or clearly mandate measures to prevent the erasure of linguistic diversity so language inclusion remains implicit rather than explicitly required.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS) explicitly addresses the environmental impact of AI focusing on Green AI carbon footprint and energy efficiency across multiple sections. Page 5 outlines under Pillar 1 has one of its aims as building AI infrastructure with 'reduced carbon footprint and improved energy efficiency” Pages 31 and 32 detail strategies for deploying energy-efficient AI powering clusters with clean energy (less than 50% grid reliance).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
fr1_element3_justif: The Strategy promotes energy efficient AI infrastructure but does not cover all the listed elements. It:targets improved energy efficiency and clean energy for AI infrastructure (1.4.2 Pillar 1 outcomes p.32). encourages powering AI clusters with clean/renewable energy (Strategy 1.1.3). However the document does not explicitly mention  (i) advanced cooling technologies or (ii) water consumption (e.g. WUE) in the context of data centres. Hence it only partially satisfies the criterion.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: The NAIS 2025 on page 28 provides that companies should develop and deploy AI systems in line with ethical principles such as fairness. Page 29 further emphasises that good data management practices  including fairness  must be upheld in the collection use and sharing of data for AI applications. In addition page 44 calls for the implementation of a comprehensive AI ethics framework that explicitly address fairness and transparency. Finally page 49 encourages companies to adopt the U.S. NIST framework for developing and deploying trusted AI systems which identifies “fairness” as a key characteristic thereby reinforcing the government’s commitment to ethical and responsible AI adoption.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: NAIS promotes fair outcomes in principle: the Vision & Guiding Principles commit to fairness non-discrimination inclusion and accessibility (pp. 13–17). The risk-mitigation section lists bias accuracy transparency and governance as core controls to reduce disparate impacts (pp. 26–28). The implementation roadmap assigns process owners/KPIs (p. 59). However it does not mandate bias testing/audits thresholds or penalties so coverage is programmatic not enforceable.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: NAIS commits to fairness non-discrimination inclusion and accessibility in its Vision & Guiding Principles (pp. 13–17) and its Risk-mitigation section names bias accuracy transparency and governance as controls to reduce discriminatory outcomes (pp. 26–28). However it does not set binding obligations on developers/deployers (e.g. mandatory bias audits thresholds reporting or penalties) nor does it specify protected-category tests. Thus it addresses the goal in principle but lacks enforceable targeted measures.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: NAIS sets expectations for fairness non-discrimination inclusion accessibility and names bias accuracy transparency governance as risk controls implying lifecycle attention to data models and deployment (Vision & Guiding Principles pp. 13–17; Risk mitigation pp. 26–28). It also provides a high-level implementation roadmap (p. 59). However it does not impose binding duties on developers/deployers (no mandatory bias testing/audits methods reporting or penalties) so obligations are programmatic rather than enforceable.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: Nigeria’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS) 2025 treats gender equality via its inclusion/ethics stance. On page 16 the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025) commits to advancing gender equality in Nigeria’s AI ecosystem including gender-specific AI learning groups and ensuring innovation is inclusive and accessible to all stakeholders regardless of gender. On page 28 it sets out measures to align AI development with gender-equality objectives reinforcing government commitment to inclusive AI governance.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: NAIS commits to ethical inclusive human-centred AI and references fairness non-discrimination transparency and bias mitigation. These address the prevention of gender-discriminatory AI in principle. However it sets no binding gender-specific safeguards (e.g. mandatory gender impact assessments audit/enforcement requirements or penalties) so protections remain strategic/principles-level not prescriptive.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: NAIS articulates expectations for fairness non-discrimination bias mitigation and inclusive human-centred AI signalling responsibilities for actors developing/using AI (sections - Vision & Guiding Principles and Responsible & Ethical AI / Governance & Implementation). However it does not set enforceable gender-specific obligations (no mandatory gender impact assessments audits or penalties). Duties remain strategic/principle-level not binding requirements.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
fr1_element3_justif: NAIS recommends initiatives to increase women’s participation in the AI workforce—e.g. gender-specific AI learning groups/capacity programmes and commitments to make AI opportunities inclusive and accessible to all regardless of gender. See p.16 and Vision & Guiding Principles

fr1_title: Nigeria Data Protection Act
fr1_justif: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sufficiently addresses Human Oversight and Determination and is AI-relevant due to its explicit provisions on automated decision-making (Section 37). In particular it establishes a right to human intervention in such scenarios (Section 37(3)(a)) which directly aligns with the indicator’s requirements.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: This Law does not apply to the processing of personal datacarried out by one or more persons exclusively for the purpose of processing by a competent authority to the extent necessary for national security (section 3).
fr1_body_name: The Nigeria Data Protection Commission
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: The NAIS does not expressly mandate “AI Impact Assessments” by name but embeds impact-assessment mechanisms within its ethics risk and governance framework. Under Pillar 4 Objective 4.1 it proposes a “standardised assessment tool” and in Strategy 4.1.3 commits to a comprehensive AI ethics assessment framework to evaluate ethical implications before deployment across the AI lifecycle (p.44). Pillar 5 also calls for a National AI Risk Management Framework to identify assess and mitigate negative impacts (p.47).  It further links AI governance to NDPA safeguards (Sec.1.1.3.5 pp.19–20).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: It promotes a culture of proactive risk management and requires the pre-deployment evaluation of ethical and safety risks but not a unified mandatory evaluation covering all aspects for every AI system before deployment. Specifically Objective 4.1 (P 44) mandates an AI Ethics Assessment Framework for pre-deployment ethical evaluation. Objective 5.1 (P 46) calls for a National AI Risk Management Framework to assess safety and security risks. While Objective 4.2 (P 45) addresses societal impacts via foresight studies and Objective 3.5 (P 43) promotes 'Green AI' for environmental well-being the document does not integrate the environmental impacts into the mandatory pre-deployment assessment required for all AI systems.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: It assigns obligations to developers and users to assess and mitigate risks to individuals and society but does not mandate a single comprehensive AI Impact Assessment. Specifically Objective 4.1 (p.44) establishes an AI Ethics Assessment Framework to address ethical considerations in AI development and deployment while Objective 5.1 (p.46) calls for a National AI Risk Management Framework to assess and mitigate safety and security risks. These obligations are reinforced by the Guiding Principles on Risk Management and Resilience which require strategies to “identify assess and mitigate potential risks and challenges” to minimise negative impacts on individuals and society (pp.28- 29).
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS) addresses reskilling and upskilling as key risk mitigation measures under Pillar 3: Accelerating AI Adoption and Sector Transformation (pp. 38 - 43) and in the Introduction. It focuses on creating a digitally competent workforce to reduce job displacement (Risk Matrix pp. 53 - 55). Through Objective 3.3: Cultivate an AI-Ready Workforce (p. 41) the strategy mandates launching a comprehensive AI skills development programme including teacher training and leveraging initiatives like the 3 Million Technical Talent (3MTT) programme aiming to equip 70% of youth with AI-related skills (Box: Talent and Youth p. 35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The NAIS includes strong government-backed objectives for reskilling and upskilling but stops short of guaranteeing dedicated funding or statutory mandates. It calls for a comprehensive AI skills development programme and identifies reskilling as the main mitigation for job displacement (Pillar 3: Accelerating AI Adoption and Sector Transformation Sec. 1.4.4 pp. 38 - 43; Risk Matrix pp. 53 - 55). It connects to initiatives like 3MTT and targets training 'at least 70% of Nigeria’s young workforce' in AI skills (Box: Talent & Youth p. 35; Regulatory Acts p. 45). On funding it promotes public-private partnerships and shared financing showing government support potential but not full funding commitment.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: The NAIS only partially addresses financial support for reskilling offering ecosystem-level incentives but not direct aid to individual workers. It promotes funding through the Nigeria Artificial Intelligence Research Scheme (NAIRS) under which the Federal Ministry of Communications Innovation and Digital Economy (FMCIDE) provides grants to 45 AI startups and researchers to expand AI capacity and training (Sec. 1.1.3 AI in Nigeria p. 15). However it includes no provisions for stipends wage subsidies or financial aid to workers. While initiatives like 3MTT (Sec. 1.4.6.2 Box: Regulatory Acts and Initiatives p. 47) subsidize training access the strategy lacks direct worker financial support.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: The NAIS addresses AI safety under Pillar 4 (Ensuring Responsible and Ethical AI Development pp.44 - 45) and Pillar 5 (Developing a Robust AI Governance Framework pp.46–47). It mandates a National AI Risk Management Framework to identify and mitigate safety and security risks (p.47) and proposes an AI Governance Regulatory Body to oversee compliance (p.46). It integrates cybersecurity measures specific to AI systems (p.20) and references the NIST AI Risk Management Framework for trusted AI systems (p.49).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The NAIS references quality and reliability concepts but does not set explicit performance thresholds. It adopts the NIST AI Risk Management Framework defining trusted AI as valid reliable secure and resilient (p.49) and proposes a National AI Risk Management Framework to assess and mitigate risks (p.47). It also calls for an AI ethics assessment framework to evaluate AI projects pre-deployment (p.44). However it does not prescribe concrete quantitative benchmarks or mandatory performance thresholds.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The NAIS proposes safeguards through a National AI Risk Management Framework to identify assess and mitigate safety and security risks (p.47) and references the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern Map Measure Manage) for managing AI risks (p.49). It also integrates cybersecurity measures specific to AI systems (p.20). However it does not set out explicit fallback procedures emergency shutdown protocols or detailed incident response mechanisms for AI system failure.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The NAIS calls for an AI ethics assessment framework to evaluate AI projects before deployment (p.44) and proposes a National AI Risk Management Framework to identify and mitigate safety and security risks (p.47). It also references the NIST AI Risk Management Framework which includes governance and risk evaluation functions (p.49). However it does not mandate specific pre-deployment testing standards validation procedures or detailed lifecycle documentation requirements.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: The NAIS integrates cybersecurity into AI governance stating that cybersecurity measures specific to AI systems must mitigate vulnerabilities and protect AI-powered applications (p.20). It also proposes a National AI Risk Management Framework to address safety and security risks (p.47) and references the NIST AI Risk Management Framework which includes security and resiliency as core attributes of trusted AI (p.49). However it does not impose explicit binding security obligations or detailed technical controls against adversarial attacks.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
fr1_justif: The Strategy links transparency to trust and accountability: it connects the Nigerian Data Protection Act (NDPA) transparency requirements with “transparency and trust” and building public confidence (p.20). It treats transparency as AI explainability noting most AI cannot explain the “how” behind outputs making accountability for harmful decisions harder (pp.26 - 27). It also highlights a policy trade-off-trust via transparency vs “system vulnerability” to attacks (p.26). Transparency is embedded as a guiding principle (p.28) and to be operationalised through a national AI ethics framework/principles and assessment tools (p.44).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: NAIS promotes transparency/explainability to build trust but does not impose specific binding disclosure duties about purpose data sources or decision logic. It: (i) directs companies to comply with NDPA transparency duties (p.20); (ii) treats transparency/explainability as core to risk assessment/mitigation (pp.27–29); (iii) calls for a national AI ethics framework and an expert group to guide transparency (pp.44 46); and (iv) encourages adopting the NIST AI RMF (p.49). It stops short of mandating detailed public disclosures.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

fr1_title: ICT Development Strategy: SMART/MK 2030 (North Macedonia)
fr1_justif: On page 33 the document focuses on priority area on implementing education and training programs for ICT skills in the educational process (of teachers and students) citizens administrative officials and potential ICT professionals. The aim is to minimize the digital divide and support the digital transformation by fostering an entrepreneurial and innovative society with a high level of employment and productivity. In accordance with the objective measures are envisaged for the development of digital competencies aimed at: preschool and school-age children high school students; students of first second and third cycle study programs according to higher education regulations; educators and researchers; active adults pensioners .
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Transformation (MDT)
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: P.34- Evolution of the digital skills of teaching staff and integration of ICT tools in formal education: The path toward ‘e-Schools’..later on same page:The key measures and directions of action primarily stem from the establishment of a national framework for digital skills...'On p. 36: The reform of educational programs will be directed towards the development of digital and technical skills among pupils and students including new trainings and scholarships for youth in the ICT field which according to p. 33 extends to primary secondary tertiary levels.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: Action Plan 2025–2027 (pages 67–68): A 2.1.2.1 Training for above-basic level digital skills for teachers in primary schools; A 2.1.2.2 Training for above-basic level digital skills for teachers in secondary schools; A 2.1.2.3 Establishment of teaching programs at faculties for the development of digital skills of teachers; A 2.1.2.4 Updating existing educational curricula to integrate digital technologies and tools in all subject areas.

fr1_title: Law on Personal Data Protection (North Macedonia)
fr1_justif: (p.19) Section 3 starting from article 39 mandates that 'Where a type of processing in particular using new technologies (here implies to AI) and taking into account the nature scope context and purposes of the processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons the controller shall prior to the processing carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data. (a): a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons which is based on automated processing including profiling and on which decisions are based that produce legal effects concerning the natural person or similarly significantly affect the
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Article 27 (Restrictions p.14) allows for certain restrictions of data subject rights and controller obligations for reasons including national security and defence but does not exclude these sectors from the law’s scope. Instead it permits the applicable law to restrict rights and obligations “where necessary and proportionate”.
fr1_body_name: Personal Data Protection Agency
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The LPDP does promote a culture of proactive risk management especially for high-risk data processing activities including those involving AI. This is primarily achieved through the mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) process (Article 39). However it focuses on the rights and freedoms of individuals but not on environmental and cultural considerations.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: ICT Development Strategy: SMART/MK 2030 (North Macedonia)
fr1_justif: The document addresses public sector skills development by strengthening digital competencies among government employees and institutions. Measure M 2.2.4 focuses on improving access to digital skills training for the public administration including the development of training programs promoting gender equality in technology (A 2.2.4.1) and the integration of these trainings into the Ministry of Digital Transformation’s Learning Management System (A 2.2.4.2). In addition Measure M 2.2.5 supports capacity building within the public sector by introducing “Digital Ambassadors” in public institutions to lead digital transformation (A 2.2.5.1).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Transformation (MDT)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes measures aimed at developing digital and ICT-related skills among public servants such as the development of training programs and their integration into the Ministry of Digital Transformation’s LMS (A 2.2.4.1–A 2.2.4.2) as well as initiatives to promote digital leadership and awareness within government institutions including the introduction of “Digital Ambassadors” in public bodies (A 2.2.5.1) and educational campaigns on digital transformation and technology use (A 2.2.5.3). However the document does not specifically establish a government-wide strategy focused on AI upskilling or reskilling nor does it address AI risks or training for members of the judiciary.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The document includes provisions for assigning dedicated roles within government institutions to support digital transformation notably through the introduction of “Digital Ambassadors” in public sector bodies to lead and coordinate digital transformation efforts (A 2.2.5.1). These roles are intended to promote digital innovation and institutional capacity within public administration. However the document does not specifically refer to AI champions AI governance roles or expert teams focused on responsible AI innovation meaning that only part of the criterion is addressed through broader digital transformation leadership roles rather than AI-specific structures.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

fr1_title: Operational Plan for Active Employment Programs Measures and Labor Market Services for 2025 (North Macedonia)
fr1_justif: The document addresses reskilling and upskilling by offering a wide range of digital and AI-focused training programs and ensuring official certification and practical experience. Pages 45-54 specifically mention the AI trainings and courses offered as eligible for government funding.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: Employment Service Agency
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The document states that the activities related to upskilling in AI area is mainly funded by the Employment Service Agency which is public institution. On page 84 section 4 it is written the amount and the exact budget line.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: On page 84 in the budget line there is a lump sum dedicated for advanced digital skills trainings of nearly 700 thousand euro for 2025 targeting 350 persons.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: ICT Development Strategy: SMART/MK 2030 (North Macedonia)
fr1_justif: It is a strategic document with action plans that identifies the weaknesses of missing AI regulation with focus on transparency privacy protection and ethical use. Concretely the Action Plan (Section 4.3.1 pp. 110) has a concrete measure for developing a legal and institutional framework for safe and ethical AI including: Drafting a national AI strategy Developing legal regulation for ethical AI aligned with the EU AI Act Establishing working groups for ethical oversight and risk analysis Creating a national AI ethics code Establishing a public register for AI projects (including legal basis).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The leading body is the National Council for Digital Transformation and Cybersecurity
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

fr1_title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (Norway)
fr1_justif: Chapter 3.2 addresses AI skills in general and the first part of it points out that AI and digital literacy needs to 'be given more prominence already at primary and lower secondary school level'. programming and technology understanding would be incorporated better in education in Norway to increase AI literacy in population in the long run. It also further addresses opportunities to increase competence in older population already in the job market inviting further education and skill improvement (see Chapter 3.2 'Courses and further education programmes'). P.7 shortly addresses: 'Institutions of higher education ought to evaluate how topics with relevance to artificial intelligence can be integrated into their programmes...'
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Page 8: 'It does not cover the defence sector.'
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: AI skills and in particular programming is to be included through a curriculum reform in disciplines like maths since the primary school. p.43 'Under The Curriculum Renewal27 natural science will be made a more exploratory and practical subject already at primary school level with a distinct technology element that also includes programming.' 'The new curricula will come into effect in 2020.'
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: p.7 'Institutions of higher education ought to evaluate how topics with relevance to artificial intelligence can be integrated into their programmes in areas that will be affected by artificial intelligence in the coming years.' p.34 'Higher education programmes should correspond to needs for advanced expertise in the different sectors both for competence in AI and in basic subjects such as statisticsmathematics and information technology.' p.43 'Programming will be introduced in more subjects; among other things programming and computational thinking skills will be included in the new mathematics subject.'
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

fr1_title: EU GDPR
fr1_justif: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).
fr1_body_name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: It is mandatory to establish an independent supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint including a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) including age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

fr1_title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (Norway)
fr1_justif: Introduction brings up language as an important aspect to consider when developing AI with the main point to strengthen the representation of Norwegian Sami and dialects that are used in Norway within language models: 'To enable Norwegian citizens to participate in increasingly advanced services in their own language we need good language resources in both Norwegian language forms and in Sami (p.6). The Government will facilitate the collection of and access to language resources.' Chapter 2.2 is fully dedicated to elaborating on these points and outlining already existing initiatives and collaborations as well as charting further steps that need to be taken by the government or other organizations.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Page 8: 'It does not cover the defence sector.'
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy addresses at least the necessity of covering the range of languages and cultures present in Norway adapting them to local realities page 19: 'To make systems like these accessible in written Norwegian and Sami and in dialects the technology must be adapted to these languages and to local conditions.' Chapter 2.2 lists important steps to be taken in this direction like making language data available expanding domains of available data collaborating with research etc.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: The government presented a white paper on language (p. 20) to reinforce that language technology in the form of speech recognition and language understanding should be accessible in written Norwegian; Sami and dialects (p. 19). The technology must be adapted to these languages and local conditions; for this purpose the government offers a service with linguistic resources (linguistic data) through the National Library of Norway. Although the government mandates the availability of linguistic resources for technological development purposes the guidelines and the white paper on the Sami language culture and society for example are still to be prepared (p. 19).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
fr1_element3_justif: To make systems like these accessible in written Norwegian; Sami and dialects the technology must be adapted to these languages and local conditions. This requires linguistic resources and the service offered by the National Library of Norway provides linguistic data for the development of language technology in Norwegian. The National Library of Norway and the Norwegian Language Council will cooperate by coordinating their efforts to further develop the resources held in the Språkbanken. Primarily the entities have a responsibility to ensure that the public sector as a purchaser and the developer communities in the public and private sectors are informed of and request these linguistic resources (p.19).

fr1_title: The Digital Norway of the Future National Digitalisation Strategy 2024–2030
fr1_justif: Chapter 3.2.1.3 Data centres (page 35) explains how artificial intelligence has a great potential to promote sustainability and contribute to green transition while at the same time this technology and data centers need to be treated as a potential threat to the environment and attention needs to be paid to the efficiency and sustainability of this industry. The Government will emphasise the development and use of the most climate-friendly AI possible and support research into climate-friendly AI models through the Research Council of Norway (p.74).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digitalisation and Public Governance (DFD)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: Page 10:'Goal 2030: The amount of electrical and electronic waste per person shall be reduced by 32 per cent. Currently this figure stands at 26.8 kilos per person.' Page 76: 'For example the new proposal for a regulation on batteries set extensive requirements for documentation of among other things production conditions quality utilisation properties and waste management that must accompany the battery in the form of a Digital Product Passport'
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_justif: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).

fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.
