fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) including the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).

fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and techniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). General-purpose AI providers and generate synthetic AI system content need to be published as technical documentation (Art.50 53). It is mandatory to register in the EU public database before deploying the high-risk AI (Art.49).

fr1_element2_justif: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); including explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. fr1_title: The Public Policy for the Safe and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems (April 2025) (Oman)
fr1_justif: The policy encourages for human-centered AI systems and to take into account peculiarity of society preservation of human dignity and Islamic principles in the deployment of AI systems emphasising the local cultural and ethical framework of the state. AI itself is defined in page 2 as encompassing fields focused on developing systems that perform cognitive functions such as understanding language placing linguistic performance under the policy's scope.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Transport Communications and Information Technology
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The Introduction of  the policy states that all development efforts must be conducted in a manner consistent with Islamic principles and values emphasising the local cultural and ethical framework of the state. AI itself is defined in page 2 as encompassing fields focused on developing systems that perform cognitive functions such as understanding language placing linguistic performance under the policy's scope. The policy provides Humanity and Social Welfare as one of the ethical principles to consider when developing AI systems which requires considering the economic and social dimensions of using AI technologies widely to ensure benefits are fairly distributed across different social groups.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: It mitigates bias or cultural stereotypes by requiring fairness non-discrimination and inclusivity in all AI development mandating that algorithms be checked regularly for bias (page 7) where continuous measures to mitigate biases must be taken including conducting regular fairness and randomness tests on the system’s generated outputs (page 7) and that diverse representative data be used in training (page 7) to avoid favoring a certain culture. The policy also protects cultural identity as personal data (page 3) ensuring that AI respects cultural and linguistic contexts given that AI is defined as performing cognitive functions such as understanding language.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
fr1_element3_justif: Under the principle of Inclusivity and Fairness the document states that developers must adhere to the principle of inclusivity which requires promoting equitable representation for all segments of society (page 3). To achieve justice and inclusivity developers must ensure the diversity of data used in training systems to include representation from different segments of society minorities and individuals with disabilities (page 7). The definition of AI encompasses systems that perform cognitive human-like functions such as understanding language. This ensures that the ethical principles still apply to the linguistic processing capabilities of AI systems (page 2).

fr1_title: The Public Policy for the Safe and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems (April 2025) (Oman)
fr1_justif: The policy defines fairness inclusivity and AI Ethics separately. Fairness ensures that AI systems are designed and used in a just and objective manner avoiding bias and discrimination in the outputs and decisions resulting from these systems across all user groups. (page 3). The policy recognises Fairness and Inclusivity as one of the ethical principles for developing AI systems which must be designed to include the principle of non-discrimination based on specific protected characteristics including race gender religion or any other personal characteristic. Developers are required to systematically check the algorithms for biases and causal factors that could lead to discrimination (page 7).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Transport Communications and Information Technology
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Developers are required to systematically check the algorithms for biases and causal factors that could lead to discrimination. There are obligations to ensure the diversity of data used in training systems which must include representation from different segments of society minorities and individuals with disabilities to avoid biased results. The policy seeks to ensure that AI systems do not contribute to widening economic disparities and that they are equally distributed across social groups to promote their use to achieve sustainable development (page 7).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: AI systems must be designed and developed to include the principle of non-discrimination based on specific protected characteristics including race gender religion etc. They are also required to ensure the diversity of data used in training. This data must specifically include representation from different segments of society minorities and individuals with disabilities. This prevents AI systems from inheriting and amplifying biases present in non-representative data sets (page 7).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: Deployers must adhere to the requirement of continuously monitoring the performance of AI systems and their outputs immediately detecting any errors or deviations and taking corrective actions (page 5). Developers are mandated to check the algorithms for biases and causal factors that could lead to discrimination in addition to being transparent in the algorithm mechanism for decision-making and clear on the logic used by the system for analysing decisions and data (page 6).

fr1_title: The Public Policy for the Safe and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems (April 2025) (Oman)
fr1_justif: This policy explicitly includes principles of inclusivity and justice specifying that AI systems must be designed so that no bias occurs based gender or other personal characteristic. It also requires using diverse datasets in training that represent different societal groups (page 7).

In page 7 it is mandated that systems are developed in a manner that avoids discrimination on gender.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: The Public Policy for the Safe and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems (April 2025) (Oman)
fr1_justif: The document addresses AI Safety and Security through mandates for continuous monitoring data protection and adherence to cybersecurity standards (pages 5 and 6). AI Systems Deployers must continuously monitor performance for errors implement strict controls to protect personal data and classify data sensitivity for appropriate protection including multi-layered encryption and compliance with local laws. Developers are required to conduct an ethical social and structural impact assessment before deployment (page 5) ensure systems are safe from breaches and do not cause any physical or psychological harm (page 7) and follow best practices for cybersecurity (page 6).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: In terms of reliability all developed and used AI systems must undergo a regular evaluation of their performance and compliance. AI Systems Deployers must ensure that AI systems have a tangible value and a clear and explicit benefit compared to alternative solutions providing a true assessment of their efficiency or quality and feasibility. This assessment must be objective and compatible with the needs and operational objectives of the concerned authority (page 4). In terms of accuracy AI Systems Developers must commit to the continuous development of sustainable and compliant models ensuring the long-term sustainability and performance maintenance of these systems and conducting regular internal performance reviews (page 5).
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: Deployers must provide effective and efficient mechanisms for human intervention in sensitive and influential decisions taken by AI systems (page 4). Deployers must ensure that future decisions resulting from the procedures are traceable and documented to ensure their future auditability and analysis. Developers must also provide full documentation and data related to the systems (page 5). Deployers and developers must provide clear and documented tools and procedures for handling errors or harms resulting from system use to ensure the provision of technical and ethical support comprehensively and transparently (page 7). It includes error-handling and harm mitigation but lacks clear technical safeguards or emergency protocols.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: AI Systems Developers are required to document the development process of the AI system clearly and transparently including the techniques and data used for audit purposes. Before deployment developers must conduct an ethical social and structural impact assessment for AI systems and retain the results in the system's documents (page 5). Developers must also conduct regular internal performance reviews for the system including independent technical evaluations to improve performance (page 6)
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: AI Systems Developers must provide strict privacy controls and secure sensitive data such as access control and data encryption. Developers are required to follow best practices for cybersecurity to address potential threats regularly update software and conduct penetration tests (page 6). AI Systems Deployers must also implement strict controls to protect the personal data used by the AI system  and classify data used in AI systems according to its level of sensitivity taking appropriate protection measures including multi-layered encryption (page 5). Continuously monitoring potential biases in the AI system output to mitigate biases related to data or algorithms (page 5).

fr1_title: Bill of Law 413 of September 24 2025 regulates the use of artificial intelligence in the Republic of Panama
fr1_justif: This document establishes equality and non-discrimination as core AI principles. Art. 4.2 (Equity) mandates equal treatment and the avoidance of unfair biases while Art. 4.9 (Inclusion) prohibits discrimination against any group and requires a gender and sexual diversity perspective in AI development. Furthermore Art. 5 reinforces human dignity and fundamental rights and Art. 6 highlights values such as respect diversity and inclusion.These provisions create a robust ethical framework for inclusive AI.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Art. 20 establishes a prior impact assessment for AI systems posing high risks to rights fairness or security analyzing biases transparency and interpretability. Additionally Art. 21 mandates that developers implement technical and organizational measures to mitigate algorithmic biases. Furthermore Art. 22 promotes the use of representative diversified datasets and requires periodic reviews and audits of algorithms to ensure equitable results. These articles create a robust lifecycle for bias management moving from ex-ante assessment to active mitigation and continuous auditing
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The article 35 establishes that the use of artificial intelligence shall be subject to rules that guarantee respect for and protection of the human rights enshrined in the Constitution of Panama as well as the international treaties or conventions signed by Panama. The use of artificial intelligence shouldn't make discriminatory decisions based on race gender sexual orientation religion disability or other characteristics protected by current legislation. Articles 21 and 22 state the obligation to mitigate algorithmic biases throughout the entire lifecycle of AI systems
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The article 22 establishes that the use of representative diverse datasets shall be promoted as well as the periodic review and audit of algorithms to correct biases and ensure equitable results. The Art. 21 states that developers of artificial intelligence systems must implement technical and organizational measures to mitigate algorithmic biases

fr1_title: Law that typifies and punishes the creation dissemination and use of deepfakes and manipulated content
fr1_justif: The draft law addresses AI-facilitated misinformation by criminalising the creation and distribution of deepfakes and digitally manipulated synthetic content. The motive of the law describes risks such as reputational harm deception sexualised non-consensual content and threats to public order caused by AI-generated media. Article 4 defines deepfakes and manipulated content while Articles 5–8 establish penalties for producing sharing or using AI-generated falsified images audio or video to harm or mislead individuals.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The draft seeks to prevent the use of AI tools to produce or spread harmful synthetic media. The justification highlights risks such as deception harassment reputational damage and violence facilitated by deepfakes. Articles 5–8 criminalise creating distributing or using AI-manipulated content directly targeting the misuse of such tools for misinformation or harm.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: It offers partial protection through criminal penalties for perpetrators. Again in articles 5 to 8 it establish offenses enabling victims to pursue criminal action against individuals who produce or distribute deepfakes causing harm. However the law does not create explicit victim rights protection mechanisms or remedies against platforms nor does it outline procedures for redress beyond criminal prosecution. It will be executed throughout the criminal justice system.
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: The draft references risks such as sexualised non-consensual deepfakes and digital gender-based violence produced through manipulated images and videos. In articles 5 to 8 penalise the creation and distribution of such content which directly contributes to preventing AI-generated gendered harassment and abuse even though gender-specific terminology is not isolated in the articles themselves.

fr1_title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
fr1_justif: Chapter II establishes enforceable rights for persons affected by AI systems including the right to information and explanation (Arts. 5 7 8) the right to challenge AI decisions with legal/significant effects and correct underlying data (Art. 9) and the right to request human intervention or review (Art. 10). Art. 6 allows enforcement before competent administrative bodies and courts (individual or collective). Chapter V establishes liability and full reparation for AI-caused harm including objective liability for high-risk/excessive-risk systems (Arts. 27–29).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The draft partially addresses this question by recognising liability and the right to reparation without creating enforcement mechanisms specific to AI-related harms. Article 27 establishes the right to full reparation of damages caused by AI systems including strict liability for high-risk and excessive-risk systems and reversal of the burden of proof in other cases. However the draft doesn't establish specialised judicial mechanisms dedicated AI tribunals or specific procedural reforms to enforce these rights. Article 6 allows individuals to pursue rights before competent administrative bodies and courts but doesn't include specific remedy provisions.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: The draft bill refers to the possibility of seeking redress before competent administrative bodies in cases of harm caused by AI systems (Art. 6) indicating the use of state-based non-judicial avenues. However it does not establish a dedicated AI ombuds regulator or complaint mechanism nor does it set out detailed procedures for handling AI-related grievances. Article 32 further provides that the Executive Branch shall designate a competent authority including functions such as the registration of high-risk AI systems but the structure mandate and complaint procedures of such authority are to be defined only after the law’s approval and regulation
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: In articles 19 & 20 the draft requires internal administrative structures & processes. Chapter VI article 30 allows codes of good practice including complaint-related procedures but it does not mandate a standardised grievance mechanism for all private deployers.

fr1_title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
fr1_justif: The Draft Law explicitly includes the right to non-discrimination and the right to the correction of discriminatory biases in AI systems (Art. 5). It also refers to transparency explainability and human oversight ensuring that AI systems operate fairly and ethically. These principles align with the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) the MERCOSUR Declaration on Human Rights in AI (2024) and the Paraguayan Constitution which guarantees the right to equality and non-discrimination.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Although it does not addresses specific groups it partially addresses fair and equitable outcomes by requiring non-discrimination bias correction and risk mitigation measures. Article 5 establishes the right to non-discrimination and to the correction of discriminatory biases in AI systems. Articles 19(c) 20(b) & 21(c) and 24 require data management algorithmic impact assessments and transparency to prevent discriminatory or disproportionate effects.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: It includes explicit provisions to prevent AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying discrimination. Article 5 recognizes the right to non-discrimination and to the correction of discriminatory biases (direct indirect illegal or abusive). Article 12 prohibits the use of AI systems that cause discrimination based on race ethnicity gender sexual orientation age disability religion or political opinions. Articles 19(c) 20(b) & 21(c) require bias-mitigation and data-management measures but enforcement mechanisms remain undefined.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: It assigns obligations to developers and deployers to identify and mitigate bias but not to measure it systematically. Articles 19(c) 20(b) require adopting data-management measures performing tests to prevent discriminatory biases and ensuring human supervision of high-risk systems. Article 24 mandates algorithmic impact assessments to detect and mitigate discriminatory effects. However it lacks detailed or continuous bias-measurement requirements across all AI lifecycle stages so coverage is partial.

fr1_title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
fr1_justif: The draft law addresses human oversight and determination through some provisions: In 3(c) it establishes human participation in the AI lifecycle and effective supervision. In 5(d) it recognises the right to human participation and determination in AI-based decisions affecting individuals. In 7 (d) & 8 (e) concern information and explanation rights requiring disclosure of the role of AI and humans in decision-making but do not themselves impose oversight obligations. In 9–11 require human review and final human determination where AI decisions produce significant irreversible or legally relevant effects. Finally arts 20–21 impose concrete oversight documentation and override obligations only for high-risk AI systems.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The draft law explicitly promotes meaningful human control supervision and accountability as core principles (Art 3(c & j). It guarantees human participation and determination in AI-assisted decisions through rights to explanation challenge human intervention and final human determination particularly where decisions have significant or irreversible impacts (Arts. 5(b & d) 8(e) 9–11). For high-risk AI systems the framework mandates human oversight mechanisms enabling operators to understand system behavior detect anomalies avoid automation bias override outputs or stop system operation altogether (Arts. 20–21).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The draft includes explicit limits on full automation in sensitive sectors that are considered high-risk. For instance regulates remote biometric identification in public security to cases with prior judicial authorisation preventing autonomous operation. It require human review intervention and final human determination for decisions with significant or irreversible impacts directly limiting automation in areas such as law enforcement and health-related high-risk applications (article 16 & 17).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The draft law assigns accountability to providers and operators requiring internal structures to ensure security and traceability across the AI lifecycle (Art. 19). For high-risk systems it mandates effective human oversight enabling designated personnel to intervene override or interrupt operations (Arts. 20–21). However it lacks an explicit requirement to designate specific individuals who are ultimately accountable for the system's final decisions.

fr1_title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
fr1_justif: The draft introduces algorithmic impact assessments as a mandatory obligation for high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems (art. 13 & 22). It requires developers and deployers to conduct ex-ante assessments identifying potential risks to fundamental rights safety and public interests including risks related to data quality bias discrimination and misuse (Chapter IV). These assessments must document the intended purpose data sources risk mitigation measures and residual risks and be updated through continuous monitoring during deployment. The bill also links impact assessments to transparency auditability and human oversight obligations (Arts. 17–26) establishing a preventive risk-based approach to AI governance.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: It promotes proactive risk management by requesting ex-ante algorithmic Impact Assessments for high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems including the identification of risks to fundamental rights safety bias/discrimination data quality and the definition of mitigation measures with ongoing monitoring obligations (Chapter IV; Arts. 17 to 26). However the framework doesn't require assessments of environmental impacts nor does it mandate a unified societal & ethical impact methodology applicable to all AI systems. As such it addresses key elements of proactive risk management but not all dimensions referenced in the statement.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The evidence will assign binding obligations once adopted to developers providers and deployers of AI systems to conduct algorithmic Impact Assessments for high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems. These assessments must identify potential risks to fundamental rights safety bias discrimination data quality and misuse define mitigation measures and be subject to monitoring and updates throughout deployment (Arts. 1718 & 22 to 26).
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: It seems that public access to assessment findings is only partially addressed. The draft includes transparency and information obligations that indirectly support public accountability such as requiring documentation of risks mitigation measures and auditability for high-risk AI systems and granting affected individuals rights to information and explanation (Arts. 5 7 to 10 & 22 to 26). However it doesn't establish a general right for the public to access or request the findings of algorithmic Impact Assessments nor does it mandate publication of assessment summaries or a public AI register.

fr1_title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
fr1_justif: Although the draft framework could not be considered as thorough regarding this indicator Article 17 (c) includes among High-Risk AI those systems that could be use within the employment sector to hire recruit select filter and evaluate candidates. It also includes AI-powered systems to manage employees and access to employment. As a consequence of this classification such systems are subject to the mandatory obligations applicable to high-risk AI systems established in Articles 19 onwards.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: It does not include specific provision related to the topic; however it does classifies AI-powered systems used in employment sector to hire promote or evaluates employees as High-risk (art. 17(c)). It does include some provisions to apply to those considered high-risk AI systems though but in general not specifically.
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
fr1_justif: The draft addresses AI safety and security through a risk-based regulatory approach. It classifies AI systems into prohibited high-risk & excessive-risk categories & establishes differentiated obligations accordingly (See chapter III; Arts. 14 to 18). For high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems it requires compliance with security accuracy robustness data quality human oversight monitoring & traceability obligations as well as the adoption of mitigation measures to prevent harmful or unsafe outcomes (Chapter IV; Arts. 19 to 26). Certain AI practices are prohibited due to unacceptable risks reinforcing preventive safety safeguards (See art. 14).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The draft bill requires accuracy robustness data quality and continuous monitoring for high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems (Chapter IV; Arts. 19 to 26) which function as qualitative reliability requirements. However it doesn't define explicit quantitative performance thresholds or standardised quality benchmarks nor does it set measurable accuracy or reliability metrics applicable across systems.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The draft requires risk mitigation measures human oversight monitoring and traceability for high-risk & excessive-risk AI systems (Chapter IV; Arts. 19 to 26) which can function as safeguards to reduce harm. It also restricts or prohibits certain uses based on risk (Art. 14). However it doesn't mandate fallback procedures shutdown mechanisms or emergency response protocols for system failures or unexpected behaviour nor does it specify standardised incident-response processes.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The draft requires technical documentation risk classification and pre-deployment obligations for high-risk & excessive-risk AI systems including documentation of system characteristics data quality mitigation measures and ongoing monitoring (Chapter IV; Arts. 19–26). These requirements imply elements of testing and validation prior to deployment. However the framework doesn't explicitly mandate standardised pre-deployment testing protocols or validation benchmarks applicable across the AI lifecycle nor does it prescribe detailed testing methodologies.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

fr1_title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
fr1_justif: The draft law addresses transparency and explainability through multiple obligations. Article 1 and 2(h&j) includes transparency and explainability as a guiding principle. Articles 5(b) 7(abei) 8(albc)–11 (pp. 12–16) grant rights to prior information clear explanations of automated decisions human review and non-discrimination. Articles 19–21 (pp. 22–24) require transparency in AI deployment disclosure of system logic documentation public consultations and publication of evaluations. Article 35 (p. 29) mandates a public database of high-risk AI systems.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: It includes several provisions requiring clarity about AI systems’ purpose data sources and decision-making logic. Article 7 (b) obliges providers to disclose the system’s purpose types of decisions operators involved and (c) categories of data used. Article 8 guarantees the subject`s right to require explanations of the logic (a) criteria factors and data that influenced an automated decision (c). Article 20(e) mandates information on how the model works and the criteria used to generate outputs supporting public trust.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The draft assigns some obligations to provide meaningful explanations of AI outputs. Article 5(b) grants a right to explanation for any AI decision. Article 7 requires disclosing automated decision-making system purpose human roles and data used. Article 8 impose obligation to providers to explain logic criteria and factors influencing a specific decision. Article 20(e) mandates information enabling interpretation of model results especially for high-risk systems.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The draft establishes rights to explanations. Again article 5(b) grants individuals the right to an explanation of any AI decision that affects them. Article 7 requires prior information on automated decision-making system purpose human roles and data categories involved. Article 8 mandates explanations of the logic criteria data sources and main factors influencing a specific outcome ensuring individuals can understand how the decision was reached.

fr1_title: Supreme Decree 115-2025-PCM (Peru)
fr1_justif: he Law defines digital literacy as a continuous process of acquiring and developing essential digital skills for functioning in digital environments including for studying working accessing goods and services socializing and exercising citizenship (Art. 6). It further establishes digital literacy as a guiding principle for AI-based systems emphasizing the need to promote skills connected to the design development implementation and use of AI (Art. 7). Art. 13 also introduces the National Digital Talent Platform (coordinated by the SGTD) which explicitly includes the use of AI to develop student competencies under the National Basic Education Curriculum aiming to prepare students for the digital future by promoting equality and cl
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Yes Article 4 of the law expressly states that the provisions do not apply to the use of Artificial Intelligence-based systems for national defense and security.
fr1_body_name: Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation (SGTD)
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The Law includes guiding principles one of which is digital literacy which highlights the need to promote the development of skills related to the design development implementation and use of AI-based systems (Article 7). This principle gives rise to a specific obligation for educational institutions which is to “implement study programs aimed at developing AI skills” in coordination with the National Authority (Article 13). The obligations apply to schools colleges and universities. According to Art. 6(f) the AI education is “promoted at all stages of a person's development” meaning it covers primary secondary and tertiary levels.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The Law includes guiding principles one of which is digital literacy which highlights the need to promote the development of skills related to the design development implementation and use of AI-based systems (Article 7). This principle gives rise to a specific obligation for educational institutions which is to “implement study programs aimed at developing AI skills” in coordination with the National Authority (Article 13). However there is no mention to the creation of institutions within the formal education system and the reference on the programs is very vague.
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The Law states that the Ministry of Education is responsible for 'promoting the responsible ethical transparent and inclusive use of AI for the development of student skills within the framework of the National Basic Education Curriculum with the aim of preparing students for the digital future by promoting equality and closing gaps. It also promotes the training of teaching staff in AI and digital technologies for their pedagogical use in public and private educational institutions' (Article 13).

fr1_title: Supreme Decree 115-2025-PCM (Peru)
fr1_justif: The law establishes that there are “Misuses of AI” which are prohibited in all cases. One such misuse is when an AI-based system is used to: 'Deceptively or manipulatively influence people's decision-making especially when: using subliminal or deliberately deceptive techniques or exploiting vulnerabilities with the aim of affecting a person's ability to make conscious and informed decisions; it exploits the cognitive emotional or socioeconomic vulnerabilities of specific individuals or population groups in order to substantially modify their behavior; and it misleads or manipulates information through an AI-based system to affect people's decision-making autonomy.' (Article 23)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Yes Article 4 of the law expressly states that the provisions do not apply to the use of Artificial Intelligence-based systems for national defense and security.
fr1_body_name: Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation (SGTD)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: As previously mentioned the law establishes that there are Misuses of AI” which are prohibited in all cases. One such misuse is when an AI-based system is used to: 'misleads or manipulates information through to affect people's decision-making autonomy'. (Article 23) However there is no mention to AI-facilitated violence or hate speech.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The law does not specifically mention protection and redress mechanisms for victims of misuse of AI (as defined by the law) but Article 36 states that in general anyone affected by the misuse of AI has the option of appealing to various administrative bodies (such as data protection consumer protection etc.) and judicial bodies.
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: Supreme Decree 115-2025-PCM (Peru)
fr1_justif: Article 12 (Protection of Vulnerable Groups in the development and use of AI) establishes that all digital services supported by AI-based systems must fully consider the differentiated needs of children and adolescents. Article 24 (Use of high-risk AI-based systems) then establishes that AI-based systems shall be considered “high risk” when these systems perform assessments of children and adolescents in the education sector. It should be noted that the regulation establishes specific obligations for high-risk systems.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Article 4 (Exceptions to the scope of application) explicitly states that the regulation does not apply to the use of AI-based systems for defense and national security.
fr1_body_name: Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation (SGTD)
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children

fr1_title: Supreme Decree 115-2025-PCM (Peru)
fr1_justif: Article 7 of the law establishes various guiding principles one of which is “Sustainability.” This principle is defined as the obligation that 'in the development implementation and use phases of an AI-based system its human social economic cultural and environmental impacts are comprehensively analyzed and evaluated (...) Likewise the adoption of sustainable practices that minimize energy and resource consumption is promoted fostering environmentally responsible technological solutions as well as their components and committed to sustainable development.' Article 27 also mentions 'c) Consider the social and environmental impact of the development of AI-based systems.'
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Yes Article 4 ('Exceptions to the scope of application') of the law expressly states that the provisions do not apply to the use of Artificial Intelligence-based systems for national defense and security.
fr1_body_name: Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation (SGTD)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: Article 27.1 of the law establishes that 'All AI developers implementers and users must behave in an honest and ethical manner for which the following actions are considered: (...) c) Consider the social and environmental impact of the development of AI-based systems.' While this is a provision associated with excessive energy consumption it is not specific enough and there are no other mentions in the law so I believe that this topic is addressed but only partially.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: Supreme Decree 115-2025-PCM (Peru)
fr1_justif: The law establishes a series of guiding principles for the development and use of AI-based systems (Article 7). One of these principles is “Non-discrimination” which it defines as the obligation that “measures are implemented to prevent mitigate and correct the generation reinforcement or perpetuation of discriminatory or biased results.”
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Article 4 ('Exceptions to the scope of application') specifically states that the provisions of the law do not apply “to the use of Artificial Intelligence-based systems for national defense and security.”
fr1_body_name: Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation (SGTD)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The law specifically states that all uses of AI-based systems must comply with the principle of being “non-discriminatory” (Article 7). Article 23 also establishes Improper Uses a catalog of prohibited conducts which includes provisions to prevent discrimination.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The law specifically states that all uses of AI-based systems must comply with the principle of being “non-discriminatory” (Article 7). In practical terms this principle is applied through various obligations such as conducting impact assessments (Article 30). In addition AI-based systems that are used “to analyze classify or infer sensitive data about individuals based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their racial or ethnic origin political opinions union membership religious or philosophical beliefs sexual life or sexual orientation” are prohibited (Article 23).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The law specifically states that all uses of AI-based systems must comply with the principle of being “non-discriminatory” (Article 7). In the case of AI-based systems considered “high risk” developers are required to conduct an impact analysis to identify and minimize potential risks ensuring that the system avoids infringing on fundamental rights and does not perpetuate inequalities or biases (article 30). Since it only covers the preliminary phase but not the entire system life cycle the document is considered to only partially address this area.

fr1_title: Supreme Decree 115-2025-PCM (Peru)

Human intervention is necessary to correct modify or stop the operation of these systems in order to prevent abuse strengthen transparency and accountability and safeguard collective well-being in compliance with current legal ethical and moral principles.'
