It requires that AI systems in Qatar be “fair and non-discriminatory” use data representative of the Qatari population identify groups adversely affected by under-sampling stereotypes and biased information conduct discrimination impact assessments with ethical and legal experts ensure systems do not contain algorithmic or historical biases favouring certain groups and perform regular audits and user-feedback monitoring for perceived bias. The rationale (p.13) links this to Qatar’s multicultural society the constitutional ban on discrimination and equal opportunities for all.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: Principle 3  “Reduce bias and avoid discrimination” (p.12 ) includes measures to prevent AI systems from reproducing or amplifying existing societal bias: developers must ensure groups are not under-represented rectify training data affected by under-sampling stereotypes or biased information and ensure systems do not contain algorithmic or historical biases that favour certain groups. The rationale for Principle 3 (p.12) links this to Qatar’s Constitution which prohibits discrimination based on gender race language or religion and stresses eradicating pre existing biases and promoting unbiased decision-making.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: Principle 3 “Reduce bias and avoid discrimination” (p.12) assigns concrete duties to AI developers and deployers: ensure data ingested by AI systems is representative of the Qatari population identify groups harmed by under-sampling stereotypes and biased information conduct discrimination impact assessments set metrics and mitigation strategies with ethical and legal experts and carry out regular audits and user-feedback-based monitoring for perceived bias over time. Principle 1 “Do no harm” (p.8) also mandates pre-deployment and ongoing risk assessments that explicitly test AI systems for bias.

fr1_title: Principles and Guidelines for Ethical Development and Deployment of Artificial Intelligence (Qatar)
fr1_justif: The Guidelines address Gender Equality chiefly under Principle 6 – “Minimise bias and promote fairness” (p.15). It warns against discrimination or unfair treatment based on gender and instructs users to: pick tools with bias-minimisation features seek transparency in algorithms/decision-making evaluate training data request validation/bias assessments and ensure human supervision for high-risk uses. Fairness and equity are also highlighted as cross-cutting aims in the framework overview (p.7).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: The Guidelines explicitly aim to prevent AI that perpetuates gender discrimination. Principle 6 :“Minimise bias and promote fairness” (pp.15–16) tells users to avoid tools that could cause discrimination based on gender to choose transparent systems evaluate training data for representativeness request validation/bias assessments and add human supervision for high-risk uses. The Summary (p.17 further warns against the “perpetuation of bias and discrimination.”
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: The Guidelines assign duties mainly to users: select transparent tools test for bias evaluate training data provide human supervision for high-risk uses and use monitoring/reporting mechanisms (Principle 6 :Minimise bias and promote fairness p.15). They also tell users to request validation/bias assessment reports from developers (p.15). But detailed obligations for developers/deployers are deferred to a separate document (Scope p.2)
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: Guidelines for Secure Adoption and Usage of Artificial Intelligence (Qatar)
fr1_justif: The Guideline embeds human oversight by requiring organizations to clearly define implement and monitor the role and intervention of humans across the AI lifecycle (Sec. 5.2.1 Risk Management p.21). It mandates user-facing safeguards: plain language disclosure of AI use reversibility opt-out options and clearly marked decision-review/feedback channels (Sec. 5.2.2.1 Stakeholder interaction p.23). Accountability is reinforced via documentation for explainability/auditability (Sec. 5.2.2.2 p.23) and logging of decision-making (Sec. 5.2.2.3 pp.22–23). It also notes human in the loop aspects in risk criteria. Finally it explicitly notes under 5.1.5 Human oversight in AI decision making different human-in-the-loop models of oversight.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Guideline explicitly promotes meaningful human control. It requires integrating human oversight in AI decision-making and outlines oversight modes human in the loop human over/on top of the loop and when to apply them (Sec. 5.1.5–5.2 pp.19–21). It mandates defining and monitoring the role and intervention of humans across the lifecycle (Sec. 5.2.1 p.21) plus user safeguards: reversibility opt out and clearly marked decision review/feedback channels (Sec. 5.2.2.1 p.23). It codifies Human oversight & Monitoring  for high impact systems (Appx. 8.1.5 p.33).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The Guideline promotes human control: it requires clearly defining implementing and monitoring the human role across the AI lifecycle (Sec. 5.2 p.21).it details oversight modes human in the loop and human over/on top of the loop and when to apply them (Sec. 5.1 pp.19–20).It mandates Human oversight & Monitoring for high impact systems (Appx. 8.1.5 p.32) and flags high stakes areas like healthcare defense and criminal justice (p.31). However it does not prohibit full automation and even defines human out of the loop models of oversight (p. 20).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The Guideline suggests that organizations should allocate responsibility & oversight to specific personnel/departments. It lists individuals with authority to address AI risks establish/monitor processes decide the level of human involvement and maintain/monitor/document/review AI models (Sec. 5.1.2 p.19). It also promotes clearly identifying and monitoring human roles/intervention across the lifecycle (Sec. 5.2.1 p.21) and to top management and the governing body on disclosure and risk appetite (Secs. 5.2.2.1 & 5.2.1 p.23). However all of these are phrased as suggestions and recommendations not as binding obligations for the entities.

fr1_title: Guidelines for Secure Adoption and Usage of Artificial Intelligence (Qatar)
fr1_justif: The guideline addresses Impact Assessments through a comprehensive AI risk-management approach. Section 5.2.1 Risk management (p. 21–23) outlines the need to identify assess prioritize and continuously re-evaluate AI-related risks including data risks societal impact explainability regulatory compliance and human oversight. It further integrates risk evaluation across the AI lifecycle (p.18) and requires documentation auditability monitoring and testing to mitigate potential harms.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The guideline promotes a proactive risk-management culture across the AI lifecycle. Section 5.2.1 “Risk management” (p 21–23) requires organisations to identify assess and prioritise AI related risks before deployment including data quality bias societal impact regulatory compliance transparency and human oversight. It also calls for ongoing monitoring testing and documentation (pp. 18–20). However environmental impacts are not explicitly & systematically addressed so the requirement is only partially met.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The guideline assigns clear obligations to both AI solution providers and AI deployers to conduct comprehensive risk and impact assessments across the AI lifecycle. Section 4 “Risks Threats Challenges” (pp.13–17) requires identifying analysing and documenting AI-related risks and implementing mitigation controls before and during deployment. Section 5.2.1 “Risk management” and the lifecycle guidance (pp.21–23) require continuous evaluation monitoring and treatment of impacts on individuals and society.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Qatar Digital Government Strategy
fr1_justif: The document addresses public sector skills development through initiatives aimed at strengthening digital capabilities within government institutions. Under “Strategic Actions to Achieve This Objective – Elevating Digital Maturity” it includes digital upskilling as a key assessment domain specifically referencing ICT training and digital literacy for government officials (p. 15). In addition the establishment of a central digital advisory hub will support entities by onboarding digital experts and providing guidance to build in-house capabilities and capacity for transformation initiatives (p. 15). These measures aim to enhance government skills needed for digital transformation and emerging technologies.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Smart Government and Digital Excellence Committee Robust governance model
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes measures related to upskilling public servants but does not specifically focus on AI or the judiciary. Under “Strategic Actions to Achieve This Objective – Elevating Digital Maturity” digital upskilling is identified as a key domain including ICT training and digital literacy for government officials (p. 15). Additional support is provided through a central digital advisory hub that helps entities build in-house capabilities and onboard digital experts to leverage emerging technologies such as AI (p. 15). However the document does not outline a dedicated government-wide AI training strategy or mention judicial training.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The document proposes institutional support structures that can function as expert guidance mechanisms but it does not explicitly designate “AI champions.” Under “Strategic Actions to Achieve This Objective – Elevating Digital Maturity” it calls for establishing a central digital advisory hub to assist government entities with digital transformation including onboarding digital experts and providing guidance on the use of emerging technologies such as AI (p. 15). While this creates expert support capacity within government the document does not specifically assign dedicated AI champion roles or teams focused solely on responsible AI innovation.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The document promotes strengthening digital skills in government but does not establish explicit requirements for ongoing AI-specific professional development. Under “Strategic Actions to Achieve This Objective – Elevating Digital Maturity” digital upskilling ICT training and improving digital literacy among government officials are identified as key assessment domains (p. 15). The document also proposes support through a central digital advisory hub that helps institutions build internal capacity and access expertise related to emerging technologies such as AI (p. 15). However it does not mandate continuous professional development specifically tied to the evolving nature of AI technologies.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy for Qatar 2019
fr1_justif: The Strategy addresses reskilling/upskilling mainly under Pillar 1: “Race for Talent in the AI+X Era” and Pillar 3: “The Changing Landscape of Employment” (p 6–9). Pillar 1 mandates AI education at all levels and “AI courses or boot camps” for those already in the workforce plus management/executive training to work in AI-related jobs with recommendations to build AI+X curricula and degree programmes (p 6–7). Pillar 3 analyses AI-driven job automation in Qatar and recommends educating/training citizens to manage build and invest in AI solutions (p. 9–10).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: data strategy office
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy partially addresses this. Under Pillar 1: “Race for Talent in the AI+X Era” it calls for AI education and training for existing workers including “AI courses or boot camps that prepare those already in the workforce to work in AI-related jobs” and management/executive training (p 6). It also calls for “significant investments in the education and retraining of its citizenry” (p.7). It does also recommend to provide financial incentives to local businesses to embrace new AI solutions and resist thetemptation of using low-cost labor as a substitute for embracing AI technology (p. 10). However it does not clearly state that these programmes are government-funded or subsidized although it is implied.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Guidelines for Secure Adoption and Usage of Artificial Intelligence (Qatar)
fr1_justif: The Guidelines address AI safety and security by requiring organizations to ensure the accuracy reliability and robustness of AI systems across the full AI lifecycle. They mandate risk assessments secure model development adversarial-attack protection data integrity controls and continuous monitoring. The document also specifies safeguards fallback mechanisms and human-oversight requirements to prevent system failure or harm. Sec 3-5 ( P.11- 17)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The Guidelines partially address AI system reliability through testing validation and continuous performance monitoring without defining explicit quantitative performance thresholds. Section 5.3.7.2 (Resilient AI – Testing) requires testing validation and verification of AI systems to ensure reliable operation under expected conditions (p.28). Section 6.2 (Understanding the limitations of Generative AI) requires evaluating system performance across a wide range of potential inputs to identify scenarios where performance may degrade (p.31). Additionally Sections 6.3 and 6.3.1 emphasize continuous performance monitoring and adversarial testing to maintain accuracy and reliability (p.31).
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The Guidelines address safeguards and response mechanisms to mitigate harm from AI system failure but do not define a formal unified emergency protocol. Section 5.3.7 (Resilient AI) requires resilience measures such as backups system-wide testing validation and simulation to ensure safe operation and recovery in case of failures (pp.28–29). Section 5.2.2.9 (Incident Reporting) requires organizations to establish reporting channels for inappropriate system behavior or incidents enabling timely human intervention (p.26). In addition Section 5.1.5 (Human oversight in AI decision making) supports fallback through human intervention when systems behave unexpectedly (p.20).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: Section 5.3.7.2 (Resilient AI – Testing) mandates testing validation and verification of AI systems—including models data business logic and underlying infrastructure—prior to deployment taking system complexity and criticality into account (p.28). In addition Section 5.2.2.6 (Integrating AI solution) requires testing AI models against business objectives at key milestones in the development cycle to ensure expected performance before operational use (pp.24–25). Section 5.2.2.2 (Record keeping – documentation) further requires maintaining documentation on design architecture models datasets and test and validation results to support robustness and auditability (p.23).
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: The Guidelines introduce explicit security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation and adversarial interference. Section 5.3 (Technology) establishes mandatory technical security controls for AI systems including access control (5.3.2 p.26) network security (5.3.3 p.27) and supply chain security (5.3.4 p.27) to prevent unauthorized access and tampering. Section 5.2.2.6 (Integrating AI solution) requires regular testing against known attack techniques such as adversarial attacks model extraction and model poisoning (pp.24–25). In addition Section 6.3.1 (Adversarial testing) mandates testing AI systems against malicious inputs and attempts to break system behavior (p.31).

fr1_title: Principles and Guidelines for Ethical Development and Deployment of Artificial Intelligence (Qatar)
fr1_justif: The document mandates transparency and explainability as core user responsibilities. Principle 4 (p.13) obligates users to 'demand transparency' from AI providers. Principle 6 (p.15) requires users to 'seek transparent AI solutions' that explain decision-making processes and to leverage 'usage-related monitoring & reporting mechanisms.' It further commands users to 'understand the AI scope' and acknowledge 'algorithmic limitations' (Principle 5 p.14) ensuring a foundational comprehension of system logic for effective oversight and informed use.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The guideline addresses purpose and data sources by mandating users to 'demand transparency' about system functionality and data used (Principle 4 p.13) and to 'evaluate training data' for diversity (Principle 6 p.15). However it lacks specific requirements for disclosing internal decision-making logic offering only general guidance to 'seek transparent AI solutions.' This constitutes partial coverage of the statement's requirements.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

fr1_title: White Book on Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The White Book addresses AI literacy through its focus on “Education and Skills Development” as a general objective and recommendation (p.1449). It calls for strengthening education research and training systems specific to AI and data governance promoting public awareness and workforce preparation for an AI-based economy (p.12). The document also highlights ethical and inclusive AI education aligned with EU and UNESCO standards ensuring citizens understand AI technologies their impacts and responsible use within society.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Sub-council for AI and Data Governance (SCIA) and the National Council on Digital Transformation
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The White Book includes objectives and recommendations on education and skills development (p.1449) and calls for training programmes awareness initiatives and integration of AI and data governance into education and workforce systems (p.12). However it does not specify curriculum reforms or delineate measures for primary secondary or tertiary levels. Instead it addresses education in a broad cross-sectoral sense promoting capacity-building and lifelong learning rather than formal curriculum changes.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

fr1_title: Draft Law on Digital Public Services (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The draft law addresses AI-facilitated misinformation and violence by mandating rapid removal of illegal content (Art.16) and establishing trusted notifiers for harmful material (Art.22). Article 35 requires testing and adapting algorithmic systems and content moderation to detect and mitigate risks of hate speech and online violence. Together with transparency obligations (Art.15–17) these provisions support proactive control of AI-amplified misinformation and harm.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The document partially addresses the indicator. It establishes platform obligations to mitigate illegal and harmful content risks through content moderation transparency of automated systems and prioritised flagging by trusted notifiers (Arts. 15–17 22). Transparency reporting includes disclosure of automated moderation tools and safeguards supporting accountability for algorithmic amplification (Art. 15). However it does not include AI-specific provisions targeting generative AI coordinated misinformation campaigns election disinformation or explicit hate-speech definitions nor proactive obligations to prevent AI-driven misinformation creation or amplification beyond general platform duties.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: Art.15–17 require providers to publish annual transparency reports disclose the use of automated moderation tools and explain how decisions to remove or restrict content are made. Art.16 establishes notice-and-action procedures for illegal content and Art.22 introduces trusted notifiers to enhance enforcement. Although AI developers are not directly regulated platforms’ AI-based moderation systems are explicitly covered.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: Art.17–21 grant users the right to receive explanations for moderation decisions contest removals and access out-of-court dispute resolution mechanisms. These ensure procedural fairness and limited protection for those affected by harmful content. The draft law also creates direct compensation or liability mechanisms against perpetrators or platforms and extends civil liability and compensation rights to users harmed (Art.54).
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: White Book on Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The White Book embeds Fairness & Non-discrimination as core governance aims. In Guiding Principles (p.16) it explicitly upholds non-discrimination equality inclusivity and diversity plus transparency and accountability to steer design development use and deployment. Inclusivity & Accessibility requires inclusive design diverse teams and measuring impacts on under-represented groups noting AI can perpetuate bias (p.10). Ethical & Socio-Economic Considerations commit to addressing algorithmic bias so AI does not exacerbate inequalities ensuring fair and rights-respecting adoption (p.12–13).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Sub-council for AI and Data Governance (SCIA) and the National Council on Digital Transformation
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The White Book promotes equitable outcomes and flags that AI can perpetuate bias calling for inclusive design diverse teams and measuring impacts on under-represented groups (p.10 Inclusivity & Accessibility). Its Guiding Principles commit to non-discrimination equality inclusivity transparency and accountability across the AI lifecycle (p.16). However it does not set concrete obligations like mandated bias audits impact assessments or redress processes so coverage remains principle-level rather than prescriptive.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The White Book acknowledges AI can perpetuate biases and recommends inclusive design diverse teams and measuring effects on under-represented groups (p.10 Inclusivity & Accessibility). Its Guiding Principles commit to non-discrimination equality inclusivity equality of opportunity and gender equality plus transparency and accountability across the AI lifecycle (p.16). However it doesn’t prescribe concrete enforceable controls (e.g. mandated bias audits or protected-class testing) so coverage is principle-level.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The White Book recommends lifecycle responsibilities for companies but doesn’t impose binding duties. It outlines pre-design assessment of societal risks and values conflicts design via risk-based portfolios development/testing with documentation traceability and data governance for training/validation/testing and post-deployment monitoring plans (p.36–37).

fr1_title: White Book on Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance (Moldova)
fr1_justif: One of the guiding principles of the White Book is inclusivity and diversity which means promoting diversity equality of opportunity and gender equality in AI-based products and services. (p.16). Another guiding principle is diversity equal opportunities and gender equality requiring AI systems to be user-centric and designed so that anyone can use AI products or services regardless of age gender abilities or other characteristics (p.18). Further p. 47 under 'steps ahead' mentions that the following principles are encouraged to underlie the design development use and deployment of AI-based technologies and the adoption of these solutions in society such as: - Diversity equal opportunities and gender.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Sub-council for AI and Data Governance (SCIA) and the National Council on Digital Transformation
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: The White Paper outlines under the section “steps ahead” (p. 47) the document highlights the need to embed diversity; equal opportunities and gender equality into the design development use and deployment of AI-based technologies and the adoption of these solutions in society (p.47).'
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: White Book on Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The White Book builds Human Oversight into governance. Guiding Principles commit to human-centered AI and accountability (p.16). The lifecycle framework requires mechanisms for human intervention when AI produces unwanted/erroneous decisions and encourages human validation of outputs with user instructions/limitations and access to performance to enable oversight (p.38–39). For higher-risk uses it envisages a High-Risk Management System (HRMS) with traceability (logs) technical documentation and post-market monitoring to support ongoing human supervision (p.38–39).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Sub-council for AI and Data Governance (SCIA) and the National Council on Digital Transformation
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The White Book promotes meaningful human control: Guiding Principles commit to human-centred AI and accountability (p.16). The lifecycle framework requires mechanisms for human intervention and encourages human validation plus user instructions/limitations and access to performance to enable oversight (p.37). For higher-risk uses it envisages a High-Risk Management System with traceability (logs) technical documentation and post-market monitoring (p.37). However it sets no sector-specific enforceable controls for critical areas and is non-binding.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The White Book does not ban full automation nor identify sensitive sectors such as law enforcement or medicine. However it introduces general human-oversight requirements for high-risk systems such as traceability through logs technical documentation data governance measures and performance monitoring (p.37). These mechanisms align with EU AI Act principles and indirectly support preventing uncontrolled automation but they are not sector-specific or binding.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: White Book on Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The White Book addresses impact assessments implicitly through its discussion of risk-based assessments and AI lifecycle governance. On p.36–37 within the section Framework for an Effective AI and Data Governance it outlines an Assessment phase requiring companies to identify societal risks classify potential harms and establish a High-Risk Management System (HRMS). This lifecycle approach includes post-market monitoring traceability and ethical compliance evaluations functioning as de facto AI impact assessments to ensure transparency accountability and safety.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Sub-council for AI and Data Governance (SCIA) and the National Council on Digital Transformation
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The White Book promotes a culture of proactive risk management but does not make it mandatory. On p.36–37 the Framework for an Effective AI and Data Governance introduces an Assessment phase requiring organizations to identify risks to society and ethics before deploying AI systems supported by a risk-based approach and High-Risk Management System (HRMS). However while it covers societal and ethical impacts environmental impacts are not systematically addressed.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The White Book encourages developers and users to assess and mitigate risks before deploying AI systems but stops short of assigning formal obligations. On p.36–37 the Framework for an Effective AI and Data Governance outlines an Assessment phase and a High-Risk Management System (HRMS) requiring companies to classify potential risks ensure traceability and monitor ethical compliance. These provisions imply impact assessment practices but remain recommendatory not mandatory.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

fr1_title: White Book on Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The White Book addresses labour protections primarily on p.13 where it highlights the need for fair working conditions skills development and safeguards to ensure an equitable transition amid AI-driven changes. It also references the obligation to respect internationally recognized labour rights (p.18). While p.16 outlines general AI principles such as transparency accountability human oversight and non-discrimination these apply broadly to AI governance rather than labour protections specifically.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Sub-council for AI and Data Governance (SCIA) and the National Council on Digital Transformation
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: The White Book promotes fairness transparency accountability and non-discrimination in AI use (p.16) which indirectly cover protections against AI-driven discrimination in employment contexts. It emphasizes the need for human oversight and ethical AI deployment to prevent bias in automated decision-making and ensure equitable outcomes (p.12–13). However it does not explicitly address hiring promotion or termination decisions or the rights of workers under algorithmic management systems.
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: The White Book establishes transparency explainability accountability and human oversight as key principles for trustworthy AI (p.16). These provisions require AI systems to be transparent in their operation and understandable to users which can extend to employment contexts. However the document does not explicitly mandate transparency or disclosure obligations related to AI-driven performance monitoring employment decisions or access to workplace benefits.
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Professional Development Program for Civil Servants for the years 2025-2027 (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The Professional Development Programme for Civil Servants 2025–2027 approved by Government Decision No. 166/2025 establishes a national framework for continuous upskilling of public servants. It introduces the development and implementation of a program on advanced digital skills and the use of AI in work processes for civil servants via Objective 2.4 activities 2.4.1 and 2.4.2 (p.29) to be implemented by the Cyber Security Agency by training at least 150 civil servants by Q4 of 2027 (p.29). The Programme mandates specialized modules e-learning resources and partnerships with institutions to strengthen civil servants’ capacity to apply AI and digital tools in governance.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: State Chancellery Cyber Security Agency
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The Professional Development Programme for Civil Servants 2025–2027 establishes a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants but it only partially addresses AI-specific competencies. Objective 2.4 introduces the development (by Q4 or 2025) and implementation (by Q4 of 2027) of a training on advanced digital skills and the use of artificial intelligence in work processes ensuring AI-related capacity building across all public authorities (p.29). However it does not include provisions for developing a foundational understanding of AI risks ethics or governance nor does it apply to the judiciary.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The programme can be read as a government-led effort to equip civil servants to adapt to a rapidly changing digital environment. It explicitly notes that “without a strategic vision training efforts can be fragmented and inefficient” and links training to “adaptation to digital government solutions/innovations and changes” emphasizing continuous training and exchange of experience to help civil servants adjust to technological and legislative changes (pp. 3 and 9). However it does not mention AI technologies specifically and it frames continuous training as a recommended approach rather than an explicit AI-focused requirement.

fr1_title: White Book on Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The White Book highlights the government’s commitment to ensuring an equitable shift to an AI-driven economy through education and training programs that prepare the workforce for new technological realities (p.12). It emphasizes education and skills development and capacity-building initiatives promoting lifelong learning professional development and talent cultivation to enhance competitiveness and adaptability in the AI sector (p.7 14 16 49).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Sub-council for AI and Data Governance (SCIA) and the National Council on Digital Transformation
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The White Book calls for investment in education training and capacity-building to ensure a fair transition to an AI-driven economy (pp. 12–13 16 48). It highlights the government’s role in providing training programs and specialized courses for the workforce and in promoting lifelong learning and professional development initiatives (pp. 12–13 16). However the document does not specify government-funded or subsidized programs or financial mechanisms for reskilling and upskilling workers to adapt to AI-driven job changes.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: White Book on Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The White Book addresses safety and security as a core requirement for trustworthy AI (p.16). It mandates that AI systems operate securely be protected against cyber threats and misuse and ensure robustness and reliability. The document promotes a risk-based approach through HRMS regulatory sandboxes testing validation and post-market monitoring (p.36–37). It specifies that the HRMS must include procedures to collect and preserve technical documentation maintain traceability (logs and records of verification teams) and enforce data governance policies for model training validation and testing. It calls for performance tracking (accuracy robustness) and post-market monitoring to ensure continued compliance safety and resilience.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Sub-council for AI and Data Governance (SCIA) and the National Council on Digital Transformation
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The White Book partially addresses performance thresholds and quality benchmarks. It introduces a risk-based approach and a High-Risk Management System (HRMS) requiring procedures for model testing validation and performance assessment including accuracy and robustness (p.36–37).
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The White Book introduces human intervention mechanisms to correct erroneous AI decisions (p. 7 Human Agency) and promotes risk-based management systems and post-market monitoring to detect and mitigate system failures (p.36–37). However it does not explicitly prescribe detailed emergency or fallback procedures for all AI system failures.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The White Book includes clear provisions for pre-deployment testing validation and documentation to ensure technical robustness. It mandates that high-risk AI systems comply with a High-Risk Management System (HRMS) including procedures for collecting technical documentation traceability and performance evaluation covering accuracy and robustness (p.36–37). These measures ensure reliability across the AI system lifecycle.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: The White Book calls for security obligations to protect AI systems from cyberattacks and misuse. It identifies safety and security as a core requirement mandating that AI systems operate securely and be protected against cyber threats and adversarial manipulation (p. 16 Guiding Principles key requirement 3: Safety and Security). It also promotes robustness data protection and continuous monitoring across the AI lifecycle to safeguard systems and maintain trust (p.36–37).

fr1_title: White Book on Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance (Moldova)
fr1_justif: The White Book outlines Transparency & Explainability as a key requirement for AI as AI systems must explain their decisions and actions in human-understandable terms (p.7). In Guiding Principles it elevates transparency and trust across the AI lifecycle (p.16). In the AI lifecycle governance framework it requires information & transparency for low-risk systems mandates technical documentation traceability and data-governance for training/validation/testing and sets post-market monitoring instructions limitations and performance access for end-users (p.36–37). It also states users should understand how the system works and why it makes decisions (p.38).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Sub-council for AI and Data Governance (SCIA) and the National Council on Digital Transformation
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The White Book promotes clarity via information & transparency requirements (purpose instructions limitations) technical documentation traceability (logs) data-governance for training/validation/testing datasets post-market monitoring and user access to performance so users understand how/why decisions are made (p.37; Guiding Principles p.16). However it doesn’t mandate full public disclosure of data sources or decision logic in all cases.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The White Book promotes clarity via information & transparency requirements (purpose instructions limitations) technical documentation traceability (logs) data-governance for training/validation/testing datasets post-market monitoring and user access to performance so users understand how/why decisions are made (p.37; Guiding Principles p.16). However it doesn’t impose explicit duties to provide meaningful explanations in specific high-stakes domains.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The White Book requires users be able to understand how the system works and why it makes decisions operationalized via information & transparency technical documentation traceability (logs) user instructions/limitations and access to performance (p.37). It also embeds human agency allowing intervention when AI decisions are erroneous (p.7 the 9 key requirements). However it does not create an explicit enforceable right to explanation and is a non-binding guideline.

fr1_title: National Strategy in the Field of Artificial Intelligence 2024-2027 (Romania)
fr1_justif: The National AI Strategy promotes AI literacy through education at secondary and tertiary levels. It identifies education as a priority sector for AI use (p.9) and outlines objectives to raise the population’s understanding of AI benefits use and regulation (p.10). Actions include creating AI undergraduate and postgraduate programmes integrating interdisciplinary modules beyond ICT (p.76) embedding AI fundamentals in high school curricula of mandatory study disciplines and optional disciplines at middle school and high school levels that address general issues of AI (p.77). Further measures encourage partnerships with international universities and support for doctoral and postdoctoral mobility (p.76).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Interministerial Commission for the Coordination of the Implementation of the National AI Strategy
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The National AI Strategy includes explicit measures for curriculum reform at two educational levels. At secondary level it proposes introducing AI fundamentals into mandatory high school curricula and optional courses addressing AI applications effects and risks (p.77). At tertiary level it calls for new undergraduate AI programmes expansion of master’s and interdisciplinary modules beyond ICT and establishing AI as a doctoral field (p.76). However no reforms are mentioned for the primary level.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The National AI Strategy includes concrete measures to establish and expand AI-related programmes within the formal education system but only on the tertiary level. It calls for the creation of undergraduate programmes specialising in AI the expansion of master’s degrees incorporating industry experience and the introduction of interdisciplinary modules beyond ICT fields (p.76). Furthermore it proposes designating AI as a distinct doctoral field and promoting partnerships with international universities for joint supervision and research mobility (p.76).
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

fr1_title: EU GDPR
fr1_justif: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).
fr1_body_name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: It is mandatory to establish an independent supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint including a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) including age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
fr1_body_name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related to gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
fr1_body_name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities including equality bodies can voluntarily investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targeting gender-specific.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
