fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) including the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: National Strategy in the Field of Artificial Intelligence 2024-2027 (Romania)
fr1_justif: The National AI Strategy prioritises developing public sector skills to enable effective AI adoption. It identifies key challenges including underfunded education low digital skills of the population and uneven access to digital education among public administration personnel (p.9). Limited resources and resistance to change further hinder progress (pp.63 68–69). To address these the strategy introduces measures such as AI training for public employees (M 1.2.1 p.77) awareness initiatives and annual conferences that put AI developers in connection with public sector employees (M 5.1.1 p.83) creating an AI curriculum for administration (M 5.1.4 p.83) and training procurement staff in advanced technologies (M 5.1.9 p.83).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Interministerial Commission for the Coordination of the Implementation of the National AI Strategy
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The National AI Strategy includes several measures aimed at developing AI-related competencies within the public sector but does not outline a comprehensive government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling all public servants and members of the judiciary. It proposes training programmes for socio-professional groups including public administration employees (M 1.2.1 p.77) establishing an AI curriculum for public administration (M 5.1.4 p.83) and conducting training for procurement staff (M 5.1.9 p.83). However these are sector-specific initiatives rather than a unified cross-government framework.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The National AI Strategy acknowledges the need for continuous skills development but stops short of establishing a formal requirement for ongoing professional training. It includes measures such as developing training programmes for socio-professional categories including public administration staff (M 1.2.1 p.77) and conducting periodic training programmes for procurement personnel on advanced technology acquisition (M 5.1.9 p.83). While these reflect an awareness of the need for regular upskilling the strategy does not define a systematic mandatory framework for continuous professional development.

fr1_title: National Strategy in the Field of Artificial Intelligence 2024-2027 (Romania)
fr1_justif: The National AI Strategy promotes reskilling and upskilling through one of its strategic objectives which stresses training AI specialists and enhancing public understanding of AI use and regulation (p.10). Measures include collaboration between academia industry and technology clusters for AI certifications and retraining (p.77) partnerships for employee digital skills (p.82) and clinical trial AI training (p.84). Continuous learning is deemed vital for employability and a future-ready workforce (p.91).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Interministerial Commission for the Coordination of the Implementation of the National AI Strategy
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy highlights the need to expand training capacity for AI specialists and raise the population’s AI literacy (p.10) while calling for collaboration between educational institutions technology clusters and companies to develop training and certification programmes for professional retraining (p.77).  Education and continuing training are framed as key government-supported tools for employability and adaptation to AI-induced labour market changes (p.91). However it doesn't state explicitly that expanding training capacity in AI should be state-funded.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
fr1_element3_justif: The National AI framework doesn't impose requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce but it encourages collaboration between enterprises and training providers to develop employees’ digital and AI skills thereby supporting AI adoption within organisations (p.82). While these initiatives promote employer engagement in workforce development the document frames them as voluntary and partnership-based.

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

fr1_title: EU AI Act
fr1_justif: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).

fr1_element1_justif: High-risk AI systems must be designed to enable deployers to understand system outputs and use them including the purpose performance levels known limitations and input data specifications (Art.13). Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and techniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). General-purpose AI providers and generate synthetic AI system content need to be published as technical documentation (Art.50 53). fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); including explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure taken and main element (art.86).

fr1_title: The National AI Policy (Rwanda)
fr1_justif: Building 21st-century skills and AI literacy is one of the six priority areas in the national AI policy. The policy also includes an implementation plan that lists several outputs and indicators. Enabling a highly skilled workforce with 21st-century skills and AI literacy is one of them. The indicator to be tracked is: the number of professionals trained in data and AI-related skills. Other outputs under the 'Building 21st-century skills and AI literacy' priority area include: (1) a solid foundation in AI university education and applied research driving the national AI skills base (2) the general public in Rwanda has a general understanding of AI etc (page 3 page 7).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Responsible AI Office at the Ministry of ICT and Innovation
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The national AI policy outlines implementation activities with priority 1 being 21st-century skills and high AI literacy. It includes activities such as developing modules to be integrated into relevant subjects in the national curriculum focused on building AI/ML and data-related skills; aligning the national curriculum at primary and secondary school levels with the '21st-century curriculum' by integrating the developed AI/ML/data modules; and establishing a task force led by the ministry of education and main universities to work out a plan to integrate AI and Data Science courses into undergraduate curricula (pages 8 9).
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The policy provides for integrating AI-related courses into the formal education system. This is done for example by developing modules to be integrated into relevant subjects in the national curriculum with a focus on building AI/ML and data-related skills. Or by setting up a Program Office or function to help Rwandan universities identify existing in-class courses to scale and to disseminate national and regional MOOCs. Or by developing modules to be integrated into relevant subjects in the national curriculum focused on building AI/ML and data-related skills (pages 8 9).
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The national AI policy calls for establishing a Train-the-Trainer Program in AI skills to train new or upskill IT/science teachers as well as non-IT and science teachers. This is elaborated under policy priority area 1: 21st-century skills and high literacy (see the table on page 9).

fr1_title: Guidelines on the Ethical Development and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence (Rwanda)
fr1_justif: The AI development ethical guidelines set requirements for ethical AI systems including fairness and non-discrimination. The guidelines call for equality and non-discrimination requirements to ensure that AI systems do not treat individuals or groups unfairly. Fairness and non-discrimination are discussed in the principles section and the ethical AI requirements (pages 6 8). AI developers implementers and users need to ensure that individuals minority groups and protected classes in Rwanda maintain freedom from bias stigmatization and discrimination (p. 6).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The guidelines’ objectives state that AI systems must be developed to promote gender equality and eliminate gender bias and discrimination (page 4). The guidelines also propose ethical principles and associated values for AI. The principle of justice encourages AI developers and implementers to ensure that AI's target users are free from bias (page 6). In what the guidelines call the requirements of ethical AI systems they clarify that the fairness of an AI system can be achieved by implementing processes and measures to identify and address biases in the system and to avoid creating new biases or reinforcing existing ones (page 8).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: According to the guidelines the equality and non-discrimination requirement aims to ensure that AI systems do not treat individuals or groups unfairly based on their characteristics such as ethnicity gender sexual orientation or age whether intentionally or unintentionally. Fairness of an AI system can be achieved by implementing processes and measures to identify and address different biases in the AI system as well as measures to avoid creating new biases or reinforcing existing ones (page 8). The principle of Justice requires AI developers implementers and users to ensure that individuals minority groups and protected classes in Rwanda maintain freedom from bias stigmatization and discrimination (p. 6).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The Principle of Justice ‘Be Fair’ requires that the development implementation use and governance of AI systems be fair. AI developers implementers and users must ensure that individuals minority groups and protected classes in Rwanda are free from bias stigmatisation and discrimination. This principle also requires clarity in the process by which the AI system arrives at decisions or takes actions. AI developers and implementers are responsible for the outcomes and impacts of the AI systems they develop or implement. This requires those developing or implementing AI to conduct independent audits of AI systems for fairness (page 6).

fr1_title: Guidelines on the Ethical Development and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence (Rwanda)
fr1_justif: The national guidelines encourage the development of AI systems that promote gender equality and eliminate gender bias and discrimination. Also one of the key requirements of ethical systems under the Guidelines - Equality and Non-discrimination requires that AI systems do not treat individuals or groups of individuals unfairly based on their characteristics such as ethnicity gender sexual orientation or age whether intentionally or unintentionally (page 8).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: The national guidelines encourage the development of AI systems that promote gender equality and eliminate gender bias and discrimination (p.4). Further the ethical requirement of equality and non-discrimination requires that 'AI systems do not treat individuals or groups of individuals unfairly based on their characteristics such as ethnicity gender sexual orientation or age whether intentionally or unintentionally' (page 8).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: Guidelines on the Ethical Development and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence (Rwanda)
fr1_justif: Rwanda's AI Development Ethical Guidelines include 'human oversight and autonomy' as one of the main requirements to attain ethical AI. This indicator is addressed under the Principle of Autonomy (page 5) and the requirement of Human Oversight and Autonomy as one of the principles of the guidelines (page 8).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The guidelines under the Principle of Autonomy ‘Preserve Human Agency’ require AI systems to be designed developed and implemented in ways that allow humans to remain in control make their own decisions and avoid becoming overly dependent on or manipulated by AI systems (page 5). Additionally the guidelines recommend respecting human oversight and autonomy when developing implementing and using AI systems (page 8). They go on to state that it is therefore crucial that AI systems help and empower individuals and provide explicit support to promote their preferences.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The guidelines under the Principle of Autonomy ‘Preserve Human Agency’ require AI systems to be designed developed and implemented in ways that allow humans to remain in control make their own decisions and avoid becoming overly dependent on or manipulated by AI systems (page 5). Additionally the guidelines recommend that human oversight and autonomy be respected while developing implementing and using AI systems (page 8). According to the accountability principle roles and responsibilities should be clearly defined (p.7). However the guidelines do not provide for the identification of a responsible person to oversee intervene in AI decisions.

fr1_title: The National AI Policy (Rwanda)
fr1_justif: The national AI policy states that the public sector is the driver of AI development in Rwanda. One of the main areas is engaging local AI solution providers through innovation-friendly procurement processes. The government is encouraged to develop procurement guidelines that incentivise AI development nationwide. The Policy also recommends: Revision of ICT procurement guidelines and contract management practices for Cloud services and products development of procurement guidelines incentivising data sharing & access for public projects including ICT/data/Al components development of procurement guidelines of Al solutions in the public sector organisation of trainings for public procurement (page 4 tables on pages 11 13 and 15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Responsible AI Office at the Ministry of ICT and Innovation
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element1_justif: The national AI policy implementation plan includes AI procurement-specific interventions such as preparing revised ICT procurement guidelines developing procurement guidelines for AI solutions in the public sector and organising training for public procurement departments on using these guidelines to evaluate AI tools and solutions (National AI Policy tables on pages 13 - 15). It is unclear however if those should incorporate ethical social and technical considerations.
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
fr1_element4_justif: An emphasis is set on local industry and local solutions (p. 17 4). The national AI policy encourages the use of policy tools and the engagement of local AI solution providers through innovation-friendly procurement processes to improve the performance and efficiency of public services by leveraging AI-enabled solutions (National AI Policy paragraph 4 page 4). However local solutions are not prioritized nor AI sovereignty.

fr1_title: The National AI Policy (Rwanda)
fr1_justif: The Rwanda national AI policy captures policy recommendations among which reskilling the workforce with 21st-century AI is number one. The policy recommends improving public service delivery using AI. It also suggests that the government will invest in raising awareness of the benefits by piloting and demonstrating and building capacity to implement and manage AI projects delivering improved public services. The Government plans to build the public sector's capacity to raise awareness of AI's potential to improve public sector service delivery (page 4). Activities 49 to 52 (p.15) of the action plan target the development of skills in the public sector.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Responsible AI Office at the Ministry of ICT and Innovation
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The policy calls for upskilling public sector servants in general to raise awareness of and develop skills in AI's potential to improve public sector delivery. Strengthening digital and AI skills starting with the public sector is the policy's first priority area. This would be done in the spirit of delivering improved public services overall. The policy addresses the public sector generally and doesn't mention the judiciary specifically (page 4). Activities 49 is: Develop a capacity building program on the use of Al in public sector and 51: Organize trainings for public procurement departments (p.15)
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The policy recommended establishing the Responsible AI Office within the Ministry of ICT and Innovation to lead AI development and implementation involving multiple stakeholders (page 6).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The implementation plan recommends establishing and developing a framework for an industry-led Apprenticeship program to support a highly skilled workforce with 21st Century Skills and AI literacy. It then lists activities to be implemented to increase the number of professionals trained in data and AI-related skills the number of PhD/Master's/Bachelor's students graduating from AI and data science courses annually and the number of Rwanda-trained AI professionals working elsewhere etc. (Rwanda National AI Policy pages 7-10) while the ongoing nature of training is not clearly mentioned.

fr1_title: The National AI Policy (Rwanda)
fr1_justif: Rwanda's national AI policy has six priority areas among which building 21st-century skills and high AI literacy are listed as critical enablers. The national AI policy recommends reskilling the workforce with 21st-century AI and data skills. The government plans to implement a Tax Relief and Grants programme to help employers upskill and reskill their employees. This aligns with the development of a National Skills Building Programme that prioritises AI and data skills together with a Young Professionals/Apprenticeship Programme to develop AI talent and career opportunities in the knowledge economy (pages 3 & 7).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Responsible AI Office at the Ministry of ICT and Innovation
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: Rwanda’s National Artificial Intelligence Policy (2023) explicitly includes government-led measures to support reskilling and upskilling and sets out concrete actions and delivery responsibilities. Under Priority Area 1: “21st Century Skills & High AI Literacy” the Policy commits the Government to invest in a National Skills Building Programme that prioritises AI and data skills; to create a Young Professionals/Apprenticeship Programme; to establish a publicly and privately funded programme for AI skills building at university level (fellowships Master’s/PhD support and research placements); and to implement tax relief and grants for employers who upskill or reskill employees (for more see implementation plan tables on pages 7-19).
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: The national AI policy recommends reskilling the workforce with 21st-century AI and data skills and suggests that the government implement a Tax Relief and Grants programme to help employers upskill and reskill their employees (see table on page 7).
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Guidelines on the Ethical Development and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence (Rwanda)
fr1_justif: The ethical guidelines address safety and security through the ethical principle of non-maleficence: 'do no harm' (page 5) and the ethical requirement of safety (page 9). Furthermore Rwanda's AI Development Ethical Guidelines feature critical aspects for ethical AI development in Rwanda. These aspects include 'safety' which concerns ensuring that AI systems operate without harming the mental and physical well-being of humans the well-being of our society or the environment (page 9).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The safety requirement as part of the guidelines ensures that an AI system operates without causing harm to the mental and physical well-being of humans to the well-being of the society or the environment. The guidelines recommend that organisations involved in AI development prioritise safety and aim to reduce unintended outcomes and errors that may arise during AI system operation (page 9). It is stated that 'this requires a systematic approach to risk management that involves identifying assessingmitigating and treating risks relevant to the intended use context of the AI system' (p.9) which might involve the development of benchmarks while those are not directly mentioned.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The Rwanda AI development ethical guidelines recommend considering both direct and indirect risks as well as residual risks after mitigation actions with a systematic approach to risk management that involves identifying assessingmitigating and treating risks relevant to the intended use context of the AI system.Safety measures must be implemented throughout the entire lifecycle of the AI system from early planning and design to proactive prevention of safety issues and throughout operation (page 9).
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

fr1_title: Guidelines on the Ethical Development and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence (Rwanda)
fr1_justif: Rwanda's national AI development ethical guidelines include the Principle of Explicability or 'Operate Transparently' which requires that AI systems be transparent understandable and explainable to users and affected parties. AI systems should be designed and implemented so that users and stakeholders can understand how they work how they make decisions and what results they produce (page 6). Also the guidelines expect developers and implementers to provide relevant information to facilitate understanding of the system make impacted humans aware of the AI interaction and enable them to understand and challenge outcomes when necessary (page 9).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: Rwanda's national AI development ethical guidelines include the Principle of Explicability or 'Operate Transparently' which requires that AI systems be transparent understandable and explainable to users and affected parties. AI systems should be designed and implemented so that users and stakeholders can understand how they work how they make decisions and what results they produce (page 6). Furthermore the transparency requirement for AI systems expects developers and implementers to provide relevant information to facilitate understanding of the system make affected humans aware of the AI's interactions and enable them to understand and challenge outcomes when necessary (page 9).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: Under the Principle of Explicability of the guidelines this Principle requires 'AI developers and implementers should develop and implement AI systems with clear and comprehensible explanations for their data algorithms processes decision-making mechanisms and business models' (page 6).
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The AI ethical guidelines advocate for clear explanations of AI processes algorithms and decision-making mechanisms. Transparency is key to building and maintaining citizens’ trust in the developers of AI systems and AI systems themselves. Technological and business models explainability matters from an ethical standpoint. Technological transparency implies that AI systems including the data used to construct them are auditable comprehensible and interpretable by human beings at varying levels of comprehension and expertise (page 6). However it does not directly provides for rights for individuals to receive an explanation.

fr1_title: National Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Digital Learning (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The document addresses AI Literacy mainly in Section 7.1: AI Curriculum for Learners (p.23) which outlines teaching AI concepts hands-on AI activities critical thinking about AI and ethical awareness. It also appears in Section 8.1: AI Skills Training for Educators (p.25) ensuring teachers can teach AI effectively. Foundational AI literacy terms and definitions are provided in the Glossary (p.4–5) supporting understanding of key AI concepts used in learning. The explicit goal is to Advanced integration of AI with entire educational systems facilitating independent learning and potential shifts in educational paradigms (p. 7).
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes clear recommendations for curriculum reforms. Section 7.1 “AI Curriculum for Learners” (p.23) outlines integrating AI concepts and skills into curricula across K–12 higher education and lifelong learning. It recommends hands-on AI learning critical thinking about AI ethical considerations and continuous curriculum updates—indicating explicit curriculum reform guidance across all education levels. The explicit goal is to Advanced integration of AI with entire educational systems facilitating independent learning and potential shifts in educational paradigms (p. 7).
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The document recommends establishing and expanding AI-related programs within formal education. Section 7.1 (p.23) calls for integrating AI concepts skills and hands-on AI activities into formal curricula across K–12 higher education and TVET. Section 8.1 (p.25) further supports creating AI training programs for educators. While it does not mandate new institutions it clearly promotes developing structured AI programs within existing formal education systems. The explicit goal is to Advanced integration of AI with entire educational systems facilitating independent learning and potential shifts in educational paradigms (p. 7).
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes explicit provisions for teacher training and resources. Section 8.1 “AI Skills Training for Educators” (p.25) outlines needs-based AI training active learning and continuous professional development. Section 3.2 (p.16) recommends AI tools to support lesson planning and content creation. Section 2.1–2.2 (p.13–14) highlights AI-generated materials and resource recommendation engines confirming strong support for educator training and resources.

fr1_title: Guidelines: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Public (2025) (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The Generative Artificial Intelligence Guidelines for Public address AI-facilitated misinformation and violence in Section 5: “Generative AI Risks and Potential Mitigations” (pp. 13–15). It warns that deepfakes and misrepresentation can enable scams fraud and identity theft and that malicious GenAI manipulation can pose safety threats to public security. The document proposes safeguards such as watermarking content moderation dataset filtering output verification and fact-checking to detect and prevent harmful biased or deceptive content promoting transparency and user vigilance to mitigate misinformation and related harms.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: In Section 5: “Generative AI Risks and Potential Mitigations” (pp. 13–15) the document addresses these risks under “Deepfakes and Misrepresentation”; “Safety Threats” and “Misinformation and Hallucination.” It recommends measures such as watermarking AI-generated content; content moderation and filtering systems dataset; filtering output verification; and fact-checking; to detect and prevent the spread of deceptive or harmful material. These provisions explicitly aim to ensure GenAI tools are not weaponized for harassment; fraud or public harm; reinforcing safe and ethical AI use.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: It includes provisions assigning responsibilities to AI developers and service providers to ensure robust content moderation and transparency in managing harmful content.In Section 5: “Generative AI Risks and Potential Mitigations” (pp. 13–15) under “Safety Threats” and “Misinformation and Hallucination” the document recommends that platforms and GenAI developers implement content moderation and filtering systems verify both user prompts and model outputs and regularly update moderation tools to counter emerging threats. It also advises output verification content labeling and watermarking to make AI-generated content transparent and traceable—ensuring accountability in how harmful content is detected managed and disclosed.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: AI Ethics Principles (September 2023) (Version 1.0) (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The document address Access to Redress and Remedy primarily through ethical guidance rather than binding obligations. In the AI Ethics Checklist – Deploy and Monitor phase (page 46) entities are asked to ensure: “mechanisms that allow for redress in case of harm or adverse impact” and to “provide information to end-users/third parties about opportunities for redress.” These provisions promote transparency and accountability by requiring organizations to establish internal accessible grievance mechanisms for AI-related harms.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The document reference remedy and redress mechanisms though not formal judicial procedures.In the “Deploy and Monitor” phase of the AI Ethics Checklist (page 46) it asks whether entities have:“Established mechanisms that allow for redress in case of the occurrence of any harm or adverse impact” and“Mechanisms that provide information to end-users/third parties about opportunities for redress.”These provisions indicate a non-judicial organizational-level redress mechanism intended to handle AI-related harms internally.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: The document includes provisions related to state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms though framed as guidance rather than enforceable mandates.In the “Roles and Responsibilities” section (page 29) SDAIA is tasked to:“Conduct investigations and audits and monitor compliance with this Framework with the support of the National Regulatory Authorities.”Additionally the “Compliance” section (page 32) notes that SDAIA may “follow up and measure the level of commitment and compliance of registered entities” and “assist entities in reviewing annual reports and make recommendations.”
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes recommendations for entities to establish accessible grievance and complaint mechanisms primarily as part of ethical accountability rather than legal obligation.In Principle 6 – Transparency & Explainability (page 23) it states that:“The model should establish a process mechanism to log and address issues and complaints that arise to be able to resolve them in a transparent and explainable manner.”Additionally in the AI Ethics Checklist – Deploy and Monitor phase (page 46) it asks whether entities have:“Established mechanisms that allow for redress in case of the occurrence of any harm or adverse impact.”

fr1_title: AI Ethics Principles (September 2023) (Version 1.0) (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The document addresses Environmental Impact under Principle 4 – Social & Environmental Benefits (pp. 19–21). It requires AI systems to prevent harm to humans and the environment promote sustainability and measure resource and energy consumption. It directs developers to ensure AI supports ecological responsibility and continuous assessment of environmental effects in line with sustainable development goals.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: The framework indirectly addresses the prevention of resource-intensive AI by advising developers to measure and maintain acceptable energy consumption and ensure AI systems do not harm environmental sustainability (pp. 19–20). While it promotes ecological responsibility it does not specify binding limits or reporting requirements on energy or e-waste.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: AI Ethics Principles (September 2023) (Version 1.0) (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The document addresses Fairness and Non-discrimination through Principle 1 – Fairness which requires AI systems to eliminate bias discrimination and stigmatization across the entire AI System Lifecycle (pp. 12–13). It mandates fairness-aware design identification of affected and vulnerable groups and selection of fairness assessment metrics during the Plan and Design phase (p. 13). The framework further requires training models on representative bias-cleansed data careful handling of sensitive attributes and continuous monitoring of fairness thresholds during Build Validate and Deploy stages (pp. 13–15). These measures aim to ensure AI outcomes are inclusive objective and non-discriminatory.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The document explicitly promotes fair and equitable outcomes through Principle 1 – Fairness. It requires AI systems to eliminate bias discrimination and stigmatization in design data development deployment and use (pp. 12–13). During the Plan and Design phase entities must identify affected and vulnerable groups define fairness objectives and select appropriate fairness metrics (p. 13). The framework further mandates training models on representative bias-cleansed datasets careful handling of sensitive attributes and defining fairness thresholds (pp. 13–14). Continuous fairness monitoring and reassessment during deployment is also required to prevent disproportionate harm to specific groups (pp. 14–15).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The document explicitly addresses the prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying societal biases under Principle 1 – Fairness. It requires eliminating bias discrimination and stigmatization across the AI System Lifecycle and explicitly references protected characteristics such as gender race religion age and other sensitive attributes (pp. 12–13). The framework mandates fairness-aware design identification of sensitive attributes and assessment of disproportionate harm to affected or historically disadvantaged groups during the Plan and Design phase (p. 13). It further requires bias-cleansed representative training data justification for any use of sensitive attributes and continuous fairness monitoring.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The document assigns clear lifecycle-wide obligations to AI developers and deployers to identify measure and mitigate bias. Under Principle 1 – Fairness entities must implement fairness-aware design identify affected and vulnerable groups; and define fairness metrics and thresholds during the Plan and Design phase (pp. 12–13). During Prepare Input Data; data must be assessed for quality representativeness and bias and sensitive attributes; or their proxies must be excluded or explicitly justified (pp. 13–14). The Build and Validate phase requires fairness metric evaluation; justification of trade-offs; and corrective action if thresholds are not met (pp. 14–15).

fr1_title: AI Ethics Principles (September 2023) (Version 1.0) (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The policy emphasizes Human Oversight and Determination as part of Principle 7 – Accountability & Responsibility (pp. 25–27) and in the AI Ethics Checklist (p. 41). The framework requires AI systems to be human-controlled ensuring decisions are monitored governed and open to intervention by authorized users. It mandates clear assignment of accountability across the AI lifecycle defining oversight processes KPIs and fallback mechanisms to prevent overreliance on automation and preserve human judgment in decision-making.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The policy explicitly promotes meaningful human control over AI systems. In Principle 7 – Accountability & Responsibility (pp. 25–27) and the AI Ethics Checklist (p. 41) the framework requires building human-controlled AI systems where decisions are monitored governed and open to human intervention. It also warns against overreliance on automation and mandates mechanisms for human oversight and fallback actions ensuring AI assists rather than replaces human judgment especially in high-impact contexts.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The policy addresses the prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors. Under Principle 5 – Reliability & Safety (p. 22) and Principle 7 – Accountability & Responsibility (pp. 25–27) the document specifies that AI systems involving irreversible or life-and-death decisions must trigger human oversight and final determination. It further requires human-controlled governance structures and authorized user intervention mechanisms ensuring that ethical judgment and human review remain integral in critical applications such as healthcare and public safety.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The policy explicitly assigns obligations to designate responsible individuals for AI oversight and accountability. The Roles and Responsibilities section (pp. 29–31) mandates entities to appoint officers such as the Chief Data Officer (CDO) Chief Compliance Officer (CCO/CO) and Responsible AI Officer (RAIO) to oversee ethical implementation monitor AI systems and intervene when necessary. These roles ensure clear accountability and human responsibility for AI-driven decisions across all organizational levels.

fr1_title: Guidelines: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Public (2025) (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The document incorporates multiple elements of AI Impact Assessments tailored specifically to generative AI risks. It requires structured risk evaluation and harm analysis under Privacy & Security (p.11) including “privacy impact assessment” and “risk management assessment” for GenAI models. It mandates reviewing data quality bias and discriminatory outputs within Fairness (p.8) reflecting known GenAI vulnerabilities. Reliability & Safety (p.9) addresses safety controls hallucination prevention and system robustness. Risks & Mitigations (pp.13–15) require output verification misinformation detection and ongoing monitoring—all core risk areas.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The document promotes proactive risk management by requiring several pre-deployment impact checks. Fairness mandates assessing bias and impacts on minority groups before use (p.8). Reliability & Safety requires evaluating system risks and embedding harm-prevention mechanisms prior to deployment (p.9). Privacy & Security requires conducting “privacy impact assessment and risk management assessment” and revisiting them regularly (p.11). Social & Environmental Benefits requires avoiding societal or environmental harm (p.12).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The document assigns obligations to developers and users to assess and mitigate risks to individuals and society functioning as impact-assessment duties even not in formal way:Fairness requires developers and users to “carefully test GenAI models to ensure no bias and understand training data” (p.8) obligating risk identification for affected groups.Reliability & Safety requires assessing system risks harm-prevention mechanisms and triggering human oversight (p.9).Privacy & Security explicitly requires conducting “privacy impact assessment and risk management assessment” and revisiting them regularly (p.11).Social & Environmental Benefits obliges actors to avoid societal or environmental harm (p.12).
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Guidelines for Government (Version 1) (2024) (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The document supports Public Sector Skills Development by requiring continuous training for government employees on GenAI use risks and data-handling practices. Appendix 2 (p. 23–24) mandates training courses to build awareness technical skills and the ability to review AI outputs. Section 4.3 (p. 12) stresses educational initiatives to enhance staff understanding of GenAI while Appendix 1 (p. 12–17) shows practical skill-building in content creation analysis translation and project planning.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The document does not include provisions for a government-wide strategy for upskilling or reskilling public servants or members of the judiciary. Its training references are limited to entity-level operational guidance tied only to responsible GenAI use. Appendix 2 – “Training and Education” (p.23) mentions “continuous training courses” but these are practice-oriented and apply only within each entity not across government. Section 4.3 – Government Entities (p.12) encourages educational initiatives but does not set national coordination mandatory AI literacy or judiciary-specific development.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The document assigns internal roles related to oversight and responsible AI use but it does not explicitly establish “AI champions” teams dedicated to innovation or expert leadership.Section 4.1 – Data Management Office assigns responsibility for approving GenAI tools auditing data quality liaising with legal experts and addressing privacy concerns (p. 11).Section 4.3 – Government Entities requires entities to establish clear policies and provide educational initiatives (p. 12).Section 4.2 – Users emphasizes that individuals must stay informed and report issues (p. 12).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes provisions for ongoing professional development.It explicitly recommends continuous training to keep up with AI tool developments addressing both technical and ethical Appendix 2 – “Training and Education” (p.23) requires that “employees undergo continuous training courses… covering the technical aspects of generative artificial intelligence tools to enhance workflow efficiency” demonstrating an explicit expectation of ongoing upskilling.Section 4.2 – Users (p.12) further requires that “users stay informed about the latest developments in the capabilities and limitations of generative artificial intelligence tools” reinforcing continuous professional learning.

fr1_title: National Strategy for Data & AI (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The Strategy links AI to reskilling / upskilling by prioritizing development of Data & AI skills specialists and experts to meet future labor-market needs. It highlights AI literacy machine-learning training programs STEM and AI bootcamps and the creation of Data & AI educational tracks and certification programs to build a domestic talent pipeline. These appear in Section 3.0 (p. 10) and Section 4.1 – Objective 2 (p. 21).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Saudi Data & AI Authority (SDAIA)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy explicitly focuses on workforce reskilling and upskilling to address labor market changes driven by Data and AI. It identifies three workforce groups—Data & AI experts Data & AI specialists and the general workforce whose AI literacy must be strengthened—and proposes targeted training efforts for each (p.21). Measures include professional training programs certification schemes recognizing professionals developing Data and AI skills and cooperation with academic institutions to expand training opportunities (p.22). These initiatives aim to equip the workforce with the skills needed to adapt to evolving job market demands created by AI.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: The strategy supports financial incentives for developing Data and AI skills but does not explicitly provide direct financial support for workers participating in reskilling programs. It proposes specialist educational tracks supported by scholarships and professional training to develop local Data and AI talent (p.22). However these measures primarily target students and specialist talent development rather than offering explicit financial incentives or subsidies for workers undertaking reskilling programs.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: AI Ethics Principles (September 2023) (Version 1.0) (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The policy address Safety and Security through Principle 2 – Privacy & Security (pp. 15–17) and Principle 5 – Reliability & Safety (pp. 21–23). These sections require AI systems to be designed with security-by-design data protection and risk-management mechanisms to prevent cyberattacks data breaches and system failures. They also mandate continuous monitoring safety self-assessments and fallback plans to ensure reliability robustness and resilience. Collectively these measures protect individuals and society from potential harms caused by unsafe or insecure AI systems.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The document establishes quality and reliability requirements to ensure AI systems operate accurately and consistently. Under the Reliability & Safety principle AI systems must adhere to predefined specifications and function as intended with mechanisms ensuring technical robustness and preventing harmful outcomes (Principle 5). It requires rigorous testing validation and reassessment of AI models using appropriate methodologies and stress-testing scenarios to verify system behavior under extreme conditions (Build and Validate). Continuous monitoring of system performance and functionality is also required to ensure ongoing reliability and alignment with the designed operational framework (Deploy and Monitor).
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The policy explicitly requires safeguards and fallback procedures to mitigate harm from AI failures. In Principle 5 – Reliability & Safety (pp. 21–23) it mandates establishing standards protocols and fallback plans to handle system errors unexpected behavior or adversarial attacks. The AI Ethics Checklist (pp. 42–45) further asks whether entities have tested fallback plans risk management strategies and predefined procedures for AI system failures. These provisions ensure emergency preparedness and minimize harm to users and society.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The policy clearly requires pre-deployment testing validation and documentation to ensure technical robustness. In Principle 5 – Reliability & Safety (pp. 21–23) it mandates rigorous testing validation and reassessment of AI systems before deployment including stress testing under extreme scenarios and stakeholder sign-off. The AI System Lifecycle (pp. 9–11) further integrates build validate and monitor phases ensuring continuous documentation and verification.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: The policy includes explicit security obligations to protect AI systems from cyberattacks and manipulation. In Principle 2 – Privacy & Security (pp. 14–17) it requires that AI systems be designed with security-by-design data protection and cybersecurity measures to withstand attacks and prevent unauthorized access or data breaches. It also mandates risk management assessments data classification encryption and continuous monitoring to ensure resilience against adversarial interference and manipulation throughout the AI system lifecycle.

fr1_title: AI Ethics Principles (September 2023) (Version 1.0) (Saudi Arabia)
fr1_justif: The Principles of AI Ethics address Transparency and Explainability in Principle 6 (pp. 23–24) emphasizing clarity traceability and justification of AI decisions. It requires AI systems to document data algorithms and decision logic ensuring outcomes are understandable and auditable. Entities must provide stakeholders access to explanations maintain logs of failures and enable complaint mechanisms. Annex A (p. 38) adds “AI Methods Explanation Report” and “Algorithm Auditing” tools to enhance interpretability and oversight.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The Principles of AI Ethics include explicit provisions promoting clarity on AI system operations purpose data sources and decision logic in Principle 6 – Transparency & Explain-ability (pp. 23–24). It requires that AI systems be traceable auditable and explainable with documented data processes and rationale for decisions. It also mandates information sections and logs to inform stakeholders how outcomes are produced—directly fostering public trust through openness and communication.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The Principles of AI Ethics assign such obligations in Principle 6 – Transparency & Explainability (pp. 23–24) and Accountability & Responsibility (pp. 25–26). They require AI system owners and developers to provide clear contextual explanations of AI outcomes to affected stakeholders ensure traceability of decisions and maintain documentation and logs for audit and redress. These duties apply particularly where AI decisions may significantly affect individuals or communities reinforcing accountability in high-stakes contexts.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The Principles of AI Ethics (SDAIA 2023) include such provisions under Principle 6 – Transparency & Explainability (pp. 23–24) and Deploy & Monitor phase of the AI Ethics Checklist (p. 45). They require entities to inform end-users of the reasons criteria and benefits behind AI decisions and ensure accessible explanations of outcomes. The framework also mandates mechanisms for complaints feedback and redress enabling individuals to request and understand how AI decisions affecting them were made.

fr1_justif: The Senegal national AI strategy explicitly addresses AI literacy by planning to integrate AI into the education system under strategic orientation 1 trainings for software development include levels from preschool to higher education (P. 7 and P.49) and focus on teachers and trainers to implement AI awareness (P. 73)

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Development Strategy (Senegal)
fr1_justif: The Senegal AI strategy provides for ethical impact and risk assessment of AI systems at the level of regulatory principles and future mechanisms. Strategic Orientation 4 states that developers and providers should assess the potential negative consequences of AI applications on human rights and fundamental freedoms and adopt precautionary approach based on appropriate risk prevention and reduction measures (P. 61) and action 4.3 (P. 62) calls for categorising types of AI according to potential risks to human rights and societal well being. Action 4.15 then proposes to “define the types of AI and deployment areas that are required to conduct an impact assessment” (P. 63).
