fr1_justif: Action 2.16 establishes a structured procurement mechanism by mandating the creation and implementation of a program to accelerate public procurement of AI including consultations to identify public-sector challenges followed by calls for expressions of interest directed at AI stakeholders to propose solutions (p. 9). This is reinforced by Action 2.17 which provides for the establishment of a dedicated organization within the State to facilitate procurement with an AI liaison in each ministry as well as Action 2.18 which promotes recurring procurement mechanisms such as annual calls and incentives and Action 2.19 which introduces legal and procedural tools such as regulatory sandboxes and simplified procurement processes.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Communication Telecommunications and Digital Economy (MCTEN)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Development Strategy (Senegal)
fr1_justif: Senegal’s national AI strategy outlines public-sector skills development with explicit references to training decision-makers and capacity-building for the judicial executive and legislative branches. Under Strategic Direction 1 Human Capital (P. 49) the strategy sets a goal to train around 90000 Senegalese in software development and AI by 2028 and states that this includes “covering the capacity-building needs of public governance judicial executive legislative branches. It also specifies “5% capacity building for decision-makers and key players from the public sector private sector and civil society central and decentralized level i.e. 4500 people” (P. 7). Further Action 1.9 calls for “a series of awareness-raising seminars for key players in Senegal on the opportunities risks and challenges of AI… prioritizing the multidisciplinary nature of the participants” and then lists participants including public decision-makers regulatory authorities (P. 51).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Communication Telecommunications and Digital Economy (MCTEN)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy makes explicit references to training decision-makers and capacity-building for the judicial executive and legislative branches. Under Strategic Direction 1 Human Capital (P. 49). However the details on its applications and risks are not specified.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation

fr1_element3_justif: The strategy outlines that capacity building should be for all levels of degree; qualification; and certification; training in initial and continuing formats for professionals; trainers; and decision makers (P. 7); but does not create requirements for continuous trainings.

fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Development Strategy (Senegal)
fr1_justif: Senegal’s National AI Strategy launched in 2023 and coordinated by the Ministry of Communication Telecommunications and the Digital Economy (MCTEN) explicitly incorporates human capital development as a core pillar:It sets ambitious targets to train tens of thousands of people in data science and AI by 2028 (about 90000 individuals) to build national capacity and prepare the workforce for AI-related opportunities. The strategy outlines actions to develop training programs for trainers create national and regional AI training institutes and establish an observatory for skills needs and training programs to ensure continuous alignment with labour needs.

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2025–2030
fr1_justif: The Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia 2025-2030 addresses AI literacy through Measure 3.2 which mandates integration of AI into primary and secondary curricula interdisciplinary AI projects and AI-enabled tools in classrooms. It sets targets for teacher training and certification and literacy monitoring. The education chapter (Section 3) also emphasizes ethical AI use personalized learning and continuous professional development for teachers. Under the implementation plan it also measures the amount of universities currently having AI Curricula in their program and sets a target to increase the number by 2030 (p. 49).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Council for AI
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: Section 6.3 explicitly highlights managerial effects on the education system through integration of AI into primary and secondary curricula reinforcing the formal adoption of AI literacy. Under the implementation plan it also measures the amount of universities currently having AI in their program and sets a target to increase the number (p. 49). Combined with Sections 3.2.1 and 3.3 the strategy establishes AI education in primary secondary and tertiary levels including curriculum updates teacher training interdisciplinary courses and standardized programs in higher education while emphasizing ethical AI use and preparation for AI-enabled classrooms.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia 2025–2030 includes specific measures for establishing AI-related programs within formal education. Section 3.2.1 details undergraduate and master’s programs in AI machine learning and data science at six universities across Belgrade; Niš; Novi; Sad and Kragujevac. Section 3.1 mandates new study programs elective and mandatory AI modules and doctoral-level courses supported by laboratories research centers and industry collaboration. Section 3.3 emphasizes standardization and inclusion of AI programs in non-technical faculties.
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia 2025-2030 explicitly mandates teacher training and provision of resources for AI education. Section 3.2 describes training teachers to apply AI in primary and secondary classrooms modernize teaching methods and promote ethical interdisciplinary and innovative learning. Section 3.2.4 emphasizes continuous professional development AI certification programs and use of AI to support personalized learning complex assessment and critical thinking.

fr1_title: Ethical Guidelines for Development Implementation and Use of Robust and Accountable Artificial Intelligence (Serbia)
fr1_justif: The Ethical Guidelines for Development Implementation and Use of Robust and Accountable AI address children’s rights by emphasizing the protection of vulnerable groups including children (p.12-13 Section 3.3). AI systems must be safe reliable and secure prevent harm and avoid malicious use. Any damage must be repaired promptly with legal compensation. The guidelines integrate civil criminal and ethical obligations to ensure AI does not cause physical mental or property harm highlighting the special care required for children in AI deployment and use.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The guidelines emphasize that AI systems must be safe secure and prevent harm and highlight protection of vulnerable groups including children (p.12-13 Section 3.3). However they do not provide detailed child-specific measures such as data anonymization encryption or explicit privacy protocols for AI interactions. They focus on general safety and liability rather than comprehensive provisions on children’s personal data and privacy.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: The guidelines require Al systems to be safe reliable and secure and to prevent malicious use that could cause harm (p.12-13 Section 3.3). They explicitly highlight the protection of vulnerable groups including children from harm. However they do not provide detailed child-specific measures addressing targeted advertising manipulation or inappropriate content so only some aspects of prevention are covered.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2025–2030
fr1_justif: The strategy addresses Cultural and Linguistic Diversity primarily through the national program for Serbian language technologies (Sections 4.3 6.4). It supports AI development for natural language processing language models annotated/unannotated corpora speech recognition and generative AI ensuring Serbian is represented in digital services education and public administration. Measures include digital infrastructure archives pilot projects and training programs (Sections 4.3 6.4) preserving linguistic heritage and improving accessibility while enabling AI-mediated interaction in the local language.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Council for AI
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy addresses linguistic and cultural diversity primarily through Measure 4.3 - National program for the development of language technologies for Serbian (Section 4.3 pages 52-54) and Section 6.4 on effects of measures focusing on the preservation and promotion of the Serbian language and culture in digital environments. It covers language-specific AI development text and audio corpora and public administration applications but does not explicitly address multiple global cultures or a broad range of languages beyond Serbian.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: Measures 4.3 and 6.4 focuses on developing language technologies tailored to the linguistic specifics of Serbian explicitly aiming to increase the presence and influence of Serbian in the digital age and preserve Serbian culture history traditions literature and journalism through improved access to digital services in Serbian. This implicitly addresses the risk of AI-driven linguistic erasure and dominance by major languages. However the measure does not explicitly require safeguards against cultural stereotyping bias or tools that favor dominant cultures nor does it set concrete anti-stereotype or diversity-protection standards.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
fr1_element3_justif: The strategy emphasizes the creation and use of annotated and unannotated Serbian language corpora and the development of AI systems for public administration and education (Measure 4.3 pages 52–54). This indirectly promotes training AI on datasets relevant to the Serbian language and local context. However it does not explicitly assign obligations to developers or users nor does it address adaptability to multiple cultural and linguistic contexts beyond Serbian.

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2025–2030
fr1_justif: It notes that AI development requires a “large amount of electrical energy” and stresses that sustainability cannot rely only on renewable energy production but also on “energy-efficient solutions” and efficient use of AI technologies. Environmental protection is embedded as a core ethical constraint stating that AI “must not negatively affect the environment” (Section 3.3) and reaffirmed in Section 6.7 which requires continuous impact assessments monitoring of AI systems and prevention of harmful effects including environmental ones.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Council for AI
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy emphasize the environmental impact of Al including energy consumption and the need for energy-efficient solutions (Sections 3.3 Prospects and Challenges and 4.2 - General and Specific Objectives). However it does not provide detailed measures on limiting e-waste or enforcing smaller efficient Al models. The focus is mainly on promoting energy-efficient Al and renewable energy use.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: Ethical Guidelines for Development Implementation and Use of Robust and Accountable Artificial Intelligence (Serbia)
fr1_justif: Section 3.4 Fairness defines fairness as the protection of rights and integrity against discrimination and emphasizes that AI systems must prevent discrimination (including against vulnerable groups such as persons with disabilities). It describes both substantive fairness (equal opportunities no unfair prejudice) and procedural fairness (ability to challenge AI decisions transparently). Section 4.5 Diversity non-discrimination and equality incorporates the principle into broader ethical requirements highlighting equal treatment and protection from bias as essential for responsible AI.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The document explicitly promotes fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems. Section 3.4 Fairness states that AI systems must prevent discrimination and protect individuals and groups from unfair prejudice discrimination and stigmatization. It also emphasizes that AI systems should provide equal opportunities in access to education goods services and technologies and should not mislead users when making decisions. In addition Section 4.5 Diversity Non-discrimination and Equality highlights that AI systems must incorporate diversity and inclusion throughout their lifecycle and be designed in ways that prevent discrimination or marginalization of vulnerable groups including persons with disabilities.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The document explicitly addresses the prevention of discrimination and bias in AI systems. Section 3.4 Fairness states that AI systems must prevent discrimination and protect individuals and groups from unfair prejudice and stigmatization. It specifically refers to discrimination based on characteristics such as race sex gender sexual orientation gender identity age ethnicity religion political beliefs social origin language disability and other personal characteristics. In addition Section 4.5 Diversity Non-discrimination and Equality emphasizes that AI systems must incorporate inclusion and diversity throughout their lifecycle and be designed to avoid marginalization or discrimination against vulnerable groups including PWD
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The document emphasizes the importance of fairness diversity and non-discrimination in AI systems. Section 3.4 Fairness requires that AI systems prevent discrimination and protect individuals and groups from unfair prejudice and stigmatization while Section 4.5 Diversity Non-discrimination and Equality states that reliable and accountable AI systems should allow for inclusion and diversity throughout their lifecycle and be designed to avoid marginalization of vulnerable groups. However the document does not explicitly assign obligations to developers or deployers to systematically identify measure and mitigate sources of bias across all stages of the AI lifecycle such as data collection model development and deployment.

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2025–2030
fr1_justif: The Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia 2025-2030 addresses gender equality by mandating that AI development deployment and education provide no preferential treatment based on gender. 'Legal and Regulatory Challenges emphasize' equal rights and opportunities for all genders in AI-related activities ensuring that women and men have the same access to education professional development and participation in AI programs and initiatives (pp. 32-33).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Council for AI
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: The document explicitly states that AI must be developed and used in a manner that prevents discrimination and respects equality among individuals. It specifies that in the education development and application of AI solutions no one should receive preferential treatment based on gender race nationality or other affiliations including gender identity or orientation. This establishes a clear expectation that AI systems should not perpetuate discrimination or bias based on gender (pp. 32-33).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: The document states that the development and use of AI must prevent discrimination and respect equality among individuals. It specifies that in the education development and application of AI solutions no one should receive preferential treatment based on gender race nationality religion gender identity or other affiliations and that minority groups must have equal rights. However while it establishes the principle of equality and non-discrimination it does not explicitly assign concrete obligations or responsibilities to specific entities developing or deploying AI systems to ensure gender equality.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2025–2030
fr1_justif: Section 3.3 highlights the need for monitoring intervention and control procedures throughout the AI lifecycle especially in education and employment acknowledging risks that require human intervention. Sections 6.7 commit to establishing a legal and institutional framework continuous monitoring of all AI systems impact assessments before deployment and oversight by competent authorities with humans 'as the measure” guiding AI use.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Council for AI
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The document promotes meaningful human control over AI systems by requiring monitoring intervention and control mechanisms throughout the AI lifecycle particularly in sensitive domains such as education and employment (Section 3.3). It further commits to impact assessments prior to deployment continuous monitoring of AI systems and institutional oversight by competent authorities explicitly emphasizing that humans should remain “the measure” guiding AI use (Section 6.7).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: Sections 3.3 and 6.7 highlight risks of over-reliance on Al bias and impacts on human rights emphasizing the need for human oversight in sensitive areas such as education employment and decision-making affecting citizens. Section 5 (Goal 1) establishes a legal and institutional framework to monitor Al deployment. However the strategy does not explicitly prohibit full automation in specific sectors like law enforcement or medicine nor mandate mandatory human review of Al outputs in these domains.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: Section 5 (Goal 1) and Section 7 (Coordination Mechanism) establish institutional oversight with the Ministry and the Council for Artificial Intelligence responsible for monitoring reporting and coordinating Al deployment. Sections 3.3 and 6.7 emphasize human oversight and ethical use. However the strategy does not explicitly require entities deploying Al to designate specific responsible individuals personally accountable for Al decisions so individual accountability is not fully addressed.

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2025–2030
fr1_justif: Measure 6.1 explicitly requires that during the implementation of AI incentives in the public sector impact assessments are considered for systems that may be classified as high-risk linking these assessments to safety security and reliability requirements. Section 3.3 outlines key AI risks including algorithmic bias discrimination privacy violations lack of transparency and insufficient lifecycle control. Section 6.7 further outlines combating challenges in data protection potential negative impacts on lifestyles and the safety of citizens and the state by requiring continuous impact assessments and reevaluation of how potential AI solutions are used before deployment.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Council for AI
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy partially addresses proactive risk management. Societal and ethical impacts are covered in Section 3.3  through discussions of bias discrimination privacy and transparency. High-risk systems are targeted in Measure 6.1 which requires impact assessments for AI deployment in critical public sector systems. Environmental impacts are noted in Section 3.3 regarding energy consumption and efficiency. and only but not covered in the impact assessments. Therefore there is ne provision fully mandating evaluation of all impacts the question listed before deployment.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

fr1_title: Ethical Guidelines for Development Implementation and Use of Robust and Accountable Artificial Intelligence (Serbia)
fr1_justif: The document identifies AI related labour harms by classifying employment related systems such as recruitment hiring evaluation monitoring promotion dismissal and labour management as high risk AI systems (p. 8) recognizing their impact on workers’ rights and conditions. It further defines high risk systems as those affecting human integrity and rights requiring analysis and impact assessment (p. 7) linking employment related AI use to heightened oversight. These concerns are operationalized through stakeholder engagement mechanisms requiring that employees are informed of AI impacts trained accordingly and that employees and trade unions can access information on relevant high risk systems (pp. 33–34).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2025–2030
fr1_justif: The strategy explicitly requires that public procurement contracts include mandatory obligations for private providers to transfer data to state authorities including specifications on structure format and timelines (p. 21) and further proposes the use of procurement law to impose enforceable obligations on contractors in cases of public-interest services (p. 44). In addition it promotes the representation of domestic AI solutions in public procurement as a strategic tool for strengthening national AI capacity (p. 37)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Information System for Planning Implementation Monitoring Public Policy Coordination and Reporting
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2025–2030
fr1_justif: Measure 5.1 focuses on capacity building in data management and data engineering including structured training programs for public servants as a prerequisite for AI use. Measure 5.3 supports skills development through workshops trainings and expert consultations on data standardization and AI-compatible formats.  Measure 6.2 directly targets AI skills by organizing trainings and pilot projects for public employees with quantified targets for trained staff. Section 6.1 (Effects of measures) highlights institutional learning coordination and the role of the AI Council in strengthening long-term skills.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Council for AI
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy partially addresses this statement. It includes provisions for upskilling and reskilling civil servants through Measure 5.1 (capacity building in data management ETL and AI tools) and Measure 6.2 (trainings and workshops on AI applications). However it does not explicitly present a single government-wide strategy unifying all training for both civil servants and judiciary covering foundational AI concepts applications and risks in a fully integrated manner.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: Section 6.1 (Effects) and Measure 6.2mention the creation of institutional roles such as the Al Council and dedicated teams to coordinate Al implementation and provide guidance. These roles support governance ethics and pilot projects fostering responsible Al use.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: Measure 5.1 establishes continuous capacity-building programs for civil servants in data management and Al skills while Measure 6.2 requires workshops pilot projects and periodic training to ensure staff stay updated on Al applications. Section 6.1 (Effects) emphasizes institutional learning and adaptation to evolving Al technologies.

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2025–2030
fr1_justif: in Section “Labor Market and Education Implications” it recognises AI-driven automation and calls for timely reskilling and continuous employee training. Measure 3.4 establishes informal AI training requalification programs certification and labour market monitoring (2025–2030). Measure 6.4 ) links AI adoption incentives with targets for upskilled workers in AI-enabled environments (5000 by 2030) and under Measure f) raise the number of participants in AI educational campaigns and workshops (also 5000 by 2030) to increase society's overall AI capabilities. Section 6.2 also notes support for professional development and AI training programs will enable employees to acquire new skills and knowledge thereby increasing productivity.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Council for AI
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy addresses reskilling and upskilling in the context of Al through Measure 3.4 Informal Education for the Use of Al-Based Solutions which includes designing courses workshops and requalification programs for employees as well as providing financial and organizational support (also acknowledged under Measure 6.3 and Section 6.2). However it does not explicitly establish government-funded or subsidized programs nationwide specifically for all workers; the focus is mainly on courses workshops and targeted support rather than a comprehensive subsidy or funding scheme.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy addresses financial support in Measure 3.4 - Informal Education for the Use of Al-Based Solutions which mentions providing financial and organizational support for courses workshops and training for employees needing Al skills. However it does not explicitly provide direct incentives or subsidies targeted specifically at individual workers participating in reskilling programs so the question is only partially addressed.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
fr1_element3_justif: The Strategy addresses this aspect in Measure 6.4 - Incentives for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Economy which includes indicators (5000 upskilled workers by 2030) for the number of upskilled workers operating in Al-enabled environments and targets for companies to achieve implementing Al solutions. This implies that companies are expected to support workforce training. However the Strategy does not explicitly mandate or require companies to invest in training to mitigate job displacement so the measure only partially covers the requirement.

fr1_title: Ethical Guidelines for Development Implementation and Use of Robust and Accountable Artificial Intelligence (Serbia)
fr1_justif: Section 3.3 Prohibition to cause damage notes that an artificial intelligence system must meet safety standards and have adequate mechanisms to prevent damage to persons and their property. Section 4.2 Technical Reliability and Security calls for risk assessment resilience against threats and validation/testing to ensure accuracy and reliable operation. Finally there is also a questionnaire checklist covering Security Accuracy and reliability (pp. 19-20).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The document requires that AI systems meet safety standards and include mechanisms to prevent harm to persons and property (Section 3.3). Section 4.2 on Technical Reliability and Security calls for risk assessment resilience against threats and validation/testing to ensure accuracy and reliable operation. A checklist also evaluates security accuracy and reliability (pp. 19–20). However the document does not establish explicit performance thresholds or specific quality benchmarks.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: Section 3.3 requires AI systems to include mechanisms that prevent harm to persons and property and Section 4.2 calls for risk assessment resilience against threats and validation/testing to ensure reliable operation. The checklist also addresses security accuracy and reliability (pp. 19–20). However the document does not explicitly define fallback procedures or emergency response protocols for system failures.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: Section 4.2 requires validation and testing to ensure accurate and reliable AI system operation and includes measures related to risk assessment and resilience against threats. A questionnaire checklist also assesses security accuracy and reliability (pp. 19–20). However the document does not explicitly require testing prior to deployment nor does it specify documentation requirements or measures covering the entire AI system lifecycle.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: Section 4.2 on Technical Reliability and Security requires AI systems to undergo risk assessment and to demonstrate resilience against threats alongside validation and testing to ensure reliable and accurate operation. The document also includes a checklist covering security accuracy and reliability (pp. 19–20) which supports assessing potential vulnerabilities. However while the document addresses security and threat resilience in general terms it does not explicitly establish detailed obligations specifically targeting cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference against AI systems.

fr1_title: Ethical Guidelines for Development Implementation and Use of Robust and Accountable Artificial Intelligence (Serbia)
fr1_justif: Ethical Guidelines address Transparency and Explainability in Sections 3.1 and 4.4 (pp. 10-11 14 26-31). Explainability ensures AI processes purposes and decisions are clear to users and stakeholders with “black box” models requiring traceability external evaluation and transparent communication. Transparency involves disclosing system parameters and decision rationale. The Questionnaire for Assessment of AI Systems operationalizes these principles promoting user understanding accountability stakeholder dialogue and context-sensitive explanations for high-impact AI applications.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The Guidelines explicitly address the promotion of clarity regarding AI operations: Purpose and potential of the system must be explained to all affected stakeholders (Section 3.1 pp. 10-11).Decision-making processes and rationale should be transparent with mechanisms for traceability and explainability including black box models (Sections 4.4 pp. 26-31).Data sources and model logic are highlighted with recommendations for external evaluation ethics-by-design and communication with users to foster trust (pp. 31).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The Guidelines explicitly require that AI systems be explainable throughout their lifecycle and state that decisions (or recommendations) made by AI systems must be clearly explained to anyone directly or indirectly affected (pp. 10–11). They further specify that when an AI system has a significant impact on people’s lives including areas such as financial and legal decisions medical diagnoses employment and university enrolment decision-making processes must be explained adequately and in a timely manner adapted to the stakeholder’s level of knowledge (pp. 29–31). The document also recommends traceability mechanisms transparency regarding input data and decision criteria and additional measures for “black box” models (pp. 29–30) t
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Bill No. 19 of 2024) (Singapore)
fr1_justif: The Act prohibits the publication sharing boosting and reposting of digitally generated or manipulated online election advertising depicting candidates (Sections 2 and 3 pp. 1-4). It targets content created by 'generative artificial intelligence' or 'digital means' that produces realistic audiovisual representations which a reasonable person would believe depicts a candidate (Sections 2(1C)-(1D) 3(5A)-(5B) pp. 2-6). Criminal penalties apply: individuals face fines up to $1000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment; platforms face fines up to $1 million (Sections 2(1E) 3(5C) pp. 2-6). Exemptions include satire parody and commentary if clearly indicated (Section 2(1F) p. 3).
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The Act prevents AI tools from creating and disseminating misinformation in the election context by criminalizing the publication sharing boosting and reposting of digitally generated or manipulated content depicting candidates (Sections 2(1C)-(1D) 3(5A)-(5B) pp. 2-6). However it does not address hate speech harassment or violence and is limited to election-related content only. Amplification by platforms is covered through obligations on online communication service providers (Sections 2(1E) 3(5C) pp. 2-6).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: Advisory Guidelines on the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) for Children’s Personal Data in the Digital Environment (Singapore)
fr1_justif: The Guidelines address children’s rights around AI-enabled data practices by requiring age-appropriate notices consent and withdrawal mechanisms for children including higher protection for those under 13 (Notification; Consent for collection use or disclosure of personal data p.4–6). They regulate AI-related practices such as age assurance profiling behavioural/telemetric data and geolocation requiring data minimisation safeguards against harmful or inappropriate content and higher security for children’s personal data (Reasonable purposes; Ascertainment of age; Geolocation data; Protection pp.6–10; Annex A DPIA pp.12–13).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The guidelines require organizations to adopt “data protection by design” for AI services accessed by children (p. 7-8) provide anonymization and minimization of personal data (p. 8 Data Minimisation) implement stringent security (p. 7 Security Measures) and ensure age-appropriate transparency and parental consent (p. 8 Ascertainment of Age). These measures directly safeguard children’s privacy whenever their data interacts with AI systems.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: The Guidelines address preventing exploitation or harm mainly via data uses that shape what children see online but do not expressly regulate AI or targeted advertising in detail. Using children’s data or profiles to target harmful or inappropriate content is unreasonable and not allowed (Reasonable purposes pp.6–7). Guidelines encourage age assurance and profiling only to gate age-appropriate content and surface safety information (Reasonable purposes; Ascertainment of age pp.6–8) and require geolocation minimisation to reduce safety risks (Geolocation data pp.8–9).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: The Guidelines impose responsibilities on organisations providing online products or services likely to be accessed by children to implement age-appropriate notices consent flows and safeguards but they do not separately classify AI developers/deployers.They recommend: age assurance and profiling only to support access to age-appropriate content and safety information (Reasonable purposes; Ascertainment of age pp.6–8) data minimisation and default geolocation limits (pp.7–9) and higher security plus DPIAs for services used by children (Protection; Accountability pp.9–12).

fr1_title: National AI Strategy - ADVANCING OUR SMART NATION JOURNEY
fr1_justif: The document explicitly links AI development to cultural context and societal diversity through its Human-Centric AI R&D Programme. It emphasises that AI systems should understand “culture and social norms (especially Asian cultures and norms)” and calls for the integration of social sciences such as psychology and sociology to account for socio-cultural differences in design and deployment (p. 19). This demonstrates a clear effort to embed cultural sensitivity into AI systems. While a newer strategy (2.0) has been introduced it shifts focus toward AI for the public good and does not formally supersede the original strategy which remains valid within its original scope.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National AI Office Digital Government Office
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: Driving a Greener Digital Future: Singapore's Green Data Centre Roadmap
fr1_justif: The Green Data Centre Roadmap links AI growth to environmental impacts by noting that generative AI and other digital technologies increase demand for compute and data-centre capacity (pp. 4–5). As data centres are major users of energy and water the roadmap proposes measures to reduce their environmental footprint including energy-efficient infrastructure and cooling solutions for high-density AI workloads such as liquid and immersion cooling (pp. 8–9). It also promotes green computing and carbon-efficient software design to optimise workloads and reduce emissions (pp. 11–12) alongside the use of low-carbon energy sources and improved water efficiency (pp. 13–15).
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: The roadmap addresses measures to prevent energy-intensive AI development through requirements and incentives for energy-efficient compute hardware advanced cooling optimized server utilization green software and AI model optimisation (pp. 8–14). However it does not directly address e-waste from AI systems (no explicit provisions on e-waste management or reduction see pp. 10–14).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
fr1_element3_justif: The roadmap provides detailed provisions to promote energy efficiency in data centers recommending renewable energy adoption (p. 13) advanced cooling technologies like immersion and liquid cooling (pp. 8–10) optimized hardware and software for efficient compute and storage (pp. 10–12) and water management practices to reduce resource consumption (pp. 15–16). These measures aim to cut carbon and water footprints in support of sustainable digital infrastructure.

fr1_title: Model AI Governance Framework (2nd Edition IMDA/PDPC) (Singapore)
fr1_justif: The Model AI Governance Framework addresses Fairness and Non-discrimination by requiring organizations to ensure AI decisions are explainable transparent and fair (pp. 15–16) and by promoting human-centric risk-based oversight (pp. 28–34). It focuses on minimizing bias in data (pp. 38–39) mitigation of discriminatory decisions regular model auditing traceability and inclusive stakeholder engagement (pp. 35–43). These measures help prevent unjust impacts and ensure equitable AI outcomes.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The framework promotes fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems by recommending measures to mitigate bias in training data monitor for discrimination and periodically review models for fairness (see pp. 13 15–16 22–24 38–40 65–66). However the recommendations are voluntary and enforcement relies on organizational adoption not regulatory mandate (see p. 13).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The framework provides detailed recommendations to help prevent AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases such as minimizing inherent bias in datasets monitoring for discrimination in outcomes and periodic review of models for adverse impacts across race gender age religion and protected characteristics (Pg 15-17 Pg 38 Pg 64). These measures are voluntary and not mandatory.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The framework sets out voluntary obligations for developers and deployers to identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle. It provides guidance on data quality minimizing inherent bias maintaining data lineage and regular review of training/testing data and model decisions for adverse impacts (pp. 36–40). However these measures are recommendations not enforceable requirements.

fr1_title: Model AI Governance Framework (2nd Edition IMDA/PDPC) (Singapore)
fr1_justif: The document contains concrete and operational mechanisms addressing gender bias within AI systems. In particular it provides detailed methodological approaches to fairness testing including the use of demographic datasets to evaluate bias across groups such as gender the application of bias ratios and the “four-fifths rule” to ensure equitable outcomes in hiring contexts and proactive de-biasing of models to prevent disadvantage based on demographic characteristics (pp. 42–43). These measures are complemented by counterfactual fairness testing which requires that AI decisions remain unchanged when sensitive attributes such as gender are altered (p. 46) thereby directly targeting gender-based discrimination at the model level.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: Model AI Governance Framework (2nd Edition IMDA/PDPC) (Singapore)
fr1_justif: The framework details three models: (1) human-in-the-loop (2) human-on-the-loop and (3) human-out-of-the-loop explaining when and how humans should intervene review and override AI outputs especially in high-risk contexts (pp. 28–34). It recommends meaningful human control responsible staff and the ability to appeal or override decisions made by AI (pp. 22–24 30–31 57–58). A risk-based approach determines the level of oversight (p. 30).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The framework promotes meaningful human control by detailing models for human oversight (human-in-the-loop human-on-the-loop) requiring human review and the ability to override AI decisions especially in critical and high-risk contexts (pp. 28–34). It emphasizes that AI should support not replace human judgment for decisions with significant impact (pp. 22–24 31).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The framework highlights that sensitive applications like law enforcement or healthcare require heightened human involvement and oversight recommending review or override mechanisms (pp. 30–34) but it does not explicitly ban full automation in any sector. Instead it urges a risk-based approach and increased human oversight in critical areas rather than prohibiting automation outright.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The framework encourages organizations to designate responsible individuals to oversee and be accountable for AI decisions especially for material outcomes (pp. 23–24 31 57–58). It sets out recommended practices but does not establish legally binding obligations or precise enforcement for all entities.

fr1_title: Model AI Governance Framework (2nd Edition IMDA/PDPC) (Singapore)
fr1_justif: The document contains clear and structured provisions requiring impact assessments of AI systems framed through a risk-based governance approach that explicitly considers impacts on individuals. It requires organisations to assess and manage risks associated with AI deployment including potential adverse effects arising from automated decision-making (p. 22) and operationalises this through a risk assessment methodology based on the likelihood and severity of harm (pp. 28–29). These harms are not limited to technical failures but include effects on individuals such as unfair or discriminatory outcomes which the framework explicitly highlights as a key risk to be mitigated (p. 14).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

fr1_title: Platform Workers Act 2024 (No.30 of 2024) (Singapore)
fr1_justif: The Platform Workers Act 2024 addresses labour protections in contexts of automated platform management. Section 6(1)–(2) (pp.11–12) defines “management control” as the use of data to determine worker eligibility allocate tasks or determine payment without human intervention on a regular or routine basis which indicate automated decision processes in platform work. The Act extends protections to such workers including mandatory records and earnings slips (ss.13–14 pp.15–16) financial protections such as priority of earnings and injury compensation (ss.16–17 pp.18–21) and collective representation through platform work associations (page 141 Part 3; Sixth Schedule).
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Manpower Commissioner for Platform Work
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: The Platform Workers Act 2024 addresses only certain aspects of this provision. Section 5 (pages 9-10) covers workers who lack traditional employment contracts but are subject to algorithmic management systems explicitly recognizing platform workers as a distinct category subject to management control defined in Section 6 (pages 10-11) as data-driven decision-making without human intervention. However the Act does not include specific provisions protecting workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion or termination decisions. It lacks requirements for bias audits human review of algorithmic decisions or prohibitions on discriminatory AI systems.
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: The Platform Workers Act 2024 regulates data-driven platform management but does not require transparency about how automated systems operate. Section 6(1)–(2) (pp.11–12) defines “management control” as the use of data to determine worker eligibility allocate tasks or determine payment without regular human intervention. While the Act does not impose obligations to explain such systems it provides indirect transparency measures including requirements for platform operators to maintain records and provide detailed earnings slips for each task (ss.13–14 pp.15–16). Workers may also raise concerns through representation and dispute resolution mechanisms (Part 3; Sixth Schedule).
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work
fr1_element3_justif: The Act strengthens collective rights for platform workers operating under data-driven app-mediated management (which includes AI/algorithmic systems). It prohibits any term that restricts platform workers from joining organising or participating in platform work associations and criminalises such clauses (Section 7 page 13). Part 3 establishes registration governance and rights of platform work associations while the Sixth Schedule amends the Industrial Relations Act so these associations can represent workers in industrial matters (including platform engagement terms) and participate in collective bargaining and dispute resolution with platform operators.

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Singapore National AI Strategy 2.0 (2023)
fr1_justif: The document addresses public sector skills development by strengthening AI capabilities within the public service. It highlights the growing use of AI in public services such as education healthcare immigration clearance and scam detection demonstrating the need for a skilled public workforce (p. 8). It promotes mass awareness and adoption of AI tools among public officers and the use of government-developed AI systems such as the Pair LLM suite (pp. 24–25). Crucially the government commits to uplifting AI literacy and proficiency of all public officers by rolling out targeted AI training courses for different workforce segments including senior management policy and operational roles (p. 26).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: AISG (AI Singapore)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: NAIS 2.0 sets a government-wide direction to uplift AI skills across the public service but does not mention the judiciary or create a single detailed civil-service training blueprint. It commits to drive mass awareness and adoption of AI across the Public Service and to uplift the AI literacy baseline and sharpen the AI proficiency of all public officers through targeted AI skills courses for different workforce segments (System 1 Action 3 p. 26).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The document assigns responsibilities within government to support AI adoption and capability building but it does not explicitly describe AI “champions” roles. It states that government agencies with specialised expertise will develop and lead sector-specific AI strategies and that agencies responsible for whole-of-government functional domains (e.g. Finance HR Service Delivery) will identify and optimise business processes using AI and build internal capabilities (System 1 Action 3 p. 26). While this indicates designated teams and leadership for AI initiatives the framework does not explicitly frame them as AI champions providing guidance across government.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes provisions promoting continuous development of AI skills within the public sector. It commits to uplifting the AI literacy baseline and sharpening the AI proficiency of all public officers by developing and rolling out targeted AI training courses for different workforce segments (System 1 Action 3 p. 26). It also emphasises the need to drive mass awareness and adoption of AI across the Public Service to ensure officers can effectively use evolving AI tools (p. 25). These measures reflect an approach aimed at keeping the public workforce updated as AI technologies rapidly advance.

fr1_title: Skills Framework for Infocomm Technology (ICT) (Skills in Generative Artificial Intelligence- Gen AI) (Singapore)
fr1_justif: The document addresses reskilling/upskilling by defining structured skill pathways for workforce adaptation to AI. It organizes competencies for two worker archetypes: AI Users (Chapter 1 pages 3) and AI Practitioners (Chapter 2 page 6 ) enabling workers to identify relevant upskilling paths. For AI Users it covers GenAI Principles and Applications (TSC #1) and Prompt Design (TSC #2) to help workers 'enhance productivity drive innovation' and adapt to AI-enabled work environments (pages 4-5). For AI Practitioners it provides seven advanced technical skills (TSCs #3-7) including Prompt Engineering Model Selection Evaluation Application Development and Model Fine-Tuning.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI (2024) (Singapore)
fr1_justif: Page 21 to 22 of the guideline speaks about security in the context of AI particularly asking for the adoption of security by design with refinements based on unique characteristics of AI as well as development of new security safeguards with new tools such as input filters to detect unsafe prompts and digital forensics tools for generative AI to investigate and analyse digital data (e.g. file contents) to reconstruct a cybersecurity incident. Page 12 to 15 discusses trusted development and development including using baseline safety practices like fine-tuning transparency via labels.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The framework recommends an initial set of standardised model safety evaluations for LLMs covering robustness factuality propensity to bias toxicity generation and data governance (Pages 14-15 Trusted Development and Deployment) it also requires industry adoption of common safety practices to reduce hallucinations and improve accuracy (Pages13-14). For evaluation it recommends benchmarking tests models against datasets of questions and answers to assess performance and safety (Page 14).
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: Pages 16-18 Incident Reporting: Establishes formal incident reporting structures for severe AI incidents including those causing death health damage or critical infrastructure disruption. Pages 17-18: Implements vulnerability reporting mechanisms similar to software security practices with typical 90-day windows for patching after discovery providing fallback procedures for addressing system weaknesses. Pages 6-8 Accountability: Requires appropriate degree of human involvement. Page 20 testing safety nets: Requires independent third-party testing to identify failures before deployment serving as critical safeguards.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: Pre-Deployment Testing Requirements (Pages 13-15 Trusted Development and Deployment): Mandates comprehensive pre-deployment evaluation through two approaches of benchmarking tests models against datasets to assess performance and safety and red teaming. Validation through testing (Pages 19-20): Establishes dedicated Testing and Assurance dimension requiring independent third-party testing with standardised methodologies and benchmarks to validate system robustness. Lifecycle Documentation (Pages 12-15): Requires risk assessments considering use case context and documentation of safety practices. Technical Robustness Standards (Pages 14-15): Specifies standardized evaluations covering robustness factuality propensity to bias toxicity.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: Security Dimension (Pages 21-22): Establishes comprehensive security obligations addressing new threat vectors that arise through generative AI models. Red Teaming for Security (Page 14 to 15): Advocates for evaluation via red-teaming acknowledging that sectors and domains may have unique needs that require additional evaluations (e.g. mandating stringent accuracy thresholds for high-risk use cases such as medical diagnosis).

fr1_title: Model AI Governance Framework (2nd Edition IMDA/PDPC) (Singapore)
fr1_justif: The framework treats transparency and explainability as core governance principles (p.15). Section 3.26–3.29 (p.44–45) defines explainability and recommends documenting model training selection design decisions and using supplementary explanation tools. It then links explainability with transparency through guidance on product descriptions and technical specifications and complements this with related guidance on transparency and consumer interactions later in the document (pp.53–56).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The framework includes specific measures for promoting clarity about how AI systems operate their purpose data sources and decision logic to foster public trust. It recommends clear plain-language explanations documentation of system purpose description of data sources and explanation of decision-making processes for stakeholder transparency (pp. 15–16 41 53–58 66).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The framework recommends meaningful user-facing explanations for AI outputs especially for material decisions (see pp. 56–58 66) but does not impose mandatory requirements or specify obligations for high-stakes contexts (like hiring or loans). It provides general guidance for organizations to consider appropriate transparency relative to risk but leaves implementation flexible.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The framework recommends channels for users to request explanations for AI-driven decisions that affect them and for organizations to provide clear reasons for important outcomes (pp. 57–58 66). However it does not formally establish an enforceable right for individuals to receive explanations or specify redress mechanisms; these are presented as suggested practices.

fr1_title: 2030 Digital Transformation Strategy for Slovakia
fr1_justif: The strategy acknowledges that based on experience of Slovak IT companies the content of education at various types of schools (primary secondary college) already contain the matter of IoT and Slovak pupils/students have excellent results in IoT and robotics at competitions for secondary school and college students and in international contests (p. 18). However it also notes that Slovakia immediately needs a comprehensive systemic change of education which will ensure that primary and secondary schools and universities offer more subjects and majors from the viewpoint of quantity and quality where pupils and students will acquire advanced digital and technological skills and high quality education. (p. 19).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Office of the Deputy Prime Minister of the Slovak Republic for Investments and Informatization
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes objectives related to curriculum reforms across different education levels. It notes that primary secondary and higher education already include topics such as IoT and robotics and highlights the strong performance of Slovak students in related competitions (p. 18). At the same time it calls for a comprehensive systemic change in education to ensure that primary and secondary schools and universities offer more subjects and majors focused on advanced digital and technological skills (p. 19). The strategy further emphasizes that these developments should be applied throughout the entire education system from primary schools to universities (pp. 30–31).
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

fr1_title: EU Digital Services Act
fr1_justif: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Digital Services Coordinators
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

fr1_title: EU GDPR
fr1_justif: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed.
