fr1_element1_justif: Initiative 1.2.5 of Annex 1 outlines the development of a “data and AI skills roadmap to guide the implementation of skills development initiatives for the public sector on data-driven decision-making and responsible public sector transformation through AI” (p. 7). Additionally Initiative 1.2.6 notes that training programs will be developed for the “judiciary and relevant regulatory agencies on Responsible AI Regulation and Governance leveraging existing online resources (including MOOCs)” (p. 7).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: Initiative 1.1.13 of Annex 1 recommends updating the Digital Government Competency Framework to include a “functional job profile for a Data Officer to be introduced in every government organization to oversee data collection management and sharing in compliance with the requisite laws and governance standards” (p. 6). Additionally section 2.2 of Annex 4 underscores the designation of “principal champions” within each agency who would advocate for the principles provide guidance and conduct internal audits to ensure principle alignment (p. 90).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes multiple provisions that support ongoing professional development and continuous training. Initiative 1.2.15 of Annex 1 proposes designing and implementing an “AI Ethics certification program for public and private sector professionals” (p. 9). Section 6.2 of Annex 4 further recommends developing “role-specific AI training modules for different levels of government officials” establishing “mentorship programs pairing AI experts with government departments” and conducting “regular AI workshops and seminars for continuous learning” (p. 98).

fr1_title: Sri Lanka's National Strategy on AI (July 2024 - Draft Strategy for Public Consultation)
fr1_justif: On page 54 of Annex 3 as part of the immediate setup and functions of the National Center for Artificial Intelligence (NCAI) capacity building and talent development are identified as a key pillar outlining efforts to “establish AI learning pathways” with a focus on up-skilling the current workforce and integrating AI modules into higher education. Initiatives 1.2.16 and 1.2.17 mention the launch of a “Data and AI Skills Development Fund” to support upskilling and reskilling initiatives alongside data- and AI-focused vocational training for professionals affected by job displacement (Annex 1 p. 9). In addition postgraduate AI programs aim to upskill existing professionals with advanced technical knowledge (Annex 7 p. 158).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: On page 9 Initiative 1.2.16 of Annex 1 outlines the launch of a “Data and AI Skills Development Fund” to support upskilling and reskilling initiatives. This is a long-term initiative to be undertaken by the NCAI the Ministry of Technology (MoT) the Ministry of Finance and industry partners. Progress will be measured based on funding allocations as well as the number of individuals and organizations benefiting from the fund. Further Initiative 1.2.17 introduces data- and AI-focused vocational training programs for professionals at risk of job displacement (p. 9). This will be measured based on the number of AI-focused vocational training programs introduced participant numbers and post-training employment rates.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: Initiative 1.2.16 of Annex 1 outlines indicators measuring the amount of funding allocated as well as the number of individuals and organizations benefiting from the Data and AI Skills Development Fund to support upskilling and reskilling initiatives (p. 9). This indicates the availability of public financial support for training activities. However the document does not clearly specify the types of financial support that would be provided to workers to enable their participation in AI skills and capacity development programs.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
fr1_element3_justif: On page 9 Initiative 1.2.17 of Annex 1 aims to introduce a “Data and AI-focused vocational training programs for professionals at risk of job displacement”. This is a long term initiative that would be undertaken by the NCAI Ministry of Skills Development vocational training institutes and Industry partners. This will be measured based off the number of AI-focused vocational training programs conducted number of participants and post-training employment rates.

fr1_title: Sri Lanka's National Strategy on AI (July 2024 - Draft Strategy for Public Consultation)
fr1_justif: The trust and safety pillar of the National Center for Artificial Intelligence (NCAI) seeks to ensure the responsible development and use of AI through legal and ethical oversight (Appendix B9 p. 83). Its mandate includes developing AI governance frameworks monitoring compliance and managing risks associated with AI deployment. Safety and security are further operationalised through performance metrics with KPIs on accuracy reliability system uptime and stability (Annex 6 pp. 118–119; Annex 7 pp. 142–143). Annex 7 additionally introduces a system-specific AI development lifecycle requiring rigorous testing to ensure functionality and accuracy prior to deployment (p. 136).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: Section 7.2 of Annex 11 sets a clear benchmark requiring deployed language models to “achieve a benchmark accuracy rate of 95% on standard language processing tasks within the first year post-deployment (p. 203).
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The evidence includes provisions related to safeguards and mitigation procedures in the event of AI system failure or unexpected behavior. For instance Section 5.4 of Annex 4 outlines risk-mitigation measures such as developing “redundancy systems and robust backup solutions” to address system downtime (pp. 95-96). It also requires agencies to “implement safeguards and monitoring mechanisms to detect and address emerging risks' (ibid).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: Section 3.1 of Annex 7 outlines the second stage of a system-specific development lifecycle for AI which “focuses on creating the actual AI models and the accompanying software system” (p. 136). Data engineers would prepare and manage the data with AI scientists developing and training the models and finally the software engineers building the application framework. As a last step this phase would include “rigorous testing to ensure functionality and accuracy before deployment” (ibid). While this confirms a requirement for pre-deployment testing the document does not specify detailed testing protocols or stress-testing procedures.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

fr1_title: Sri Lanka's National Strategy on AI (July 2024 - Draft Strategy for Public Consultation)
fr1_justif: On page 19 Action 3.4 of Annex 1 states that an AI Governance Framework must be developed in line with Sri Lanka’s AI governance approach addressing harm disclosure impact assessments transparency risk mitigation human oversight and redress mechanisms. Annex 4 further notes that government agencies are to use AI to enhance efficiency transparency and accessibility for improved public service delivery (p. 86). It emphasises that trustworthy and transparent AI is “fundamental to building public trust” and requires robust ethical standards privacy safeguards and security protocols aligned with international frameworks (p. 88). Subsection 9.2 further outlines criteria to ensure transparency in government AI decision-making (p. 102).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: On page 90 subsection 2.3 of Annex 4 states that clear AI transparency guidelines must be developed which could include “AI Fact Sheets” for each deployed system ‘detailing its purpose data sources decision-making process and potential limitations which must be made accessible to the public to foster trust and understanding’. Meanwhile subsection 5.2 emphasizes prioritizing “open-source and open standards technologies to promote interoperability” though this serves as a technical standard rather than a transparency-related provision clarifying how AI systems operate (p. 94). Additionally subsection 9.2 calls for the creation of public registries of AI systems used in government decision-making.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: On page 88 subsection 2.1 of Annex 4 outlines one of the core principles as following a human-centric approach implying that government AI systems must be designed to ‘augment human decision-making and improve efficiency while maintaining human oversight especially in critical areas’. Further subsection 9.2 states that mechanisms must be implemented “to provide citizens with explanations of AI-driven decisions affecting them” (p. 102). However there is no specific provision outlining whether citizens or government employees have the right to request specific data points an AI system used to make a decision about them.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy in the State of Palestine
fr1_justif: The framework addresses the indicator by including a project on “artificial intelligence in culture protecting Palestinian content and natural language processing” (p. 10) thereby linking AI development to cultural context and local content preservation. It also promotes the use of Arabic language processing technologies to enhance accessibility and usability of AI systems in the local context (p. 10). In addition the strategy recognises the role of AI in fostering inclusion noting its potential to “integrate marginalized groups into initiatives that promote human development and self-improvement” (p. 7).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research the Ministry of Entrepreneurship and Empowerment
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy in the State of Palestine
fr1_justif: While the strategy includes broad capacity-building measures across public and private sectors it also contains specific provisions targeting the public sector bringing it within the scope of the indicator. In particular the guidance media and implementation plans explicitly provide for building and developing governmental capabilities and skills in artificial intelligence and supporting exchange programs (pp. 8 11–12 18). In addition the strategy mandates raising awareness of artificial intelligence across all government agencies (p. 9) and emphasizes the necessity of digital transformation within the government sector (p. 5).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research the Ministry of Entrepreneurship and Empowerment
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Policy (Palestine)
fr1_justif: The framework explicitly identifies the need to “build capacity and adapt to the rapid changes in skills and requirements of the intelligence-based labor market” (p. 3) directly linking AI deployment to workforce transformation. It supports this through measures such as training and education across sectors and levels from foundational skills to lifelong learning (p. 4) and integrating AI and data competencies into the education system including training for teachers and administrators (p. 8). It further calls for reskilling and upskilling in response to labor market changes (p. 10) alongside workshops awareness programs and investment in local talent through scholarships and training (pp. 8 10).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: National AI Team
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Federal Act on Data Protection (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: The law serves as a pillar to combat manipulation disinformation or violence when it involves the processing of personal data by AI systems: profiling high-risk profiling (Art. 5) high-risk profiling carried out by private entities or any profiling by federal agencies (Art. 6); protection against manipulation and automated decisions (Art. 21); impact assessment (Art. 22); and sanctions (Art. 60). The communication from the Federal Commissioner clarifies that the law is directly applicable to data processing by AI (https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/update-current-legislation-directly-applicable-ai). It states that 'the use of programs that allow the falsification of faces images or voice messages of identifiable people must be indicated.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The communication states that the use of programs that allow the falsification of faces images or voice messages of identifiable individuals must also always be clearly indicated. This is based on Article 6 of the law and appropriate measures to correct erase or destroy data that is incorrect or incomplete with respect to the purpose for which it was collected or processed. The adequacy of the measures depends on the scope of the processing and the risk that the processing entails. Article 21 mandates the provision of information in the case of automated individual decision-making. However there is no preventive measure.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: Federal Act on Data Protection (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: The data subject may request that the automated individual decision be reviewed by a natural person. (Art. 21) The data subject may request that incorrect personal data be corrected; an individual can request that a specific data processing activity be prohibited and that the personal data be deleted or destroyed. (Art. 32) A person can view automated decisions they have the right to stop the unlawful processing of the personal data concerned redress the consequences of unlawful processing declare the processing to be unlawful. (Art. 41) While protection in the context of automated decisions is clearly stated a specific connection to redress and remedy in the context of AI is missing. However such connection can be implicitly assumed.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: The data protection law applies to AI (https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/update-current-legislation-directly-applicable-ai). According to the law article 32 regarding data processing the applicant may also request that any correction deletion or destruction prohibition of processing or disclosure to third parties marking as contested or judgment be communicated to third parties or published. In the public sector (Article 41) any person with a legitimate interest may request the responsible federal agency to remedy the consequences of illegal processing.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: The law suggests that companies to have a data protection officer (Art. 10). The data protection law applies to AI (https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/update-current-legislation-directly-applicable-ai). Article 21 is based exclusively on automated processing in accordance with information obligations. The FDPIC as a complaint or grievance body. (Art. 23 49).  The entity opens an investigation against a federal body or a private individual who must provide all information and documents necessary for the investigation. If the data subject has filed a complaint they must be informed of the measures taken in response and the outcome of any investigation (art. 49 4).
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The data protection law applies to AI (https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/update-current-legislation-directly-applicable-ai).  The law suggests that companies establish internal mechanisms to handle complaints for example by appointing a data protection officer (Art. 10). Individuals have the right and companies have the duty to provide information (Art. 19). The data controller must provide the information free of charge. The Federal Council may provide exceptions particularly if the effort required is disproportionate. The information must generally be provided within 30 days (Art. 25). However there is no incentive for accessible mechanisms.

fr1_title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: Guideline 1: Putting people first (p. 3) states that the use of AI should help improve people's quality of life and sustainably develop our society. Guideline 2: Regulatory conditions for the development and application of AI: AI should help ensure high-quality living standards based on the principles of sustainable development (p. 3). AI offers the potential for economic growth prosperity security and employment as well as for reducing the ecological footprint and energy consumption and this potential should be explored in the best possible way (p. 4).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: The guidelines defined that the AI offers the potential to reduce the ecological footprint and energy consumption and this potential should be explored by developing new business models. Regulatory conditions for digital solutions should be designed in a way that does not hinder innovation and contributes both to greater value creation and sustainable development (p. 4). AI systems must be designed to be safe robust and resilient in order to have a positive impact on people and the environment (p.5).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: Individuals groups and genders must be protected from discrimination and stigmatisation (page 3). The Confederation must ensure well-balanced high-quality data are used or that 'suitable compensatory safeguards' are put in place to counter inherent bias (page 3). The use of AI should actively create equal opportunities for people and 'encourage and facilitate their access to education goods services and technology (page 3). AI applications likely to affect fundamental rights should be accompanied by an 'Equality Impact Assessment' (EIA) as a frame of reference in addition to continuous monitoring and safeguards (page 3).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The primary directive is that individuals groups and genders must be protected from discrimination and stigmatisation. The use of AI should create equal opportunities for people and encourage and facilitate their access to education goods services and technology. The Confederation must ensure that well-balanced high-quality data are used or that 'suitable compensatory safeguards' are put in place to counter inherent bias. (page 3) AI applications that are likely to affect fundamental rights should be accompanied by an 'Equality Impact Assessment' (EIA) continuous monitoring and appropriate safeguards.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: AI applications that may affect fundamental rights must be accompanied by appropriate technical and organizational safeguards and controls. Therefore individuals groups and genders must be protected against discrimination and stigmatization (p. 3). Generally applicable norms include the prohibition of discrimination and the promotion of equality guaranteed by the Federal Constitution the Gender Equality Law the Law on Discrimination Based on Disability the Swiss Civil Code on the protection of personal privacy the International Covenant on Economic Social and Cultural Rights the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (p.9).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

fr1_title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: Preservation of Human Agency: The guiding principle is to prioritize people mandating that Self-determination should be preserved and that individuals must be able to participate in life in an autonomous manner. The role of AI is to complement and enhance human activities and skills. (page 3) Non-Delegation of Responsibility: The framework strictly limits AI's authority under Guideline 4 (Accountability) which explicitly states: 'It must not be possible to delegate responsibility to machines' (page 5) Legal Mandate for Human Review: The Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP) provides the mandatory 'human-in-the-loop' mechanism: Individuals have the right to review automated decision(page 10)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The guidelines prioritize human control by establishing that 'It must not be possible to delegate responsibility to machines' (page 5) under Guideline 4: Accountability. In critical decision-making contexts the framework ensures AI remains a tool by granting individuals the right to have any automated decision that significantly affects them 'be reviewed by a natural person' (page 10)  thereby preserving human judgment.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: There are general requirements for AI developers. Civil and criminal law dictates that traffic accidents or medical errors can constitute cases of liability attributed to the use of AI-based software (p. 9). The Data Protection Act plays a key role in terms of profiling AI including health-related data. There are requirements applying to the processing of particularly sensitive personal data related to genetic and biometric data. There is a duty to provide information in the case of automated decision-making and this can be reviewed by the data subject (p. 10). However there are no longer measures for total prevention.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: In the case of an automated decision the data controller must inform the data subject about any decision based exclusively on automated processing when such a decision has legal consequences for the data subject or significantly affects him or her (p.10). So the obligation applies only in case of consequences and advance supervision for intervention.

fr1_title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: The document's core purpose for mandating Impact Assessment is to achieve proactive risk management and prevent harm across multiple dimensions. The guidelines mandate proactive assessments by requiring that AI applications be designed with 'ethics by design'. This ensures safeguards are integrated from the planning stage to eliminate or mitigate risks early preventing reactive crisis management. Assessments are explicitly required where AI is likely to affect fundamental rights necessitating the upfront evaluation of potential societal harm including discrimination and bias. They demand the tracking and assessing of impact across a broad scope: individuals society the economy and the environment.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: In the document it is explicitly stated that AI applications which are likely affecting fundamental rights should be accompanied by an impact assessment. (page 3) Specifically also in Guideline 5 (Safety) it says: 'By adequately tracking and assessing the impact of the use of AI the risks for individuals society the economy and the environment can be identified at an early stage and either eliminated or mitigated.' (page 5) Ethics by design is considered a inherent feature of designing and using AI. (page 3)
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The document explicitly mandates an assessment whenever fundamental rights are at risk. (page 3) It requires developers to integrate risk assessment and ethical considerations into the AI system's design phase making the process itself a tool for proactive risk management mentioning using the principle 'ethics by design'. (page 3)
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

fr1_title: Federal Act on Data Protection (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: The document addresses specifically profiling which means any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of the use of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person in particular to analyse or predict aspects concerning that natural person's performance at work. (Art. 5)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: Regarding automated decision-making (Article 21) the data controller must inform the data subject of any decision based solely on automated processing that has significant legal consequences or adverse effects for the data subject. The data subject must upon request allow the controller to express their point of view. The data subject may request that the automated individual decision be reviewed by a natural person. However there are no specifications regarding adverse effects such as any type of discrimination.
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: Concerning automated decision-making (Article 21) the data controller must inform the data subject of any decision based solely on automated processing that has significant legal consequences or adverse effects for the data subject. The data subject must upon request allow the controller to express their point of view. The data subject may request that the automated individual decision be reviewed by a natural person. This does not apply when there is a contract in place and consent for the decision to be automated.
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems
fr1_title: Strategy Use of AI systems in the Federal Administration (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: The strategy sets parameters for the Federal Administration's digital transformation using AI. It emphasizes that the administration must lead by example and use AI systems in accordance with shared principles including legal/ethical principles ensuring public interest and placing high value on trustworthiness including explainability transparency data protection accuracy. (page 3) The main goal for public disclosure is found under field of action 2 'Earning trust': The expected benefit is that internal and external stakeholders from the general public will 'gain transparency about which Al systems are used in the Federal Administration and how their use is monitored'. The use of AI systems 'must remain traceable'. (page 6)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Federal Digital Transformation Council
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
fr1_element2_text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
fr1_element2_justif: The strategy's most direct objective is for the general public to 'gain transparency about which Al systems are used' (page 6) and it includes a non-prioritized goal to maintain a 'comprehensive overview' of systems. (page 10) This fulfills the need for an inventory and public access. However the document does not include an explicit measure that requires public disclosure of all specific key information for high-risk systems such as training data the rationale for use and the results of impact assessments (pages 6 10). It addresses these topics internally but lacks the specific public mandate for all listed elements.
fr1_element3_text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
fr1_element4_text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

fr1_title: Strategy Use of AI systems in the Federal Administration (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: The document addresses public procurement of AI primarily by linking it to the overarching core principles for AI use. It includes an unprioritized strategic goal explicitly stating that procurement legislation and organizational principles must 'enable and promote procurement of Al systems in accordance with the principles for the use of Al systems in the Federal Administration' (Appendix page 10). The goal integrates specific requirements into the procurement process namely the core principles (page 3) which mandate that procured systems must be: trustworthy (explainability transparency data protection accuracy); governed by clearly defined responsibilities and accountability across the entire Al system's life cycle. (pages 3 10)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Federal Digital Transformation Council
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy requires that AI acquisition guidelines go beyond traditional IT but this is not defined (p. 3). Although acquisition legislation and organizational principles allow and promote the acquisition of AI systems in accordance with the principles for the use of AI systems in the Federal Administration this requirement was not prioritized in the current strategy and 'will be evaluated during each sub-strategy review and reprioritized if necessary' (p. 10).
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
fr1_element4_justif: The strategy requires that procurement aligns with AI principles and mandates defining the approach to digital sovereignty specifically including open-source requirements  (page 11). However it is only partial because while it connects procurement and sovereignty to high-level principles it lacks explicit provisions that prioritize local AI developments as a concrete strategy to achieve that sovereignty. Also it is related to the governance of the AI system and not directly to procurement.

fr1_title: Strategy Use of AI systems in the Federal Administration (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: The document addresses public sector skills development as its dedicated field of action 1: Developing skills (page 4). The strategic objective is to ensure the Federal Administration has the necessary skills and knowledge to competently design and use AI systems (page 5). The primary goal is that employees have access to training and further education programmes on the use of AI that are appropriate to their level and role and that they are prepared for changes resulting from AI use (page 5). New skills are explicitly required in fields such as AI data science law and business management (page 4).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Federal Digital Transformation Council
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes a government-wide strategy with objectives for upskilling the public servants (Federal Administration) covering their foundational understanding of AI's use and risks. Specifically field of action number 1: Developing skills mandates access to training and further education programmes to help employees manage risks and gain skills in AI data science law and business management. However the strategy does not include specific provisions measures objectives or recommendations targeting members of the judiciary. (pages 45)
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The document includes objectives and mechanisms for assigning expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI through existing roles and interdepartmental structures but it does not include specific provisions for assigning dedicated 'AI champions' or new teams strictly for that purpose. The strategy mandates interdepartmental interdisciplinary coordination structures in place to share experiences (page 5) and relies on internal and external service providers to offer support (page 5 10). It aims for strategic knowledge management (page 10) but lacks the specific provision to create new dedicated roles for this function.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The strategic goal for Field of action 1: Developing skills is that employees have 'access to training and further education programmes on the use of Al that are appropriate to their level and role' (page 5). The term 'further education' directly implies continuous upskilling. The document acknowledges the necessity of staying current by stating the Federal Administration must design its use of AI systems 'in lockstep with technological developments' (page 5). The strategy emphasizes continuous adaptation by stating it has 'no set validity period' because 'Al is developing rapidly' (page 9) and its goals can be 'reprioritised by the Federal Digital Transformation Council in order to respond to advancements in Al technologies' (page 9).

fr1_title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
fr1_justif: The document addresses specifically safety in the context of AI namely Guideline 5 discusses the safety of AI systems and that they have to be designed to be safe robust and resilient. (page 5) Importantly it does not include security.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: AI systems must be designed to be safe robust and resilient in order to have a positive impact on people and the environment. (page 5) The data policy must strike a balance between the protection of privacy and the use of data. It should work towards ensuring that data used for AI applications are of sufficient quality and are documented. (page 4)  Decision-making processesbased on AI should be designed in such a way that ensures that they are traceable for directlyand indirectly affected persons and the mode of action must also be verifiable for experts. (page 4) However no quality limits or parameters were developed.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: AI applications that may affect fundamental rights should be accompanied by an impact assessment continuous monitoring and appropriate safeguards and controls especially in the case of self-learning systems. (page 3) Thus individuals groups and genders must be protected against discrimination and stigmatization. To this end adequate technical and organizational safeguards and controls must be provided. Furthermore balanced and high-quality data should be used or appropriate compensatory safeguards should be implemented. fr1_justif: In the NAIS Strategy 3: Enhancing Human Resource Capacity and Advancing AI Education aims to promote AI literacy among the public by equipping people with the knowledge understanding and skills needed to use artificial intelligence responsibly and beneficially in ways that are appropriate and aligned with their level of education and age group. (pp.147-148)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Minister of Education and Ministry of Higher Education Science Research and Innovation (p149)
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The strategy addresses education and skill training in relation to AI by strengthening core competencies from the school-age period through lifelong learning. It emphasises developing analytical thinking problem-solving creativity collaboration and technological proficiency among students which are foundational for AI literacy (p.13). It also highlights the need to strengthen domestic capabilities through AI skills and education to support the development and application of AI particularly in public services (p.88).
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: This is a requirement of the strategy. AI-related undergraduate programmes are offered by public and private universities including King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology Ladkrabang Chulalongkorn University and Chiang Mai University mainly through faculties of engineering science and information science. At the basic education level the Institute for the Promotion of Teaching Science and Technology (IPST) provides AI curricula covering awareness core concepts models and integration supporting the development of AI competencies in the formal education system (pp. 231–232).
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

fr1_title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
fr1_justif: AI systems should be designed developed and deployed to generate benefits for humans society and the environment throughout their lifecycle (p.17). The document requires accountability mechanisms including internal and external audits of data algorithms deployment and outcomes to identify and mitigate environmental and societal risks (p.19). Designers and developers must ensure data integrity ethical compliance and environmental protection (p.20). AI should be developed sustainably adapt to different environments and include built-in risk mitigation security recovery mechanisms and continuous testing under real-world conditions to avoid harm to human life and the environment (pp.23–33).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element2_justif: It can be considered “partially” as although the provision is not specific and appears non-binding it states that data integrity accuracy availability personal data protection and impacts on ethics human life and the environment should be taken into account and that relevant actors should comply with these requirements. While explicit measurement mechanisms are not clearly specified they appear to be implicitly reflected in the requirement that these factors be considered.
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

fr1_title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
fr1_justif: The Guideline embeds fairness and non-discrimination across the entire lifecycle of AI systems. It requires AI design and development to recognise social diversity and actively reduce exclusion and bias with the aim of maximising benefits for society particularly for disadvantaged and vulnerable groups. It also mandates that key decisions in AI research design deployment and use be demonstrably fair rather than assumed to be neutral. To achieve this the Guideline emphasises diverse research teams representative datasets and technical and procedural mechanisms to assess and verify fairness in practice (p. 13-14).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: AI should be researched designed and developed with an understanding of diverse user needs including minority and disadvantaged groups such as persons with disabilities while respecting human abilities and potential. Stakeholders who may be affected by bias or unfairness should participate in the design and development process. AI systems must also be reviewed and corrected when they produce unintended biased outcomes which may result from interactions with different groups or incorrect assumptions about users. (p.29-30)
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The document provides guidance to prevent artificial intelligence systems from perpetuating or amplifying societal bias and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age disability or other protected characteristics. It promotes the use of bias detection tools and encourages testing on unseen data and underrepresented populations to ensure equitable performance. The Guideline also recommends involving persons with disabilities in testing and design processes to enhance accessibility and inclusion and advises developers and service providers to provide appropriate training tools and access channels for users (p.31).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: It can be considered partially as the provision states that significant decisions related to the research design development deployment and use of artificial intelligence should be demonstrably fair. The term “demonstrably” implicitly suggests that bias must be identified and assessed and the reference to research design development and deployment reflects a lifecycle approach. However the provision does not establish clear or binding obligations for developers and deployers.

fr1_title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
fr1_justif: Under the topic of Laws Ethics and International Standards the AI Ethics guideline clearly states that artificial intelligence should be designed based on a human-centred approach with humans as the final decision-makers.(p.10)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: A human-centred (Human-Centric) approach should guide the design and deployment of artificial intelligence ensuring that humans retain the authority to make final decisions. AI systems should be designed so that their tasks and decision-making can always be transferred back to humans. They must also allow human intervention in all decision-making processes preserving human autonomy to reject AI-generated outputs. Appropriate mechanisms should be included to ensure that humans can override or interrupt the operation of the AI system whenever necessary. (pp.23-24)
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
fr1_justif: Under the topic of Laws Ethics and International Standards the AI Ethics Guideline states that public procurement should require AI developers and service providers to comply with transparency principles conduct impact assessments on how data processing affects human rights and privacy and assume responsibility for any negative consequences arising from the use of artificial intelligence (p.18).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The document states that artificial intelligence should be reviewed and assessed to ensure that its research development and deployment generate benefits and promote the well-being of humans society and the environment (p. 22). It also encourages organisations to establish dedicated oversight bodies to supervise AI development and deployment provide legal ethical and human rights guidance assess potential risks and negative impacts and ensure accountability of researchers designers developers and service providers (p. 23). However it does not explicitly specify that such reviews or assessments must be conducted prior to deployment and therefore does not clearly establish a mandatory pre-deployment evaluation requirement.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: There should be support for establishing organisations and regulatory bodies overseeing the development and use of artificial intelligence. These bodies should provide guidance to AI researchers designers developers and service providers on legal ethical and human rights implications assess risks that may result in negative impacts and ensure appropriate accountability mechanisms for those involved in AI research design development and service provision. (p.18)
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: There should be mechanisms to ensure accountability for AI researchers designers developers service providers users and other stakeholders throughout the system’s entire life cycle. This includes auditing datasets algorithms design methods deployment and outputs through internal and independent external reviews. Audit results should be reported risks assessed and mitigation measures implemented to prevent adverse impacts on people and the environment (p. 19). However while this creates obligations for developers and stakeholders it does not grant the public the right to access these audit findings.

fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: It can be considered partial as Objective 2 (p.147) aims “to improve the skills of the workforce in the industrial sector.” Page 148 provides further details on measures supporting scholarships work placements and talent mobility by offering financial aid to develop expertise in science and technology within high-capability target fields particularly at the Master’s Doctoral and Postdoctoral levels. These provisions indicate an intention to promote reskilling and upskilling through grants and educational support. However the measures are primarily focused on advanced academic training and highly skilled personnel rather than the broader workforce suggesting limited inclusiveness in comprehensive workforce-wide skill development.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: Scholarships also support work placements in the private sector and promote talent mobility. (p.148)
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
fr1_justif: Under the topic of Security and Privacy the AI Ethics guideline states that AI should be created to serve but must not be used to deceive oppose or threaten human beings. AI should be designed with risk-prevention principles to protect against attacks and other threats ensuring the security of data and systems. This includes safeguarding personal data ethics and the safety of human life and the external environment throughout the system’s entire life cycle. It should also have the capability to detect report and respond in order to avoid or mitigate negative impacts. (p.12)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: Artificial intelligence should be designed and developed with the capability to implement fallback plans for system recovery from various failures including mechanisms to revoke data and services in order to ensure that users’ rights and interests are not violated and that no harm is caused to human life or the environment during recovery operations. (p.35)
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: AI models should be tested under conditions that reflect the dynamic nature of real-world environments to ensure the safety of users and the surrounding environment. They should also be continuously monitored reviewed and appropriately updated. However as pre-deployment testing is not explicitly specified this provision only partially addresses the requirement (p. 39).
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: The document requires AI systems to be designed developed and deployed with strong risk-prevention measures to protect system security prevent misuse and safeguard critical data personal information human life and the environment (p. 27). Systems must include capabilities to monitor detect and respond to threats resolve incidents restore normal operations after attacks and implement fallback plans including mechanisms to revoke data or services to protect users’ rights (p. 29). Researchers and developers should continuously update their skills to reduce emerging risks (p. 29). Public and private organisations must also comply with the Cybersecurity Act 2019 to ensure the cybersecurity of AI systems (p. 34).

fr1_title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
fr1_justif: Under the topic of Transparency and Explainability the AI Ethics guideline clearly states that AI should be researched designed developed provided and used in a transparent manner with explainable and predictable outcomes and with the ability to audit and review past activities. Also AI should have the capacity for traceability to monitor and detect anomalies and to diagnose system failures.(p.11)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: AI systems should transparently disclose their purposes decision-making reasons datasets capabilities limitations algorithms processes and reliability. The information should be explained in a way that affected individuals can understand considering different levels of knowledge and varied use contexts. This allows users to question how the AI works and to detect bias errors and unintended outcomes more easily. (p.25)
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: Stakeholders who may be affected by AI should be properly informed and have the right to request information about why AI is used on them and the impacts of such decisions. They should also be able to participate directly or indirectly in the design and development of AI throughout its life cycle. Users must be notified when they are interacting with an AI system rather than a human and made aware that decision outcomes are generated by AI. (p.26)

fr1_title: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system (PTTS/ISO/IEC 42001:20XX) (Trinidad and Tobago)
fr1_justif: It does not create dedicated rules for deepfakes election interference or gender-based or child-focused harms. Instead it addresses these risks through its general AI governance and risk-management framework. Clause 4.2 requires organisations to assess impacts on affected stakeholders while Clause 6.1 mandates identification and mitigation of risks from foreseeable misuse. Annex C lists social psychological and reputational harm and B.5.5 explicitly refers to misinformation for political gain and deepfakes. However no sector-specific prohibitions safeguards or victim-redress mechanisms are established.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: National Digital Transformation Strategy 2024-2027 (Trinidad and Togo)
fr1_justif: While the NDTS 2024-2027 is a broader digital strategy it contains explicit provisions addressing AI fairness and non-discrimination. Page 69 commits to removing bias from systems to ensure they are representative of and relevant to the diverse needs of society directly addressing algorithmic fairness in AI systems. Page 59 establishes that the e-ID system must focus on preventing discriminatory practices providing a concrete non-discrimination requirement in an AI-relevant context. Together these provisions demonstrate a demonstrable and explicit link to the Fairness and Non-Discrimination indicator
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Public Administration and AI (MPAAI)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Partially covered: Commitment to bias removal and representative systems (p.69). Non-discrimination principles (p.59) Recognition of vulnerable groups (p.29 59). Ethical research framework (p.30 69).  The framework establishes aspirational goals for fair AI outcomes but defers concrete measures to future policy development (p.68: forthcoming AI strategy).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: There are broad commitments to bias removal and non-discrimination (p.59 69)  recognition of some not all vulnerable groups: gender age disability (p.29 59 75).   Human rights framework (p.26 31). The document defers detailed provisions to the forthcoming AI Policy Strategy (p.68) making current protections aspirational rather than operational.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

fr1_title: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system (PTTS/ISO/IEC 42001:20XX) (Trinidad and Tobago)
fr1_justif: The standard establishes a dedicated AI impact assessment process through Annex B.5 requiring evaluation of effects on individuals groups and society. Annex B.5.4 (p. 31) addresses impacts on individuals/groups; Annex B.5.5 (p. 32) covers broader societal and health/safety impacts. Annex A (p.20) summarises these controls. Supporting clauses include: Clause 6 (risk-based planning) Clause 8 (operational controls) Clause 9 (performance monitoring) and Clause 10 (corrective action). Together these establish a lifecycle-wide framework for both ex-ante & ex-post AI impact assessment.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The standard doesn't explicitly require pre-deployment assessment of ethical and environmental impacts specifically making current provisions partial. Yet it promotes proactive risk management through Annex B.5 (AI impact assessment process) B.5.4 (impacts on individuals/groups) and B.5.5 (societal and health/safety impacts) alongside Clauses 6 8 and 9.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The standard explicitly assigns obligations to organisations developing & using AI to conduct structured impact assessments. Annex B.5 establishes a mandatory AI impact assessment process; B.5.4 requires assessment of impacts on individuals and groups; B.5.5 requires assessment of broader societal impacts. Clause 6 further requires organisations to identify and treat AI-related risks systematically. These are explicit obligations to conduct comprehensive impact assessments identifying and mitigating risks to individuals and society.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

fr1_title: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system (PTTS/ISO/IEC 42001:20XX) (Trinidad and Tobago)
fr1_justif: The Draft TTS/ISO/IEC 42001:2023 embeds safety & security throughout its AI management system architecture such as safety policy update requirements (B.2.3); assignment of roles & responsibilities (B.3.2); inclusion of diverse trustworthiness experts including safety specialists (B.4.6); assessment of societal impacts (B.5.5); AI system verification against safety requirements including acceptable error rates (Clause 6.2.4); structured risk assessments (Clause 6.2); impact assessment (Annex B.5.4); incident communication plans for safety problems (B.8.4); and safety explicitly listed as a risk source in Annex C (p.50). Lifecycle-wide monitoring & corrective a action mechanisms (Clauses 9-10) further ensure ongoing safety compliance.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: It is partially. The standard addresses reliability and accuracy through B.6.2.4 which requires organisations to document evaluation criteria based on safety requirements including acceptable error rates and B.5.5 which requires assessment of societal impacts on health and safety. However the standard doesn’t establish specific numerical performance thresholds or minimum accuracy requirements before deployment it assigns obligations to define and document such criteria organisationally rather than prescribing fixed benchmarks.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The draft standard provides organisational safeguards through operational controls (Clause 8.1) continuous monitoring (Clause 9.1) corrective-action requirements (Clause 10.1) and risk identification in Annex C. Yet it doesn't prescribe specific technical fallback mechanisms or emergency-shutdown procedures for AI system failures.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The draft promotes lifecycle robustness through impact-assessment provisions (Annex B.5.4) AI system verification requirements including documentation of evaluation criteria & acceptable error rates (Clause 6.2.4) data provenance & accuracy documentation requirements (Annex B.7.2-B.7.3) general documentation obligations (Clause 7) & monitoring obligations (Clause 9.1). However the standard doesn't impose detailed or standardised technical testing and validation procedures prior to deployment though it establishes governance & documentation obligations rather than prescribing specific technical validation protocols.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: The draft includes general security-related governance through risk-management requirements (Clause 6.1) operational controls (Clause 8.1) information-control provisions (Clause 7) and explicit identification of malicious or adversarial threats in Annex C. However it doesn't impose detailed or technical cybersecurity obligations tailored specifically to AI systems.

fr1_title: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system (PTTS/ISO/IEC 42001:20XX) (Trinidad and Tobago)
fr1_justif: Transparency is identified as a core principle within the standard and is to be incorporated into the design of organisational processes information systems and control mechanisms (p. x). Clause B.5.4 specifies that AI impact assessments must take account of transparency and explainability considerations. Clause 7.2 further requires that data-management practices address transparency and explainability including how data are used to determine system outputs. Clause 9.3 lists transparency among the objectives guiding the responsible use of AI. In addition Annex C.3 highlights a lack of transparency as a key AI-related risk that organisations should assess and mitigate.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust

fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: A.8.2 and A.8.3 assign transparency and reporting obligations to organisations but without sector-specific explainability requirements for high-stakes contexts.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

fr1_title: Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 (Uganda)
fr1_justif: The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 provides several specific sections that relate to access to redress and remedy including in contexts relevant to automated processing and decision making. Section 27 Rights in relation to automated decision-taking (p. 11 - 12) gives a data subject the right to challenge a decision significantly affecting them if that decision is solely based on automated processing. It mandates notification to the data subject gives a right to require reconsideration and allows a complaint to the regulator.' to include specific wording about automated decision taking and remove non-AI specific sections about redress and remedy.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: According to Section 7 subsections 2 (ii) and (iii) personal data collected for purposes of national security or the prevention detection investigation and prosecution of offenses are exempt from the standard consent requirements. Subsection (3) further clarifies that while data subjects generally have the right to object to data collection this right does not apply to data processed under the aforementioned legal exceptions in subsection (2)
fr1_body_name: The Personal Data Protection Office

fr1_title: Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 (Uganda)
fr1_justif: In Section 27 (Rights in relation to automated decision-taking p. 11-12) a data subject may require a data controller to ensure any decision that significantly affects them is not based solely on automated processing of personal data. If a significant decision is based solely on automated processing the controller must notify the data subject as soon as reasonably practicable and the data subject may require the controller to reconsider the decision within 21 days. In response the controller must inform the data subject in writing of steps taken. Also the data subject may complain to the Personal Data Protection Office (PDPO) if unsatisfied.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: According to Section 7 subsections 2 (ii) and (iii) personal data collected for purposes of national security or the prevention detection investigation and prosecution of offenses are exempt from the standard consent requirements. Subsection (3) further clarifies that while data subjects generally have the right to object to data collection this right does not apply to data processed under the aforementioned legal exceptions in subsection (2)
fr1_body_name: The Personal Data Protection Office
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 (DPPA) does not explicitly mention  AI or the phrase “meaningful human control.”However it indirectly promotes and enforces human oversight in automated decision-making processes. Section 27 gives a data subject  a right to give a notice in writing to a data controller require that a decision which significantly affects him or her is not based solely on automated processing of personal data. Where a decision which significantly affects a data subject is based solely on automated processing the data controller shall notify the data subject as soon as reasonably practicable.And a data subject may request reconsideration of such a decision within twenty-one days.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
