fr1_title: Law of Ukraine on Personal Data Protection
fr1_justif: Article 8 addresses automated decision-making by granting individuals the right to be protected from automated decisions that have legal consequences for them (Art. 8(13)). It also establishes avenues for redress by allowing data subjects to lodge complaints with the Commissioner or courts and to use legal remedies in case of violations of personal data protection legislation (Art. 8(8)–(9)).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Article 25 of the Law explicitly provides for restrictions on the application of Articles 6 7 and 8 in the interests of national security. This constitutes an explicit exclusion of defence and security domains from the core obligations of the framework.

fr1_element1_justif: The law establishes the Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights as an ombudsman responsible to receive complaints and other appeals on issues of personal data protection (p.10) allowing data subjects to lodge complaint where their data are processed unlawfully. fr1_title: Advisory on responsible use of artificial intelligence by public servants (Ukraine)
fr1_justif: (p.2) These tips are one of the components of the roadmap for regulating artificial intelligence (hereinafter referred to as AI) in Ukraine. The text outlines a systematic approach to the implementation and responsible use of artificial intelligence in professional activities by public servants. Basically the document's aim is to improve the civil servants' skills and capacities to engage with AI responsibly and ethically.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: (p.13) Public servants can use educational series available on the Diia.Osvita platform (a government-led resource) to further study and understand the basics of cyber hygiene and digital security. - there is a reference to multiple educative materials that build up an ecosystem of AI literacy for state sector. Most of such materials are located on the state-governed platform Diia.Osvita.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: (p.8) The implementation of AI systems in the public service requires the application of additional principles of using AI in the professional activities of a public servant namely: 7. adaptability (constant improvement of the principles of responsible implementation of AI in accordance with the technological development of AI systems and changes in legal regulation). This implies the need for professional development of the workers although it is not mentioned explicitly.

fr1_title: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Ukraine
fr1_justif: The Concept explicitly addresses workforce reskilling and upskilling in response to AI-driven labour market transformation. It directly acknowledges the risk of job displacement due to automation (p. 3) and provides targeted workforce measures most notably the development of a roadmap for retraining individuals whose work may be automated in the next five to ten years (p. 5). In addition the framework includes provisions for advanced training and professional retraining of personnel including adult education programs in artificial intelligence and support mechanisms such as scholarships for individuals undergoing such retraining (p. 4).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

fr1_title: Recommendations on responsible development of systems using AI technologies (Ukraine)
fr1_justif: (p.4)The objectives of these recommendations are:To guide AI system developers in adhering to ethical principles in the development and use of AI including risk-based security and reliability privacy and data protection fairness and justice transparency and accountability human oversight and monitoring leadership and awareness-raising and protection of intellectual property rights.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Scope limitations — contextually specific challenges in the development and use of AI systems such as industry differences data access restrictions privacy etc. that cannot be fully covered by general recommendations. These recommendations do not cover issues related to the national security and defense sector. (p.4)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: (p.14) The fifth factor is benchmark results. Comparing models using standardized tests helps to choose the most effective solution. The main metrics for evaluation include classification accuracy (Accuracy / F1-score) the balance between correct detection and avoidance of false positives (Precision / Recall) prediction execution time (Inference time) and the amount of memory required (Memory footprint). Using open platforms such as Papers with Code Hugging Face Leaderboard Chatbot Arena or MLPerf you can evaluate competing solutions based on real-world performance metrics.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: First of all it is necessary to clearly allocate responsibilities for the supervision of the AI system. Depending on the scale of the model’s functionality; the number of people in the field and the risk issues identified during the human rights impact assessment and risk assessment; it is necessary to determine: the number of people responsible for carrying out professional supervision; clear areas of their responsibility depending on their expertise and profile; an accountability system; a crisis protocol in case of incidents. (p.27)
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: (p.46) While the evidence includes provisions for the need to test and train data sets it does not include further requirements for pre deployment testing. However it extends requirements to the quality and origin of datasets.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: (p.45) The evidence indicates that developers should pay special attention to risks from cyber attacks such as attacks through data or model poisoning creation of backdoors (hidden access) for abuse or model inversion. There are no further measures for obligations or legal responsibility for non-compliance.

fr1_title: White Paper on Artificial Intelligence Regulation in Ukraine: Vision of the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine
fr1_justif: The document provides for a list of measures to be introduced within the governance and regulatory framework. One of such measures is Voluntary Labeling of AI Systems. Quote: Labeling of AI systems is the provision of clear and structured information about the design functions algorithms and other aspects of artificial intelligence systems. This process is aimed at ensuring transparency and openness regarding the way intelligent systems operate. Following the disclosure of information about the system by the developer such a system receives the appropriate labeling tags. - p.20
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Defence Sector is Not Subject to Regulation. While implementing our approach during the full-scale invasion of the Russian Federation were main aware of the importance of developing innovative solutions to repel aggression and in noway intend to propose regulation of AI systems in the defence sector. This is due to both the national interests of the state and the real state of affairs in the security sector – unilateral regulation (restriction) of the use of AI in the defence sector at the level of national legislation will only put our country in a less favorable position compared to the aggressor which will not implement such regulation. - p.10
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The document provides for 'building trust' as one of key priorities of state policy in AI sphere. Quote: User trust: labeled and therefore transparent AI systems help to build trust among users. Knowledge of AI system operations and information about its capabilities and limitations allow users to make informed decisions about their interaction with the technology similar to how end users can choose their diet through food ingredient labeling. Industry Trust: in the industry transparency fosters trust between companies researchers and developers of safety policies and regulations. Open sharing of information about AI systems encourages collaboration and thedevelopment of best safety practices.- p.21
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: There are no obligations however there is the suggestion of voluntary labelling of AI systems for both public and private sector which pursues the purposes of ensuring accountability ethics and compliance as well as building trust - p.21. The document generally refers to the need to establish risk-based classification of AI systems and apply safeguards according to the risk level including explainability - p.22
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: Building Trust. User trust: labeled and therefore transparent AI systems help to build trust among users. Knowledge of AI system operations and information about its capabilities and limitations allow users to make informed decisions about their interaction with the technology similar to how end users can choose their diet through food ingredient labeling. Industry Trust: in the industry transparency fosters trust between companies researchers and developers of safety policies and regulations. Open sharing of information about AI systems encourages collaboration and the development of best safety practices. - p.21

fr1_title: Federal Decree by Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data (United Arab Emirates)
fr1_justif: The Data Subject has the fundamental right to object to any decisions resulting from automated processing including profiling that adversely affect them(18). The Controller shall include the human element in reviewing automated processing decisions upon request providing immediate remedy against algorithmic error or bias. Data Subjects have the right to submit complaints to the UAE Data Bureau if a violation occurs(24). The Bureau examines complaints and can impose administrative penalties against the Controller/Processor if the violation is proven serving as a formal redress action. Individuals may communicate directly with the DPO regarding their rights and submit requests and complaints related to their personal data processing.(12)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Provisions of the Decree by Law shall not apply to Personal Data held by the security and judicial authorities. Provisions also shall not apply to Government Data which often encompasses defence and security-related information. However the framework includes a caveat regarding international data transfer stating that the cross-border transfer of data requires the Data Subject's consent provided that such transfer shall not contradict the public or security interest of the State
fr1_body_name: The UAE Data Bureau (Office)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: It focuses on administrative and internal non-judicial remedies: Individuals must submit a complaint to the UAE Data Bureau if a violation occurs (Art 24 c1). The Bureau examines the complaint and imposes administrative penalties (Art 24 c2 & 3). Stakeholders can submit a written grievance to the General Director of the Bureau against any penalty or decision it issues (Art 25). It is not permissible to challenge the Bureau's decision until this grievance is submitted (Art 25). The Data Subject has the non-judicial remedy to request the Controller include the human element in reviewing automated processing decisions (Art 18 c4). The Decree explicitly states its provisions shall not apply to Personal Data held by judicial authorities (Art 2).
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: The UAE Data Bureau (Office) is established as the primary regulator and state-based non-judicial body responsible for: receiving complaints imposing administrative penalties if a violation is proven. and dealing with any grievances against any decision or penalty imposed by the Bureau in the first instance.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: Companies (Controllers and Processors) must maintain internal grievance mechanisms for issues related to AI-driven processing (Art 11 c1b). The Data Protection Officer (DPO) is required to receive and manage complaints on personal data (Art 11 c1b). Data Subjects may directly contact the DPO about any data processing concerns including automated decisions (Art 12 c2). Controllers must provide clear accessible channels for such contact (Art 19). These internal mechanisms complement the external complaint process overseen by the UAE Data Bureau ensuring layered recourse and accountability. (Art 24 c1)

fr1_title: AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (United Arab Emirates)
fr1_justif: The framework explicitly addresses the protection of children in AI systems particularly under the Human-Centered AI (Principle 6) which require that AI systems capable of influencing behavior must be designed to distinguish between adults and children and implement additional safeguards for vulnerable populations such as children “when informed consent cannot be obtained or when it may not be a sufficient safeguard” (p. 35).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children

fr1_title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
fr1_justif: The policy addresses the UAE's diversified culture (over 200 nationalities) as its greatest advantage for AI development (p40). This diversity provides unique 'impeccable' data sets essential for machine learning and Artificial Intelligence applications specifically citing diagnostics for diseases like Tuberculosis (p40). The document also seeks to contextualize global AI debates for young Arab countries and leverage the strong regional talent pool in MENA (p7). For Linguistic Diversity the AI Office will establish an open-access digital library of research and papers in both English and Arabic (p39). This initiative aims to boost the research sector and close the research gap in the region (p39).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: UAE AI and Blockchain Council
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The UAE's 'diversified culture with more than 200 nationalities' is deemed its 'greatest advantage'. This results in 'impeccable' data sets that can be used for responsive applications such as diagnosing diseases like Tuberculosis (TB) using Artificial Intelligence.For language the AI Office will create an 'open-access digital library of research and papers in both English and Arabic'. This aims to 'boost the research sector in the region' making knowledge culturally and linguistically accessible. The Strategy also required contextualizing debates for 'young and ambitious Arab countries'.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: It addresses prevention indirectly through ethical data and linguistic measures. The strategy focuses on a 'values-driven approach to AI' and mandates a National Governance Review of 'ethics'. This moves beyond abstract principles to 'useable guidelines'. Quality control is established via the UAI Seal of Approval recognizing 'high quality ethical AI companies' through a 'robust rigorous and comprehensive certification methodology'. The strategy leverages the UAE’s diversified culture as an asset for developing 'impeccable' data sets countering bias inherent in limited training data. To prevent linguistic erasure the AI Office will establish an 'open-access digital library of research and papers in both English and Arabic.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (United Arab Emirates)
fr1_justif: The document addresses fairness and non-discrimination under 'Fairness (Principle 1)'. It mandates that AI systems 'should not discriminate against people or groups' and must be 'provably fair' especially for 'significant and critical decisions'.To ensure this organizations must define their context-specific meaning of fairness and undertake 'Discrimination Impact Assessments'. Guidelines require mitigating and disclosing 'biases inherent in datasets' and ensuring data is 'accurate and representative of the affected population'. The framework emphasizes 'inclusiveness equality human benefit and rights' and requires considering whether subjects receive 'equal treatment' in the same circumstances
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The core principle of the guidelines is that the UAE 'will make AI systems fair'(3.1.1). Guidelines ensure that benefits are 'available and accessible to all'(3.1.2.1) & that AI systems respect 'inclusiveness equality human benefit and rights'(1.3). AI systems should be designed to achieve a 'fair and just society'(3.6.2.4). AI systems 'should not discriminate against people or groups in a way that could have an adverse impact'(3.1.2.1). Organizations must implement 'Discrimination Impact Assessments' (3.1.2)
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: It states AI systems 'should not discriminate against people or groups in a way that could have an adverse impact'(3.1.2). Requires assessing 'demographic groups that may be adversely impacted' and ensuring data is 'representative of the affected population'(3.1.2). Under Privacy (3.8) the document explicitly lists characteristics such as 'race descent gender age language religion political opinion national origin ethnic origin social origin... or disability' as sensitive data that must be fully secured due to potential for damage injury or hardship if disclosed. Steps must be taken to 'mitigate and disclose the biases inherent in datasets' & evaluate all datasets to assess 'inclusiveness of identified demographic groups'(3.1.2)
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The framework assigns proactive obligations to developers and operators to address bias throughout the lifecycle: Data must be 'accurate and representative of the affected population' to avoid 'non-operational bias'(3.1.2).Organizations must 'mitigate and disclose the biases inherent in datasets'(3.1.2).They are advised to use 'Discrimination Impact Assessments' & identify 'demographic groups that may be adversely impacted'(3.1.2).The goal is to ensure 'equal treatment' (3.1.2) respecting 'inclusiveness equality human benefit and rights'(1.3)& achieving a 'fair and just society'(3.6.2.4). Sensitive characteristics are protected under Privacy ensuring data is not used to 'unlawfully or unfairly discriminate' (3.8.2)

fr1_title: DIFC Regulation 10 – Accreditation and Certification Framework For Autonomous and Semi-Autonomous Systems Processing Personal Data (“Framework”) (United Arab Emirates)
fr1_justif: DIFC Regulation 10 addresses gender equality indirectly through its mandatory principle of Fairness. It requires high-risk AI systems to be certified and designed to 'treat all individuals equally and fairly regardless of race gender or other specifically subjective factors'. The framework also mandates that systems must be designed to avoid or mitigate 'unjust bias' and 'discrimination'. This creates an enforceable auditable mechanism to challenge gender-based harm from AI within the DIFC's jurisdiction.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Regulation 10 Advisory Committee
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: The document provides general provisions for the assignment for obligations and responsibilities to developers of AI systems which are applied to protect gender equality.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: Federal Decree by Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data (United Arab Emirates)
fr1_justif: The framework ensures human oversight in AI through explicit rights and obligations on automated processing (Art18 c.4). Under Article 18(p21) individuals may object to decisions made via automation or profiling that have legal or adverse effects (c.1). When an objection is raised the Controller must include human review(c.4) ensuring a person reassesses the outcome. For high-risk automation a Personal Data Protection Impact Assessment (PDPIA) is required to evaluate risks and safeguards (Art 21 c.1) p23. Together these provisions guarantee that AI-driven decisions remain subject to meaningful human intervention.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection explicitly excludes defence security judicial authorities and government entities from its scope (art 2 c.2). This carve-out preserves state sovereignty and public order as such data is governed by specialised security and intelligence laws. The exemption ensures national security operations aren’t constrained by data-subject rights like erasure or objection(art17 c.2 & art18c2.b). The law further allows processing and transfers tied to judicial or security procedures confirming that critical state functions operate under separate higher-level legal regimes (art 4 c3 & art 23 c. 1(ce)).
fr1_body_name: The UAE Data Bureau (Office)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 promotes meaningful human control by ensuring human judgment can override automated decisions with serious consequences. Data Subjects have the right to object to automated or profiled outcomes and Controllers must include human review upon request. For high-risk automation a Data Protection Impact Assessment is required to evaluate and mitigate risks. Transparency is ensured through information rights on automated decisions while DPO oversight strengthens accountability and safeguards against uncontrolled automation.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 ensures human intervention and ethical judgment in automated decisions with significant impact. It grants individuals the right to object to automated or profiled outcomes and requires Controllers to conduct human review when requested. For high-risk automation a Data Protection Impact Assessment must evaluate potential harms and mitigation measures. Although security and health data may fall under other laws the Decree guarantees human oversight for any automated decision that adversely affects individuals within its scope.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 assigns clear accountability for oversight and intervention in high-risk data processing. It designates the Controller and Processor as responsible entities and mandates appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO) for sensitive or automated processing. The DPO verifies compliance advises on risk evaluations and ensures timely involvement in data protection matters. Controllers must keep records of authorized access and are accountable to the UAE Data Bureau which may impose penalties for violations ensuring strong human oversight and accountability.

fr1_title: AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (United Arab Emirates)
fr1_justif: The guidelines addresses Impact Assessments (IA) through specific non-mandatory guidelines (p5 1.1). It recommends Discrimination Impact Assessments (DIAs) for fairness which should be conducted both pre-release and regularly after as an ongoing evaluation (p17 3.1.2). For Privacy preserving AI algorithmic systems require adequate Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) that must also include societal and ethical considerations (p42 3.8.2). Operators should consider internal risk assessments and human rights impact assessments (p37 3.6.2.4). The document also mandates that AI applications be assessed through critical examination of resource usage and environmental impact throughout the AI lifecycle (p.38 3.7.1).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The document promotes proactive risk management and requires ex-ante evaluation for AI systems making 'significant decisions'. Mechanisms mandated for evaluation before deployment include:Recommending formal Discrimination Impact Assessments (DIAs) (p17 3.1.2) pre-release & requiring Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) that cover societal & ethical considerations (p40 3.8.1). Developers must identify & mitigate significant inherent risks and requiring critical examination of resource usage and energy consumption(p38 3.7.1). Efforts must be made to estimate and understand sustainability and environmental impact (e.g. CO2 emissions) throughout the AI lifecycle making carbon impacts a core consideration during model development. (p38 3.7.2)
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The guidelines assign obligations to AI developers and operators to conduct risk and impact assessments before and after deployment. (3.1.2.1 p17) They recommend Discrimination Privacy and Human Rights Impact Assessments to ensure fairness data protection and ethical use. (3.1.2.1 p17) Under Accountable and Robust AI principles actors must identify and mitigate risks (3.2.1 p20) assess the impact of incorrect decisions prevent harm and perform vulnerability and safety assessments. These measures promote fairness safety and accountability in AI systems making significant decisions. (1.1 p5)
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The guidelines recommend public release of audit findings for AI systems making critical decisions of civic interest to ensure accountability (p22 3.2.2.3). Under Accountable AI such systems should undergo external audits (p20 3.2.2) with results publicly released where outcomes significantly affect individuals or society (p22 3.2.2.3). The guidelines also promote transparency through responsible disclosure of data algorithms and decision factors and suggest public sector AI systems may share source code and explanations (p26 3.3.1). Documentation of impact assessments and traceability records further supports accountability.(p22 3.2.2.3)

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
fr1_justif: The strategy contains explicit targeted measures for public sector AI skill development most notably under Objective 5 which introduces dedicated “Government Training” programs designed to equip civil servants with AI competencies (p. 33). These include advanced courses for government employees mandatory engagement projects tied to their institutional roles and the stated goal that “100% of senior leadership in government… are trained and versed in AI” (p. 33). The document further recognizes the urgency of reskilling public sector workers due to automation risks explicitly identifying government employment as a key area requiring intervention (p. 32).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: UAE AI and Blockchain Council
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

fr1_title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
fr1_justif: The strategy explicitly addresses workforce reskilling and upskilling in response to AI-driven labour market transformation particularly under Objective 5. It recognises that a significant share of jobs may be affected by automation and identifies retraining as “particularly critical” (p. 32). It outlines concrete pathways such as professional upskilling through specialised AI training secondments and study opportunities (pp. 34–35) as well as employment transition support including career guidance and training for workers at risk of displacement (p. 35). It further presents a structured multi-tiered approach encompassing apprenticeships short courses scholarships and project-based learning (p. 34).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: UAE AI and Blockchain Council
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: The UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (July 2024)
fr1_justif: Under Safety the UAE places great importance on ensuring that all AI systems comply with the highest safety standards (p3 s2). The country also actively encourages modifying or removing systems that pose risks (p3 s2). Regarding security the Charter emphasizes that the development of AI must ensure peaceful coexistence with the technology (p5 s10). This peaceful coexistence is crucial to ensure technology enhances well-being without compromising human security or fundamental rights(p5 s10).Furthermore the principles of Human Oversight Governance and Accountability and Commitment to Treaties and Applicable Laws collectively enforce a robust and responsible environment that ensures safety and protects the rights of the UAE community (p5.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

fr1_title: Federal Decree by Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data (United Arab Emirates)
fr1_justif: The document addresses AI transparency and explainability through specific controls on 'Automated Processing' and 'Profiling'. Processing must be transparent. Data Subjects have the right to information regarding 'Decisions made based on automated processing including profiling' and the right to object to adverse decisions resulting from such processes. Crucially the Controller must include the human element in reviewing automated processing decisions upon the Data Subject's request. Furthermore automated processing involving systematic assessment or high risk requires a Personal Data Protection Impact Assessment and a Data Protection Officer.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The Scope of Application (Article 2) mandates that the provisions of the Federal Decree by Law No. (45) of 2021 shall not apply to personal data held by the security and judicial authorities. This clause ensures that data processing activities handled by authorities responsible for security functions are exempted from the law's obligations.
fr1_body_name: The UAE Data Bureau (Office)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The framework assigns clear obligations to Controllers using automated processing or profiling (AI) to ensure explainability and accountability. Controllers must inform individuals when decisions are made through automation and disclose the basis for those decisions. Data subjects have the right to object and request human review of AI-driven outcomes ensuring meaningful explanations and human oversight. For high-risk or high-impact processing such as credit or employment decisions Controllers must conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment that documents decision logic and processing purposes in advance.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The framework grants individuals explicit rights to understand and challenge AI-driven decisions affecting them. Data subjects can request information on automated or profiled decisions including their purpose and outcome. They have the right to object to such decisions especially when legally or personally significant and to demand human review ensuring meaningful explanation of key factors behind the outcome. For high-risk processing controllers must conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment detailing the system’s logic and rationale before deployment promoting transparency and accountability.

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: National AI Strategy (2021) (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The strategy addresses AI literacy under Pillar 2: Skills and Talent (pp. 40–47). It promotes access to AI data and digital skills via computing education in schools Skills Bootcamps and lifelong learning. It backs teacher training through the National Centre for Computing Education and calls for inclusive pathways into AI careers. The strategy emphasizes AI literacy as vital for public understanding equity and preparing the workforce for the AI-driven economy.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Office for AI
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy supports AI programmes in schools (e.g. via the National Centre for Computing Education) (Summary of key actions pp. 8–9).  It also backs tertiary provision via AI/data science Masters conversion courses across universities (pp. 22–23). However it does not set out explicit curriculum reforms across all primary/secondary/tertiary levels.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: It describes new/expanded formal education programmes: '2500 new Masters conversion courses in AI and data science…delivered across universities' (Skills & Talent pp. 22–23). It also cites '16 new AI Centres for Doctoral Training…delivering 1000 new PhDs' (From Sector Deal to AI Strategy p. 18). It further commits to support the National Centre for Computing Education so AI programmes for children are accessible (Pillar 1 Actions / Summary of key actions pp. 38–39 / pp. 8–9).
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The Strategy commits to supporting the National Centre for Computing Education (NCCE) so AI programmes for schools are accessible (Summary of key actions pp. 8–9; Pillar 1 Actions pp. 38–39). However it does not explicitly set out dedicated teacher training measures in the text.

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Online Safety Act 2023 (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: While the Online Safety Act 2023 framework is relevant as it regulates the algorithmic systems through which such content spreads. Section 152 (p. 158) establishes an advisory committee on disinformation and misinformation to guide OFCOM. Sections 9(5)(b) and 11(6)(b) (pp. 8 11) require providers to assess risks considering 'algorithms used by the service and how easily quickly and widely content may be disseminated.' Section 231(10) (p. 229) defines 'proactive technology' utilising 'artificial intelligence or machine learning' for content identification and moderation. Thus the Act addresses the infrastructure enabling harmful content dissemination
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Defence and security are explicitly excluded from the Act's scope. Schedule 1 paragraph 9(3) (p. 248) states that the provisions do not apply to services provided by the Crown which includes government departments and agencies such as the Ministry of Defence and intelligence bodies. The Act's duties apply only to commercial online services not to state-run defence or security systems.
fr1_body_name: The Office of Communications
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The Online Safety Act 2023 addresses the prevention of AI tools being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation hate speech harassment and violence. It requires providers to assess and mitigate risks arising from algorithms and other service functionalities that may amplify illegal or harmful content (s. 9(5)(b) p. 9). Providers must take proportionate measures relating to the design and operation of algorithms and features to reduce such risks (s. 10(4)(b)–(e) pp. 9–10) including the use of proactive technology. The Act mandates removal of illegal content such as terrorism threats and hate-based abuse (s. 10(2)–(3) pp. 9–10).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: The Online Safety Act 2023 assigns clear obligations to platforms but not to AI developers as a distinct actor. Providers of regulated services must implement robust content moderation systems to address illegal and harmful content including duties to use proportionate systems and processes and proactive technology (ss. 9–10 pp. 8-9). The Act also requires transparency including mandatory provider transparency reports on content moderation practices (s. 77 pp. 80–81) and empowers Ofcom to require information about algorithms and systems (s. 85 pp. 87–88). However the framework does not impose standalone obligations on AI developers focusing instead on platform-level moderation and transparency.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Online Safety Act 2023 establishes protective and redress-related mechanisms for individuals targeted by misinformation and tech-facilitated violence but does not create a direct individual right to sue platforms. Providers must offer accessible reporting and complaints procedures and act on reported illegal and harmful content (ss. 17–18 pp. 15–16). Users may escalate unresolved complaints to the Office of Communications which can investigate and enforce compliance against platforms (Part 7 ss. 131–147 pp. 133–147). However it does not provide a standalone civil redress mechanism against platforms; enforcement is regulator-led not victim-initiated.
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 addresses Access to Redress and Remedy in the AI context primarily through safeguards for automated decision-making. Articles 22A–22C (pp. 95–96) define significant decisions based solely on automated processing and require protections for individuals affected. These safeguards include providing information about the decision enabling individuals to make representations obtain human intervention and contest the decision ensuring meaningful avenues for redress. Further provisions on meaningful human involvement and reconsideration of decisions are set out in Article 22D and related sections (pp. 96–98) reinforcing the right to challenge and remedy AI-driven outcomes.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: In the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 defence intelligence and national security are treated as explicit exclusions from the general framework through dedicated exemptions and carve-outs for intelligence services and national security processing (pp. 105–108). These sections remove such activities from the ordinary application of safeguards and rights meaning defence and security are effectively excluded from the framework’s scope for the purposes of this assessment.
fr1_body_name: Information Commissioner
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 explicitly relies on state-based non-judicial mechanisms to handle grievances arising from automated and AI-driven decision-making. The Information Commissioner is empowered to supervise compliance receive complaints investigate controllers’ reliance on exemptions and enforce safeguards related to automated decisions (Articles 22A–22D pp. 95–99). Individuals can challenge automated decisions and seek remedies through the Commissioner making this a clear use of an existing regulatory body as a non-judicial complaint mechanism for AI-related harms.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 imposes mandatory safeguards on controllers using automated or AI-driven decision-making requiring them to enable individuals to make representations obtain human intervention and contest decisions (Articles 22C and 50C pp. 96–98). These function as internal grievance and review mechanisms within organisations. However the Act does not require companies or developers to establish standalone or formal complaints systems nor does it provide incentives such as trust marks. Therefore it addresses access to grievance mechanisms in substance but not in full scope (pp. 95–98).

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Online Safety Act 2023 (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The Act protects children from AI-driven harms by requiring regulated services to assess and mitigate algorithmic risks (ss. 9–13 pp. 9–15). It obliges providers to consider how algorithms automated decision-making and design features affect children’s exposure to harmful content (s. 11 (6)(b) p. 11). Services must use proportionate age-verification or estimation technologies (s. 12 (4–8) pp. 12–13) and apply safety-by-design principles. Ofcom enforces these duties ensuring AI systems used online uphold children’s safety and wellbeing.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Defence and security are explicitly excluded from the Act's scope. Schedule 1 paragraph 9(3) (p. 248) states that the provisions do not apply to services provided by the Crown which includes government departments and agencies such as the Ministry of Defence and intelligence bodies. The Act's duties apply only to commercial online services not to state-run defence or security systems.
fr1_body_name: The Office of Communications
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: Sections 9–13 (pp. 9–15) require regulated services to assess and mitigate risks to children arising from algorithms and data-driven features indirectly protecting privacy. Section 12 (4–8) mandates proportionate age verification or estimation measures limiting children’s data use. However the Act does not establish standalone provisions on personal data or AI-specific privacy rights which remain under data protection law.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: Sections 9–13 (pp. 9–15) require services to assess and mitigate risks to children from the design and operation of algorithms and functionalities. Section 11(6)(b) (p. 11) specifically includes “algorithms used by the service” as potential causes of harm. Section 12 (4–8) mandates measures to prevent children’s exposure to harmful or manipulative content including AI-driven recommendation or targeted advertising systems.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: Sections 9(2) and 11(6)(b) (pp. 9 11) require service providers to assess and mitigate risks to children arising from the design of functionalities and algorithms. Section 12(4–8) (pp. 12–13) mandates age-appropriate design and proportionate measures to ensure children’s safety. These provisions assign clear obligations to developers and operators of AI-driven systems to design platforms that are safe and suitable for child users.
fr2_title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (United Kingdom)
fr2_justif: The Act strengthens children’s privacy in AI contexts by amending UK GDPR data-protection-by-design duties to include “children’s higher protection matters” (Bill cl.81) and by requiring ICO codes of practice on AI/ADM and EdTech. It also revises ADM rules with safeguards (info challenge human intervention). DSIT’s guidance highlights a dedicated section on Children’s Data Protection and ADM safeguards.
fr2_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr2_defence_and_security_justif: In the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 defence intelligence and national security are treated as explicit exclusions from the general framework through dedicated exemptions and carve-outs for intelligence services and national security processing (pp. 105–108). These sections remove such activities from the ordinary application of safeguards and rights meaning defence and security are effectively excluded from the framework’s scope for the purposes of this assessment.
fr2_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr2_element1_justif: The Act amends UK GDPR Article 25 to require data-protection-by-design that takes account of “children’s higher protection matters” for services likely to be accessed by children (Art.25(1A)–(1B)). ADM provisions add safeguards (info challenge human intervention contestation) where decisions are solely automated.
fr2_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr2_element2_justif: The Act limits harmful automated decision-making via restrictions and safeguards (Arts.22B–22C) and strengthens design duties for children (Art.25(1A)–(1B)) reducing manipulation risk. However it does not directly regulate content or targeted advertising to children (addressed primarily by Online Safety law).
fr2_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr2_element3_justif: Controllers must factor children’s higher protection matters into technical/organisational measures (Art.25(1A)–(1B)). Where decisions are solely automated controllers must implement safeguards (provide info enable representations human intervention contestation) and additional measures can be set by SoS regulations.

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: National AI Strategy (2021) (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The diversity focus is limited to workforce representation (gender race disability) on pages 16-17 (Reflecting and protecting society section) and page 23 (conversion courses diversity statistics). Page 31 addresses algorithmic bias through representative datasets and mentions bias detection using sensitive data. The Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities is referenced on page 51 regarding algorithmic bias concerns not cultural/linguistic preservation.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Office for AI
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: The document addresses bias prevention but not cultural/linguistic diversity specifically. Page 31 states 'Poor quality datasets can also be un-representative especially when it comes to minority groups and this can propagate existing biases.' It commits to permitting data collection 'to monitor and mitigate bias in AI systems.' Page 51 acknowledges 'concerns around fairness bias and accountability.' Page 58 references CDEI's work on 'algorithmic bias.' However there are no provisions addressing cultural stereotypes linguistic diversity erasure or AI favoring dominant cultures.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: AI Opportunities Action Plan (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The document addresses Environmental Impact minimally primarily in Section 1.1 'Building sufficient secure and sustainable AI infrastructure' (pages 7-9). Recommendation 5 (page 9) calls on government to 'mitigate the sustainability and security risks of AI infrastructure' and support companies demonstrating 'sustainability or security advancements.' Recommendation 4 (pages 8-9) references accelerating 'clean power' provisioning for AI Growth Zones.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The UK Sovereign AI and Digital Centre of Government
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
fr1_element1_justif: The document makes limited reference to sustainability by stating that government should “mitigate the sustainability and security risks of AI infrastructure” and support hardware that demonstrates “performance sustainability or security” improvements. However these mentions remain general and aspirational. There are no specific provisions measurable targets or concrete policy tools addressing excessive energy consumption resource-intensive AI development or e-waste management. (pp. 7-9).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
fr1_element3_text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
fr1_element3_justif: The plan partially addresses renewable energy: Recommendation 4 (page 8) specifies AI Growth Zones should be provisioned with 'clean power' and Recommendation 5 (page 9) references mitigating 'sustainability risks' and leveraging sustainability 'advancements.' This covers renewable energy sourcing at a high level. However no provisions address advanced cooling technologies optimised hardware water consumption or carbon footprint reduction targets.  Only one of the four aspects (renewable energy) is partially addressed.

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The Act addresses fairness and non-discrimination through Section 80 on Automated Decision-Making. Article 22B restricts significant decisions based solely on automated processing when involving special categories of personal data (e.g. race ethnicity health political opinions) under Article 9(1). Article 22C mandates safeguards including: (a) informing data subjects about automated decisions; (b) enabling representations; (c) providing human intervention; and (d) enabling individuals to contest decisions. Section 50B-50C extends similar protections for law enforcement contexts. These provisions protect against discriminatory AI outcomes by limiting automated decisions on protected characteristics and ensuring redress mechanisms.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: In the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 defence intelligence and national security are treated as explicit exclusions from the general framework through dedicated exemptions and carve-outs for intelligence services and national security processing (pp. 105–108). These sections remove such activities from the ordinary application of safeguards and rights meaning defence and security are effectively excluded from the framework’s scope for the purposes of this assessment.
fr1_body_name: Information Commissioner
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Article 22B (Page 95) restricts automated decisions based on special categories of personal data (race ethnicity religion health) under Article 9(1) preventing discriminatory processing. Article 22C (Pages 95-96) requires safeguards including human intervention and the right to contest decisions providing redress mechanisms. The Act lacks explicit requirements for: proactive bias auditing of AI systems fairness metrics or testing bias impact assessments pre-deployment monitoring for discriminatory algorithmic outcomes or mandates to ensure equitable results across demographic groups. The focus is on procedural safeguards and individual rights rather than systemic measures to promote fair AI outcomes.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: Article 22B (Page 95) prohibits significant automated decisions based solely on processing of special categories of personal data under Article 9(1) which includes race ethnicity religion political opinions health and biometric data. This restricts discriminatory automated processing based on protected characteristics. Article 22C (Pages 95-96) mandates safeguards and Section 50B (Page 97) extends restrictions for sensitive processing in law enforcement contexts.However the Act does not explicitly require measures to prevent AI systems from perpetuating historical biases in training data auditing algorithms for discriminatory patterns monitoring for bias amplification or proactive detection of systemic discrimination.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: AI Opportunities Action Plan (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The Plan promotes gender equality by committing to “increase the diversity of the talent pool” in AI noting that Only 22% of people working in AI and data science are women and that the government needs to focus on increasing the representation by targeted education and initiatives (pp. 11-12).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: AI Opportunities Unit
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
fr1_element3_justif: The Plan commits to “increase the diversity of the talent pool” in AI noting that only 22% of AI and data-science workers are women (pp. 11–12). It calls for expanding the representation by targeted education initiatives (p. 12).

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Data Protection Act 2018 (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The Act hardwires human oversight into AI decisions. Part 2 s.14 (p.14) supplementing UK GDPR Art.22 requires that when a 'qualifying significant decision' is made solely by automated processing the controller must notify the person and if asked within one month reconsider or take a new non-automated decision. For law enforcement (Part 3) ss.49–50 (pp.50–51) and ss.50A–50D (pp.52–54) enable individuals to obtain human intervention make representations and contest decisions; reconsideration must involve 'meaningful human involvement.' For intelligence services (Part 4) ss.96–97 (pp.93–94) provide similar rights.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The Act contains broad national security exemptions (e.g. Section 26) and a separate regime for intelligence services (Part 4) which allow the government to disapply many GDPR-style protections including Article 22–type rights. As a result human oversight is not legally guaranteed for individuals in security and defence contexts although institutional oversight mechanisms (e.g. commissioners and parliamentary committees) still exist.
fr1_body_name: Information Commissioners Office (ICO)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: Article 22 of the UK GDPR restricts decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect individuals and grants the right to human intervention promoting meaningful human control. However the law applies only when decisions are solely automated and significantly impactful and it does not explicitly emphasize human oversight in all AI uses or critical systemic areas. Thus while it supports human judgment in some contexts it does not fully address all elements of the statement.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: Article 22 of the UK GDPR prohibits solely automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects unless certain conditions are met ensuring human review in high-impact scenarios. This offers protection in some sensitive sectors (e.g. public services credit or employment) but the law does not explicitly target or prohibit full automation in specific fields like law enforcement or medicine. Thus it partially addresses the prevention of full automation in critical sectors.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: The UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 assign accountability to data controllers requiring them to ensure lawful processing including for automated decision-making. Controller obligations are set out in s.6 (p.8) and the general obligations in Part 3 s.56 (p.58) while automated decision-making safeguards appear in s.14(4)–(5) (p.14). While data protection officers must be designated for law enforcement processing under ss.69–71 (pp.66–68) the law does not explicitly require the appointment of named persons to oversee or intervene in AI decisions specifically. Therefore while accountability is mandated designation of specific individuals for AI oversight is not directly stated.

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Data Protection Act 2018 (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: It addresses impact assessments primarily through Section 64 which mandates Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) when processing is 'likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals.' Controllers must conduct DPIAs prior to processing including a description of operations risk assessment mitigation measures and safeguards. Section 65 requires prior consultation with the Information Commissioner when a DPIA indicates high risk. These requirements apply directly to AI systems processing personal data particularly those involving automated decision-making or profiling. Court-case proving application of the law to AI: https://www.judiciary.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/R-Bridges-v-CC-South-Wales-ors-Judgment
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The Act contains broad national security exemptions (e.g. Section 26) and a separate regime for intelligence services (Part 4) which allow the government to disapply many GDPR-style protections including Article 22–type rights. As a result human oversight is not legally guaranteed for individuals in security and defence contexts although institutional oversight mechanisms (e.g. commissioners and parliamentary committees) still exist.
fr1_body_name: Information Commissioners Office (ICO)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: The Act promotes proactive risk management by requiring controllers to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before processing that is likely to pose a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms (s.64(1)). The DPIA must assess the nature of the processing risks to data subjects and the measures and safeguards planned to mitigate those risks (s.64(3)). Where the assessment indicates a high risk that cannot be adequately mitigated the controller must consult the Information Commissioner prior to processing (s.65(2)). Together these provisions require risks to be evaluated and addressed before deployment of potentially harmful data processing activities.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The Act assigns obligations to data controllers to conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) where processing is likely to pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals (s.64(1)). The DPIA must include a description of the processing operations an assessment of risks to data subjects and the measures and safeguards planned to mitigate those risks (s.64(3)). Where the assessment indicates that risks remain high the controller must consult the Information Commissioner before processing begins (s.65(2)). These provisions require organizations to systematically assess and address potential harms before deploying high-risk data processing activities.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: The Data Protection Act 2018 establishes accountability mechanisms enabling individuals to hold organizations accountable for AI system impacts. Section 165 (page 155) grants data subjects the right to lodge complaints with the Commissioner regarding data protection violations. Section 167 (page 157) provides the right to apply to courts for compliance orders. Section 168 (page 159) enables compensation claims for contraventions. Section 124C (page 121) requires the Commissioner to publish impact assessments for codes of practice.

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Data Protection Act 2018 (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: Article 22(1) provides workers the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing including profiling which produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect them. Recital 71 explicitly references employment contexts including 'e-recruiting practices without any human intervention' and decisions evaluating 'performance at work.' Article 22(3) mandates safeguards including the right to obtain human intervention express one's point of view and contest automated decisions. Articles 13(2)(f) and 14(2)(g) require employers to provide meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decision-making and its significance and consequences.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The Act contains broad national security exemptions (e.g. Section 26) and a separate regime for intelligence services (Part 4) which allow the government to disapply many GDPR-style protections including Article 22–type rights. As a result human oversight is not legally guaranteed for individuals in security and defence contexts although institutional oversight mechanisms (e.g. commissioners and parliamentary committees) still exist.
fr1_body_name: Information Commissioners Office (ICO)
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: Article 22(1) protects individuals from decisions based solely on automated processing producing 'legal effects' or 'similarly significant effects' covering hiring promotion and termination. Recital 71 explicitly references 'e-recruiting practices without any human intervention' and evaluation of 'performance at work.' Article 22(3) mandates safeguards including human intervention and the right to contest decisions. Article 22(4) restricts automated decisions based on special category data including race and ethnic origin. However the framework does not explicitly address 'discrimination' as a concept which falls under separate legislation (Equality Act 2010). It also does not specifically reference 'algorithmic management systems'.
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: Article 5(1)(a) establishes transparency as a core principle requiring processing to be 'lawful fair and transparent.' Articles 13(2)(f) and 14(2)(g) mandate controllers provide 'meaningful information about the logic involved as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences' of automated decision-making. Article 15(1)(h) grants workers the right to access information about 'the existence of automated decision-making including profiling' and its logic. Recital 71 references employment contexts including 'performance at work' and the right to 'obtain an explanation of the decision reached.' Article 12 requires information to be provided in 'concise transparent intelligible and easily accessible form.'
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems
fr1_title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS): Mandatory Scope and Exemptions Policy (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The ATRS establishes mandatory public disclosure of government algorithmic systems. Section 1 (Summary) mandates publication of ATRS records on GOV.UK. Section 3 (Organisations in scope) defines covered entities: ministerial departments non-ministerial departments and arm's-length bodies providing public services. Section 4 (Algorithmic tools in scope) requires disclosure for tools with 'significant influence on decision-making with public effect' or that 'directly interact with the public.' The framework requires proactive transparency through a standardised template capturing purpose data risks and human oversight.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The ATRS Mandatory Scope and Exemptions Policy explicitly provides for national security exemptions stating that 'situations where no information can be safely published are expected to be unusual (e.g. in cases where even the existence of a tool cannot be made public for security reasons).' The policy also notes that national security was a key consideration in finalising the detailed scope of the mandatory requirement.
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
fr1_element1_justif: The ATRS addresses all aspects. Public registry: Section 2 (Introduction) establishes 'proactive publication of information on algorithmic tools in the public sector' via a repository at gov.uk/algorithmic-transparency-records. Purpose: Section 4.2 requires disclosure for tools with 'significant influence on decision-making with public effect' or that 'directly interact with the public' capturing each tool's purpose. Description of function: Section 4.1 requires information on how tools 'support or solve a specific problem using complex algorithms.' Responsible agency: Section 3 (Organisations in scope) mandates identification of responsible organisations; records must identify the owner department and team.
fr1_element2_text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
fr1_element2_justif: High-risk systems are covered in Section 4.2 (pages 7-8) which targets tools with 'significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect' or that 'directly interact with the general public.' Rationale for use is addressed in Section 5.3 (page 12) stating the ATRS focuses on 'the use case that a tool is deployed into and the steps taken to ensure that a tool is appropriate in that context.' Data for training is partially covered:Section 5.2 (page 11) shows a 'Dataset purposes' field exists in the template but provides limited detail on specific disclosure requirements. However the document contains no provisions requiring disclosure of impact assessment results; there are no references to impact assessment frameworks.
fr1_element3_text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
