fr1_element3_justif: The document provides a framework for distinguishing public disclosure from protected information though it offers broad recommendations rather than detailed guidelines. Section 2 (page 3) establishes that 'Transparency...should be our default position.' For national security Section 5.1 (page 9) addresses cases 'where even the existence of a tool cannot be made public for security reasons' ' For privacy Section 5.1 (page 10) notes the ATRS captures 'tool-level information rather than personal information'. However rather than providing specific disclosure criteria the document broadly aligns exemptions with Freedom of Information Act 2000 and offers guidance on documenting exemptions.
fr1_element4_text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Guidelines for AI procurement (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: AI-specific guidelines beyond IT requiring bias/risk checks vendor transparency (avoid ‘black box’) and lifecycle accountability. ‘Top 10 Considerations’ covers data assessment iterative AI impact assessment SME/VCSE-friendly market engagement governance/info assurance and avoiding ‘Black Box’ algorithms/vendor lock-in. In ‘AI-specific considerations’: Publication asks bidders to address data quality/bias and disclose algorithms/models (incl. possible independent audits); Selection/Evaluation lists robust practices (accountability non-discrimination reproducibility testing); Contract Implementation/Ongoing Management requires lifecycle monitoring and end-to-end auditability.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element1_justif: The guidance is AI-specific and goes beyond IT procurement by embedding ethical/social and technical safeguards. “Top 10 Considerations” covers data ethics bias/non-discrimination transparency/explainability governance and avoiding “black box” and vendor lock-in. “AI-specific considerations within the procurement process” adds Data Protection Impact Assessment/data governance data quality and bias checks robust evaluation (testing/reproducibility) and contract-stage monitoring/auditability.
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element2_justif: The Guidelines require vendors to evidence bias fairness and robustness through multiple stages of the procurement process. In “Publication” bidders must explain how they mitigate bias/discrimination and manage data quality and governance; in “Selection Evaluation and Award” authorities are advised to assess testing verification reproducibility and accountability; and in “Contract Implementation” suppliers must ensure ongoing monitoring auditability and lifecycle assurance.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element3_justif: The Guidelines explicitly warn against “black box” AI and recommend requiring vendor transparency on how systems work. “Top 10 Considerations” includes “Black Box AI systems” and advises obtaining sufficient information from suppliers about the model/algorithm and how it uses data and flags independent assurance/audits. In “Publication” and “Selection Evaluation and Award” it advises setting transparency/explainability requirements in the Invitation to Tender and evaluating suppliers’ ability to explain models and data use. This is intended to prevent procuring opaque systems.
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
fr1_justif: The document addresses public sector skills development through capacity building initiatives and training programs for civil servants. Principle 9 (p.14) establishes the competency requirement that civil servants gain skills to 'use design build and maintain AI solutions.' The Acquiring Skills and Talent section (pp.30-31) operationalises this through five learning pathways targeting different civil service roles from beginners to senior leaders. Training programs include free AI courses on Civil Service Learning covering AI fundamentals generative AI machine learning deep learning NLP and computer vision. The Digital Excellence Programme provides specialised AI training for senior civil servants while sandboxes enable practical e
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The document establishes a government-wide strategy for upskilling civil servants but excludes the judiciary. Principle 9 (p.14) requires civil servants gain skills to 'use design build and maintain AI solutions' and understand 'risks and opportunities of AI.' The Acquiring Skills and Talent section (pp.30-31) provides a comprehensive strategy with five learner pathways covering foundational AI understanding. Learning Resources (p.31) include courses on 'fundamentals of AI and generative AI including their capabilities and limitations' and 'understanding AI ethics.' However the framework exclusively targets 'civil servants' with no provisions for judges or judicial training.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The document addresses all three aspects. For dedicated AI roles the Governance section (pp.96-97) recommends 'AI governance boards' or 'AI expert representation on an existing governance board' providing oversight and strategic guidance. Ethics committees (p.97) assess ethical implications with specialized experts. For expert guidance the AI community of practice (p.32) offers 'monthly meetings for people working on or interested in AI in the public sector' to share best practices. For fostering responsible AI culture the Leaders pathway (p.31) targets senior civil servants 'responsible for creating an AI-ready culture in government' focusing on governance ethics and strategy.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The document establishes clear ongoing professional development requirements. Principle 9 (p.14) states civil servants should 'proactively keep track of developments in the field.' The Acquiring Skills section (p.30) mandates 'Every civil servant can take up to 5 days of learning per year' and emphasises that 'upskilling current digital and data professionals on AI remains crucial.' The Working Collaboratively section (p.32) recommends 'cross-government and industry events that will help your team stay updated on the latest developments and best practices.' The Governance section (p.96) requires frameworks focus on 'continuous improvement through the inclusion of new knowledge methods and technologies.'

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: AI Opportunities Action Plan (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: In Section 1.3 (“Training retaining and attracting the next generation of AI scientists and founders” pp.10–13) the Action Plan sets an AI skills agenda: it proposes training “tens of thousands” of AI professionals by 2030 (p.11) and expanding pathways into AI careers via further education apprenticeships and employer- or self-led upskilling (Recommendation 17 p.12). It also states the lifelong skills programme must be “ready for AI” ensuring opportunities for workers to reskill into AI and AI-enabled jobs (Recommendation 19 p.12).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Skills England
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The Plan covers the objective of reskilling/upskilling for AI-driven labour-market change: it says the lifelong skills programme must be “ready for AI” and that government should ensure “sufficient opportunities for workers to reskill both into AI and AI-enabled jobs” (Recommendation 19 p.12). It also recommends expanding pathways such as further education apprenticeships and employer/self-led upskilling (Recommendation 17 p.12). But it does not set up a specific subsidised programme or funding line in the text.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
fr1_element3_justif: The Plan supports the idea that employers should upskill workers by recommending expansion of pathways into AI and AI-enabled roles including “employer- or self-led upskilling” (Recommendation 17 p.12) and by calling for sufficient opportunities for workers to reskill ( Recommendation 19 p.12 ). But it does not impose binding requirements on companies to invest in training to mitigate automation-related job displacement (no mandated duties enforcement tools or penalties).

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The Code establishes 13 principles across 5 AI lifecycle phases to address cyber security risks specific to AI systems (Introduction). It mandates security obligations including: threat modelling and risk management for AI-specific attacks like data poisoning and model inversion (Principle 3); pre-deployment testing and security assessments (Principle 9); safeguards requiring systems to withstand adversarial attacks and failures (Principle 2); incident management and recovery plans (Principle 6); and monitoring for anomalies and security breaches (Principle 12). The Code applies to all AI supply chain stakeholders including developers system operators and data custodians (Audience section).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: The Code partially addresses this through security-focused provisions but lacks specific quantified thresholds. Principle 2 requires AI systems be 'designed and implemented to withstand adversarial AI attacks unexpected inputs and AI system failure' (2.2). Principle 9 mandates security testing before release (9.1). Principle 12 requires monitoring 'to ensure AI models continue to produce desired outputs' and to 'detect anomalies security breaches or unexpected behaviour over time' (12.2). However no specific minimum accuracy requirements quantified performance thresholds or quality benchmarks are established. The focus remains on security robustness rather than accuracy or reliability metrics.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: The Code comprehensively addresses all three aspects. For safeguards Principle 2 (2.2) requires systems 'designed and implemented to withstand adversarial AI attacks unexpected inputs and AI system failure.' For fallback procedures Principle 5 (5.3) mandates 'disaster recovery plans to account for specific attacks' and (5.3.1) requires ensuring 'a known good state can be restored.' For emergency protocols Principle 6 (6.5) requires 'an AI system incident management plan and an AI system recovery plan.' Principle 11 (11.1.1) mandates 'contingency plans to mitigate security risks.' Principle 10 (10.3) requires support during incidents 'to contain and mitigate the impacts.'
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: The Code fully addresses all aspects. For pre-deployment testing Principle 9 (9.1) mandates 'all models applications and systems...have been tested as part of a security assessment process' and (9.2) requires 'testing prior to the system being deployed.' For validation Principle 7 (7.3) requires re-running 'evaluations on released models.' For documentation Principle 8 (8.1) mandates 'a clear audit trail of their system design and post-deployment maintenance plans' including 'security-relevant information such as sources of training data intended scope and limitations guardrails...and potential failure modes' (8.1.1). The Scope section confirms lifecycle coverage across all five phases.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: This is the Code's primary focus. The Introduction explicitly addresses AI-specific threats including 'data poisoning model obfuscation indirect prompt injection.' Principle 2 (2.2) requires systems to 'withstand adversarial AI attacks unexpected inputs and AI system failure.' Principle 3 (3.1) mandates threat modelling addressing 'AI-specific attacks such as data poisoning model inversion and membership inference.' Principle 6 (6.2) requires 'controls that mitigate attacks on the AI system via the API' and (6.5) mandates incident management and recovery plans. Principle 12 (12.2) requires monitoring to 'detect anomalies security breaches or unexpected behaviour.'

country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
fr1_title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (United Kingdom)
fr1_justif: The Act hard-codes transparency and explainability for automated decision-making. It defines when a decision is 'solely automated' and 'significant' (Art. 22A p. 95) and mandates safeguards (Art. 22C pp. 95–96) that must: provide information about the decision let people make representations obtain human intervention and contest outcomes. It also amends UK GDPR Articles 13–15 to require information about automated decision-making in notices and access rights (Sch. 6 paras 3–5 p. 198) and ties penalties to breaches of 22B/22C (Art. 83(5) p. 199). In addition restrictions for sensitive data apply (Art. 22B p. 95).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: In the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 defence intelligence and national security are treated as explicit exclusions from the general framework through dedicated exemptions and carve-outs for intelligence services and national security processing (pp. 105–108). These sections remove such activities from the ordinary application of safeguards and rights meaning defence and security are effectively excluded from the framework’s scope for the purposes of this assessment.
fr1_body_name: Information Commissioner
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The Act requires controllers to provide information about automated decisions and enable representations human intervention and contesting (Art. 22C(2)(a)–(d) pp. 95–96) which promotes clarity for affected individuals. It also amends transparency and access duties so notices and rights requests reflect the new automated decision-making regime (Sch. 6 esp. paras updating Arts 12–15 to reference Arts 15–22D p. 198). However it does not mandate full public disclosure of model internals (e.g. full datasets or comprehensive decision logic documentation).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The Act assigns duties to controllers using solely automated decision-making to give affected individuals information about the decision let them make representations obtain human intervention and contest outcomes (Art. 22C(2)(a)–(d) pp. 95–96) i.e. an explanation focused on the particular decision's basis. It also updates transparency and access duties so privacy notices and access rights reflect automated decision-making use (Sch. 6 updates to Arts 13–15 p. 198). However it does not generally require developers to explain system outputs beyond these automated decision-making contexts.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The Act guarantees safeguards for solely automated decisions that give individuals access to information about the decision and rights to make representations obtain human intervention and contest outcomes (Art. 22C(2)(a)–(d) pp. 95–96) which supports explanation of the result affecting them. It also amends transparency and access duties so notices and access requests reflect automated decision-making use (Schedule 6 updates to Articles 13–15 p. 198). However it doesn't require disclosure of all 'key factors' behind the model beyond these duties focused on automated decision-making.

fr1_title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
fr1_justif: The document directly addresses AI literacy as a core objective. On page 9 Objective (i) explicitly commits to 'Elevate AI literacy and specialized skills' across the workforce. This is to be achieved through inclusive national education and training initiatives including specific skills-building programs focused on AI and data literacy complemented by apprenticeship programs to nurture local talent. This establishes a clear strategic focus on building foundational public understanding and technical capacity in AI.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: Yes the document includes a direct recommendation for higher education within the formal system (Pg. 9). Under the objective 'Foster Innovation and R&D' it explicitly proposes to 'Set the foundations for world-class AI university education and applied research by initiating public-private funded programs.' This clearly advocates for the creation and enhancement of advanced specialized AI programs within tertiary educational institutions moving beyond general literacy to establish dedicated centers of excellence and formal advanced learning pathways in the field of artificial intelligence.
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

fr1_title: The Personal Data Protection Act (Tanzania)
fr1_justif: 1. The Act classifies “data related to children” as sensitive personal data (Sec. 3) and prohibits processing without prior written consent (Sec. 30). 2. Since minors cannot consent parents or guardians must provide it (Sec. 30(4)) processing of children’s data. 4. Consent can be withdrawn anytime without cost (Sec. 30(2)). 5. Guardians may also require that decisions affecting the child are not based solely on automated processing (Sec. 36(1)).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Personal Data Protection Commission
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: A data subject including a child’s guardian may demand that decisions significantly affecting the child are not based solely on automated processing (Section 36(1)).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children

fr1_title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
fr1_justif: The document proposes measures to enhance cultural and linguistic diversity. The Diversity and Inclusion guideline (Page 12) suggests AI training data be 'representative of different genders races ethnicities and other diverse factors.'
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: The draft strategy includes provisions to promote AI systems that are representative and culturally responsive. Digital Inclusivity (Paragraph 10.4.1) which aims to integrate diverse human attributes in AI development management and use. It also addresses objectives (Paragraph 11.3.1) by focusing on a Swahili-centered ecosystem ensuring AI responds to local language and cultural contexts. Further specific measures include investment in Swahili resources (Paragraph 11.3.2.4). Additionally the draft establishes technical committees (Paragraph 10.4.2) and promotes media initiatives (Paragraph 13.6.3) to ensure AI development considers inclusivity and cultural relevance.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: The draft addresses bias mitigation through data and algorithm design to prevent cultural stereotypes (via Principles 3 & 5 and Guidelines 2 & 6). However it does not explicitly cover preventing the erasure of linguistic diversity or AI tools favoring dominant cultures as no specific provisions target these aspects.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
fr1_element3_justif: The draft partially addresses the query through the high-level goal-oriented obligation in Paragraph 10.4.1 to promote inclusivity of diverse human attributes in AI. This applies broadly but is not a specific enforceable rule. The document does not assign explicit mandated obligations to entities to ensure their AI systems are trained on diverse datasets or are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts. Other principles (e.g. 3 5) and guidelines (e.g. 2) on bias and data diversity remain advisory recommendations.

fr1_title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
fr1_justif: The document proposes that fairness and non-discrimination are core principles in AI. Principle 3: Managed Bias (Page 10) acknowledges bias risks mandates proactive bias minimization and emphasizes human oversight. Guidelines 2 and 6 (Pages 12-13) call for diverse inclusive training data and ongoing vigilance against bias. Proposal 5 (Pages 20-21) and Recommendation 5 outline measures such as real-time analysis pre-emptive data checks bias-free design user feedback diverse teams objective mechanisms decommissioning biased systems and early testing. Fairness is linked to Transparency (Pages 10-11 19) Accountability (Page 11) and Safety (Page 10).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The document proposes proactive management of bias as a core AI principle. Principle 3: Managed Bias (Page 10) mandates that AI must not unjustifiably impair human rights sets standards for bias minimization and emphasizes human oversight. Guidelines 2 and 6 (Pages 12-13) focus on diverse inclusive data and ongoing vigilance against bias. Proposal 5 (Pages 20-21) and Recommendation 5 outline measures including real-time bias detection bias-free design pre-emptive data checks user feedback diverse teams structural mechanisms decommissioning biased systems and continuous testing.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The document proposes measures to prevent AI from perpetuating or amplifying societal biases. Principle 3: Managed Bias (Page 10) mandates AI must not unjustifiably impair rights and requires bias minimization before deployment. Guidelines 2 and 6 (Pages 12-13) emphasize diverse inclusive data and ongoing vigilance. Proposal 5 (Pages 20-21) and Recommendation 5 outline real-time bias detection bias-free design pre-emptive data checks user feedback diverse teams and decommissioning biased systems. Transparency (Pages 10-11 19) and Accountability (Page 11) support fairness.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The document proposes a proactive duty to manage bias in AI. Principle 3 (Page 10) requires defining bias minimization standards before deployment and assigns humans to spot and correct unintended behaviors. Guidelines 2 3 and 6 (Pages 12-13) address bias across the AI lifecycle covering diverse data ongoing monitoring and careful training analysis. Proposal 5 (Pages 20-21) recommends detailed measures including real-time analysis pre-emptive data checks mitigation via design and multidisciplinary teams continuous testing and mechanisms to eliminate bias. Principle 6 (Page 11) and Proposal 1 (Pages 13-15) reinforce accountability and human oversight for bias management.

fr1_title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
fr1_justif: The document addresses Human Oversight and Determination through Proposal 1: Human  Agency and Control which emphasizes that AI systems must remain under constant human monitoring and control supported by proper documentation (Page 13). It further details steps for implementation (Page 14) including providing technical documentation designing systems for effective monitoring and enabling human choice between AI outputs. Finally it assigns responsibility to system designers requires training of designated personnel and establishes clear criteria for system use and intervention (Page 15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The document embeds Human Agency and Control as a core principle (Page 13) requiring AI to remain under constant human monitoring and control. (Pages 13–15) outline concrete safeguards: documenting AI limitations enabling human shutdown designing for oversight and allowing human choice between AI outputs. These apply strongly in critical areas like health justice and education reinforced by principles on safety accountability transparency and risk management (Pages 10–21).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
fr1_element3_justif: Yes. The document clearly assigns obligations to designate responsible individuals for AI oversight and accountability. Page 15 Article VII Under Recommendation 1 Principle 1: Human Agency and Control specifies mandates for the clear assignment of obligation for a person who will monitor and control the operations of the AI system. Proposal 6 (Page 22 Article II ) reinforces accountability by requiring defined roles rules and responsibility across the AI lifecycle.

fr1_title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
fr1_justif: The guidelines require developers and deployers to proactively identify and mitigate risks before and during AI deployment. Guideline 9 mandates anticipating risks from data algorithms and system use. Proposal 1 requires early detection of harmful impacts on equality and human rights and Proposal 6 defines risk management as timely identification assessment documentation and minimization of potential harms. Impacts cover societal ethical environmental and economic consequences. Guideline 10 and Proposals 3–5 mandate ethical reviews bias detection data quality checks rigorous testing and thorough documentation with accountability assigned to all responsible parties.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: Yes. The document includes provisions that promote a proactive culture of risk management by requiring evaluation of societal ethical and environmental impacts before AI deployment. Objective (p.9): Calls for ethical AI use through transparency accountability and privacy safeguards. Principles (p.10–11): Require prevention of harm and continuous assessment of impacts. Guidelines (p.12–13): Emphasize anticipating risks and conducting ethical reviews. Recommendations (p.13–22): Call for early detection of harmful impacts and accountability for environmental and societal effects.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: Yes. It assigns obligations to AI developers and users to conduct comprehensive impact assessments for identifying and mitigating risks to individuals and society. Principle 6 (p.10–11) makes developers accountable for system outcomes and their effects on employees. Guidelines 9–10 (p.12–13) require anticipation of risks and regular ethical reviews to detect and address potential harms. Proposals 1 and 6 (p.13–22) call for early detection of harmful impacts documentation and clear accountability while Proposal 3 (p.17–19) mandates data management policies to minimize privacy and societal risks.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

fr1_justif: The guidelines prioritize reskilling and upskilling to build local AI capacity. A core objective is to 'Develop Human Capital' by elevating AI literacy through national skills-building programs and apprenticeships to nurture local talent (Pg 9). It also mandates educating employees on ethical AI use (Pg 12-13) and promotes ongoing team education on emerging threats (Pg 17-18) ensuring a skilled workforce for Tanzania's digital economy.

fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: While the document explicitly calls for national skills-building and apprenticeship programs (Page 9) it does not definitively specify that these initiatives will be government-funded or subsidized. The language outlines objectives and recommendations rather than concrete funding mechanisms.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
fr1_justif: The Guideline provide for guide and principles in deployment and use of AI in the country. Among the principles is 'safe' i.e. AI deployment and usage must conform to safety expectations for the environment in which the AI is used - not to cause or exacerbate harm.(p. 10).It require the conduct of risk assessment (p. 21) guideline to ensure privacy and security concerns (p.12) and requires routine monitoring of AI systems to anticipate risks identify ethical use and potential bias (p.12-13)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: Yes. The document explicitly requires establishing performance thresholds and benchmarks. Page 15 (“Proposal 2: Technical reliability and security”) sets the foundation stating that reliability is achieved when a system “functions as intended” which directly refers to performance benchmarks. Page 14 (Rec. 1.ix) mandates defining metrics and thresholds for system use. Page 16 (Rec. 2.i) details benchmarks such as false-positive and false-negative rates user feedback and validity. Pages 16–17 (Rec. 2.iv) require rigorous testing with quality datasets to confirm reliability.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: On p. 14 there are recommendations for 'technical documentation AI system designs its subsystems and components & mechanisms for monitoring and control of its operation including ex-post analysis of the processing results against the input data' and 'early detection of harmful impacts or side effects to equality and human rights.' To ensure technical reliability and security (p.15) 'Rigorous testing'(p. 16) 'and real-time system monitoring @ p. 17. to mitigate and prevent harm p. 20-21.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: On Proposal 2: Technical reliability and security @ p. 15 the Guideline provide for detailed recommendation on testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle. However the guideline is not specific on pre-deployment testing.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: Yes the document includes specific provisions and recommendations related to protecting AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference. Key sections are:    Resilience (p. 10): Defined as the degree to which AI can withstand and recover from cyber-attacks.Technical reliability and security (p. 15-17): This core section mandates that security is a key requirement. It details specific adversarial risks like training data poisoning avoidance attacks model theft and adversarial attacks (p. 16). It recommends developing rigorous threat models conducting proactive 'red team' attacks and establishing procedures to remove threats (p. 17)

fr1_title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
fr1_justif: The document proposes the following AI principles and guidelines. Principle 5: Transparency (Pages 10-11) encourages users to know when AI is used understand its functions and receive clear explanations. Principle 7: Explainable and Interpretable (Page 11) emphasizes technical traceability and the right to explanation. Guideline 5 (Pages 12-13) proposes disclosure of data algorithms and decision processes. Proposal 4 (Pages 19-20) offers recommended measures for implementing these guidelines detailing traceability explainability and communication at data algorithm and process levels.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: Yes. The document proposes measures and recommendations to promote clarity in AI operations and foster public trust. Proposal 1 (Page 13) suggests documenting AI functionalities use scenarios limitations and areas where the system is not designed to operate. Guideline 5 (Page 12) proposes transparency regarding data sources.  Traceability and Explainability are also discussed in pages 19 & 20. Principle 7 (Page 11) and Proposal 4 (Page 19) recommend explainable outputs and traceable decision logic with Recommendation 4 (Page 20) focusing on clarity at the algorithm and process levels.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The document proposes obligations for AI explainability. But clear obligations are not provided. Principle 7 (Page 11) suggests that individuals be 'meaningfully informed' and understand the reasons and logic behind AI decisions. Principle 6 (Page 11) proposes accountability for designers and deployers emphasizing shared responsibility. Recommendation 1 (Pages 14-15) and Proposal 4 (Page 19) recommend technical documentation ex-post analysis and extra measures for “black box” models to support explainability.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: Yes. The document proposes provisions establishing the right for individuals to receive explanations for AI-driven decisions affecting them. Principle 7 (Page 11) states that individuals must be 'meaningfully informed' and have access to the reasons and logic behind decisions presented in an understandable manner. Principle 5 (Pages 10-11) supports this by requiring affected persons to understand how decisions are made.

fr1_title: Advancing Artificial Intelligence Education for American Youth
fr1_justif: The document addresses AI literacy primarily in Section 1 (Background.) noting to equip students with essential AI skills and competencies it frames AI literacy as essential for preparing youth to “understand use and help develop AI technologies.” Section 2 (Policy) establishes AI literacy and proficiency as national priorities emphasizing early exposure critical thinking and ethical understanding of AI systems. Section 4 (Developing an AI-Ready Task Force) and Section 5-7 (Supporting Educators) direct the Department of Education to expand K-12 AI literacy resources integrate AI concepts across subjects and prioritize teacher training and professional development using federal grants.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: White House Task Force on AI Education
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The document promotes systemic integration of AI literacy across the education system. Section 2 (Policy) emphasizes early exposure to AI for “America’s youth” indicating primary and secondary (K–12) education while Section 4 references postsecondary pathways such as certifications and Registered Apprenticeships extending AI education into tertiary education and workforce preparation. Together these provisions outline curriculum integration across all educational levels.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The document addresses this area partially. In Section 4 (Developing an AI-Ready Workforce) it promotes the expansion of AI-related courses certifications and Registered Apprenticeships and encourages partnerships to increase student exposure to AI. Section 3 establishes a White House Task Force on Artificial Intelligence Education to coordinate such initiatives. However it does not explicitly establish new dedicated AI institutions or formal degree programs.
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The document clearly includes provisions on teacher training and resources. Sections 5-7 (Supporting Educators) directs the Secretary of Education to prioritize the use of federal discretionary and formula grant programs to support professional development and training for educators so they can integrate AI fundamentals across subjects and offer stand-alone AI and computer science courses. It also emphasizes equipping educators with the skills and tools needed to teach AI literacy effectively.

fr1_title: Public Law 119-21 'Take it down Act' (USA)
fr1_justif: The TAKE IT DOWN Act targets AI-enabled harms mainly via “digital forgeries” (AI/ML-generated intimate images) and treats them as a driver of abuse/harassment and coercive threats. It (1) defines “digital forgery” as content created using “machine learning” or “artificial intelligence” (p.1 Sec.2(h)(1)(B); (2) criminalizes knowing publication of such forgeries intended to cause or causing harm and for minors where intent is to “abuse humiliate harass or degrade” (pp.3–4 Sec.2(h)(3); (3) covers threats made to intimidate/coerce/extort or cause “mental distress” (p.5 Sec.2(h)(6); (4) requires platform removal within 48 hours and efforts to remove.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: Federal Trade Commission
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: It prevents certain AI-enabled harms by targeting harassment/abuse via nonconsensual intimate images (including AI “digital forgeries”) and related threats plus a takedown mechanism. It does however not address preventing AI tools from creating/amplifying misinformation or hate speech broadly. Relevant provisions: p.2 Sec.2(h)(1)(B); pp.3–4 Sec.2(h)(3); p.5 Sec.2(h)(6); pp.6–7 Sec.3(a).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: The Act assigns content-handling obligations to “covered platforms” via a notice-and-removal process required on-platform notice and mandatory removal within 48 hours plus reasonable efforts for identical copies (pp.6–7 Sec.3(a)(1)–(3)). It does not set comparable obligations for AI developers nor does it require broader transparency reporting on how systems moderate harmful content beyond the notice/process disclosure (pp.6–7 Sec.3(a)(2)).
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: The Act gives targeted individuals a protection/takedown pathway by allowing a notice from an affected person (or representative) and requiring “covered platforms” to remove the content within 48 hours and address duplicates (pp.6–7 Sec.3(a)(1)–(3)). It also provides redress via criminal penalties against perpetrators (pp.3–4 Sec.2(h)(3)) and FTC enforcement for platform noncompliance (p.7 Sec.3(b)). However the provisions focus specifically on AI-generated intimate forgeries and related harassment and do not establish broader rights covering misinformation or all forms of tech-facilitated violence nor do they provide a comprehensive redress framework against platforms.
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: The framework addresses a major form of gender-based harassment/violence—nonconsensual intimate visual depictions including AI-enabled “digital forgeries” plus related threats and a platform takedown process. It does not cover gender-based harassment/violence beyond this NCII/deepfake context. (p.2 Sec.2(h)(1)(B); pp.3–4 Sec.2(h)(3); p.5 Sec.2(h)(6); pp.6–7 Sec.3(a)).

fr1_title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
fr1_justif: On p. 17 it states that under 'Offer Consistent Remedies or Appeals' that Agencies must ensure that individuals affected by AI-enabled decisions have access to a timely human review and a chance to appeal any negative impacts when appropriate. If an agency already has an appeals or human review process in place such as appeals of adverse actions it may extend or adapt that process to cover decisions made with AI consistent with applicable law. Any remedy process should be designed to avoid placing unnecessary burdens on the individual and should follow established guidance for minimizing administrative burdens.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Appendix §1(c) “Applicability to National Security Systems” (p.5) states: “This memorandum does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System” (as defined in 44 U.S.C. §3552(b)(6)). Additionally Appendix §1(a) (p.4) says it applies to “agencies” per 44 U.S.C. §3502(1) which excludes certain national defense GOCO facilities.
fr1_body_name: Chief AI Officer Council
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: Partially because M-25-21 strengthens existing administrative (state-based) pathways but does not create a new ombuds/tribunal/regulator. It requires agencies for high-impact AI to offer remedies/appeals—including timely human review and an opportunity to appeal adverse outcomes and it allows agencies to extend existing review/appeals processes to AI-enabled decisions (Sec. 4(b)(vi) p.17). It also mandates channels to receive public feedback/concerns about high-impact AI use cases (Sec. 4(b)(vii) p.17).
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

fr1_title: Children´s Online Privacy Protection Rule Amendments (USA)
fr1_justif: The document addresses children's rights in the context of AI by expanding the definition of 'Personal information' (p.7) to include biometric identifiers (such as facial templates voiceprints and gait patterns) that can be used for automated or semi-automated recognition (pp.33-35). This change is a direct response to the rapid advancement of technologies like facial recognition and machine learning intended to strengthen the protection of this sensitive immutable data (p.7). The Commission noted concerns about AI/ML tools being used for mass profiling targeted advertising and engagement-maximizing techniques (pp.8 17).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
fr1_element1_text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: COPPA includes specific provisions measures and objectives aimed at protecting children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems. The 2025 amendments to COPPA introduce enhanced requirements relevant to AI such as - (a) Verifiable Parental Consent (b) Data Minimization and Retention Limits (c) Transparency and Clear Privacy Notices (d) Prohibition on using children's data for targeted advertising or marketing (e) Security Measures and (f) Restrictions on third-party sharing (pp.7-8 33-35). The Commission shares concerns about practices operators employ to maximize children's engagement with online services (often using AI/ML techniques) and notes it may pursue enforcement under Section 5 of the FTC Act (pp. 8 17).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
fr1_element2_justif: Yes particularly concerning data collection targeted advertising and sensitive biometric information. Separate Consent for Disclosure: Operators must obtain separate verifiable parental consent for disclosures to third parties and disclosures for advertising purposes are not integral to the service.§312.5(a)(2) on Page 63 (Rule Text) and discussion in Part II.D.1.b on Page 30-33. Definition of 'Support for the internal operations of the website or online service' in §312.2 on Page 61-62. Definition of 'Personal information' in §312.2 on Page 61 (Rule Text). The discussion of this as a response to AI's ability to misuse this data is in Part II.B.3.b on Page 7-8. Contextual advertising Discussion in Part II.B.4.e on Page 19
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
fr1_element3_justif: It was pointed out that profile-based personalization can be beneficial in contexts such as‘‘delivering age-appropriate contentrestricting display of adult contentrestricting contact by adults serving content that is relevant to the user [and]enriching the functionality for a user.’’  (p.18) although the commission decided against this amendment. Nevertheless services - including AI - being age appropriate is being actively discussed (p.47) although not to the level of the assignment of obligations.

fr1_title: Algorithmic Accountability Act 2025 (USA)
fr1_justif: The bill operationalizes fairness/non-discrimination by mandating impact assessments for “covered algorithms” used in “critical decisions.” It requires testing for differential performance by protected and other characteristics (Sec. 4(a)(4)(E) pp. 18–19) and identifying needed resources to improve “fairness including bias and non-discrimination” (Sec. 4(a)(11)(B) pp. 24-25). It also mandates consultation with civil-rights and impacted communities (Sec. 3(b)(1)(G) pp. 9–11) and mitigation of material harms (Sec. 3(b)(1)(H) p. 11). FTC must publish aggregated findings and a public repository (Sec. 6 pp. 31–36).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: The bill includes explicit provisions to promote fair and equitable AI outcomes. It requires algorithmic impact assessments to evaluate differential performance and outcomes across protected classes (Sec. 4(a)(4)(E) pp. 18–19) directly addressing biased results. Covered entities must identify and implement measures to improve fairness including bias and non-discrimination (Sec. 4(a)(11)(B) p. 25). It also mandates mitigation of material harms arising from algorithmic decision-making (Sec. 3(b)(1)(H) p. 11) and consultation with civil rights experts and affected communities (Sec. 3(b)(1)(G) pp. 9–11) reinforcing equitable treatment objectives.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The bill explicitly aims to prevent AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying societal biases and discrimination. It requires algorithmic impact assessments to test for disparate outcomes and performance across protected characteristics such as race sex age and other legally protected classes (Sec. 4(a)(4)(E) pp. 18–19). Covered entities must document and implement measures to reduce bias and advance fairness and non-discrimination (Sec. 4(a)(11)(B) p. 25) and mitigate material harms linked to discriminatory impacts (Sec. 3(b)(1)(H) p. 11). The requirement to consult civil rights experts and affected communities (Sec. 3(b)(1)(G) pp. 9–11) further reinforces bias-prevention objectives.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The bill assigns proactive obligations across the AI lifecycle to entities that develop or deploy covered algorithms. It requires algorithmic impact assessments that identify risks stemming from training data design and deployment contexts (Sec. 4(a)(1)–(4) pp. 16–19). Entities must test for biased or discriminatory outcomes document data sources and limitations and assess how design choices affect outcomes (Sec. 4(a)(3)(B)–(D) pp. 17–18). They must also identify and implement mitigation measures to improve fairness and prevent discrimination before and after deployment (Sec. 4(a)(9)(C) p. 24; Sec. 4(a)(11)(B) p. 25).

fr1_title: Executive Order 14110 Safe Secure and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligene
fr1_justif: Gender Equality is addressed through its equity/civil rights mandate: AI must not “disadvantage” groups denied equal opportunity (Policy & Principles Sec.2(d) pp.2-3/36). It directs action against algorithmic discrimination and unlawful discrimination in hiring and housing/tenant screening (Sec.7.1–7.3 pp.21–24/36). In health it requires “equity principles” using disaggregated data and monitoring bias across population groups (Sec.8(b)(i)(C) p.25/36). It also requires agencies to assess/mitigate disparate impacts and provide human remedies (Sec.10.1(b)(iv) p.29/36). Under Sec10.2(a) the Director of the Gender Policy Council among others is also tasked with identifying priority mission areas for increased Federal Government AI talent.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: The Attorney GeneralAssistant Attorney General in charge of the Civil Rights DivisionHeads of Federal civil rights officesDepartment of Justices Civil Rights Division
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: The document explicitly requires action against algorithmic discrimination and unlawful discrimination including in contexts such as hiring and housing/tenant screening (Sec.7.1–7.3). It further mandates that AI systems must not disadvantage groups denied equal opportunity (Policy & Principles Sec.2(d)) and requires agencies to assess and mitigate disparate impacts and provide remedies where harms occur (Sec.10.1(b)(iv)). However these provisions address discrimination broadly under civil rights protections and gender equality is not explicitly singled out as a distinct category.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: The document assigns responsibilities to agencies and entities using AI to prevent discrimination and uphold equality. It requires that AI systems must not disadvantage groups denied equal opportunity (Policy & Principles Sec.2(d)) and directs action against algorithmic and unlawful discrimination in areas such as hiring and housing/tenant screening (Sec.7.1–7.3). It also obliges agencies to assess and mitigate disparate impacts and provide human remedies when harms occur (Sec.10.1(b)(iv)). While these obligations cover discrimination generally gender equality is implied rather than explicitly specified as a targeted requirement.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

fr1_title: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights MAKING AUTOMATED SYSTEMS WORK FOR THE AMERICAN PEOPLE
fr1_justif: The framework explicitly operationalizes human oversight as a core principle of AI governance through its “Human Alternatives Consideration and Fallback” section which establishes that individuals must have access to human review (p. 8) and the ability to contest automated decisions (p. 7). It further requires that automated systems especially in sensitive domains such as employment healthcare and criminal justice incorporate human oversight mechanisms and ensure “human consideration before any high-risk decision” (p. 50–51)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: 'These principles are not intended to and do not prohibit or limit any lawful activity of a government agency including law enforcement national security or intelligence activities.' p. 2
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: Advancing Governance Innovation and Risk Managment for Agency Use of AI (USA)
fr1_justif: M-24-10 makes AI Impact Assessments a pre-use gate for “safety-impacting” and “rights-impacting” AI: agencies must complete and periodically update an “AI impact assessment” documenting purpose/expected benefit (metrics or qualitative analysis) risks/mitigation stakeholders & failure modes and data quality/provenance/representativeness (§5(a)(iv)(A) pp.17–18). It pairs AI with real-world performance testing (§5(a)(iv)(B) pp.18–19) and independent evaluation using the IA + test results integrated into release/ATO processes (§5(a)(iv)(C) p.19). For rights-impacting AI agencies must record equity/fairness issues and algorithmic discrimination in the AI (§5(a)(v)(A)(1) p.21).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The memo explicitly excludes national-security/defense use: “Applicability to National Security Systems. This memorandum does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System” (§2(c) p.4). It also carves out defense/security actors from specific requirements—for example agencies must publish annual AI use-case inventories “except for the Department of Defense and the Intelligence Community” (§3(c)(iv) p.5) and some requirements “do not apply to elements of the Intelligence Community” (§2(a) p.3).
fr1_body_name: Chief AI Officer (CAIO) with defined governance/risk-management duties
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: M-24-10 requires pre-deployment risk management for “rights-impacting” and “safety-impacting” AI including completing an AI impact assessment documenting purpose/benefit risks mitigations stakeholders and data issues (§5(a)(iv)(A) PDF pp.17–18) and real-world testing/independent evaluation before release/ATO (§5(a)(iv)(B)–(C) PDF pp.18–19). It also covers societal/ethical aspects via equity/fairness and discrimination duties (§5(a)(v)(A) PDF pp.21–22) and consultation (§5(a)(v)(B) PDF p.22). However it does not require environmental impact evaluation.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: It assigns mandatory obligations to federal agencies (as users/procurers and sometimes developers) to complete and periodically update an AI impact assessment for covered “rights-impacting” and “safety-impacting” AI documenting purpose/benefits risks mitigations stakeholders and data issues (§5(a)(iv)(A) PDF pp.17–18) and to test/evaluate the system before release/ATO (§5(a)(iv)(B)–(C) PDF pp.18–19). It does not impose direct standalone IA duties on all private-sector developers/users (only when acting “on behalf of” an agency) so this obligation only arises in a very specific case as an exception.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: It requires some public-facing disclosure but not a general right to obtain AI Impact Assessment findings. Agencies must post a public AI Use Case Inventory online (§3(a)(iv) “AI Use Case Inventories” p.5) and ensure inventory entries provide plain-language public notice/documentation (§5(a)(v) item “I. Provide public notice…” p.21). For high-risk determinations/waivers agencies must publicly release a summary with justification (§5(a)(ii) “Certification and Publication of Determinations and Waivers” p.14). It does not require publishing the full AI impact assessments.

fr1_title: Bipartisan House Task Force Report on Artificial Intelligence (USA)
fr1_justif: According to the document labour protections are addressed in “Education and Workforce” under “Labor Laws for Modern Needs”: employers using AI must comply with anti-discrimination and labor laws and Congress should consider workplace AI transparency to protect workers’ rights (p.104). It states workplace AI must respect NLRA rights (noting NLRB work on emerging tech and protected activity) and calls for OSHA to monitor/update standards as AI enters workplaces (p.104). It also recommends: “Monitor the interaction of labor laws and worker protections with AI adoption” (p.110).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: In Education & Workforce – “Labor Laws for Modern Needs” (p.104) the Report states employers using AI in the workplace must still comply with anti-discrimination and labor laws and it urges Congress to consider workplace AI transparency to protect workers’ rights. It also recommends monitoring how labor laws and worker protections interact with AI adoption (Recommendation p.110). But it does not provide explicit protections spanning hiring/promotion/termination and does not clearly name non-contract/gig workers under algorithmic management as a specific category.
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: The Report explicitly raises the need for “workplace AI transparency” as a way to protect workers’ rights when AI is used by employers (Education & Workforce – “Labor Laws for Modern Needs” p.104). This supports transparency as an objective/recommendation.But it does not spell out specific obligations to explain AI use for performance monitoring employment decisions or effects on access to benefits nor does it set a defined disclosure standard or enforcement mechanism in that section.
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work
fr1_element3_justif: In Education & Workforce – “Labor Laws for Modern Needs” (p.104) the Report notes that AI-driven workplace practices remain subject to labor laws and points to the relevance of NLRA/NLRB protections as emerging technologies affect workers’ protected activity/rights. This acknowledges organizing and/or collective-rights frameworks in the AI workplace context.But it does not propose concrete AI-specific measures to strengthen collective bargaining and it does not specifically address gig-dominated sectors in this section.

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems
fr1_title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
fr1_justif: M-25-21 advances public disclosure mainly through proactive publication requirements: Each agency (except for the Department of Defense and the Intelligence Community) must inventory its AI use cases at least annually submit the inventory to OMB and post a public version on the agency's website. Agencies are encouraged to update the public versions of their inventories on an ongoing basis to reflect their current use of AI. OMB will issue detailed instructions to agencies regarding the inventory and its scope (pp. 12-13).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The memo draws a hard boundary around defense/security uses that qualify as National Security Systems (NSS): in the Appendix Section 1 “SCOPE” subsection (c) “Applicability to National Security Systems” (p. 4) it states the memo “does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System.” It also clarifies NSS AI is governed “through other policy” (footnote 8) reinforcing that this framework’s transparency/governance duties don’t apply to NSS contexts.
fr1_body_name: Chief AI Officer (CAIO) agency AI Governance Board Chief AI Officer Council
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
fr1_element1_justif: The memo mandates a public inventory: agencies “must inventory [their] AI use cases… and post a public version on the agency’s website” (Appendix §3(b)(v) “Update AI Use Case Inventories” p.12). It implicitly identifies the responsible entity (each agency publishes its own inventory). However it covers AI “use cases” not “all AI systems” and it does not itself require the public inventory to include purpose function description and responsible office—it defers scope/details to OMB: “OMB will issue detailed instructions… regarding the inventory and its scope” (p.13).
fr1_element2_text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
fr1_element3_text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
fr1_element3_justif: It sets high-level boundaries but not detailed disclosure-vs-exemption rules. It explicitly excludes National Security Systems: “does not cover AI…component of a National Security System” (Appendix §1(c) p.4). For privacy/disclosure it requires agencies “must inventory [their] AI use cases… and post a public version on the agency’s website” (Appendix §3(b)(v) “Update AI Use Case Inventories” p.12).
fr1_element4_text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

fr1_title: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government (USA)
fr1_justif: M-25-22 is a federal AI acquisition/procurement framework: it sets scope/applicability to contracts for “AI systems or services” (§2 pp.2–4) mandates agency-level procurement controls (privacy terms IP/lock-in mitigation limits on use of government data for training and documentation/transparency needs) (§3(d)–(f) pp.5–6) and gives AI acquisition lifecycle guidance—cross-functional teams market research product demos/tests performance-based acquisition and ongoing performance/risk management—so agencies buy AI that is fit-for-purpose and preserves public trust (§4(a)–(c) pp.6–8).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The memo excludes national-security/defense acquisition by stating it “does not apply to AI acquired for use as a component of a National Security System” (§2(d) Applicability to National Security Systems p.4). It also notes it does not apply to elements of the Intelligence Community (§2(a) Covered Agencies p.2) reinforcing the security carve-out.
fr1_body_name: Senior Agency Officials for Privacy
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element1_justif: M-25-22 creates AI-specific acquisition guidance beyond standard IT buying by adding ethical/social safeguards (privacy protections and limits on use of govt data for training: §3(d)–(f) pp.5–6; risk controls for high-impact AI: §4.D p.10) and technical requirements (documentation/transparency expectations; testing & evaluation; and ongoing monitoring: §4(b)–(c) pp.7–8 and §4.E pp.10–11).
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element2_justif: Safety/performance testing is addressed: agencies are told to include product demos and testing before award (§4(c) pp.7–8) and contracts must enable ongoing testing/monitoring to evaluate performance risks and effectiveness at set intervals (§4.E pp.10–11). High-impact AI must follow minimum risk-management practices (§4.D p.10). But the memo does not mandate a universal vendor “proof” of bias/fairness testing as a standalone requirement for all procurements.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element3_justif: It requires/encourages documentation and transparency to support explainability and tracking performance (“Documentation Transparency and Accessibility” §3(e)(v) p.6) and tells agencies to set reasonable transparency/documentation requirements on vendors for (potential) high-impact AI (“Solicitation Development – AI Use Transparency Requirements” §4(c)(1) pp.7–9). It also references data/model portability and pricing/licensing transparency to avoid lock-in (§4(c) p.9–10).
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

fr1_title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
fr1_justif: M-25-21 embeds public-sector skills development in three places: (1) “Agency AI Strategies” requires agencies to plan to “recruit hire train retain… an AI-ready workforce” and achieve “AI literacy for non-practitioners” (p. 6). (2) “Enabling an AI-Ready Federal Workforce” links training/upskilling to responsible AI adoption and prioritizes developing and retaining AI talent (p. 9). (3) Minimum practice “Ensure Adequate Human Training and Assessment” requires periodic system-specific training for AI operators (p. 17).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: The memo draws a hard boundary around defense/security uses that qualify as National Security Systems (NSS): in the Appendix Section 1 “SCOPE” subsection (c) “Applicability to National Security Systems” (p. 4) it states the memo “does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System.” It also clarifies NSS AI is governed “through other policy” (footnote 8) reinforcing that this framework’s transparency/governance duties don’t apply to NSS contexts.
fr1_body_name: Chief AI Officer (CAIO) Agency AI Governance Board
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: M-25-21 establishes government-wide expectations to build an AI-ready federal workforce and foundational understanding through training/upskilling (civil service) but it does not cover the judiciary. It requires Agency AI Strategies to plan to “recruit hire train retain… an AI-ready workforce” and achieve “AI literacy for non-practitioners” (p.6 Agency AI Strategies). It also includes a dedicated section on “Enabling an AI-Ready Federal Workforce” (p.9). Scope is limited to covered executive agencies (p.4 §1 Scope).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: M-25-21 makes the CAIO and Agency AI Governance Board responsible for advancing an AI-ready workforce. The CAIO’s duties include advising agency leadership and helping drive the agency’s transformation toward an “AI-ready workforce” (p.10 Sec. 3(a) Agency Governance Roles and Bodies). The Governance Board provides cross-office oversight and coordination for AI governance (which includes workforce readiness activities tied to the memo’s training/upskilling expectations) (p.11 Sec. 3(a)) aligning with the memo’s workforce/training provisions (p.9 “Enabling an AI-Ready Federal Workforce”).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: For public-sector skills development M-25-21 explicitly requires ongoing training: under the Minimum Practices “Ensure Adequate Human Training and Assessment” states agencies must ensure “sufficient and periodic training assessment and oversight” for AI operators and that “Training should be conducted on a periodic basis … and should be specific to the AI system” (p.17 Sec. 4(b) practice iv). It also promotes continuous upskilling by urging agencies to “leverage AI Trainings and Resources to Upskill Existing Staff” (p.9 “Enabling an AI-Ready Federal Workforce”).

fr1_title: America´s AI Action Plan
fr1_justif: In “Empower American Workers in the Age of AI” (pp. 6–7) the Plan calls for a “serious workforce response” including DOL funding for rapid retraining for AI-related displacement and guidance so states can use Rapid Response funds to proactively upskill workers at risk; it also proposes pilots under WIOA to address AI-driven workforce challenges (p.7). In “Train a Skilled Workforce for AI Infrastructure” (pp. 17–18) it recommends skills frameworks/competency models industry-driven training CTE and Registered Apprenticeships and partnerships with community/technical colleges to transition the existing workforce into critical AI roles (pp.17–18).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: AI Workforce Research Hub (under the US Department of Labor DOL)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: In “Empower American Workers in the Age of AI”; “Recommended Policy Actions” (pp. 6–7) the Plan calls for government-funded/subsidized reskilling/upskilling by directing DOL to (1) fund rapid retraining for workers affected by AI-related job displacement and (2) enable states to use Rapid Response funds to proactively upskill workers at risk (pp. 6–7). It also recommends piloting workforce approaches under WIOA to address AI-driven labor-market challenges (p.7).
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
