fr1_element2_justif: The Plan supports financial support pathways through public workforce funding mechanisms—e.g. in “Empower American Workers in the Age of AI” (pp. 6-7) it recommends DOL use Rapid Response funds to proactively upskill workers at risk and fund rapid retraining for AI-related displacement (pp. 6-7). However it does not consistently specify direct worker-facing benefits like paid leave or individual grants; many incentives are routed via programs/states/employers rather than support to workers themselves directly.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
fr1_element3_justif: The Plan encourages and incentivizes employer investment in training but it does not create mandate for companies to fund reskilling. In “Train a Skilled Workforce for AI Infrastructure” (pp. 17–18) it promotes industry-driven training and employer involvement to transition the existing workforce into critical AI roles (pp.17–18). It also points to incentive-based approaches (e.g. employer-supported training/education assistance mechanisms) rather than compulsory company obligations.

fr1_title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
fr1_justif: M-25-21 links AI Safety/Security to “high-impact AI” and requires “minimum risk management practices” prioritizing AI that is “safe secure and resilient” and mandates a plan to discontinue non-performing high-impact AI or cease use if risk mitigation isn’t possible (Main memo pp.2-3). In the Appendix it requires processes to measure monitor and evaluate ongoing performance (p.10) and mandates termination of non-compliant AI (Sec. 4(a)/4(b) pp.13–14) plus pre-deployment testing and risk mitigation plans (Sec. 4(b)(i) pp.14–15).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: M-25-21 explicitly states: “Applicability to National Security Systems. This memorandum does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System” (Appendix Section 1 ‘SCOPE’ subsection (c) p. 4).
fr1_body_name: Chief AI Officer Council
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element1_justif: M-25-21 requires use-case metrics and testing/validation—e.g. for high-impact AI it mandates pre-deployment testing reflecting “expected real-world outcomes” and AI impact assessments with benefits “supported by specific metrics” (Appendix Sec. 4(b)(i)–(ii) pp. 14–15). It also requires processes to “measure monitor and evaluate… performance and effectiveness” (Sec. 3(a)(i)(F)(2) p. 10). While it also necessitates to implement minimum risk management practices for AI (pp. 2-3) it does not set a universal minimum accuracy/quality threshold applicable across systems so this remains quite broad and unspecific.
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: For high-impact AI M-25-21 requires agencies to implement safeguards including human oversight and contingency planning: it calls for a plan to “discontinue” high-impact AI that is not performing as intended and to “cease use” when risks can’t be mitigated (main memo pp.2-3).  In the Appendix it requires human review/oversight mechanisms and procedures to manage failures/harms and implement remedies/appeals where relevant (minimum practices for high-impact AI Sec. 4(b)(v)–(vi) pp. 15–16).
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: For high-impact AI M-25-21 requires pre-deployment testing and risk mitigation plans reflecting “expected real-world outcomes” (Appendix Sec. 4(b)(i) pp. 14–15). It mandates an AI Impact Assessment before deployment to be updated periodically throughout the AI lifecycle and documented (Appendix Sec. 4(b)(ii) p. 15). It also requires agencies to document implementation of minimum practices and be ready to report them (Appendix Sec. 4(a)(1) p. 13).
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: M-25-21 recognizes adversarial evasion/manipulation as an AI risk factor (Appendix Sec. 7 “Methods of Understanding AI Risk Management” p. 23). It also requires agencies to test and periodically review high-impact AI to detect adverse impacts to the “performance and security of AI functionality” and to design monitoring to detect changes post-deployment (Appendix minimum practices p. 16). However it does not prescribe detailed technical cybersecurity controls; it instead directs agencies to update internal policies on “cybersecurity and privacy” (Consolidated Table of Actions p. 24).

fr1_title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
fr1_justif: OMB Memorandum M-25-21 embeds Transparency and Explainability as core governance requirements for federal AI use.Transparency is mandated through public disclosure mechanisms including publicly released AI Strategies (Section 2(a) pp. 5–6) AI Use Case Inventories (Section 3(b)(v) pp. 12–13) and public reporting of high-impact AI determinations and waivers (Section 4(a)(iv) p. 15).Explainability is operationalized via documentation and traceability duties requiring agencies to document AI capabilities limitations intended use data provenance and model performance (Section 2(d)(ii) p. 9; Section 4(b)(ii) pp. 16–17). Agencies are also encouraged to favor models that are “inherently more explainable” (Section 3(b)(iii) p. 12).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Defence and security are explicitly excluded from the scope of OMB Memorandum M-25-21. The Appendix states that the memorandum “does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System” (Appendix §1(c) p. 5). It further clarifies that elements of the Intelligence Community are exempt from multiple obligations including minimum risk management practices and public reporting (Appendix §1(a) p. 4; Sections 3(b)(v) and 4 pp. 12–15). Additionally agencies are directed to rely on separate defense- and intelligence-specific AI policies for such systems confirming a clear exclusion from this framework’s scope
fr1_body_name: Chief AI Officer (CAIO)Agency AI Governance BoardChief AI Officer Council (interagency chaired by OMB)Office of Management and Budget (OMB) (oversight coordination reporting authority)
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes explicit provisions promoting clarity on how AI systems operate to foster public trust. It requires agencies to document AI purpose capabilities limitations intended use data sources and data provenance as well as to conduct and document AI impact assessments (Sections 2(d)(ii) and 4(b)(ii) pp. 9 and 16–17). It also mandates public transparency measures including publicly available AI Strategies AI use case inventories and public reporting on high-impact AI determinations (Sections 2(a) 3(b)(v) and 4(a)(iv) pp. 5–6 12–13 and 15). These measures directly advance clarity explainability and public trust. It also advocates for using AI models that are inherently more explainable where possible (p. 12).
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 addresses AI-facilitated misinformation through Line 1.2 Action F (p. 38) which explicitly commits to addressing the impacts of AI on disinformation and the integrity of democratic processes in a manner consistent with freedom of expression through a holistic and systemic approach. Line 1.2 (p. 37) more broadly commits to developing risk-based regulatory frameworks that protect human rights democracy and the rule of law throughout the AI lifecycle. The Strategy does not address gender-based AI-facilitated violence hate speech deepfakes platform content moderation obligations or redress mechanisms for victims of AI-facilitated harm.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
fr1_element4_justif: Principle 4 (p. 30) requires proactive measures to prevent gender-based discriminatory stereotypes and biases from being reproduced in AI systems. However this addresses bias and discrimination in AI design broadly — it does not specifically target AI-facilitated gender-based harassment or violence.

fr1_title: Law No. 18331: Personal Data Protection Law (Uruguay)
fr1_justif: Article 16 of Law 18.331 protects individuals from decisions made solely on the basis of automated decision-making that significantly affects them granting the right to demand human intervention review and explanation. It is mentioned in the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2030 as part of the legal basis for regulating the automated processing of personal data. The Strategy explains that the Personal Data Regulatory and Control Unit (URCDP) is empowered to “establish the criteria and procedures that must be observed by those responsible and in charge in the automated processing of personal data indicated in Article 16 of the aforementioned Law.”
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: Article 3 lit. b) of Law 18.331 explicitly excludes from the law's scope databases whose purpose is public security national defence State security and activities related to criminal investigation and repression of crime. Accordingly the rights established under the law — including the automated decision-making right under Art. 16 and the Habeas Data remedy under Art. 37 — don't apply to databases operated by armed forces police or intelligence bodies for these operational purposes. Note that administrative data held by these bodies & personal background data provided to judicial or administrative authorities remain subject to the law under Art. 25.
fr1_body_name: Personal Data Regulatory and Control Unit (URCDP)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: Article 37 establishes the Habeas Data process by which any person who needs to enforce the rights granted by the Personal Data Protection Law can go to court including the right under Article 16 not to be subject to automated decisions with significant legal effects. Note that this judicial remedy does not extend to databases explicitly excluded from the law's scope under Article 3 lit. b) namely those operated by armed forces police or intelligence bodies for public security national defence or criminal investigation purposes.
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: Article 63 of Law 20.075 (2022) amended Article 34 of Law 18.331 to empower the URCDP to establish criteria and procedures for automated processing of personal data under Article 16. As the body responsible for enforcement of Law 18.331 URCDP has sanctioning powers and receives complaints from data subjects regarding violations of their rights including rights related to automated decision-making. Note that as of the assessment period URCDP has not yet published specific criteria or guidance on automated processing and the same exclusion applicable under Article 3 lit. b) limits URCDP's jurisdiction over security and defence operational databases.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: Article 16 of Law 18.331 requires data controllers to provide individuals with information about the criteria and programs used in automated decisions affecting them implying an obligation to respond to individual requests. However it does not mandate companies to establish formal accessible grievance mechanisms or proactive human review processes for AI-related harm.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 addresses cultural diversity in AI through three provisions. Principle 4 (p. 29-30) requires AI actors to prevent ethnic-racial and national-origin biases in AI systems mandates diversity in AI development teams and calls on the public sector to address structural underrepresentation of diverse social groups in training data. Line 2.2 Action a (p. 43) explicitly requires generating training datasets reflecting Uruguay's culture and social diversity. In p. 15 cite as a milestone the Montevideo Declaration which establishes cultural and geographical diversity as a guiding principle for responsible AI. Linguistic diversity is not addressed.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element1_justif: Line 2.2 Action a (p. 43) mandates generating training datasets reflecting Uruguay's culture and social diversity. However there is no mention of linguistic diversity or responsiveness to a wide range of languages.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element2_justif: Principle 4 (p. 30) requires AI actors to prevent ethnic-racial and national-origin biases from being reproduced in AI systems and addresses algorithmic and automation bias. However there are no specific provisions against erasure of linguistic diversity or dominance of specific cultures.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
fr1_element3_justif: principle 4 (p. 30) requires the public sector to address structural underrepresentation of diverse social groups in training data. Line 2.2 Action a (p. 43) mandates culturally representative datasets. However obligations are limited to cultural diversity; linguistic and contextual adaptability are not addressed.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: Principle 4 of the Strategy addresses'Equity and non Discrimination' setting the standard for this issue. (Page 29). It requires AI systems to respect equality and explicitly address both algorithmic bias and automation bias recognizing risks of reproducing gender racial social and disability-based inequalities (pp. 29–30). The Strategy promotes proactive measures such as improving training data quality fostering diversity in development teams and ensuring equitable access to AI benefits (p. 30). 'This principle covers both discrimination based on algorithmic bias and discrimination based on automation bias—the human tendency to rely excessively on the support of algorithms even when they make mistakes.' (p.30)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: mainly under the guiding principle of Equity and Non-Discrimination and in Section 5. It explicitly requires preventing discriminatory stereotypes and biases based on gender ethnicity social status or disability and calls for improving data quality and diversity in design teams to reduce biased results (pp. 29–30). In Axis 3 (Sustainable Development) it mandates instruments such as indicators protocols and good-practice guidelines to measure social impacts and address differentiated effects on vulnerable groups (p. 48).
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy requires proactive measures to avoid reproducing discriminatory stereotypes and structural inequalities based on 'gender ethnic or racial identity social status national origin or disability' throughout the AI lifecycle (pp. 29–30). It also promotes improving training data quality fostering diversity in development teams and using open public data to reduce underrepresentation and algorithmic bias (p. 30).
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: Page 29 of the Strategy covers this point partially because it establishes a general duty of AI actors to adopt proactive measures to prevent discrimination and reduce unwanted biases but it does not impose detailed enforceable technical obligations. It requires stakeholders to consider all phases of the AI lifecycle and to adopt measures to improve data quality promote diversity in design teams and avoid discriminatory outcomes (p. 29). However these obligations are framed as principles and guidelines rather than as concrete requirements such as mandatory bias impact assessments auditing duties or lifecycle monitoring mechanisms.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: Principle 4 'Equity and Non-Discrimination' (pp. 29-30) mandates public & private sector actors to adopt proactive measures to address AI's impact on gender equality & other structural inequalities throughout the entire AI system lifecycle preventing discriminatory stereotypes & biases based on gender ethnic-racial identity social status & national origin from being reproduced in AI systems. It further requires all AI actors to reduce undesired biases in training data & models & obliges the public sector to promote AI models using quality data to overcome the structural underrepresentation of diverse social groups. Line 2.4 Action d (p. 45) promotes women's enrolment in technology & STEM careers to strengthen their participation in AI.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
fr1_element1_justif: Principle 4 (pp. 29-30) explicitly addresses gender discrimination and bias requiring all AI actors to adopt proactive measures to prevent gender-based discriminatory stereotypes from being reproduced in AI systems throughout their lifecycle. It further mandates measures to ensure training data quality to overcome the structural underrepresentation of diverse groups. The principle covers both algorithmic bias and automation bias. However these remain guiding principles rather than specific binding provisions or procedural requirements targeting gender discrimination.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
fr1_element2_justif: Principle 4 (p. 30) assigns responsibilities to public sector actors to promote equitable access to AI benefits and address digital divides and encourages private sector civil society and academia to contribute to this goal. The public sector is further required to promote AI models using quality data to overcome structural underrepresentation. However these are framed as responsibilities to be encouraged rather than binding legal obligations assigned to specific entities.
fr1_element3_text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
fr1_element3_justif: Line 2.4 Action d (p. 45) explicitly commits to continuing through various initiatives the fostering of women's enrolment in technology and STEM careers to strengthen their participation in the AI ecosystem. This constitutes a named objective and concrete action within the Strategy's implementation plan directly targeting women's representation in the AI workforce.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: Action 3 of the Strategy focuses on “Respect for Dignity and Human Rights” requiring AI systems to be developed and used in accordance with ethical principles human dignity and internationally protected human rights including autonomy privacy equality and non-discrimination (p. 27). The Strategy warns that the use of AI in decision-making poses significant risks to these rights if decisions are not fair transparent and accountable. As emphasized on page 29 meaningful human oversight and human decision-making are essential particularly in high-risk applications through controls over data and systems monitoring outcomes and ensuring the reliability of AI outputs before decisions are made.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy includes recommendations related to the promotion of meaningful humancontrol over AI systems. Under Action 3 (page 29) it explicitly states that human oversightand decision-making are essential to prevent AI from negatively impacting human rights. Itrecommends that whenever AI is used to make or support decisions particularly in highrisksystems there must always be human oversight over AI outputs including monitoringtheir reliability and establishing controls over data and systems. These recommendationsensure that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replace human judgmentaddressing all aspects of the question.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy includes provisions related to preventing full automation particularly in highrisksystems where human oversight is essential (Action 3 page 29). However it does notexplicitly specify sensitive sectors such as law enforcement or medicine. Therefore whilethe recommendation addresses the need for human intervention and ethical judgment incritical contexts it only partially covers the aspects mentioned in the question.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: Under the guiding principle of 'Respect for Human Dignity and Human Rights' the State is required to maintain or adopt frameworks and procedures to identify assess prevent and mitigate adverse impacts on human rights according to the risk and intended use of AI systems (p. 28). In employment the document mandates studies and projections on labor impacts monitoring mechanisms and retraining policies (p. 51). Línea 3.2 includes a specific action to investigate the social economic and environmental impact of AI and develop measurement instruments protocols and good practice guides (p. 48). The Strategy also includes indicators to evaluate economic impact and public services (Línea 3.4 action e p. 50).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: Principle 1 (Page 25) “AI for people’s well-being and sustainable development” where the Strategy states: “…and the continuous evaluation of the social economic and environmental repercussions involved in the development and application of AI systems.” In page 28 it refers explicitly to the need for ex ante impact assessments:”These measures should include frameworks and procedures that make it possible to identify assess prevent and mitigate as appropriate ex ante or iteratively throughout the lifecycle of AI systems adverse impacts on human rights based on the risk and intended use involved.'
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy’s section on “Respect for dignity and human rights” establishes that private actors must implement due diligence processes to identify prevent mitigate and account for how they address their impacts on human rights (Page 27-8).
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
fr1_element3_justif: Although the Strategy does not explicitly establish a public right to access impact assessment findings the principle of 'Strengthening Democracy' calls for transparency public accountability and access to information in the context of AI governance (p. 26). Additionally Line 3.4 calls for implementing indicators and monitoring mechanisms to evaluate AI processes and public policy which implies a degree of public accountability (p. 50). However the Strategy does not explicitly define a right for the public to access the findings of impact assessments.

fr1_title: Law 20.396/2025 on Minimum Protections for Workers Performing Tasks through Digital Platforms
fr1_justif: Law 20.396/2025 establishes minimum protections for digital platform workers. Article 4 requires companies to respect equality and non-discrimination in algorithm implementation and mandates disclosure of automated monitoring and decision-making systems. Article 5 requires disclosure of key parameters used in automated decisions. Article 7 grants workers the right to a written explanation within 48 hours of any automated decision affecting their working conditions including account suspension or termination. Article 8 guarantees digital reputation portability and data access. Article 10 requires risk assessment of automated systems. Article 19 upholds collective bargaining rights for autonomous workers.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Labour and Social Security - General Labour and Social Security Inspectorate
fr1_element1_text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
fr1_element1_justif: Article 4 requires companies to respect equality and non-discrimination in algorithm implementation and mandates disclosure of automated decision-making systems affecting working conditions including account suspension or termination. Article 7 grants the right to a written explanation for automated decisions. However the law covers only platform delivery and transport workers not broader hiring or promotion decisions across sectors.
fr1_element2_text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
fr1_element2_justif: Articles 4 and 5 require disclosure of automated monitoring and decision-making systems including the parameters used. Article 7 mandates a written explanation within 48 hours for any automated decision significantly affecting working conditions. Article 10 requires risk assessment of automated systems for worker health and safety.
fr1_element3_text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work
fr1_element3_justif: Article 19 explicitly guarantees autonomous platform workers the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining enabling them to negotiate conditions more favourable than the legal minimums.

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems
fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 31) requires public sector entities that use AI whether in service delivery or decision-making support to guarantee public access to information about those systems in accordance with Law 18381/2018 (Uy's Access to Information law). It further mandates public sector compliance with Law 19179/2013 (regulated by Decree 44/2015) on open software & the use of open AI models as mechanisms to ensure transparency of AI systems developed used & acquired by the State. These provisions establish a government-specific disclosure obligation grounded in existing access to information law directly addressing public accountability for government algorithmic systems rather than general AI transparency principles.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
fr1_element2_text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
fr1_element2_justif: In the Axis of Governance the Action Line 1.2 (Regulatory Frameworks) establishes the need to Generate frameworks for transparency and accountability in developmentActions and use of AI establishing requirements appropriate to the contexts intended uses and specific risks associated with this technology. Although it does not discriminate specifically about high risks the intention is the same as the premise.
fr1_element3_text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
fr1_element3_justif: The document does include provisions and recommendations related to distinguishing between information that can be made public and information that must be protected particularly for privacy reasons.Specifically it states that AI actors (public or private) must ensure that the data they collect and use comply with current regulations on the protection and privacy of personal data and with the guidelines of the Personal Data Regulatory and ControlUnit (URCDP).It explicitly refers to compliance with Law No. 18331 (Personal Data Protection Law)and Law No. 20212 which establish the principles of legality purpose consent data security confidentiality and proactive responsibility.  (PP 30 and 42).
fr1_element4_text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
fr1_element4_justif: The document states that AI stakeholders must ensure transparency and explainability by providing “meaningful information appropriate to the context and the specific situation”. The goal is to make results intelligible and to allow people to challenge decisions that affect them.Although it does not specifically mention avoiding “technical jargon” the emphasis on making information meaningful intelligible and appropriate to the context implies that explanations should be clear and understandable to the public in general rather than overly technical.(PP 31).

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: Uruguay's National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 38 Axis 1 Action G) calls for the establishment of a public procurement policy specifically covering the development use acquisition and implementation of AI solutions incorporating principles of ethical responsible and safe use. However this remains a prospective commitment — no AI-specific procurement guidelines vendor requirements or accountability mechanisms are yet in force.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
fr1_element1_justif: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 38 Axis 1 Action G) calls for establishing a public procurement policy specifically covering the development use acquisition and implementation of AI solutions incorporating principles of ethical responsible and safe use of this technology and considering necessary regulatory adjustments. This explicitly goes beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical and technical considerations.
fr1_element2_text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
fr1_element2_justif: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 30 Principle 4) requires AI stakeholders to collaboratively reduce unwanted biases in data and models promoting training data quality team diversity and openness of public data. While this implies testing for bias and fairness it does not specifically require vendors to demonstrate their systems have undergone such testing prior to procurement.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
fr1_element4_text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: Uruguay's National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 49 Section 3.4 'Public Management') explicitly addresses AI capacity-building for public servants. Action d mandates the design and implementation of a comprehensive training plan in collaboration with AI experts targeting technical specialised and operational roles across all levels of government including the legislative body justice system and regulatory agencies. Action e introduces monitoring mechanisms to assess the effectiveness of these training initiatives. Source: National AI Strategy 2024-2030 p. 49.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: Page50: Action D of Line 3.4: Design and implement a comprehensive training plan in collaboration with AI experts from different sectors aimed at people involved in technical specialized and operational roles across all sectors and at all levels of government decision-making.This plan will include specific actions aimed at those in the legislative body the justice system and regulatory agencies.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element2_justif: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (pp. 42–44 Axis 2) supports the creation of specialised AI governance roles and expert teams within government to strengthen internal capacity for responsible AI deployment. However the Strategy stops short of mandating dedicated AI champion roles in every agency or establishing a formal cross-government expert network making this a partial rather than full commitment.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 mandates comprehensive training plans for all State personnel across technical specialised and operational roles at all government levels including the legislature justice system and regulatory bodies (Axis 2 Line 2.4 Action F p. 45; Section 3.4 Actions D and F p. 50). The Strategy further commits to strengthening Uruguay's government AI community to develop ongoing institutional capabilities supporting a culture of continuous professional development in AI.

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 addresses reskilling and upskilling through two dedicated lines of action. Line 2.4 (Talent Management pp. 44-45) commits to incorporating AI training across all educational levels and mandates that all labour training plans include content on AI's impact on work strengthening occupational re-conversion. Line 3.5 (Impacts of AI on Employment p. 51) establishes a specific line of action to address AI-driven job displacement including studies on labour market impacts programmes to maintain employability for both active and inactive workers and engagement with employers and workers' organisations to identify human capital development opportunities.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: Line 2.4 (pp. 44-45) commits to generating instruments and incentives to strengthen university capacity for AI talent and designing a comprehensive training plan for all State personnel. Line 3.5 (p. 51) includes implementing training programmes for both active and inactive workers. These actions imply institutional support and public funding but stop short of explicitly establishing government-funded or subsidised reskilling programmes.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element2_justif: Page 51: Design tools to maintain the employment status of individuals and implement training and capacity buildingprograms for those currently or not currently employed. Does not explicitly says that will provide financial support but to 'design tools' a broad concept.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: Uruguay’s National AI Strategy explicitly incorporates the principles of safety security reliability and responsible innovation. The Strategy dedicates guiding principles to “Reliability and Security” (p. 32) and “Responsible and Safe Innovation” (p. 33) establishes a governance framework to ensure ethical responsible and secure AI (p. 21–22) and contains a cybersecurity section (p. 44). These provisions collectively align with the accuracy reliability and risk-management mechanisms.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
fr1_element2_text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
fr1_element2_justif: Onpage 32 it states that “AI systems must be reliable secure and resilient capable ofrecovering from failures or attacks” but no specific implementation requirements orprocedural measures are provided.
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
fr1_element3_justif: Principle 9 (p. 33) establishes that responsible and safe innovation requires incorporating security and privacy measures from design and throughout the entire AI system lifecycle and continuously evaluating and adjusting innovations based on feedback. However no specific pre-deployment testing validation protocols or documentation requirements are established.
fr1_element4_text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
fr1_element4_justif: Principle of Reliability andSecurity (p. 32) requires that:“ AI must be reliable secure and resilient capable of recovering from failures or attacks and generating consistent outcomes and actions. ... function properly and do not pose security risks and that they comply with information-security principles by design.”It further states that actors must adopt “measures and procedures to ensure robustness and resilience of systems … and security against potential cyberattacks” Under “Cybersecurity” (44 the document establishes concrete measures and actions including: “Establish specialized areas for AI cybersecurity… to develop response mechanisms to the threats posed by AI for early threat detection...

fr1_title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
fr1_justif: Principle 6 is Transparency and Explainability: (page 31)Transparency and explainability play a crucial role in ensuring the effectiveness of all the above principles. AI stakeholders must ensure transparency and explainability in relation to AI systems. This involves providing meaningful information appropriate to the context and the specific situation balanced with the protection of other rights that may be involved. The information disclosed must make the results intelligible and must be appropriate to enable people to challenge them when they are affected. In addition transparency is specifically linked to strengthening democracy (page 26) regulatory frameworks (page 37) and public management (page 49).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: In the specific case of the public sector the implementation of this principle also implies that public entities that use AIwhether in the delivery of public services or in supporting decision-making guarantee access to the respective public information in accordance with the provisions of Law No. 18381 of October 2008 and its regulatory decrees (Access to Public Information Law). The implementation by public sector actors of Law No. 19179 of December 27 2013 regulated by Decree No. 44/015 ofJanuary 30 2015 (Free Software Law and Decree)  and the use of open AI models are also fundamental elements to ensure the transparency and explainabilityof the systems developed used and acquired by the State. Pp. 39 and 40.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: The Strategy requires AI actors to ensure transparency and explainability of systems (p.31) providing meaningful intelligible and context-appropriate information that allows individuals to challenge decisions affecting them (p.31). It also mandates human oversight in AI-supported decision-making especially for high-risk systems (p.29) and requires decisions to be fair transparent and accountable (p.29). These obligations apply to any AI system whose outputs may impact people However it does not assigns specific obligations to entities and does not explicitly mentions loan applications or hiring.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: The Strategy requires AI actors to provide meaningful intelligible and context-appropriate information that allows individuals to understand and challenge decisions that affect them (p.31). It mandates transparency and explainability for all AI systems (p.31) and requires that AI-supported decisions be fair transparent and accountable (p.29). Together these provisions ensure that people can know the key factors behind AI outputs and contest adverse outcomes. However it does not establish a right to receive and explanation or to understand key factors.

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (Uzbekistan)
fr1_justif: Chapter 3 section 5 promotes enhancing knowledge and skills of the population and developing human resources. Chapter 3 par.3 introduces game-based and experimental learning for early ages.  promotes AI learning “for youth and across all segments”. Par. 5 of Chapter 3 includes measures to improve teacher/professor skills (foreign training upskilling programmes); establish AI labs at universities; provide online courses with foreign experts; build training systems for school and university staff. However it provides no specific measures targeting  measures targeting: rural schools low-income students gender gaps people with disabilities.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Coordination Commission for the Implementation of the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy covers tertiary-level curriculum reforms only. Chapter 2 states that AI-focused subjects were introduced in 15 higher education institutions and that 572 students were admitted to new AI degree programmes in 12 universities.  Target Indicators for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 includes establishing  AI laboratories in major universities and expand specialized training. For primary and secondary levels the Strategy mentions early interest-building and programming for schoolchildren but does not mandate curriculum reforms.
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

fr1_title: Draft Law on the protection of the rights of users of online platforms and websites (Uzbekistan)
fr1_justif: The draft addresses AI-facilitated misinformation and violence through Article 12 (content moderation) which obliges online-platform owners to: (1) strengthen content-moderation systems and (2) ensure AI technologies operate in compliance with the Law. These duties directly target AI-driven harms by requiring platforms to improve detection/removal workflows and to govern their AI tools accordingly.
fr1_scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: Article 13 (Grounds for Illegal Content): On online platforms and users should prevent distributing “Illegal content” that includes:  false information threatening public order/safety;  incitement of national/racial/ethnic/religious hatred; obscene content showing disrespect to society/state/symbols; drug propaganda; pornography cruelty incitement to suicide; inducement (incl. of minors) to actions threatening life/health; other content advocating criminal/administrative offenses. This article defines takedown grounds that also apply when such content is created/amplified by AI (e.g. deepfakes inciting violence or coordinated harm) giving platforms a legal basis to remove AI-driven illegal content.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: The draft assigns obligations to platforms: Article 12 (Content moderation) requires online-platform owners to improve content-moderation systems and ensure their AI technologies operate in compliance with the Law—a clear duty to implement robust moderation. Chapter 4 / Article 13 defines categories of prohibited content guiding moderation practice. However no explicit transparency duties (e.g. reporting on how systems handle harmful content) and no direct obligations on AI developers apart from platform use is available.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element3_justif: Art. 10 grants users a right to file complaints to platform owners about harmful content or platform (in)action requires an accessible mechanism and a response within 15 days. Coupled with Art. 12 (platform moderation duty) and Art. 13 (prohibited content) this enables users to seek takedown. However no explicit rights to protection measures appeal/escalation to a regulator compensation/damages or platform liability or remedies against AI developers available.
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (Uzbekistan)
fr1_justif: The Strategy does not contain any direct references to cultural or linguistic diversity multilingual AI localization or the protection of minority languages. However the Strategy outlines framework for the development of a National AI Language Model that takes into account the linguistic characteristics of the region. Par. 4 states 'forming specialized datasets for tasks such as voice video and communication analysis in the Uzbek language'.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Coordination Commission for the Implementation of the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

fr1_title: Draft Ethical Rules for Artificial Intelligence Development and Usage (Uzbekistan)
fr1_justif: The Draft ethical rules addresses Fairness and Non-discrimination by defining key risks and required safeguards. It explains that AI systems must avoid biased or discriminatory outcomes noting that algorithmic bias arises from underrepresented or flawed data and can disproportionately harm protected groups (p.1–2) . It highlights the human-rights basis for non-discrimination and stresses preventing AI from amplifying societal inequalities (p.2–3). The document identifies measures such as bias audits fairness metrics mitigation duties and rights to explanation and redress (pp.3–5).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
fr1_element1_justif: Section 4.5 (Fairness and Non-Discrimination) explicitly requires that AI systems be developed implemented regulated and used without discrimination based on gender race nationality language culture religion belief social origin or social status — directly supporting fair and equitable outcomes for all groups.Section 6 (Obligations of Developers and Implementers) mandates assessments and tests to identify and mitigate potential biases ensuring AI systems do not produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups.Section 10 (Risk Assessment) requires a preliminary analysis of AI’s impact on human rights including the prevention of bias and discrimination reinforcing the commitment to equitable outcomes.
fr1_element2_text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
fr1_element2_justif: Section 4.5 (Fairness and Non-Discrimination) prohibits any discrimination in the development implementation regulation and use of AI systems based on gender race nationality language culture religion belief social origin or social status. This directly targets the risk of AI reinforcing societal biases.
fr1_element3_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
fr1_element3_justif: The framework includes explicit actionable obligations requiring developers and implementers to address bias:Section 6 (Obligations of Developers and Implementers):obliges them to “organize assessments and tests to identify and mitigate potential biases” — a direct requirement to proactively detect and address bias;requires transparency documentation of limitations and regular updates — all elements of lifecycle bias-mitigation practices.Section 10 (Risk Assessment): mandates a pre-deployment risk assessment including analysis of “prevention of bias and discrimination” — confirming obligations across data collection model development and deployment stages.

fr1_title: Draft Ethical Rules for Artificial Intelligence Development and Usage (Uzbekistan)
fr1_justif: The document treats Impact Assessments mainly as pre-deployment and ongoing checks. P.4 §6 Rights & Obligations of AI Developers/Implementers requires developers to “organize assessments and tests” to detect/mitigate bias and to document system limits/potential impacts. On p.5 Part III it §8 Internal Control & Monitoring implies risk identification + safety-measure effectiveness recommended. §9 annual External Audit recommended and §10 Risk Assessment before implementation; includes human-rights impact bias/discrimination safety privacy/security threats.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
fr1_element1_justif: Clause 4.2. Prioritization of the Interests of Individuals Society the State and the Environment. AI systems must be developed implemented regulated and used without harming human rights and freedoms the lives and health of citizens state and public security and the environment.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
fr1_element2_justif: The document assigns duties that developers and implementers must organize assessments tests to detect or mitigate risks (p.4 §6) and must conduct a risk assessment before implementation covering human-rights impacts bias discrimination safety privacy security (p.5 §10). It also adds internal control and monitoring with recommended external audit (p.5 §§8–9). But it doesn’t clearly require comprehensive impact assessments for all users nor set a detailed impact assessment methodology.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

indicator: Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (Uzbekistan)
fr1_justif: The Strategy addresses public-sector skills development by requiring government bodies to strengthen AI competencies among civil servants. Chapter 3 sets the objective to enhance skills in the use of AI technologies digital skills data analytics and big data for specialists and public employees. Paragraph 5 of Chapter 3 expands training through AI laboratories programming and machine-learning modules and professional retraining programmes for personnel involved in digital-government tasks. Appendix 2 assigns ministries concrete tasks to deliver AI training for staff.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Ministry of Digital Technologies
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy establishes a government-wide plan to enhance AI competencies among public-sector employees. Chapter 3 sets nationwide objectives to improve skills in AI technologies digital skills data analytics and big data for specialists and ministry personnel. Appendix 2 assigns AI-training tasks to multiple ministries confirming a whole-of-government approach. However no section references the judiciary or judicial training so the provision does not extend to members of the judiciary.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr1_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr1_element3_justif: The document emphasizes continuous upgrading of knowledge and skills for public administration employees and those responsible for digitalization and calls for specialized AI training programs (Chapter 3 5-§; Appendix 2 assigns ministry implementation responsibilities). However it does not establish a binding or explicit requirement for ongoing professional development (eg mandatory continuing training cycles).
fr2_title: On Measures to Radically Improve the System of Training Highly Qualified Personnel in the Field of Justice
fr2_justif: The decree addresses public-sector skills development in the judiciary by embedding AI-related competencies into judicial training. Section I(1)(d) requires candidates judges and court staff to acquire skills in the “practical application of modern information technologies and the capabilities of artificial intelligence.” Section III(6)(i) expands professional retraining through virtual court modules and classes on using AI technologies. Section VI(18) authorises use of the Adolat digital systems complex to support AI-enabled learning and research
fr2_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr2_element1_text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
fr2_element1_justif: The decree creates an AI-related upskilling framework exclusively for the judiciary. Section I(1)(d) mandates training in modern technologies and AI capabilities for judicial personnel and Section III(6)(i) requires virtual-court and AI-technology modules in retraining programmes.
fr2_element2_text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
fr2_element3_text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
fr2_element3_justif: The decree clearly promotes continued skills-building in AI within the judiciary by mandating that candidates judges and court staff develop competence in the practical use of modern information technologies and AI (Section I(1)(d)) and by strengthening retraining through virtual court modules and dedicated classes on AI technologies (Section III(6)(i)) supported by the Adolat digital systems complex for AI-enabled learning and research (Section VI(18)). However it does not set out a formal recurring continuing-professional-development obligation (eg periodic mandatory refresher training).

fr1_title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (Uzbekistan)
fr1_justif: The Strategy addresses reskilling and upskilling by prioritizing AI-skills development across education and the workforce. Chapter 3 sets the objective to “enhance the knowledge and skills of the population in the use of AI technologies” and expand human-resource capacity . It calls for teaching programming and AI technologies to students and improving the competencies of teachers and specialists. Chapter 5 introduces AI labs at universities and foreign training programs and expands access to online AI courses and professional retraining to prepare workers for an AI-driven economy.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Coordination Commission for the Implementation of the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy
fr1_element1_text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
fr1_element1_justif: The Strategy sets out state-supported measures to expand AI-related skills. Chapter 3 establishes the objective to enhance the population’s competencies in AI technologies and develop human-resource capacity. Chapter 5 and Appendix 2 (Action Plan) include government-led actions such as creating AI laboratories expanding training programmes in universities providing online AI courses and supporting professional development and retraining—constituting government-funded or supported reskilling and upskilling initiatives.
fr1_element2_text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
fr1_element3_text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

fr1_title: Draft Ethical Rules for Artificial Intelligence Development and Usage (Uzbekistan)
fr1_justif: The Rules directly addresses transparency and explainability through Section 4.6 which requires AI systems to produce clear understandable and explainable outcomes and obliges developers to ensure transparency of training databases including sources limitations and potential biases.Section 6 further obliges developers to ensure transparency and understandability of AI algorithms and provide detailed documentation on functionality and risks. Section 7 grants users the right to receive explanations about AI system algorithms.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_element1_text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
fr1_element1_justif: Section 4.6 (Transparency and Openness) explicitly requires that AI systems be developed to provide “clear understandable and explainable outcomes” and that users be informed about their interaction with AI systems. It further requires developers to ensure transparency regarding the databases used to train AI models including their sources limitations and potential biases which directly supports clarity about system purpose data origins and logic.Section 6 obliges developers to ensure the transparency and understandability of AI system algorithms and to provide documentation describing system functionality and risks—reinforcing public trust by making AI operations more comprehensible.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
fr1_element2_justif: Section 4.6 (Transparency and Openness) requires that AI systems deliver clear understandable and explainable outcomes establishing an obligation for developers to ensure meaningful explanations of outputs.Section 6 (Obligations of Developers and Implementers) further mandates developers to ensure the transparency and understandability of AI algorithms and to provide comprehensive documentation describing functionality limitations and risks upon request.Section 7 grants users the right to receive explanations regarding AI system algorithms reinforcing the expectation of meaningful output explanations including in high-stakes use cases.
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
fr1_element3_justif: Section 7 (Rights of AI Users) explicitly grants individuals the right to “receive explanations regarding AI system algorithms.” This provision ensures that users can understand how an AI system produced an outcome that affects them.Additionally Section 4.6 (Transparency and Openness) requires AI systems to provide clear understandable and explainable outcomes obliging developers to make key factors—such as data sources limitations and potential biases—available. Together these sections establish a right to explanation and insight into the factors influencing AI decisions.

fr1_title: Resolution of the Politburo on breakthroughs in education and training development (Resolution No. 71-NQ/TW)
fr1_justif: The document stresses the importance of redefining a new vision and strategy for the education system that contextualizes digital technology and artificial intelligence (P12). It set the objective of II.1 (p3) pursuing universalization of technological capacity artificial intelligence and English proficiency at the 12-K school level. This objective shall be achieved by III.4 (p7) Comprehensive universal digital transformation and strong application of digital technology and artificial intelligence in education and training; 7 (p10) Strongly renovating training programs according to international standards; integrate content on data analytics and artificial intelligence and entrepreneurship.
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_body_name: Party Committee of the National Assembly
fr1_element1_text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
fr1_element1_justif: The document promotes curriculum reforms across multiple levels of the education system. It calls for introducing knowledge of digital competencies and artificial intelligence into the general education program covering primary and secondary education (p.8). It also promotes modernization of higher education curricula by integrating content on data analytics artificial intelligence entrepreneurship and innovation into training programs (p.10). These reforms are part of a broader strategy of digital transformation and modernization of education including new teaching methods and updated program standards (pp.7–8).
fr1_element2_text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
fr1_element2_justif: The document promotes the development of AI-related education within the formal education system. It calls for introducing digital competencies and artificial intelligence knowledge into the general education curriculum (p.7–8) and for improving technological and AI capacity across the school system by 2030 (p.3). In higher education it directs institutions to modernize training programs by integrating content on data analytics and artificial intelligence to support research innovation and the development of high-level human resources (p.10). These measures support the establishment and expansion of AI-related courses within formal education programs.
fr1_element3_text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
fr1_element3_justif: The document includes measures to support teacher training and resources for AI education. It calls for improving digital and artificial intelligence competencies for both learners and teachers and incorporating these competencies into educational programs (pp.7–8). It also encourages policies that mobilize enterprises and higher education institutions to participate in training and fostering teachers and learners in digital capacity and AI. These initiatives are part of a broader strategy for comprehensive digital transformation and the application of AI in teaching learning and educational management (p.7).

fr1_title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Vietnam)
fr1_justif: AI-facilitated Misinformation and Violence is listed as one of the prohibited cases of AI applications with the potential of causing serious harm to social order safety and national security (Art 11.7 p7). Therefore AI-facilitated Misinformation and Violence is perceived as a threat to information security and social order security and lies under the responsibility of the Ministry of Public Security (Art 66.2 p36). Moreover AI-facilitated Misinformation and Violence is also referred in the context of AI applications in journalism publishing media and cultural and social fields as AI-generated content that violates the law and lies within the monitoring responsibility of the Ministry of Culture Sports and Tourism (Art 66.3 p36).
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: As mentioned in Article 2.1 (page 1) this Draft Law applies to activities related to artificial intelligence systems taking place in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam or having artificial intelligence system products and services that affect the market users national security social order and safety and the legitimate rights and interests of Vietnamese organizations and individuals. The only explicit exclusion regards AI applications developed deployed and used exclusively for defense security and intelligence purposes (in Article 2.3 page 1)
fr1_element1_text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
fr1_element1_justif: The document includes provisions aimed at preventing the misuse of AI systems to generate and disseminate harmful or misleading content. Article 11 explicitly prohibits the production or dissemination of AI-generated fake content that is likely to cause serious harm to social order safety or national security (Art. 11(7)). In addition Article 10 requires transparency and labeling measures to clearly identify AI-generated or deepfake content when published publicly (Art. 10(1)–(2)). Together these provisions establish safeguards aimed at and intended to prevent AI tools from being used to create or spread harmful or deceptive content.
fr1_element2_text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
fr1_element2_justif: Partially is selected because the obligation to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent is mentioned but not explicitly linked to Ai-facilitated misinformation and violence. According to Article 15 on General Obligations for High-Risk AI Systems Providers and implementers of high-risk AI systems have the following obligations: 1. Establish maintain and operate a risk management system throughout the life cycle of the system. 5. Ensure a level of accuracy safety and cybersecurity appropriate to the declared purpose of use. 6. Implement transparency obligations to affected persons including notification of the nature of the system decision-making mechanisms and the right to request human review (p9 10).
fr1_element3_text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
fr1_element4_text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

fr1_title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Vietnam)
fr1_justif: Article 60 (p33). Liability for compensation for damages in the artificial intelligence value chain. 1. Organizations and individuals who violate the law in artificial intelligence activities and cause damage to the legitimate rights and interests of other organizations and individuals must compensate according to the provisions of the Civil Code and the provisions of this Chapter. Article 61 (p34). Liability for damages in the artificial intelligence value chain. Article 62 (p3435). Civil liability in cases where artificial intelligence systems cause damage. Article 63. Right to request the Court to force the disclosure of evidence. (pages 33-35)
fr1_scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
fr1_defence_and_security_justif: As mentioned in Article 2.1 (page 1) this Draft Law applies to activities related to artificial intelligence systems taking place in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam or having artificial intelligence system products and services that affect the market users national security social order and safety and the legitimate rights and interests of Vietnamese organizations and individuals. The only explicit exclusion regards AI applications developed deployed and used exclusively for defense security and intelligence purposes (in Article 2.3 page 1)
fr1_element1_text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
fr1_element1_justif: Article 62. Civil liability in case of damage caused by artificial intelligence systems. 2. In order to ensure fairness in determining the causal relationship the Court has the right to request the defendant the supplier or the party implementing the artificial intelligence system to provide information documents and technical data necessary to clarify the system's operating mechanism the risk management measures applied and the factors related to the case. Article 63. Right to request the Court to force the disclosure of evidence (pages 34-35)
fr1_element2_text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
fr1_element2_justif: Partially is selected because there is no explicit reference to creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms yet Art 17.2 page 11 and Art 23.2 page 15 mention that 'Based on collective complaints serious incidents or information from reliable sources competent state management agencies have the right to request a reassessment or temporarily apply management measures corresponding to a higher level of risk. The Government shall specify in detail the procedures time limits criteria for applying temporary measures and inter-agency coordination mechanisms.' However it does not detail mechanisms to submit and respond to collective complaints.
fr1_element3_text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
